Uniform title: Hāhārāvatantra Manuscript: NGMCP 5-4798 Reel number: A 204/6

Description: The *Hāhārāvatantra* (The Tantra of the Roaring *Hā*, *Hā*) teaches the worship of Kaula goddesses, particularly various forms of Kālī, with a distinct preference for Guhyakālī. Guhyakālī is one of the most popular forms of Kālī in the Kathmandu Valley, though she is scarcely known outside of it. The primary scripture of Guhyakālī is the voluminous *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, which was likely redacted in the Kathmandu Valley, probably after the fourteenth century. It is probable that the *Hāhārāvatantra* is likewise of Nepalese origin, given its preference for Guhyakālī and the absence of manuscripts or references to it outside the Valley. Further evidence for this is the presence within the text of the characteristic Nepalese corruption *mahākarmārcana* for *mahaakramārcana*, a term denoting the Kaula liturgy for the worship of Kaula goddesses. This tantra refers to itself as an *atharvanasaṃhitā*, thereby affiliating itself with the tradition of the Atharva Veda. This is likely due to its extensive treatment of magical rites, incantations, and magical potions.

The worship of Guhyakālī is the subject of chapters 1, 3, 4 (as Śiva), 6 (the thousand names of Guhyakālī), 11, and 12–14. Chapter 2 is dedicated to Pratyaṅgirā, who is another form of Kālī. Chapter 5 contains a lengthy exposition of a mantra known as the Kālikākavaca. Chapter 7 deals with the worship of the goddess Turīyā.
Chapter 8 contains a description of the visualized forms (*dhyāna*) of numerous Kaula goddesses. Chapter 9 contains descriptions of *yantras* and their worship.
Chapter 10 deals with magical rites (*indrajāla*), including magical remedies for disease.

Chapter 11 deals with milder magical rites (*prayoga*) which may also be performed for the benefit of others. The texts repeatedly state that these rites—some of which are performed in cremation grounds—should be carried out without conceptual thought or doubt (*nirvikalpena*).
Chapter 15 describes the *Kaula* worship (*kaulikārcana*) of Kālī using eight sacrificial vessels. Notes: Revision 0: December 17, 2003.
Country of publication: India 1a) Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The illustrious Vīranātha said:
Having bowed her head to the Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāśa, the Goddess asked about the slayer of Kālikā.
Oṃ, salutations to Guhyakālikā. Now, therefore, [is the section] in the Atharvaṇa Saṃhitā.
The illustrious Goddess said:
Oṃ, salutations again and again to the one who strikes the vital points (marmans).
The Goddess, who dwells within her own [nature], free from duality and non-duality,
the Mistress of the World, Kālikā, questioned Bhairava.
Resembling the fire of universal dissolution, intent on protecting the world,
the supreme deity of the gods, Bhīṣma, the establisher of both duality and non-duality.
By which they are satisfied, for them there is great fruit therein;
therein lies their great dharma, insofar as these exist eternally.
"Duality and conceptualization as well—tell me of non-duality.
Thus did the Goddess, known by the name Dakṣiṇā-Kālikā, inquire.
Having prostrated before the lineage of Guhyakālī, which is worshipped according to the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya),
the illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this great secret which resembles the fire of universal destruction; I shall explain it to you in brief, for it must be guarded with great effort.
O Goddess, I shall tell you this most secret of secrets, which bestows liberation and grants all desires; therefore, become a practitioner who observes the samaya.
When the non-dual state is established in the mind, it strikes the vital points of all worlds everywhere, and for those [who abide therein], there is neither sin nor merit.
Bhairava does not enter the interior of that place where Kālikā is worshipped;
therefore, this worship of Kālikā, which destroys the two-fold fear, is of great merit.
Through the yoga of non-dual conduct, the practitioner shall become a possessor of perfection;
however, for those for whom there is both duality and non-duality, perfection does not arise.
Success is attained through devotion to the Guru by means of the yoga of dualistic practice;
one should always contemplate the oneness of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra.
And this [teaching], which is always the vessel for the destruction of Māra through its various methods, is the supreme mantra, and the Guru alone is the deity; the Guru alone is the deity.
The Guru himself shall become Kāla, and the supreme [consort] shall become Kālikā;
especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth lunar days.
One should perform the occasional great worship (naimittika-mahāpūjā) during the transition [of the sun], on the full moon, or on the new moon;
it should indeed be done only at night, never by day.
One should perform daily worship at home with pure and supreme joy,
or in a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an inaccessible place, or in a temple of Śiva.
1b) At a crossroads, under a solitary tree, in an empty house,
in a deserted place, at the foot of a *bilva* tree, or even at a tree with *javā* flowers.
One who has received the lineage from the Guru should worship the secret Kālikā according to the tradition.
I shall now describe the sādhana of the Goddess, whether in a cremation ground or in a house.
Combined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and especially with the five foods (pañcakhādya)—
namely, liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union.
The five [deities] beginning with the letter *ma* are the goddess Kālikā, who bestows satisfaction;
as well as the washerwoman, the outcaste woman, the leather-worker, and others.
The Kaivarttī and the Kālinī are indeed remembered as the most excellent Brāhmaṇīs;
among them, one should be chosen if one desires spiritual perfection.
O Guhyakālī, these goddesses who bestow accomplishment have been described;
one should recite their meditation.
I shall now declare the form of the Goddess according to the sequence of her birth.
By the mere knowledge of which, Kālikā is said to bestow perfection. || 1 ||
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, born from the circle of light,
the Great Goddess has ten faces and is adorned with thirty eyes.
She has fifty-four arms, possesses a human face, holds staffs, and has an upward-facing mouth;
she is considered Caṇḍayogeśvarī. (3)
Below that, one should meditate on Siddhikālikā, who has a lion’s face and is white;
below her, one should remember Saṃkarṣiṇī, who has a jackal’s face and is black.
The face of the Lord of Monkeys on the left is red and is known as Kubjikā;
the smoke-colored Śūkara is on the right, as is Trailokyadāmarā.
On the right and left is the yellow-colored Śrī Sundarī;
on the right is Nakrahāriṇī, who is known as Mahāhuṃkariṇī.
The elephant-faced [deity] is white, and on the left is the goddess Pratyaṅgirā;
on the right is the horse-faced [deity], who is dark blue, and the face of Siddhiyogeśvarī.
The nine-faced one of the Great Goddess, all intent on protecting the world, with fangs formidable [and] roaring with the sound of their own birth. 8.
Her brows were knitted in a crooked, terrifying manner; she had a dark face and an excellent, beautiful countenance.
Her tawny matted locks stood upright, and her crown was adorned with the moon and white fireflies.
She is celebrated as being adorned with garlands made of twenty-seven severed heads, terrifying with their gushing blood, and resembling full-blown hibiscus flowers.
He holds the gesture of fearlessness, a sword, a khaṭvāṅga, a noose, a spear, a severed head, a bow, a discus, a bell, a young corpse, and a chowrie. || 11 ||
A skeleton, no lineage, a snake, a hexagon, many courtesans, a water-pot, a fire-vessel, a triple staff, a garment, and a mallet. (12)
The left hand of Akṣa holds a trident, a hand-drum, and a lion;
[the right hands hold] the gesture of granting boons, a skull-cup filled with blood, a trident, and a bundle of kuśa grass. || 13 ||
A jar full of wine, an arrow, five lotuses,
an elephant, a mandāra flower, a dagger, a spear, a javelin, and a garland of flowers.

2a) A drum, a *bhūśuṇḍī* weapon, an iron club, a *tomara* spear, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a sacrificial ladle (*śruva*), a battle-axe (*parśu*), a small sword (*putrī*), a river-turbance (*nadyāvarta*), and an earring (*kuṇḍala*). || 15 ||
Holding a piece of flesh, a citron, and a sacrificial ladle in her right arms,
she wears a tiger skin and has a black antelope skin as an upper garment.
Adorned with ornaments such as bone-ornaments and garlands, resounding with the ringing of hero-bells,
terrible with a gurgling roar, and fearsome with the sound of her auspicious anklets.
The goddess has bracelets, necklaces, and armlets, beautified by large bones; a garland of severed heads hangs from her neck down to her feet.
She wears a garland made of red lotuses, adorned with withered flowers and the like;
her neck is radiant with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), and she has a meditation belt (yogapaṭṭa) as an upper garment. || 19 ||
She is endowed with gentle and foremost ornaments, adorned by the king of serpents and others,
and seated upon the five-fold time-throne (pañcakālāsana) while wearing red earrings.
Above that is the seat of Śiva, blue and marked with the sign of a bull;
it is of great value, fleshy, black in color, and four-armed.
He has one face and three eyes, is marked by Bhairava and Haraṇa,
holds a chisel and a skull in his hands, and carries a hand-drum and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Thus, the seat of the Goddess is called the Bhairava-pīṭha;
beneath that are the five corpses, which are the five elements beginning with Brahmā. (23)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these five causes possess yellow, dark-blue, red, smoke-colored, and white lusters respectively.
Bearing weapons such as the staff, discus, spear, trident, and khaṭvāṅga,
they stand beneath Śiva, who is three-eyed and has placed his forefinger in their mouths.
Tawny-red, with three secret places, they are as terrifying as the *phetkāra* sound;
possessing adamantine fangs and nails that pierce, these supreme auspicious ones rest upon the backs of lotuses. (26)

The jewels such as Śacī’s husband (Indra) and the colors of the directions along with their corresponding deities: Indra is yellowish in luster, the thunderbolt (vajra), and Fire is red together with his spear (śakti). || 27 ||
Yama is black and richly endowed with a staff; Nairṛti is smoky-colored and holds a sword; Varuṇa has a white face and holds a noose; and Vāyu is dark-blue and holds a banner in his hand.
Kubera with a saffron-colored mace, and Īśāna with a white trident;
the Kṛta Yuga is white, Tretā is yellow, and Dvāpara is red. || 29 ||
Kali is black, the Ṛgveda is white, the Yajurveda is yellow, and the Sāmaveda is red; the Ātharvaṇaveda and others are black. This seat, which grants all desires, [is formed] by these.
2b) A seat of red lotuses in union, adorned with a thousand petals; this is proclaimed as the seat whose tip is the flame of a thousand suns. 31.
The Goddess stands upon a lotus, dancing and ever-radiant;
or else she sits comfortably, presiding over all the gods.
One should meditate on her emitting the sound "Hūṃ," causing the world to tremble,
standing firm in the pratyālīḍha posture, and victorious over all prosperity.
Thus should Mahākālī be meditated upon at the tip of the tongue, possessing the freshness of youth;
she who is Maheśvarī, abiding in the center, having been ascended through contemplation in the Ineffable.
Having meditated thus.

Through the differentiation of the syllables of the mantra and the differentiation of meditation, there arises a variety of forms for the Goddess. She may have one thousand, one hundred, fifty-four, twenty-two, eighteen, eight, or four arms; she may be black in color, holding a red lotus, and her faces may consist of a lion, a jackal, a monkey, a bear, a garuḍa, an elephant, a horse, a lotus, or light.
Adorned with fifty-four horses and various weapons and missiles, seated upon twenty-seven skulls,
wearing a great garland of severed heads, filled with human blood in her skull-cup, her mouth dripping with blood,
and decorated with all kinds of ornaments;
In this manner, they pierce the sixty-four vital points of the goddess Kālikā, who stands as the destroyer of the vital organs within the threefold [mandala].
Three-faced and eight-armed, dark-complexioned, and adorned with a garland of skulls,
they drink divine blood with their wide eyes rolling.
The practitioner, having painted [the image] on a cloth, should worship it with diligence;
she bestows the fruit of all desires. One should meditate upon Kālikā together with her mantra, mixed with human blood and wine.
She should be diligently painted on a cloth by one who accomplishes all aims. Or, [an image] fashioned from a great conch shell or human bone [may be used].
A wooden image should be fashioned, either carved or engraved with human skin;
it should be adorned with a noose, a goad, a vajra, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga, and a mallet.
Holding a corpse, a child, and a skull in its hands, it is worshipped with blood-red offerings.
O beloved, he who constantly meditates upon her as she has been thus described, [attains success].

Having performed the meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*pūjā*), dismissal (*visarjana*), and all other observances (*niyama*) according to one's capacity, one should request forgiveness (*kṣamāpayitavya*). At the time of death, the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla*) and others should be employed in the worship.

Mahāmṛtyu is indeed always stationed at her side; these [deities] too must be visualized according to the ritual injunctions, established on the path of non-dual conduct. The female gatekeeper holds a skull and a trident in her hands, is clad in a tiger skin, and possesses earrings, leaf-shaped ornaments, and so forth; she has a severed head, snakes, jewels, hibiscus flowers, lotuses, and the like adorning all her limbs.
Adorned, that goddess of gods, together with her retinue, clad in a human skin and joined with a necklace of skulls,

with a face terrifying with fangs and a fierce countenance, let out a loud, boisterous laugh; she laughed with a nature and voice characteristic of her own kind, dancing with her hair standing on end, her hands blazing with craving.

She holds a noose and the staff of Yama at the same time, and brandishes a severed head with her index finger; she is adorned with ornaments of garlands of skulls, is black in color, and inspires fear. She is adorned with garlands of skulls by Bhairava, Mahākāla, Krodha, and Mṛtyuñjaya; she is black in color, possesses a massive body, is mounted upon a Vetāla, and laughs with a loud, boisterous laugh.

Surrounded by those bearing skulls as weapons, tridents, jackals, crows, vultures, owls, dogs, herons, vetālas, and rākṣasas; stationed at the corners of the circle along with Nandin, Mahākāla, Kṣetrapa, and Gaṇeśvara—O Thousand-Eyed One! Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ chrāṃ phreṃ oṃ namo bhagavati mahābhairavī!

Vikaṭotkaṭa! With fierce fangs! Rauṃ! Hrīṃ 2! Hrūṃ 2! Phaṭ 2! O you with upward-pointing hair, with a flickering tongue, with two thousand hands and feet, and three hundred thousand eyes! Grind everything to powder! Reduce it to dust! O you who are fond of human flesh and blood! Seize! Seize! Chrīṃ 2! Strīṃ 2! Phreṃ 2! O you of great energy!

O Mahāmāyā, you who perform all actions, grant [success]: *ghrīṃ 2 strīṃ 2 trī 2 hūṃ 2 kṣrīṃ 2 hrīṃ 2*. Make it long-lasting, make it twice, make it twice; protect, protect; dry up, dry up. Homage to the illustrious Mahāyoginī! O Maheśvarī, bring all states of being to fulfillment, bring them to fulfillment: *hūṃ strīṃ 2 hūṃ 4 phre& chre& hūṃ*.
O you who assume various forms! Hrīṃ 2 Trīṃ 2 Prīṃ 2 Nrīṃ 2 Hrīṃ 2 Prīṃ 2 Hrīṃ 2! Grant me great accomplishment! Protect me! Kṣraṃ 3 Sroṃ 3 Hraiṃ 3 Hrāṃ 3 Strāṃ 3 Chrīṃ 3 Śrīṃ 3!
Act according to your will through mind and speech! Trīṃ 2 Hrīṃ 2 Strīṃ 2 Chrīṃ 2 Hūṃ 2 Phaṭ!

O Śrī Guhyakālī! Hrīṃ 2 * * *? Kṣrīṃ 3 Hrāṃ 3! O you who shine intensely! Kili 2! Bring them here 2! Having entered, cause them to enter 2! Move 2! Act 2! Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Phreṃ Pheṃ! O Mahāmṛtyukarālinī! Āḥ 5 laḥ 5! O you who bring death to me, with skull in hand, seated upon blood, drink the blood! Huṃ 2 hai 2! Act! Act! Do! Do! Blaze! Blaze eternally! O dweller in the cremation ground, Phreṃ 2 Phaṭ 2! Haiṃ 2 Hūṃ 2 Kraṃ 2 Prūḥ 2 Kṣūḥ 2 Śrūḥ 2 Yrūḥ Srūḥ 2 Vrūḥ 2 Huṃ 2 Hrūṃ 2 Phreṃ 2 Hūṃ 2 Phaṭ 2!

Consume, consume! Slay, slay! Strike, strike! O you who possess consciousness, make the one without consciousness conscious! Hrīṃ hrīṃ! Bhiri bhiri! Ciri ciri! Huṃ phreṃ! O Aṭṭahāsinī! At the end of the eon, wander, wander! Cause to wander, cause to wander! Strike down, strike down! Render unconscious, render unconscious! Cause to wander, cause to wander! Cause to step forth, cause to step forth! Shake up, shake up! O enemy of all villages, O thread-wielder, O Mahāmāyā! Hrīṃ huṃ phreṃ!
Phaṭ! O life-taker, consumer of vital breaths, strike at every vital point, strike! Huṃ phaṭ phreṃ!

O Kālikā, Karālī, kiri kiri, kili kili, hrīṃ śrīṃ strīṃ phreṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ! O you who are surrounded by a mass of great bones, O tiger-like one whose body is covered with human skin, O you who always delight in blood, O most terrible one, take away, take away the vital breaths; seize, seize them!

Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī phreṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Nhrī Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī ṭhnī dhroṃ throṃ phaṭ | Having gone secretly to the cremation ground and performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) there according to the previous ritual procedure forty-six times, one should perform worship with scents, flowers, and so forth at the sites of the goddesses, [using] a skull-cup (*kapāla*).
Having offered incense made from powdered guggulu and having performed the great ritual commitment (mahāsamaya), one should recite the mantra at the cremation ground at night;

then the ritual succeeds in the fire of spirits (bhūtāgni). Having gone to the cremation ground at night, taking a *vahelikā* staff and nine *guñjā* seeds, one should wrap them in a cat skin [and recite] one hundred and eight times.

One should recite the mantra one hundred times over [the substance] in a cremation ground. Having offered it into the fire, one should draw [the figure]; having drawn it, one should bury it with a needle on either the eighth or the fourteenth day. Taking that [substance], one should recite the mantra one hundred times and scatter it over those [enemies]. Having struck them all with the *yantra*, one should offer it to the Goddess; she will do whatever one desires.
Having recited the mantra over cemetery ashes one hundred times, if they are thrown at whomever [one desires],
each of them becomes instantly deluded; by the mere recitation over the ashes, even the gods become stupefied.
How much less, O base man, have I not spoken [of this] even to the Asuras, Suras, and all the gods?
Even Brahmā and the others do not know it; how much less can it be accomplished by me?
For whomsoever [it is used], a piece of wood eight fingers long—whether from the *vaheḍikā* tree or from a cremation ground—if it has been consecrated eight times with mantras...
In his house, at the door, and on the road, all sufferings cease; even the dogs and others do not rise until the sun has risen.
Taking the dust from the sandals of the practitioner and the skull of a king, he consecrates it with the *siddhyārka* mantra.
During the recitation, whether at the time of the moon being in its watery phase (*ārdrakale*) twice or thrice, whatever he desires or contemplates, that very thing [is attained].

It performs everything; by means of a powder from a flower in a cremation ground, recited once, whoever is touched by it follows behind that very moment. *Phreṃ caṇḍa caṇḍeśvarī huṃ phaṭ*. One should repeat the mantra of the Goddess without meditating on her as previously described. Struck on the head with a flower, she trembles at that very moment.

Within the midst of the world, she rolls about, weeps, and likewise laughs. On the eighth day of the first season of a Brāhmaṇa maiden, by constantly placing a pill consecrated one hundred and eight times into her mouth,
she becomes invisible and effects a transformation of her own form [into that of] a jackal or a cat.
Taking the form of a vulture, a crow, or a hawk, he assumes whatever shape he desires. He should wander together with these intoxicated Yoginīs;

having seen those who do not observe the pledges (asamayin), he should go and inform the Yoginīs. Having made a mark with cemetery ashes on his eye, he should cast it upon the house of anyone, or even upon a piece of wood.

If one buries grass and other such items in the house, it becomes a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). One should destroy [the effect] with cowherd’s oil (*gopāla-tailika*), fisherman’s oil (*śauṇika*), net-maker’s oil (*kaivarta*), oil from sesame seeds (*tailika*), sesame oil, or ashes; or with wood from a cremation ground. This corrupts all buying and selling. What more need be said? Whatever one desires, that he accomplishes. [The powder of] a skull (*kapāla-cūrṇa*)...

Incense mixed with *mahāpala* and *guggulu*, consecrated seven times, should be offered to the Goddess; one should burn it while reciting the name of the person [targeted] twenty-one times. Alternatively, one may throw sugar into it; by that, whatever the Bhaṭṭārikā desires is seized, and she brings about every transformation. She constantly liberates [the victim].

4b) When seized by a fallen spirit, [the victim] undergoes all manner of transformations; it slays the lineage of enemies. No one else can liberate [the victim], but one is liberated by the incense of *guggulu*. Saying "Release! Release! (*muñca muñca*), [one should offer] mustard seeds...
If one strikes the head with the *yaṃ* syllable, which has been deprived of its seven seeds, the Bhaṭṭārikās must always be propitiated for that reason;
then all the siddhis come to be. One should place them in darkness; therein, O Blessed One, the goddess Cāmuṇḍā deludes even the gods.

Crushing all the asuras, gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras, she is not present everywhere, yet she is constantly devoted to recitation; with her mind, she accomplishes everything. Always remaining in non-duality, she should cause the narrative of the Daityas to be performed.

The liberator from the bonds that delude the world and cause great confusion for the Daityas and others— whether one should worship or offer libations to this *kandalī* plant with the mantra of the Goddess using water drawn up by the root,
one should contemplate the auspicious *Śivā*, who delights the senses; one should meditate on her as having the form of the deity and indeed as the Goddess herself.
First, surrounded by his entire retinue in the form [of the deity] within the heart, he revolves the mantra; one should utter the syllable *huṃ*.
At that very moment, [the enemy] becomes distressed; indeed, from that state he falls, suffers a breaking of the limbs, and even contracts fever.
This application of proof should be known, and this great mantra should be bestowed upon those who observe the commitments (*samayin*).
And he himself, with eyes wide and fierce in agitation,
laughing a loud, boisterous laugh, with disheveled hair, adorned with skulls, and wielding blazing weapons, assumed the form of a jackal.
He is divine, holding a noose and a goad, endowed with celestial weapons,
bearing a skull-cup filled with blood, and adorned with a garland of bones.
Having meditated upon oneself as Bhairava, one will then swiftly attain success.

One should draw [the figure] on a cloth from a cremation ground with oil, while the Goddess sits facing all directions and remains protecting [the practitioner] from every side. For the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), one should draw [it] with lac.
One should write [the name] of the person whose name has been consecrated seven times in a cremation ground; he will cause the enemy to speak incoherently.

For the purpose of killing, one should write [the name] on a cloth in a cremation ground using charcoal from a funeral pyre and clay from a cremation ground, fashion an image [of the victim], and have it rubbed with the three pungent spices (*trikaṭu*).

Having placed a mustard seed within his heart and cast it [into the victim], one should give it; it should be given into fire and heated. Within a day and night, the victim dies. One may cause [an enemy] to be driven away (uccāṭayet). Having written [the name] on a cloth from a cemetery and wrapped it with a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree, one should write it at the door. Wherever he steps, he causes [the enemy] to be driven away. It should be consecrated with the recitation of the "Three Fragrances" (*trigandha*).
A maiden who is fortunate should draw [the figure] with vermilion;
she will attain good fortune. Honey and *tāptā* [plant] fibers bring one under control.
Without that which is bestowed by the Ācārya, accomplishment does not arise;
those deluded by other systems will act in vain.
Indeed, these are quickly accomplished by reciting them ten thousand times at night;
he who knows this Kālī-mantra is a guru who bestows liberation and immortality.
Having performed the supreme worship with betel leaves, areca nuts, and so forth,
as well as with fragrant flowers and pleasant offerings, one should indeed worship the Guru.
Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should satisfy the guru;
having performed worship of the guru, one should then offer gold and other gifts with faith.
One should receive all the secrets of great prosperity from the mouth of the Guru;
empty-handed, one should grasp the Tantra, the Sūtra, and the Paddhati.
The Great Goddess is not accomplished even by reciting [the mantra] for hundreds of years,
if she is not offered to the Guru, who is deluded by all the world.
Having always performed worship of the preceptor with garments, gold, ornaments, vehicles, elephants, and sacrificial fees, one then quickly attains success.
But he who listens to the secret mantra without having performed worship of the guru, his mantra will not be accomplished; furthermore, he shall become a partaker in hell.
In the teaching of the Śrīkula, followers of the Śākta tradition do not recognize divisions by caste or stage of life;
for the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, woman, and even the Cāṇḍāla are all equal.
For by performing worship of the Guru, one attains success; not otherwise.
Through conceptualization one perishes, but through non-conceptualization one succeeds.
Whether it be worship, the offering of oblations, recitation, hymns, or ritual feasts,
the Supreme Goddess should be meditated upon in the same manner as one's own self.

This heart-mantra of the Goddess,

which performs all rites and was swiftly spoken by Bhairava himself— this *māṃ* mantra, the root-vidyā of the planets, spirits, and so forth— bestows all previous accomplishments through prior practice.

He performs [whatever he wills]. He does whatever he desires. He performs many magical illusions (*indrajāla*); with a peacock feather, he can block the currents of the Gaṅgā. Whatever he wishes, that he accomplishes; he paralyzes, destroys enemy forces, and conquers them.
By scattering sand from the branches of a *vānasa* tree and other such materials, he paralyzes great weapons; he even brings trees under his control.
He becomes common to all yoginīs. He assumes unmanifest forms beyond measure and agitates the *nāgas*.

By the previously mentioned method, he inflicts a blow to the vital points (*marmābhighāta*). He performs everything according to his own will; there is no doubt in this. On the fourteenth, eighth, and ninth days of the lunar fortnight, one should offer the *bali* at night on a Tuesday.

One should offer libations with water according to one's ability; when there is the capacity, one should offer the fivefold oblation (*pañcaka*) consisting of clarified butter, milk, curd, sweets, and meat. One should satisfy Kālī with food, drinks, and so forth, excluding those that are chewed, sucked, drunk, and so on, as well as those from land-dwellers and water-dwellers. One may perform this through mental recitation alone. What more need be said? This indeed is the domain of the Lord of Yoga (*Yogeśvara*).

Success is never achieved without the permission of the Guru. No one else has the authority; this [attainment] is established in the Lord and in non-duality, and it is accomplished without delay through devotion to the Guru. O Maheśvarī, by means of all edible offerings and the like, the Guru should favor him with everything. Having given even a single leaf of the Guru, he should seek forgiveness for that night. [This leads to] all success.

One shall become a partaker [of success]. At midnight, one should summon a Yakṣiṇī, a Nāśinī, a Gandharvī, a Rākṣasī, or a Mānuṣī. Even when other mantras have failed, by throwing cemetery dust, one pacifies fevers, planetary afflictions, and the like.
It accomplishes everything; one should follow behind women with the left hand. This is the Great Passion.

It becomes auspicious. O Śiva, within your house, the ground becomes auspicious. For the purpose of killing, having tied [the object] three times with a cemetery thread in a large vessel, it becomes inexhaustible. By beholding Śiva residing in its heart, liberation is attained. Having consecrated it with the mantra, saying "Hara 2," one should [bind] the waist with a cemetery thread.
The bride should eat from a hundred plates.
"Bring! Bring! Do this! Do this!"—thus [she speaks]. The Yoginī, who has a sister who brings [offerings], holds a skull-bowl, a noose, and a goad. She is radiant.
With the *mudrā* of "Hūṃ fallen," a single knitting of the brows, and a downward gaze, she is utterly dissolved;

Mahāsucaṭī has a dry tongue that licks the forehead and brows of the Yoginīs. The goddesses and all others endure her desire; how much more so other means of livelihood? Or rather, she is the worship of them all. Aiṃ Śrīṃ.

The sādhana is performed with the syllable *phreṃ* for the eight Kṣetrapālas and the Kula-mothers. In the midst of the Yoginīs of Guhyakālī, the seed-syllable of Māyā—*hrīṃ 2 hreṃ phreṃ*—causes a shower of blood. This application for attaining siddhi is extremely difficult to find anywhere; subsequently, by means of this, one enters the body of another, such as that of a cat, a jackal, or a crow.
Having taken blood, one then prepares any substance such as food or drink mixed with red dye;
the heart mantra is recited.
Thus, the application of the [astrological] days should be guarded with great effort.

Having grasped Śiva with the left hand, it is recited at the heart. Alternatively, by the mere touch of a woman, men become intoxicated with passion through the Bhairava mantra. Having bound the waist with a cord from a cremation ground...

She moves according to her own will; by means of her, one brings the three worlds under control, and she fulfills whatever desires are wished for. Furthermore, they become faint at every step. Such an application for attaining perfection is difficult to obtain even for the gods. Having taken up the Śivāstra weapon with the Mahāmṛtyu mantra...
Having consecrated it with mantras, if one touches the breast of a woman with that hand smeared with the ointment, she enters [the state of being possessed].

By means of the mantra, one should touch the *liṅga* of a great *yakṣa*; furthermore, one should not touch the breast of another woman. With the *Bhairavahṛdaya* mantra, one should bury a human bone (*śivāsthi*) eight finger-breadths deep in the house.

6b) He dies together with his livestock and kinsmen. Having taken a *śivālāṅgula* root with the *mahākāla* mantra, one should recite it at night within another village; then every *yakṣiṇī* comes. She gives whatever one desires according to one's wish.

He departs. By means of the *Nandihṛdaya*, if one casts an owl’s bone [into a dwelling], they go to ruin and abandon their place of residence. By means of the mantra of [Yama], if one casts funeral pyre embers wrapped in a jackal’s skin into someone’s house, the destruction of that person’s lineage occurs. [This is done] by means of Yama’s heart-mantra.

Taking a corpse from a cremation ground and tying it with a jackal’s skin into a bundle, whoever he touches becomes unconscious; he is seized by a spirit (*bhūta*). If one strikes with a *śivartā* [weapon], he is struck down by Yama’s staff, and everyone perishes. If it is buried eight finger-breadths deep in someone’s house, that house becomes an abode of ghosts (*pretālaya*).

It comes to pass: with the *mṛtyuhṛdaya*, one should anoint a female cat, human blood from a cremation ground, and vulture blood; one becomes invisible and assumes all forms. O Blessed One, with the *hṛdaya*, one should anoint with vermilion, head-unguent, and white [substance] together with human oil using the blood-stained ring finger.

In the form of desire, she creates the form of desire; she deludes the three worlds. Alternatively, having fashioned a *tilaka* and a pair of sandals from the skin of a jackal, and having recited the heart-mantra over human blood with a mouth full of blood, O Sister, she causes one to wander through the seven continents. Whatever one desires, she accomplishes that. Having seized the tongue of a jackal...

By placing [a substance] encased in the three metals into the mouth, one becomes Śiva. With the tongue of a cat, one makes a cat; with a dog, a dog; with an owl, an owl—one assumes the form of all. With the heart-mantra consecrated [substance], together with *śivakusuma* flowers, one acts like a mute toward all; likewise, with a handful of *śivā* hair.

Having performed the recitation (*jāpya*) with the Heart-mantra, whoever one laughs at will be seized by that planetary spirit (*graha*). Liberation [from the seizure] occurs through incense of *guggulu*. By reciting the Heart-mantra over a jackal’s eye, one produces a pair of eyes; one sees Nirvāṇa, one sees a *vīla*, and one sees a treasure-trove. One should observe the tracks of a jackal and a cat in a cremation ground.

That which is struck by him after he has consulted [the divination] a hundred times becomes devoid of its sovereign; this very [victim], such as a cat and so forth, when struck by him, becomes a ram and so forth.

One becomes invisible and transforms one's form; one does whatever one desires. By means of incense mixed with the flesh of a jackal and an owl, the immobilization of anyone occurs. Having consecrated the heart of a great preta born from a dog-womb, whomever one touches in the private parts dwells together with him wherever he stays.

*Guhyakāli phreṃ phaṭ*. There is no liberation through wine. By means of the Heart-mantra of the Goddess, measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*), the virgin becomes twelve finger-breadths. By rotating [the instrument] upwards, the *liṅga* of others becomes paralyzed (*tuṣī*). Into that vulva (*bhaga*), nothing else whatsoever enters. [This is done] with a mixture of *gṛdhra-netra* and collyrium (*añjana*).

With cat’s blood and collyrium, one causes the appearance of a *preta* or *piśāca*. This should be given to one's own disciples and to no others whatsoever; it must indeed be bestowed by him according to the scriptures for the sake of authority.

Then, he should have him cast a flower. Or else, facing east and free from fear, he should enter into the *kaula* [tradition] which is beyond all doubt.

8a) Dwelling in forests and mountains, dwelling in battle, bestowing victory and triumph; dwelling on every path, dwelling under every tree; O All, O All-Gone, O Victory, O Victorious One, Unconquered, Unvanquished! Śrīṃ Strīṃ!
*Staranī pūriṇī hrīṃ namaḥ samasamayati dviprabhavati praviśati khphreṃ khphreṃ chrīṃ strīṃ cūṃ phreṃ namaḥ svāhā*. This is the *samaya-vidyā* of all the *yoginīs*.
*Hūṃ*, together with Bhairava, O Mother of the Three Worlds! *Heḥ veṃ chreṃ namaḥ svāhā*. Of these...
This is the *samaya-vidyā* of all yoginīs;
it is the *mahāsamaya-vidyā* of Bhairava and Bhairavī, of all siddhis, of all śākinīs, and of all [beings]. When this is uttered, [it overcomes] all yoginīs and all gods.
He becomes honored everywhere among the *vidyādharas* and others, the *yakṣas* and others, in all fields (*kṣetra*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*).

He is victorious everywhere; he remains unbound everywhere, and even amidst everything, he is liberated. At the conclusion of the worship consisting of the sounds "jihvātvo," "khphreṃ," "kāra," "dada," and "hāhākāra," during the time of the commitment (*samaya*), the goddesses are present in the sandalwood [of the heart]; mind within mind.
If it occurs, one should roll the head about. Being joyful and well-nourished, one should mutter [the mantra] three times at each of the three junctions (saṃdhyā) while observing silence everywhere.
In the presence of the deity, one should mentally utter "HŪṂ PHREṂ. He becomes pleased.
By means of this *samaya-vidyā*, one accomplishes whatever one desires. The first mantra of the Goddess has been immediately consecrated.

One should recite [the mantra] three times a day using a great conch shell, a thread, or a rosary. By reciting it twenty-eight times, one succeeds; all mantras become effective. When used with a garment from a corpse burnt in a cremation ground, she appears visibly through the power of recitation. If invoked with anger, she causes [the enemy] to fall. This is offered to the Goddess; by that, there is great liberation. [The rite is performed with] water.

Having recited this, one strikes [the enemy], by which he is brought down; by whichever [substance] is employed, one achieves whatever one desires. By taking charcoal from a cremation ground and reciting [the mantra] a hundred times, whomsoever one seizes, or by using ashes from a cremation ground over which the mantra has been recited as clothing, one shall mount [him]; by that means, all become motionless like the dead.

One should sprinkle with the Heart-mantra of the Goddess; one becomes healthy. As Bhairava does, so she performs [the rite]. With the left [hand] all rites [are accomplished], and with the right. This Blessed Lady bestows accomplishment and assumes whatever form is desired.
One becomes like Mahābhairava himself; like old age and death, yet one becomes free from old age and death.

Liberated from all diseases and devoid of all defects, one scorches all enemies like fire. One asks what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. [One obtains] the sword, the sandals, and the collyrium.

Having worn the pill, one attains accomplishment. One achieves the eight great accomplishments (*siddhi*), such as the various elixirs of alchemy (*rasāyana*), as well as many kinds of minor accomplishments. One cannot be slain by anyone. By constant recitation with the mind, one accomplishes whatever one desires.
It destroys the poison of those who harbor malice. It causes an enemy to be seized by fever.

By means of the mere word, one grasps everything; one shall obtain the knowledge of Bhairava, which is difficult even for the thirty gods to attain. By this mere knowledge, the deity finds [himself] spontaneously; one becomes the creator of dissolution and creation.
Recitation alone must always be performed by the lords of yoga, whether standing, walking, eating, or drinking.

Even during sexual union, one should not abandon the mental recitation (*japa*). Upon seeing him, all people become infatuated; they become deluded. One should always perform the recitation at night; [the deities] become manifest within the body. One should always perform the worship of virgins according to the power of one's means. Thereafter, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the *yoginīs* occurs, even for a woman.
He desires accomplishment; he becomes like a cloud; he causes a burst [of power]; by his command he overcomes the god;

he wards off the sun—by this, accomplishment occurs. Bhairava himself is the conjunct [deity]. When Bhairava is ever present, the Goddess is necessarily accomplished; otherwise, even a deity never attains accomplishment.
This king Maṃtreśvara, the leader of the mantras and the lord of the pretas, will deliver [the merit] to the son of the Goddess;
indeed, no mockers shall attain it otherwise. Just as the Goddess accepts it, so too is it obtained through faith, even for a man whose death has occurred among a thousand vessels.
(What need is there for much? Command is success. Or the heart-mantra is all success;
all mantras perform all tasks. In his cremation ground...)
Or rather, even when unmanifested, he who is bowed down before the supreme, non-dual,
and vast secret of the Goddess succeeds through the ritual procedure of mantra-recitation performed with his mouth.
O highly fortunate ones, *bhairava*, *hrīṃ*, *chrīṃ*, and *cūṃ* are each the heart-mantra of the Goddess.
Maheśvarī: Oṃ, salutation to Bhairavī. The first is the Goddess Kṣobhiṇī, the second is Mahāpralayakāriṇī, and the third is Marmā.

Upon striking the vital points (marmas), one should write "tritraya" three times; then write the fourth word, "kili kili"; then the fifth word, "kici kici"; and then: "hrīṃ chrīṃ amukaṃ kāryaṃ me kuru kuru svāhā."

Oṃ namo hrīṃ khphreṃ hūṃ phreṃ bhairavī kṣobhiṇī mahāpralayakāriṇī marmamarmābhighāte kili 2 kici 2 hrīṃ chrīṃ [name of person] perform this task for me, svāhā! This mantra, O God, is difficult to obtain; by means of it, the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are brought under control.

If one recites this vidyā three times daily during the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*) for ten thousand repetitions, and remains devoted to the worship of the guru within the great observance (*mahāsamaya*), through that, accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises. Thereafter, one performs the task previously indicated.
By reciting it even once, she brings all the worlds under one's control.

One performs everything previously described. *Phreṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. It is heard that even those not mentioned are subdued. When recited with anger, it accomplishes whatever one desires. It causes agitation through fever, burning sensations, and pain. Then, by means of the foot-drawing [mantra], one seizes [the target] in the house. By the power of the mind, one goes [wherever desired].

She does whatever she desires. She destroys the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), tears it apart, and divides it into two pieces. By her will, O Blessed One, the perfected Advaitabhairavī and Tripurā likewise perform all actions, whatever resides within their minds.

Having heard the mantras of those who follow Bhairava and maintain firm vows, as well as those of others, they may be bestowed even without the command of Bhairava. Such a one shall indeed wander through the three worlds and always fill the realms.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious [mantra] which bestows constant success.
By whose will the knowledge spoken by Bhairava proceeds,
that which is to be avoided by the mind must be observed even while performing one's duty; having eaten, there is no destruction by the wearer [of the linga].

Or they may remain satisfied. Having understood that this was spoken by others, then, when the substance is in hand, the *siddhas*—specifically the *raktanihasacarās*, the *gṛdhraśiras*, and especially those endowed with auspicious knowledge (*jñāna*)—should anoint the pair of eyes. When mixed with the left eye of all [the aforementioned beings], one enters the seven netherworlds (*saptapātāla*).

He assumes a form at will. Or else, by merely applying collyrium made from a pill (guḷikā), one becomes a perfected master of yoga (siddhiyogī). Taking the blood of a female owl, a doe, a female monkey, a female serpent, a female warrior-leader, a female yoginī, and a female elephant—one should always place a pill wrapped in gold in one's mouth on the ground of accomplishment.

Having cast it into *nīlī* and smeared with it, one should worship *nīlikā* once more and cause its essence to flow out from the middle. By performing this, one may travel hundreds of *yojanas* to the south and anoint oneself; one reaches the sky in an instant.
One causes the world to revolve—the circle of Meru, Kailāsa, the seven continents, and the fourteen [worlds].
The supreme goddess Siddhiyoginī thus brings about even that illumination which is extremely difficult to attain; it may be performed by recitation once, or according to one's desire.
I shall now declare another rite involving the supreme mantra of Kālikā.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Guhyakālikā, Siddhibhairavī, Cāmuṇḍā!

O Bhairava, established in the limbs of the triple yoga, one shall attain the mudrā; indeed, through this mudrā of great power, accomplishment is achieved in no time at all. The yogin, abiding in the five syllables, is completely filled with all the principles (tattvas).
When the sound *kili* occurs twice at the letter *ṛ*, one perceives pure knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), which arises at the time of death.
This is indeed the supreme reality; the attainment of yoga is difficult to achieve.
Yet, by the mere state of this [knowledge], it bestows omniscience.

10a) The Goddess Kādī is her consort; she is the cause and the means for attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*). By that which is secret, the Supreme Sovereign (*parameśvarī*), known as the Seed (*bīja*), is held in the secret hand. In the application to the body, there are one hundred and eight [syllables]. Whether it be one or all of them, what then?
Salutations to you! Even if it is not accomplished by means of salutation, one should not act; one should abandon what is unwholesome.
Oṃ phreṃ hrūṃ Guhyakālī hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ! O Siṃhakā, [protect] from all calamities! Herein are the mantra-yogas: Khphreṃ hara 2 hūṃ phaṭ Daṃṣṭrākarālī phreṃ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā!
One should recollect the three cycles of the *vidyā* of Pratyaṅgirā Siddhimukhī; that which [is thus recited] effects eradication in times of misfortune.

In times of distress, in fear of enemies, or in battle, success is attained through recollection. Nothing has power over that practitioner of recitation (*jāpin*), even against the great lords (*maheśvara*s). Having performed sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with this [mantra], one should consume food and drink without fear. Likewise, having offered supreme flowers and incense, one should engage in meditation and recitation. Authority.

One should perform worship on the eighth, fourteenth, and ninth days, as well as daily worship; furthermore, one should perform worship on the eighth, ninth, fourteenth, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), the full moon, and on Tuesdays. Great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) ensues.
Fever, planetary afflictions, and misfortunes are destroyed by mere remembrance.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

Having performed the great *saptaka* with reference to whomsoever [one desires], one should recite this. O beloved, this supreme knowledge of Kālikā is dearer to me than my own life; it must be kept secret by those intent on attaining all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

Now it is said, O Supreme Goddess, regarding the distinction of the divisions of action: by the mere knowledge of yoga, the yogi becomes a destroyer of the gods (Tridaśahā). [The sequence of the body] is from both shoulders, the chest, the movement of the head, the hands and forearms, the two previous eyebrows, the armpits, the tip of the nose, the throat, the belly, the navel, and the root of the big toe.

On the three parts of the eyebrows, the sides, the head, the back, the two eyes, the heart, the root of the tongue, the ankles, the roots of the thighs, and the tops of the feet—Śiva dwells in these vital points (*marmapradeśa*) of the body;
therefore, one should touch them. Furthermore, in the two steady secret places, the penis, the belly, the anus, and all the joints are the supreme vital points (*paramarma*).

It moves through the navel, the neck, the testicles, and the heart; it always dwells in the supreme Śiva. It vibrates at the edge of the ear, the neck, and both cheeks; it wanders everywhere at all times. Aiṃ.

Daṃṣṭrāka eli aiṃ hūṃ phreṃ marme marmābhi phreṃ hana 2 hana 4 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! By whomsoever [this is recited], whether by one born in a cremation ground or by means of striking the vital points (marmas), [the effect is achieved].
This should be chanted at the three junctions of the day (trisaṃdhyam) over a square measuring sixteen finger-breadths (ṣoḍaśāṅgula). Thus, it should be applied everywhere, including above the feet.

The worship mantra: One should protect the substance according to the sequence. By means of the fingers, [the measurement is] two fingers, two, three, and four in succession. Half a finger, a leaf, and a pala of substance—[yielding one who is] golden, joyful, contented, prosperous, and very wise. A finger [is equal to] five palas; likewise, by half [a finger] more, there are ten palas. Two [fingers]... [are equal to] five palas.

Twelve [units] are hurried in sequence and well-loosened; having made the substance finger-to-finger, one should take a portion by means of a fraction. Having made it finger-to-finger, one should take the portion with one's own hand;
the remaining substance is likewise for the specific calculation of Śivalocana and Gṛdhra.
One should contemplate cats' eyes, an owl's head, and burnt [substances] within all collyriums.
One should anoint both eyes with human oil (*narataila*) empowered by the recitation of the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).

By the mere act of anointing, one becomes invisible and beholds the number and measure of all substances produced since birth. This is a perfected yoga (*siddhiyoga*); everything occurs according to one's will.
The yoga of meditation: for killing, it is black in form; for subjugation, red is proclaimed;
for expulsion, smoke-colored; and for pacification, white is proclaimed.
O Maheśvarī, in the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana), the form is yellow and takes on whatever shape is desired;
this is the supreme secret and the very determination of reality.

Oṃ khphreṃ siddhikarālī hrīṃ chrīṃ hūṃ strīṃ phreṃ namaḥ svāhā. This is that supreme goddess who should always be recited by the wise; indeed, all actions are accomplished according to whatever is desired by the mind.
Furthermore, what need is there to speak of how the Mistress of Yogins (*yogīśvarī*) brings about accomplishment through the yoga of the secret mind? She effects a meeting with the *yoginīs*;
she reveals all dreams;
and the assembly of *yoginīs* arises of its own accord.

By this, one accomplishes all tasks. The fulfillment of desires occurs through mind and speech. 11a) By a single utterance, one may assume various forms; one enters the sphere of accomplishment and beholds the form of Śiva.

Then, having offered a blood-oblation with the heart-mantra of the goddess known as Guhyā, who is the foremost of all Yoginīs, and having prepared the central maṇḍala, the Bhairava-yoginīs are to be drawn; they must never be drawn by anyone else. O Kumārikā, one should focus on the secret place; they are to be drawn with the consumption of liquor and with the supreme secret heart-mantra.
Having offered an oblation (*bali*) with blood, one should purify [the substances] with the *hṛdaya-mantra* starting from the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Having approached all the substances, such as wine and so forth, it effects their extraction. It cuts through the supreme obstacles.
The warding off of those mantras becomes successfully accomplished. By means of this mantra, one should cause the authorities to grant permission.
Having bestowed the authorities upon one's own disciple, one should cause them to recite; by reading it with a pure mind along with one's lineage, what person would not see [the truth]?

By the recitation of the *hṛdaya*, one perceives all beings. Whatever one desires, that one accomplishes. One should bring about the mental disposition of the Guru. By means of this cause for all accomplishments, one shall become a lord of that tantra. [This is] the Tantra of the Yoginīs.
Perform the *ḍiḍā* of illusions within the non-dual heart situated in every field and field.
This indeed is the supreme knowledge proclaimed to you, O Goddess;
it has not been given by me to anyone else, for it is a secret, supremely auspicious.
Behold that merit of the Goddess; it is not found even in good fortune.

Where Bhairava is established, by the mere remembrance of Him, the Yoginī Bhairavī and Guhyakālī, together with all the principles (tattvas), act according to one's desire. By means of the water recited over the support of that path of Yoga—

He causes [the world] to revolve. Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times as if it were his own home, he becomes a yogin; that yogin is Bhairava himself. The other eight crores of Bhairavas reside within the pores of his skin.
Alternatively, the Bhairavī mantra should be recited eight thousand times.
Indeed, O Bhairavī, one should meditate upon and recite this single [mantra] for protection.
And thus, for the practitioner, there shall be great accomplishment through speech;
however, by writing or at the commencement of recitation, someone may be killed while still alive.
And when writing, O Goddess, it should be like wine and red lac;
the seed-syllable of Bhairava and Carcikā should indeed be red.
11b) One should not begin the yoga at all during the pair of *māyāvī* [nakṣatras]; rather,
alone or even in a secluded place, one who has been consecrated with wine [should practice] with a conch-shell rosacea that possesses a radiance equal to a blazing fire.
For one who recites [the mantra] until the names of all the Bhairavas have been fully declared—
whether at the junction of day and night or during the night— the supreme recitation must be performed.
Accompanied only by his own power and mantra, consecrated with wine, and becoming filled with bliss,
he should wear a great conch-shell rosary and red garments; for him who thus recites, the name "Bhairava" is proclaimed in its entirety.
The supreme recitation (japa) should be performed during the twilight or at night;
or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, one should diligently worship the sacred book.
In the monastery (ārāma), however, both of these should likewise perform [the rite] with great effort.

A yogi who is always established in the state of non-dual conduct and observance, having approached the vow of Līlā, should then put on a pair of blue garments, let his hair hang loose, apply red unguents to his limbs, and recite [the mantra] while intoxicated with the joy of wine. He should remain joined with the Śakti.
Through the practice of non-duality (*advaitācāra*), one becomes Bhairava directly. Furthermore, by the recitation (*jāpya*) of the seventeen-syllable mantra, one shall become Bhairava before long.
By the recitation of the sixteen-syllable mantra, or by performing the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) three times during the night, one attains supreme success (*siddhi*).
One whose body is enveloped in the supreme [state] may, through the practice of mantras, uphold all scriptures and the like. Merely by remembering [it], [one attains this].

In battle, no one shall stand before him. By throwing a tiger, a bear, a cock, a *veṣṭika*, and *śivakusuma* flowers at the entrance of an enemy's house, he turns them into the form of beasts. One should grind a jackal, a cat, and a dog with blood; with this, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times against the enemy.

One steals wealth; one sees everything in another's house; one becomes invisible. Alternatively, having ground together a pill (*guṭikā*), mercury (*śivarasa*), goat’s mercury (*chāgarasa*), and [the plant] *kapilā* with cow’s milk, one should apply it as an ointment; this paralyzes fire. If one places a pill mixed with the blood of a cat in one's mouth, one becomes invisible.

With frog powder impregnated with blood, mixed with the blood of a *cāṇḍālī* and water, one should always apply it as collyrium to the eyes and below the face; this paralyzes water and causes [the enemy] to wander like a house.

If one uses the eye-salve mixed with the blood of a *caṇḍālī*, one becomes invisible. Whatever is written with her blood, that it accomplishes. By rubbing [the substance] together with a portion of her [blood], one becomes imperishable. Having bound wine, blood, and so forth with a cemetery thread, one should recite the mantra over it while holding it in the left hand, or by drinking the blood. He...
One becomes deformed; by applying the powder of a skull to the head, one becomes deformed. These are always the applications for attaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
They must be kept secret; Bhairavī does not reveal them. Among thousands of other mantras, these have been declared as the most excellent, fashioned to bestow success.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Bhairavī, Queen of the Gods, to that which destroys all sins;
for the sake of destroying the sins of the world, you have held your Guru within your heart.
How indeed can one call it the *Bhairavī* scripture when it is merely the literal meaning of the words of the *Nārāca*?
Those who do not know that it consists of one, two, four, five, six, seven, or more syllables, and who— though being sinful—
desire success (*siddhi*) by reciting it, claiming that the eight great successes (*aṣṭamahāsiddhi*) are attained in an instant, shall find no success.
Combined with the aggregate of sins,
the Mālā-mantra bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment, O Mahādevī;
through practice, O Mahādevī, even after hundreds of millions of births.
Single-syllable [mantras] do not succeed due to the absence of a hundred-fold practice;
by that success, O Goddess of Gods, one becomes Bhairavī herself.
Success is always attained for a single-syllable mantra through seven hundred thousand recitations;
for a five-syllable mantra, through sixteen hundred thousand; for a nine-syllable mantra, through nine hundred thousand;

for a sixteen-syllable mantra, through seven hundred thousand; for a seventeen-syllable mantra, through the same [seven] hundred thousand; and for a twenty-syllable mantra, through twenty hundred thousand.
With twenty lakhs [of recitations], it becomes a forty-four-syllable mantra; with nine lakhs, a ninety-syllable mantra; with four lakhs, a hundred-syllable mantra;

with three lakhs of recitations, a fifty-syllable mantra; and with two lakhs, a thousand-syllable great garland (mahāmālā). By performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) with these numbers of recitations, success is attained. Men must observe celibacy (brahmacarya) while doing so.
In the Kali age, these [rites] must be performed at night with four times the number [of repetitions]; having become armored with power (*śakti*),
gladdened by the joy of wine, and with hair disheveled.

Having performed the *puraścaryā* (preliminary rite) either with the fivefold method (*pañcaka*) or by the left-hand path (*vāmapatha*) according to the prescribed number, the success of the *puraścaryā* is attained. Even single-syllable mantras consisting of two,
three, four, five, six, seven, or more syllables— though they may not be known [by others]— become effective when brought into the *mantra-samaya* (the observance of the mantra) through recitation.

Those who desire accomplishment (siddhi) obtain the eight great accomplishments (mahāṣṭasiddhi). However, as long as the mass of sins accumulated in previous births remains, one does not achieve success. Through the preliminary recitation (puraścaraṇa-jāpa), sins are destroyed and accomplishment is attained. The Great Garland (Mahāmālā), the Great Goddess, is the swift bestower of accomplishment.
O Great Goddess, by means of practice over hundreds of millions of births.
Single-syllable mantras do not succeed through a mere hundred repetitions;
by that [practice], O Goddess of Gods, they are perfected, and one becomes directly equal to Śiva.
O Great Goddess, this great mantra bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment;
by the mere knowledge of it, a yogin becomes a conqueror of the gods.
Having understood this with effort, [one should keep secret] Caṇḍī Maheśvarī,
the bestower of great siddhis, O Kālī, through the grace of the Guru’s feet.
Having abandoned all scriptures, all yogas, and all vows;
having abandoned all mantras, one should practice the mantra of Kālikā alone.
In the Kali age, however, by the command of Śiva, the Kālikā mantras become perfected;
this great Vidyā, free from all impurities, bestows the status of a Guardian of the Quarters.
O Goddess of the Gods, for those who are devoted to these mantras spoken by Bhairava,
the three worlds shall become imperishable by the mere utterance of those words.
Oṃ, homage to Guhyakālikā! Hana 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
By reciting this root mantra, one accomplishes all siddhis. This is Bhairavī, the root mantra of the goddess who performs these special deeds.
The supreme goddess of all traditions, Kālikā, who is secretly manifested:

The Great Heart-Vidyā: 5. Oṃ hrīṃ khphreṃ hskhphreṃ khphreṃ ktīṃ namaḥ Amāvāsī. What need is there for another mantra? Having abandoned [all others], Śrī Guhyakālī is the one; both gods, grahas, and nāgas—all of them are subject to her command. She is the perfection that brings about success; O Maheśvarī, her perfection is these [mantras].

The Great Goddess, the bestower of excellence, having been made manifest, shall burn away the impurities accumulated in previous births through one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*). By the second hundred thousand, one becomes purified; by the third, there is the presence (*saṃnidhāna*) of the Goddess; by the fourth, there is the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*); and by the fifth, one should extract the mantra. Through six hundred thousand, success (*siddhi*) is attained. Thereafter, according to one's desire...

One should perform the mantra: *Oṃ phreṃ jāmahadahapacamānamoṭaya ānaya gṛhnaya veddhā cavadajalpajāt praviśya marmeti*. By this, she performs everything. With five hundred thousand recitations, one becomes worthy of worship by all the Yoginīs; with six hundred thousand, by those whose nature is Rudra; and with nine hundred thousand, by the Mahābhairavas.

"One becomes the omniscient Sadāśiva. Thus, through recitation (*japa*), one accomplishes everything. Through the yoga of the union of the mantra of consciousness and the flame of consciousness, all things are accomplished by a hundred thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt. In this way, as long as the purification of the mind has not occurred through recitation, how can accomplishment (*siddhi*) arise from mantras? [As stated] in the *Karmakāṇḍa*:
Having observed that honor, worship,
and so forth were not beneficial, he then recited the Caṇḍī [hymn]. He desired, "May there be success once again," [and thus he performed] the rite for evil karma.
Success is achieved when [the practice] is performed. I have declared that the mantra of Kālikā grants success when recited.

From where else could there be success in the Kali Yuga? The Great Goddess is attained through the gradual repetition of her mantra. Minor rites are accomplished by mere recitation; but what is the use of those minor rites for one who is a doer of evil? Therefore—
Śrī Guhyakālī necessarily bestows accomplishment; thereafter, the mantras for final liberation are declared: *khṃ* at the end of the divisions, *phreṃ*, *hskhphreṃ*, *khphreṃ*.
This is to be kept secret, O Great Goddess, and is difficult even for the gods to obtain.

Without the instruction of the Guru, there is no accomplishment. O Goddess, even the gods do not study that which has not been revealed; those who do so go to hell at that very moment. This is inevitable, O Maheśvarī; what then need be said of human beings? Therefore, I myself, Bhairava, remain as the self-arisen one to guard against the fault of [unauthorized] disclosure. Always.

For those who follow the dualistic doctrine, the Goddess is necessarily accomplished, just as it is for yoginīs in deep sleep. This must not be told to anyone; it is to be kept secret with great effort. Like the secret of fire, it should be concealed by means of the mandala and so forth, and likewise in the yoga of the offering of *mahāmāṃsa*. Everything is accomplished through mental service (*mānasopacāra*). Thus says Bhairava.
It occurs thus: all rites, such as ritual actions and mantras, are accomplished mentally at dawn.
It is certain in the Kriyātantra that those [beings] who are to be slain are to be killed by means of incense containing meat and by the offering of meat oblations (māṃsahoma).
The Śrīdevī said:
O Maheśvara, since you are pleased with me, O Bhairava, O terrifying one,
O Lord of Gods, O Master, tell me even that which is unspeakable, for it has been revealed.
O God, those mantras which are traditionally held to grant success through the mental [practices] of yogins—
Guhyakālikā grants success through the pervasion of feeling and the mind.
"O Bhairava, tell me what the activities of the yoginīs are.

To those who are self-conceited and revilers of their teacher, the *Kālikā* should not be explained. One should perceive the Guru as Bhairava himself—the one who has reached the further shore of all principles, the omniscient, the creator of all—and should offer him the reality of Śiva.
O Goddess, that disciple becomes a vessel for accomplishment; he must not transgress the shadow of his Guru.

For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others, even from a Śūdra, that attainment is achieved; therefore, for all those extending from Brahmā down to the end of the principles (tattvas), who follow that [tradition], one should receive the instruction of the mantra after making the lineage-teacher (kramaguru) the object of prostration. Because of that, O Sage, one should never fail to prostrate to the Samaya [teacher].

One should not treat [the Guru] like one crow pecking at another. Thus, by merely transgressing against the Guru, success (siddhi) departs and one sinks oneself into the netherworld (rasātala). One should never utter the name of the Guru, nor likewise that of the Yoginīs; otherwise, there will be a fall into a great hell.
The virtues of the Ācārya are to be grasped, and his faults never at all. Through virtue alone is success declared.

Through hatred one goes to hell. One should meditate on the true mantras upon all the limbs; having meditated, one should initiate one's own disciples. One should offer everything to the guru. In case of deficiency, horses, land, jewels, garments, ornaments, and so forth should be given. Gold, silver, and whatever else is desired by the mind—all this must indeed be given to the guru. Having prepared the assembly of commitments (*samayasāmagrī*) consisting of the *saṃhārikī*, the mortar, the five grains, the mallet, the *saṃhāriṇī* Yoginī, the weapon, the threshold, the grinding stone, the water-strainer, the jar, the breast-cloth, the *muhārikā*, the dust-heap, the crossroads, the *liṅga*, the solitary tree, the secret place, and the cremation ground;

By mere will, having fashioned a second body, one effects entry into another's body. With the syllables *hreṃ hreṃ*, there is the substitution of *jaḥ* and *hrīṃ*. *Aiṃ namaḥ cāmuṇḍe siddhikāli marmemarmābhighāte chrīṃ 2 hrīṃ 2 hūṃ māra 2 dara 2 bhakṣa 2 khāda 2 saha 2.*

Having recited [the mantra] once, one should offer oblations; by that, there is no doubt. By means of the root-mantra, one destroys the three worlds.
How much more so, then, cruel men? It strikes hundreds of millions of vital points in all those who have come before it.
If accomplished through mere desire, one may even kill or slay one's own ancestors; what need is there to mention [the result] when maintained with wrath?

I shall now proclaim the root mantra for the destruction of enemy armies for the sake of the knower; by the mere knowledge of which one may shatter even hundreds of millions [of troops]. Having known the other world, drive away! [create] great terror!
*Kuru 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ 5 phreṃ hrīṃ 2 hūṃ mahāmoha hanaḥ hraṃ 5 phaṭ 5 svāhā*.

This indeed is the supreme *avidyā* (spell) spoken by Siddhibhairava; when recited, one should sprinkle it at the tip of the banner of the venerable Siddhibhaṭṭārikā, or else one should conquer [the obstacle] before her while meditating, having bound it with the *nāgapāśa* (serpent-noose).
O Mahākṛṣṇa, grey with dust and smoke! Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ! May he cause the wicked thieves to fall!

Having performed the great worship, one should bury that sword which has descended through illusion. Through the state of mantra and devotion in the worship of the Bhaṭṭārikā, Brahmā and the other gods abide within her heart.

18a) How much more so, then, would one who writes the wheel of the vidyā in the house of a lowly man, having installed it according to the prescribed rite and worshipped it, destroy all calamities caused by wicked thieves, fire, water, and the like? Thus it is.

The mantra for worship is as follows: Oṃ namo hūṃ phreṃ marmemarma saṃvinī vadha 2 nāgapāśena sarvamadhyāt kuṭṭa 2 mahāṅkuśena tāḍaya 2 sphoṭaya 2 hana 2 dama 2 hana 2 hūṃ hrīṃ 2 meghasādhinīnāṃ sādhaya 2 ājñāpaya 2 daha 2 paca 2 māraya 2.

The accomplisher of all enemies, bearing many various weapons— conch, discus, trident, vajra, goad, noose, arrow, bow, tomara-spear, mallet, vajra-needle, dagger, lance, axe, club, sword, and shield— the accomplisher, *hrūṃ ha hrīṃ*, Great Māyā, Great Gaurī.

One shall accomplish all weapons; all weapons become [one's own]. Having assumed the actual form of those weapons, one should bring them forth. By this, when the mantra is favorable, the tongue of the practitioner—shaken by the performance of the offerings—becomes subdued.

The remnants of the agent should be taken; for him, that becomes the weapon. Having grasped it, he performs what he desires. What need is there to mention Amoghasiddhi? Whatever accomplishments (siddhis) have not been heard of—[all are attained].

For the practitioner who performs those various rites with the Kālikā mantra, Mahākālikā appears; having meditated upon her again and again as he pleases, according to his desire and through various modes of invocation, the yogi shall attain accomplishment by virtue of the state of non-dual yoga.

One who possesses supreme knowledge may consume all [substances]. For the non-dualist, the Goddess becomes the elixir of the essence of flavors (*rasa-rasāyaṇa*). By this [mantra], perform all [rites] such as the rules (*niyama*) according to the scripture: *Namo siddhi-cāmuṇḍā-sugaṃdhavati*.
*Oṃ hūṃ hreṃ bhakṣa 2 khāda 2 praviśya 2 śuddhāni śraddhava daha 2 paca 2 paritrāpa 2 duṣṭadravyāṇi bhasmīku 2 phreṃ heṃ kāriṇī svāhā*. [This is for] the consumption of all things.

Of all things and all substances: Aiṃ Huṃ! In the tumultuous great sound, may limb meet limb; Hrīṃ 2! O Vācavatī, Śrīṃ! Fill my speech! Enter the heart, throat, and mouth; Kruddha 2! Descend 2! Vadahne! Hūṃ Śrīṃ! O Omniscient One! Śrīṃ Svāhā! This is the Great Vācavatī.

It is known that this Great Goddess (Mahādevī) becomes the accomplisher of consciousness (*saṃjñā*). She is to be recited and meditated upon; indeed, she is to be recited according to the rules with various kinds of Vedas and a mind well-versed in all the scriptures. Then, one may move about as one pleases, or take the form of a woman, possessing a fragrant body and clothed in garments. When the Veda is mastered, [success is attained].

He causes [the disciple] to grasp all the scriptures. Together with that, one is not able to remain outside; there, the Yoginī, who performs all actions and is victorious, having reached her full age, becomes accomplished (*siddhā*). One should cause her to bestow [the teaching] even through secret qualities: *Oṃ namo mahāmāye huṃ phreṃ trailokya-trāṇe chrīṃ chrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dhāraya dhāraya yatra*.

O Mahāgaurī, you who possess wealth, grain, gold, silver, and children; O cave of great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*); O Smṛti and Medhā; O Vāse; O you whose form is like a cloud; O bestower of good fortune (*saubhāgya*) and the fulfillment of all desires; O Siddhicāmuṇḍā, fulfill [our wishes]! Grant, grant the eightfold sovereign powers! Grant, grant the eightfold sovereign powers! Grant sons, wealth, long life, and good fortune! Grant, grant riches and grain!

In the continuous fire offering (*saṃtata-homa*), perform that increase of all things, twice; O Giver of Wealth, twice; *hrīṃ* twice; *strīṃ phreṃ*; O Ratnamegha, rain down [wealth], twice; command all the *yakṣas*, twice; give orders, twice; grant glory and sovereignty, twice; make everything auspicious, twice;
make it free from obstacles, twice; homage to the Great Yakṣa King and Queen! *hrīṃ strīḥ chrīṃ* three times.

"O Mahādhanadā, grant me all wealth! O Siddhigaurī, huṃṭha, namaḥ, svāhā! (3 times). This supreme vidyā destroys the suffering of poverty; one should recite it and meditate upon it, and it bestows all mantras. Having worshipped according to the ritual rules and having written [the mantra] on birch bark, one should wear it. One who is childless obtains a son.
Good fortune, wealth, grain, and the attainment of both worldly success (*siddhi*) and spiritual perfection (*siddhi*) arise. One becomes completely liberated from all calamities.

Through *homa*, it bestows all prosperity upon the household. Furthermore, one should constantly recite this Great King-Mantra (*mahārājavidyā*); it makes one a lord of great wealth, brings about good fortune, and grants internal peace. O Blessed One, such is the accomplishment (*siddhi*).

One should cause [the victim] to be bound without end. By this, that practitioner of yoga becomes as resplendent as a lord of wealth with ten million [treasures]. *Namaḥ svāhā*. When recited, it is perfected; it accomplishes desired rites. It neutralizes all weapons and water, and it removes what is harmful from enemies. By maintaining the power of Manu, it destroys all evil planetary influences and strikes down all sins. It destroys all calamities.

Hāritā huṃ chrīṃ; in the center, the syllable *kṣreṃ* and the syllable *hrīṃ*, above and below. One should pierce [them]. How much more so, then, lowly men? What need be said if they are within a thousand *yojanas* nearby?
Thus: *khphreṃ yāṃ khphreṃ rāṃ khphreṃ lāṃ khphreṃ vā khphreṃ śāṃ khphreṃ vāraṃ* (54 times). Having burned one's own body with the breath, again with the breath...

There shall be no fear of misconduct and the like, nor of poison, fire, weapons, or missiles employed by others, nor of untimely death, wild beasts, and other such dangers; these are all dispelled at that very moment.

He sees [it] below the navel. For this is the supreme knowledge, the destroyer of old age and death; it is secret.

The supreme secret, which should not be disclosed even to one’s own mind, is encircled by a vajra; when yellow, it rains down a stream of yellow [light], and for the purpose of paralyzing (stambhana), the syllable *Eṃ* is desired by the mind as the form of Varuṇa. When joined with the arrival of the letter *Ya*, O Goddess, it brings about all misfortunes through the yoga of the arrival of the limbs (*vyaṅga*). The supreme knowledge, *hā hī*, which possesses equal radiance for a person, should be brought into union through the yoga of going and coming. Embracing it, one brings [the object] under control;
one does not cause expulsion (*uccāṭana*) among kings, but seizes all their possessions. One contemplates it within one's own mouth, brings it under control, and captivates the mind.

The goddess Cittinī should be meditated upon as having a lion, tiger, buffalo, gaṇḍa-bear, gavaya, hyena, boar, and elephant as her mounts; likewise Śravaṇā and Kārtikī, and Siṃhinī with the aforementioned mounts. One should meditate on one's own secret self as equal to the yoga of Kālikā, established upon a white lotus seat, the lord of yogins who has assumed the form and name of Siddhi, and who presides over the seven continents.
She is known as the Yoginī, the Paralyzer (Jambhinī), the Enchanter (Hāriṇī), the Accomplisher of Siddhis, the Omniscient, and the One who can assume any form at will.
O beloved, you are the Yoginī, the paralyzer, the captivator, the accomplisher of siddhis,
the embodiment of all desires, the medicinal herb, and the bestower of perfection.
By means of this, one who consumes the eight great siddhis becomes a long-lived one, enduring for an eon (*kalpa*).
One may perform all rites such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and so forth. Those who are devoted to it, those subjects, shall accomplish all hundreds of millions of scriptures without exception;
they perform whatever actions are desired by the mind. These herbs are perfected (*siddha*) and are supreme for all ritual acts.
O Yoginī, by the application of foot-ointment, you are the paralyzer, the deluder, and the destroyer of enemies;
you are the Goddess who attracts the three worlds and brings them under your command. Likewise, through worship for the attainment of siddhis, you are the dispeller of all diseases.
Oṃ hrīṃ bhamva 2 laya 2, O you of omniscient and desire-forming nature, [bestow] the elixir of mercury and the collyrium.

It is obtained near the great mountains. All the pills (guṭikās) perform all rites. Now, in the Atharvaṇa Saṃhitā: I shall describe the possession (āveśa). If a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*) is undertaken after the *puraścaraṇa*,

When one takes a flower, such as dūrvā grass or the like, in the hand and warms it while the thread is being rotated, and a transformation is manifested, then, having understood that procedure, one should take that flower and touch it in silence; having gone into the presence of whichever young girl one desires, one should do so with devotion.

When, after placing a flower on the head, [the disciple] exhibits signs such as weeping or physical disturbances like pain in the abdomen or head, then, having led them to a secluded place, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and so forth;

having worshipped [them], one should recite the mantra for possession (*āveśamantra*) one hundred and eight times. Then, having worshipped with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one performs the threefold worship, offers the three hymns of praise (*stotra*), and presents the *añjali* gesture.
One should cause [the disciple] to see it.

In that increase of the dog [the sign]: she does not touch the ground with her big toe; she opens her eyes upward.

He makes [others] hear; he moves his tongue, thinking, "What shall I do with the wholesome or the unwholesome?";

in returning a salutation, she displays the *kapāla-mudrā*. She touches the crown of the head.
He assumes a form at will. He displays the Great Hook Mudrā (*mahāṅkuśamudrā*). The accomplishment of the task is the Sword Mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*);

the attainment of desired objects is the Prayer Mudrā with palms joined (*añjali-mudrā*). "May it be well with you. He fondles his two arms; "I shall destroy the fever. O, he fondles his jaw; "I shall eat. His eyes fondle his forehead; "By you I have been brought under another's power.
