"Give me incense, flowers, and incense smoke," he says. He touches her back and says, "I shall lie down," while displaying the *triśūla* (trident) mudrā. "I have come," he says. *Rudrāṇī* displays her thumb. *Brahmāṇī* [displays] the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).
If Rudrāṇī touches with her thumb, Vaiṣṇavī with her left middle finger, Indrāṇī with her ring finger,

Kaumārī with her little finger, Lakṣmī with the *yonimudrā*, Vārāhī with her formidable fangs, and Cāmuṇḍā licks her lip with her tongue; if she touches the ground with the tips of her nails, there will be separation from what is dear to you.

If he strikes the ground with his left hand, it means: "Death will come to you. If he raises his hand, it means: "Your enemy will be destroyed. From looking to the side, one becomes unconquerable. By the *abhaya* [mudrā], "you have no fear. In the accomplishment of the great siddhis, one moves according to one’s will. By means of one’s desired form, one becomes an achiever of various ritual offerings (*caru*). One should conquer eye diseases and blood-bile (*raktapitta*) with collyrium (*añjana*). The supreme method for becoming invisible is as follows: [one should perform] a thousand [recitations] with the blood of a *caṇḍāla* mixed with [the substance] consecrated by the mantra of one’s desire, assuming various forms.
He steals wealth; he causes one to enter another's house invisibly; by his will, weapons and such become manifest.
A pill wrapped in gold, the first flower of the *cāmuṇḍālī*, and the yellow [flower] of the *caṃpaka* and *kāva*—wrapped in gold and placed in the mouth of whomever [one desires].

One becomes happy at that very moment. Blue honey, pigeon [blood], and the blood of a black snake should be applied as an ointment for those who suffer from the contraction of limbs. One should cook palāśa, ativisa, and other poisons with sesame oil;

Furthermore, yellow orpiment powder and likewise the seed of the Kanakī plant.

With those [syllables], preceded by *kṛt*, with four, two, and likewise two;

this body of Oḍīśimbara is thus fully described. This weapon [of knowledge] should be employed by a Brāhmaṇa who is a guru and a benefactor, for one whose mind is desirous of victory. Therefore, O Kula, even the ocean of the limbs of these places [should be mastered].

That scripture is inexhaustible, by which the guardians of the moon [are established] in their function.

Honey, crab, white ants, and the house-lizard—

One who has cut or split sesame seeds goes to the world of Yama, the abode of destruction;
having seized a vulture’s head, one should then fill it with salt.

This is the method for bringing back [the lost power], which is difficult to perform and brings success:

within seven nights, severe boils will undoubtedly arise.

The hair from a monkey's skin, asafoetida, and bhallātaka—

Taking the *sāvarṇika* [seal] and placing it upon the head of the *vedana*,

And by means of a preparation made from *bhallātaka*, one's enemy is deprived of his senses.

Upon whose head one should cast it— whether that be a woman or a man—

In great and terrible fears, in fears of lightning and fire, in the onset of diseases, of fanged beasts, and of elephants, and at the occurrence of calamitous days.

"O Lord, O Mother of the Gods, tell me these sciences.

At terrible crossroads, in battles, and during planetary seizures;

Whatever one remembers with the hand, and whatever one consumes with the tongue, that shall become nectar for him; there is never death for him at any time.

Recited in the forest of mantras with various divine mantra-words that grant happiness to all beings,

Destroy, destroy! Devour, devour! Pierce, pierce! Annihilate, annihilate! Cause destruction, cause destruction! Terrify, terrify! Tear asunder, tear asunder! Protect me and my retinue from all calamities! O Great Cloud, you who are the Samvartaka and Vidrutaka, fly up! Fly up!

O Bhūrūhavi, when the divine golden lotus has been struck, you who wear a garland of *ūca* and *moca*, with a white throat and a skull, holding the staff of the Jina and the lamp of the Kakkadīpa, remaining in your true form, terrifying, terrifying— drive away, drive away the Dravidas,

Paralyze the world-protectors! Kiraya kiraya! Slay, slay! Delude, delude! Subdue, subdue that spell of mine which has arisen through ritual action! Cut it down, cut it down! Paralyze, paralyze those who perform spells against me with great force; kiraya kiraya! Slay, slay! Delude, delude! Oṃ!

In the left nostril: *khphreṃ strīṃ*, Śrīpāda Makaravaktra; in the right nostril: *khphreṃ chrīṃ*, Śrīpāda Hayavaktra; in the left ear: *khphreṃ plūṃ*, Śrīpāda Gajavaktra; in the right ear: *khphreṃ hskhphreṃ*, Śrīpāda Kālikāvaktra. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the faces. *Oṃ*.

*Phreṃ līṃ phreṃ* to the right nostril, one step; *phreṃ hrīṃ phreṃ* to the left ear, one step;

The first *pāda* [ends] at the crown of the head (*mastaka*). This is the deposition (*nyāsa*) upon the body. Then follows the deposition of the three-syllable mantra:
*oṃ* at the navel, one *pāda*; *hrīṃ* at the heart, one *pāda*; *phreṃ* at the *bindu*, one *pāda*; *oṃ* at the heart, one *pāda*;
*oṃ* at the navel, one *pāda*; *siyonau*, one *pāda*; *hriṃ* at the root-tuber (*kanda*), *khphreṃ* at the *mūlādhāra*; *hskhphreṃ* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

*Khphreṃ bhrūṃ* in the middle of the brows; *kaṃ* on the left cheek; *hrīṃ* at the tip of the nose; *khphreṃ* on the upper lip; *hskhphreṃ* on the lower lip; *khphreṃ* at the tip of the tongue; *phreṃ* on the chin; *oṃ* at the navel; *svā* at the throat; *hāṃ* upon the heart.

The deposition of the piercing of others (*parabheda-nyāsa*): *Phreṃ hrīṃ*, fill the universe with the skull, *svāhā*. On the right shoulder: The Weapon-Placements (*astranyāsa*). *Phreṃ Phreṃ*. In the Kṛta Yuga, to Muṇḍī, on the left foot, the sole of the left foot (twice).

In the Tretā Yuga, to Muṇḍapāda, on the toes of the left foot (twice). In the Dvāpara Yuga, to Muṇḍapāda, on the nails of the toes of the left foot (twice). In the Kali Yuga, to Muṇḍāsana, on the left foot, above the left foot (twice).

*Atharvaveda-muṇḍāsana-āyapāda*: on the top of the right foot (2). *Indra-muṇḍāsana*: on the left ankle of the feet.

Having drawn an eight-spoked [wheel], an eight-petalled [lotus], and likewise ten, twelve, and sixteen petals, one should draw the perimeter of severed heads (*muṇḍaprākāra*). One should draw the bestower of desires: a cremated corpse burnt in the fire of liquor (ali), along with Śṛṅgāla, Ulūka, Bhairava, Kāka, Vetāla, and Caitya; and eight liṅgas in the cremation ground. Therein, [one should draw] a dot, a triangle, a pentagon, a nonagon, an octagon, and an eight-petaled lotus.

Having drawn a twelve-petaled, a sixteen-petaled, and a four-fold *kavandha* [diagram], as well as an eight-spoked trident (*śūla*), eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), and a wheel (*cakra*), one should meditate upon the Goddess. The preparation of the vessel (*pātrasādhana*) consists of the great vessel (*mahāpātra*) of the Brahmin caste, or else the preparation of the vessel using the finger-nails of a young girl. *Phreṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, O pervasive mandala, O venerable feet, *phreṃ*.

Mahākālī is blue in color, with three faces and nine eyes.
The southern face is yellow, while the northern one is like fire.
He has a circular face, wide eyes, eight arms, and holds a bow;
his tawny matted locks are piled upward, and he wears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
She is joined with twenty-six shaven-headed attendants and the blood-stained Viṣṇu;
she is richly adorned with earrings of bone and wears a garland of skulls upon her head.
With the tinkling sound of her small bells, she was the best among those who roar with heroic pride;
mounted upon a jackal-ghost, she had streams of blood flowing from her mouth.
Indra and the others, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudreśvara, and Sadāśiva,
possess complexions that are yellow, black, dark-blue, red, smoke-colored, white, and dark respectively.
They hold a vajra-staff, a discus, a spear, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga;
with their index fingers placed in their mouths, they are three-eyed and stand upon Śiva.
The goddess sits in the full lotus posture (vaddhapadmāsana), her breasts are full and elevated,
and in her left hand she holds a most beautiful skull-cup filled with blood.
They hold a trident with a skull in their right hand,
as well as a vajra, a goad, and a mallet in the right hand.
In her left [hands] she holds a noose, a khaṭvāṅga, and a corpse with its hair;
she stands in the midst of the subtle vibration of consciousness, consisting solely of the form of light.
One should install the Great Goddess, who bestows the state of Nirvāṇa, who transcends all existence, who is beyond the reach of the senses, and who possesses nine faces, within this image.
One should worship the thirty-syllable mantra in three ways according to the distinction of enjoyment (*bhoga*), authority (*adhikāra*), and liberation (*bhedena*).
This goddess is proclaimed to have nine faces as her supreme form (*parārūpa*).

[Then follow] Kalā, Niyati, Avidyā, Rāga, and Puruṣa. Then...

I constantly offer as an oblation into the fire of the Self—the fire illuminated by dharma and adharma—along the path of Suṣumnā, the impure mental modifications that arise from the senses. Khphreṃ! In the fourth state (turīya), I offer the seed-syllable of Śiva, which is born of the quality of Tamas, the supreme sign, bodiless, led by the mind of the Self, the steam of Śiva, and the essence of the auspicious Śiva-tattva, so that it may become as it truly is.
In that same manner, I purify; salutation! Salutation to the Śiva-tattva!

I offer into the fire of the void, with the hand of dharma and adharma, the entire universe—consisting of Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā, as well as the verses, the manifestations of light, the two thousand [mantras], the contemplation, and the ears—into the fire of the void.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Khphreṃ! O Great Fourth-I, you who are born from all qualities!
The body, known as the gross, subtle, and supreme *liṅga*, brought forth by the Self— within the seed-syllable *aiṃ phreṃ khphreṃ* which is the crest-jewel of self-knowledge—
I purify all principles (*tatva*) exactly as they are; *namaḥ* to the principle of *prakṛti*,
*namaḥ* to the principles of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), ear, skin, eye, [tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals].
Tongue, vital breath, speech, hands, feet, wind, genitals; sound, touch, form, taste, smell;
ether, air, fire, water, earth; *māyā*, time, necessity, limited agency, knowledge, ignorance;
the individual soul (*puruṣa*), supreme Śiva, power (*śakti*), Sadāśiva, Īśvara, pure knowledge (*vidyā*); then the verse.
38a) This "this-ness" (idaṃtā), born from the vessel [of the body], is the supreme "I-ness" (parāhaṃtā); as the supreme nectar,
I offer it into the fire consisting of supreme "I-ness," which has the nature of Śiva.
Contemplation of reality:
May the hungry ghosts and Kuṣmāṇḍas perish; may the malevolent men who cause corruption perish;
may there be auspiciousness for the practitioners who protect the tradition.
Victory to all the Mothers! Victory to the hosts of Yoginīs!
Victory to the Siddhas and Ḍākinīs! Victory to the words of the Gurus!
Victorious are all the practitioners who are purified;
victorious are the men who are worshippers, perfected in the conduct of their commitments.
The adepts of *aṇimā* and others [worship] Nanda; Bhairava and the others [worship] Nanda;
and all the deities, such as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, [worship] Nanda.
Those ministers who are pure of soul through love, completely purified,
and whose hearts always delight in bliss, are indeed protectors of the shore.
May the deities beginning with Indra be present; may Nārada be the presiding deity;
and may the gods, such as the Moon and the Sun, be satisfied according to the power of my mind.
May the lunar mansions, the planets, the yogas, the karaṇas and others,
as well as the days and the lunar dates— whether they bring happiness everywhere or are devoid of expectation— proceed on their course.
May all the Mothers, the seasons, the years and so forth,
as well as those who move in the sky and those who move upon the earth, be satisfied through my devotion.
Those who move on land and those who move in the sky, the cows, other deities and so forth—
all of them are happy today, as are all rivers and birds.
May the cattle, the trees, the mountains, the hands, and the deep caves,
as well as all the sages and Brahmins, grant peace at all times.
May the sacred fords, the many cows, and whatever other holy places there are, as well as the elders, those observing vows, and noble women, grant me auspiciousness. May they carry [me] across.
May Śiva grant his will everywhere; may sons, wives, wealth, and so forth be attained;
may kings be happy, and may my path always be secure.
On that auspicious day, the worshipper remained constantly present;
and those of sinful mind who were desirous of seizing his ornaments, [were thwarted].
In worship, he whose heart is ruined by conduct contrary to the ways of the gods is wicked and a destroyer of dharma.

Having seen the unprecedented wheel, those Kaulikas who are corrupters of the heart were filled with joy; yet for me, that very [wheel] was a source of destruction. O Śrī Bhairavī, this is to be known by practitioners as the two doors of the divine tradition (devāmnāya). Thus it is stated in the Atharvaṇasaṃhitā of the Śrī Hāhārāva Tantra.
The Chapter on the Specific Worship of the Lineage of Śivās, whose Essential Nature is the Illustrious Guhyakālī.
38b) On the northern peak of Sumeru, having bowed to the god whose banner is the bull, the goddess spoke with supreme devotion to the god, the teacher of the world.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures;
O Lord, the *Kālikākavaca* has been indicated and now revealed.
"O Lord, I do not know by what means her armor may be removed;
therefore, tell me today if I am dear to you. (3)
The Lord said:
"O bold one, O great queen, do you desire my meat?
Truly, truly, O great queen of virtuous vows, what has been spoken is not so. (4)
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
Listen, O Lord of Life; indeed, I am not merely your beloved, but I beautify my mind with the white purity of affection for your true devotees.
O Kālikā, tell me again that divine armor;
otherwise, I shall give up my life, there is no doubt.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess of noble gait; how that came to be, I shall relate to you.
Nevertheless, I will speak, for you are as dear to me as my own life.
I know the goddess Kālikā, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; she is the form of the Kula-kuṇḍalinī, intoxicated, and the abyss of knowledge.

Bhairava is its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *uṣṇik* meter (*chandaḥ*), the deity is Śmaśānaguhyakālikā, and the seed-syllables are the [syllables] beginning with *lajjā*. The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are those beginning with *drutayadri*. This is the application (*viniyoga*) for recitation (*japa*) for the sake of attaining all goals, such as poetic inspiration and the like.
In the cremation ground, however, one should meditate upon the goddess Mahākālī,
who is naked, whose face is formidable with fangs, and who is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
On the right and likewise on the left, O Rāma, the lower noose and the upper [noose] are proclaimed in that sequence. || 11 ||
Having meditated thus upon Mahākālī, all accomplishments arise.
*Krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*, may she protect my head; *hūṃ hūṃ*, may the Sovereign of the Gods protect [me]. (12)
" Hrīṃ hrīṃ," the pair of seed-syllables of modesty, may they always protect my heart; and "dakṣiṇe kālike," may they protect me at the region of the navel. (13)
KṚĪM KṚĪM KṚĪM, may it protect my male organ; HUṂ HUṂ HUṂ, again on the lower lip;
HRĪM HRĪM HRĪM, may it protect my nose; SVĀHĀ, may it protect my Brahma-randhra. || 14 ||
Oṃ may always protect the feet; krīṃ krīṃ [protect] the dissolution into Brahman;
kroṃ [protect] the right [side], and so forth; krīṃ krīṃ kuṃ kuṃ [protect] the eyes and the head. 15.
KṚĪM KṚĪM KṚĪM—may this three-syllabled mantra protect my navel and heart again. AIṂ OṂ OṂ—may the one ending with the letter ṬHA (ṬHAṂ) protect [me]. AIṂ OṂ OṂ HRĪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. || 16 ||
May Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā protect [me] with *krīṃ krīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ huṃ huṃ*,
and may Sāṅkarī protect [me] with *śrī dakṣiṇe kālike svāhā*.
Hūṃ śrīṃ hūṃ, O Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā! Oṃ aiṃ, again the twelve-syllable mantra.
Oṃ oṃ, again śrīṃ sauṃ svāhā; protect me, Kālina! || 18 ||
Oṃ krīṃ krīṃ huṃ me svāhā, this six-syllabled [mantra] of Kālikā has revealed my entire true nature. || 19 ||
O Indrāṇī, listen: first is the Gāyatrī in the form of Brahman;
then "ṅe" and "ntā," and likewise Kālikā, and after that "vidmahe. (20)
"Śmaśānavāsinī" and "Dhīmahi" follow thereafter; then the "Ghoramāyā-tantu" is declared, and after that again, "Pracodayāt. || 21 ||
Again, the *pāyātmā* (the soul of the lower part) extends to the two divisions and reaches up to the *brahmaraṃdhra*;
the *dhīmahiti* (the soul of the middle part) extends from the throat to the region of the navel.
Then, one should protect the pair of feet from the navel against terrible desire;
the word "pracodayāt" is declared for the entire body, moving clockwise.
May Kālī protect my heart; may Kapālinī protect my throat;
may Kulā protect my cheeks; and may Kurukullā protect my eyes. (24)
May Virodhinī protect my ears; may Vipracarcikā protect my teeth; may Ugrā protect my hands, and may Ugraprabhā protect my speech.
May the radiant Nīlā protect my two feet; may Meyā protect my private parts;
may Dhanā protect my nose; and may Valākā protect my chin. || 26 ||
May your mother protect my two teeth and my belly; may the auspicious Mudrikā protect the tip of my tongue. || 27 ||
May all these together protect me once again in every limb;
may Brahmāṇī protect me, and likewise Nārāyaṇī.
And may Māheśvarī always grant me protection once again;
may Kaumārī, together with her attendants, protect me from cruel and wicked beings. (29)
May Cāmuṇḍā, who dwells among the Pracaṇḍa gaṇas, protect me constantly;
and may Aparājitā grant me protection throughout the three worlds. (30)
May Vārāhī, joined with Kālikā, protect me always; and may Nārasiṃhī grant me protection in the Mandula of men. (31)
May Indrāṇī, who fulfills all desires, protect me at the eastern gate;
may these goddesses, the digits of the art of desire, protect my feet once again.

Huṃ huṃ hauṃ māṃ— may she who is present even face-to-face protect me, for she is indeed like the world itself; Oṃ kroṃ, O you whose nature is Brahman, dāṃ dīṃ duṃ daiṃ dauṃ daḥ— may Śrīvidyā-Ḍākinī protect me once again.
May the three-syllabled Śrīvidyā—Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauṃ—protect [me] always;
may Nīlasarasvatī—Strīṃ Strīṃ Ūṃ Ūṃ Ū Strīṃ Strīṃ—protect [me]. || 34 ||
And may these great vidyās, as well as Eka-jaṭā, protect me once more—she who is joined with the mantra: "Āṃ hīṃ śrīṃ, O you whose garment is the tree of joy! (35).
Oṃ juṃ saḥ hauṃ—may he, joined with the mantra and possessing the eyes of a woman, protect me.
Gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ ḍīṃ gaiṃ gaḥ—may Gaṇeśa protect me within the circle of the Gaṇas. (36)
KṢĀṂ KṢĪṂ KṢUṂ KṢAI KṢAUṂ KṢAḤ—may Kṣetrapāla, the eternal protector, guard [me]; VĀṂ VĪṂ VŪṂ VAṂ VAUṂ VAḤ—may Vaṭuka, joined by the sky-farers (khecaras), protect the waist. || 37 ||
Hskhphreṃ va māṃ pātu śkṣmlvryī; furthermore, O you whose form is the primordial seat, protect me, you who possess the nature of the piercing of the six cakras! 39.
May Kulakuṇḍalinī, who resembles a mass of lightning, protect me once more;
O Vāgrūpiṇī, [you whose mantra is] *trī trūṃḍe ca mama aṃ iṃ puṃ? eṃ*. 40.
May she who is in the form of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' protect me;
may she who encompasses the letters from 'kṣa' back to 'ka' protect me. (41)
Aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ may she protect; hrīṃ śrīṃ may she protect; krīṃ krūṃ strīṃ hauṃ klīṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ skeṃ?
sphreṃ svāhā—may she, O Sarasvatī, protect you from obstruction! 42.
Īśvara said:
Now I shall describe the pill of the Great Goddess that grants all desires:
having inscribed the armor-mantra together with the incantation upon birch bark, || 43 ||
Then, either the Guru or he himself, using unground vermilion,
should draw the syllable Hrīṃ— the Goddess— directly in front of the Yantra.
To the right of that very [seat], one should then write the syllable HŪṂ for the Goddess;
listen, O Queen of Gods, and one should likewise write the syllable HRĪṂ to the north. (45)
40a) Furthermore, the mantra-practitioner should write [the name] preceded by "svāhā" at the end; O Beloved, the Great Goddess herself, with undistracted mind, should write this yantra. 46.
Having written this armor (kavaca), O Goddess, one should wear it on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight or the ninth day of the bright fortnight within a golden cave.
O beloved of my life, having worshipped the goddess and the pill,
one should worship her according to the prescribed rite through the application of the sequence mentioned in the Nyāsa.
And this pill, O Goddess, bestows glory when placed upon the head;
and when placed upon the neck, it bestows the Great Goddess-knowledge—of this there is no doubt. (49)
If she is offered what is most desired in the heart, she bestows inexhaustible wealth;
when the Goddess is at the waist and hips, it becomes the supreme rite of immobilization (staṃbhana).
Whenever the Goddess holds her left foot, whatever desires one may have, those one obtains; of this there is no doubt. (51)
O beautiful one, listen now to the illumination of this very armor-mantra:
one should write the complete twelve-syllable vidyā upon a copper plate. (52)
Having recited the armor-mantra (kavaca), O Goddess, one should strike [the heart] with red sandalwood;
then, having recited it again, O Mistress of the Gods, one should offer an illumination with fragrant paste.
O Goddess, bestower of boons with perfect limbs, life itself has been restored; for this is indeed the threefold consecration that illuminates the armor-mantra.
Having recited the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the goddess should then contemplate the root-vidyā;
O Great Goddess Guhyakālī, she should likewise perform the threefold consecration (*saṃskāra*).
At night, the practitioner, with a steady mind, [should visualize] the Goddess wearing white garments, her mouth full of betel-leaf, and possessing a countenance as radiant as the full moon. 55.
One should hold the Goddess on the left side, and then perform the ritual of the seat (pīṭha).
Having recited the armor (kavaca), one should then perform the union with Śambhu for that Goddess.
In that very state of enjoyment, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
there, one should worship the auspicious Kālikā, the Great Goddess of the Yoni.
Āṃ hrīṃ bhagavati bhagarūpe svāhā. With this mantra, one should worship the Goddess with hrīṃ śrīṃ in the vulva. || 58 ||
This *puraścaraṇa* is indeed secreted in all the tantras;
it must not be spoken [of], O Great Goddess—listen, O beloved of my life! (59)
KṚĪṂ HŪṂ GUHYAKĀLIKE KṚĪṂ HŪṂ SVĀHĀ | May this twelve-syllable mantra protect [us].
By means of this mantra, O Goddess, one [attains] this Vidyā which has been well-guarded.
O Great Goddess, if by the power of fortune a human being attains this goddess in the Kali age, his merit cannot be equaled even by hundreds of millions of sacrifices.
O Great Goddess, even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of tens of thousands of aeons, it would not be possible to describe his auspiciousness.
O Goddess of gods, listen as I speak of the fruit that comes from even a single portion of this very knowledge; I am never capable of describing it fully. (63)
This great goddess of knowledge is to be strictly guarded even among the Āmalas; it has now been told by me as it was received within the Kavaca.
Sages, gods, and yogis alike will honor this;
thus it has been told, O Goddess, that such a thing is rare throughout the three worlds.
When the Kali age has arrived, there will be some who,
having resorted to a secondary science (upavidyā), will not perform [the rites] but will merely mutter [mantras], O lowest of men.
If they do not attain success therein, they would utter a most terrible curse;
however, O beautiful one, the Great Goddess would bestow the vidyā upon one who is well-established.
To one who is learned, devoted, and endowed with the respective mantras;
and likewise not to an atheist, one of evil conduct, or a slanderer. (68)
Listen to the fruit of the sin of one who bestows this great vidyā:
after a month has passed, the Great Goddess shall go to the house of the son of the Sun (Saturn). 69.
If one should again employ Kālikā without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca),
Kālī and the Yoginīs shall devour his limbs and all his members.
One must never speak [of this] to kinsmen;
indeed, even after thousands of tens of thousands of kalpas, there shall be no transformation for him.
O Goddess, this armor of yours is once again the enchantment of the three worlds;
O Goddess, both the mantra and the armor are truly real, there is no doubt.
He who always recites this at the three junctions of the day, which bestows all accomplishments,
finds speech consisting of both prose and verse emerging from the depths of his mouth.
Indeed, by the splendor of Śrī Rāmaharavārya alone,
even Durvāsas was subdued in his anger, just as Kubera, the lord of wealth, was subdued by Dhanada.
In beauty, he is equal to Kāma; in speed, he is like me;
and in truth, he is like Mahādevī—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
He who knows all this is indeed I; of this there is no doubt.
This is the Kālikā-avaca, fashioned by Kālabhairava.
Thus ends the chapter on the Armor of Kālikā, as fashioned by Kālabhairava residing on the northern ridge of Mount Sumeru, in the venerable Hāhārāva Tantra.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the three worlds, to Brahmā who possesses the universal form,
to the Sovereign, the Supreme Lord, the Guru in the form of Śiva.
I bow to that Supreme Sovereign Goddess, the all-pervading Ishvari, by whose power even the omniscient Lord Shiva becomes such.
I bow to that Guhyakālī, who is intent on devouring Kāla and by whom millions of cosmic eggs are reduced to ashes.
By whom she extends everything, into whom all enter again and again,
and at whose worship even the omniscient Śiva, the knower of yoga, is not a god.
And the Supreme Lord is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer, who is imperishable; He is Śiva, the peaceful Īśāna, free from old age and death.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Yuga, Rudra, together with Śakti, sustained [the world] through the Guṇas;
he attained supreme knowledge, the King of Hymns, the great Mantra.
Śiva gave it to Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu gave it to Brahmā;
by Brahmā it was given to Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha gave it to Manu.
Desiring the kingdom of contemplation, with his mind always focused on the single-pointed recitation, Manu ruled the earth girt by the oceans as if it were held in his two hands.
Without vows, without meditations, without worship, recitations, or hymns,
and without heroic practices (*vīrasādhana*), fire offerings (*homa*), and so forth, she bestows her fruit swiftly.
There exists no hymn equal to this within the belly of the universe;
therefore, setting aside everything else, one should recite the Thousand Names.
By whose thousand names one is not born again in a womb;
therefore, it should be recited with all effort by those who are composed in mind.
Having drawn [the form] with one-pointed concentration and having performed the ritual acts (*kṛtya*), one should meditate upon Maheśvarī.
41b) Oṃ, for this Thousand-Name Mantra of the deity Śrī Guhyakālī, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Sadāśiva.
The meter (chanda) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is Śrī Guhyakālī; Oṃ is the seed-syllable (vīja); Phreṃ is the power (śakti); Hrīṃ is the peg (kīlaka);
the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of all desired perfections.
Meditative absorption.

I bow to the Supreme Goddess, the ten-faced Mistress of Yogīs, who dwells upon a lotus with petals like coral, shining like ten autumnal moons, situated above the head of Bhairava— himself atop the heads of the guardians of the directions, from Brahmā down to the five pairs of Yugas— while she is mounted upon a lion, a boar, a monkey, a bear, a horse, Garuḍa, a crocodile, and a human.
She has five faces, holds a staff, a trident, a *kuśa* grass-bundle, an axe, a mallet, a noose,
and a vessel in her hands, and her lotus-like palms are marked with a *khaṭvāṅga*, a peacock feather, and a human head.
Oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ chrīṃ huṃ strīṃ namaḥ | Oṃ Guhyakālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, Sumaṅgalā, Parāpareśvarī, Dhūmrā, Parameṣṭhī, Varapradā!
Caṇḍikā, Carcikā, Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, Śavarohiṇī—
she whose face is beautiful and serene, the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Caṇḍaghoṣā, Mahārāvā, Cārucakrā,
Prakāśinī, Caṇḍeśvarī, Prāṇacarī, and Caṇḍapherucarāṇī.
She who destroys the pride of the fierce Daityas, who removes all sins,
the auspicious Mistress of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, the formidable one, the terrifying beloved of Bhairava.
May you become one of great fortune, worthy of enjoyment, and a liberator;
O Bhavānī, you who destroy the disease of worldly existence and awaken the devotion of your devotees.
She who pacifies great delusion, who gladdens with great enthusiasm,
whose splendor is patience and beauty, whose radiance is like moonlight, the fierce Mistress of Yoga, the Auspicious One.
She whose form is splendor, composed of splendor, illuminating with divine luster;
she whose face is light, the Great Caṇḍī, the Mistress of Yoga, the Bestower of Great Boons.
She has the face of a lion, the face of a jackal, the face of a monkey, and the face of an elephant;
she has the face of Garuḍa, the face of a spike, the face of a dancer, and the face of a horse.
She has the face of a man, is blue in color, and possesses fifty-four arms;
she holds a jewel of consciousness as a seal on her hand and is adorned with human skulls.
With a garland of dry skulls and adorned with various jewels,
Kālikā is the fierce subduer of the wicked, riding upon a lion.
Adorned with human skulls and decorated with dried skulls,
she is Kālakālī, the radiant Kālī, the Roaring One who devours the sacrificial offering.
Victorious Jayā, Jayantī, Vijayā, the destroyer of evil dreams,
seated upon the throne of Brahmā and the Pretas, the beautiful Kamalā, beloved of the lotus.
She whose tongues are blazing, whose tongue is flickering, and whose tongue is like lightning; she who removes old age;
she whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; she who is seated upon the corpse of Viṣṇu.
Seated in the center of the solar disc, bestowing the fruits of various karmas,
she is Rudrī, fierce with her seat of a corpse, passionate, and lotus-eyed.
Seated in the posture of Īśvara, she is the Sovereign, beloved by the Lord;
she possesses great power, is the Great One, and bestows supreme sovereignty.
The goddess seated on the throne of Sadāśiva is known as Sudhā, the Mother;
established in Kroṣṭu-rāva, she is Māyā, known as the bearer of great nectar.
Mahāpheru, Varārāvā, Rāvaruddhā, Bhayaṃkarī,
the auspicious mother of Mahāsena, Pratiṣṭhā, and Pālanī.
She who shatters Niśumbha and Śumbha, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
she who crushes Dhūmrākṣa and the maiden who utterly destroys Viḍālākṣa.
She who withers the seed of passion, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
the fierce and violent one of terrible form, who strikes down formidable enemies.
She who brings about the destruction of fierce evil, she who upholds the formidable command;
she who wields terrible weapons, the sustainer of all, adorned with formidable ornaments.
The pacifier of great sins, the performer of fierce deeds,
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍī, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍanādinī,
Yoginī, Mahācaṇḍā, Caṇḍarūpā, and Caṇḍikā.
She who wields the sword and the trident, the terrible one, who utters the roar of the syllable "Hūṃ."
Vāhinī, Śaktinī, Caṇḍī, Mahākandaradhāriṇī,
Khaṭvāṅginī, Muṇḍinī, Cāpinī, Cakriṇī, and Parā.
Ghaṇṭārāva, Priyā, Nityā, Kharīṇī, Kuṭṭinī, Mahā, Vālā,
Pretadhṛtavatī, and Mahākaṅkāladhāriṇī.
Na-kulinī holds a serpent and a weapon; Śiti is indeed clad in white. Ṣaḍasraḍoḍikā has a hand [holding] a fire-vessel and a triple staff (tridaṇḍa).
Śruvahastā holds a *śruva* ladle; Siṃhī holds a garment and a mallet.
Huṃkāriṇī, Ḍiṇḍinī, Śrīkarī, and Kartṛdhāriṇī;
she who wields the great goad and sounds the great ḍiṇḍima drum.
She holds a trident and a staff, she carries a cow and a water-pot;
she bears a lotus, a goad, and a book, and she rides upon a corpse.
From the Churikā flows the Maravatī and the Mahākusumamālinī; these two rivers, which bestow supreme bliss, she holds within herself.
The Supreme Goddess, the Great Fierce One, who brings devotees under her control, who loves worldly existence;
she is the Mistress of the Left in the Void, the Leftward One, the Sky-walker, the Quarter-walker, and Steadfastness.
Gocarī, Bhūcarī, Saumyā, Mātaṅgī, Pālakī, Śivā,
Naravallī, Varāhā, Gosarpāsyā, and she of various faces.

She is the embodiment of bliss, the embodiment of virtue, the embodiment of the sun, and the refuge of all qualities; she is the embodiment of the moon, the embodiment of great joy, the embodiment of splendor, and the one with the great mouth.
She whose form is milk, the great remover of obstacles, the great banner, the auspicious wielder of the thunderbolt;
she who possesses a flag, the source of compassion, the primordial nature, and the Sovereign Goddess.
She who moves within the orb of the sun, who is fond of the vermilion tilaka,
who possesses the form of a thousand stars, and who is the fierce-formed Great Goddess.
Mahāhaṃsamati, Viṣṇumati, Vimalasiṃhikā,
Mahācaṇḍamati, Siṃhamati, Vimati, and Prabhā.
Ahīramatī, Mātaṅgī, she of great intellect regarding the perishable and the imperishable,
Vicitracitritamatī, and the supreme Vīrasiṃhamatī.
Bhaurūsiṃhamatī, Jñānā, Mahārasmimatī, Kṛśā,
Mahātrikoṇasaṃsthānā, Mahā, Īḍā, and Marīcikā.
She who moves everywhere, she whose gait is divine, the great fish, the great goddess;
the great Caṇḍī with most divine limbs, the great Vidyā born of the earth.
In the great intermediate space, she is Tejomvā, Siddhiyoginī, and Kāminī;
she is Gaganāmbā, Mahābhaṭṭī, and the emaciated Mahānilombharā.
Mahācaṇḍā, Maṇḍalāmbā, Śauṇakī, Jhaṣaṇī, Ghṛṇī,
Padukīrī, Padukī, Gandhakālī, and Mataṅgī.
Kaivartinī, Caṃpakā, Marta?, Kāminī, Rākṣasī,
Bhajakiṃbhikṣuki, Śrotri, Dhūmrā, Daṃṣṭriṇī, and Rūpiṇī.
Jvālinī, Gaganeshī, Madiyāgā, Dhāriṇī, Nadi, Vigavā, Śāntī, Mahāmāyā, Subhagā, Ānandinī, and Dhruvā.
Umānandā, Śriyānandā, Mahānandā, Sunandinī,
Iḍā, Marīci, Vidyāmbā, Mūkajāmbā, and Prabodhinī.
Caṃdrinī, Raudrīṇī, Divyā, and Siddhyantarikṣajā are remembered;
likewise Ambikā, Vālikā, and Ambā, who is directly worshipped by virtuous people.
Vidyādharī, Caṇḍinī, and Mārutā are always remembered;
likewise Ulkāmukhī, Lokamukhī, Varṇeśī, and Varṇamālikā.
Bhīmānanā, she who is called Anaṅgā, the one who sets the time of the Vidyā in motion,
Unmanī, Sundarī, Svāhā, and she who moves within the orb of nectar.
Karālā and Vikarālā, Khagā and Khagavāhinī,
Śṛgālī, Pūtanā, Vajrā, Vyomakālī, and Kaulinī.
The source, the source of accomplishment, the great source, born of a good source;
the source of accomplishment, the source of truth, the great source, and the source of the bones of the great number.
Divyayoni, Mahādivyayoni, Padmākṣayoni,
Mahābhakṣaṇabhakṣī, and the auspicious Mahāsaṃhāriṇī.
The Great Mistress of Passion, the Fierce One, the Destroyer of the Great Ender;
she who devours the great sacrifice and whose voice is the sound of the destruction of time.
Kālarātrī, the most terrible Mahāraudrī, Cāṇḍālī, the destroyer of Time; Vīreśvarī, worshipped by heroes, who removes the fear of the fire of time.
The great Bhairavī, the destroyer who wanders within the cosmic egg,
is the auspicious Saṃhārakālikā, the dispeller of great fear.
The Great Divine One at the time of creation, the Most Radiant One at the time of maintenance, the Terrible One at the time of withdrawal, and she who devours Time at the time of dissolution.
Raktakālī, Mahogrā, Kālī, Yamamārgikā,
Mṛtyukālī, Bhadrakālī, and Mahāmārtaṇḍakālikā.
Mahākālāgnikālī and Paramārkārka Kālikā;
Kālakālī, Mahāghorā, and Caṇḍabhairavakālikā.
Maṃtrakālī, Haṃsakālī, Kramakālī, and Ḍāmarī;
Jñānakālī, Cakrakālī, and Cakra-oṃkārakālikā.
Mahāgagaṇakālī, Ekābhāsā Kālikā,
Mahāśabdakālikā, and Mahābalāttakālikā.
Ṛddhikālī, Śuddhikālī, Bhāsāśrī, Haṃsakālikā,
Caṇḍabhāsākālikā, and Bhāsāḍāmarakālikā.
The light-bearing dark-blue,
the light ending with the bears, the light of the source,
the great light, and the light of the sky.
Sūryakālī, Candrakālī, Agnikālī,
the most terrifying Vāyukālī, Vyomakālī, Manaḥkālī, and the all-pervading Suvyāpinī.
Sarvakālī, Siddhikālī, Nirālambā, Āstukā, and Ālikā; Kālikā, Daṃṣṭriṇī, Mudrā—she is that Lelihānakā mudrā.
The skull-gesture (kapālamudrā) is the destroyer of time; that gesture is the annihilator of time.
The terrible gesture (ghoramudrā) is the destroyer of the pledge (samaya), as well as the formidable and the whirling one (bhrāminī).
Śrī-kuṇḍalā is that mudrā, and the head-bowl mudrā;
the yoni-mudrā, the supreme mudrā, and the twelfth is the mahāmudrā.
Chippilī, Dhīvarikālī, Prakṣepaṇī, Mudrīkā,
Prabhā, Veśyā, Śauṇḍinī, Ghorā, Kaivarttī, Kheṭakī, and Manī.
Bhāgarā, Jakīchippilī, Jñānā, Aṭakī, Kośaghaṇṭikā,
Agnivaktrā, Piṅgākṣī, Ramaṇī, Maṇī, and Jarā.
Gokarṇī, Gajakarṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, Aśvakarṇikā,
Vidyunmukhī, Prasannāmbā, Lokamātā, and Prabhāvinī.
Brahmānanā, Brahmabalā, Kapilā, Pūtanā, Bhayā,
Nagnanāśā, Bhagnakarṇā, Bhagnoṣṭhā, and Rājamātṛkā.
Guhyeśvarī, Sāradā, Jalpeśvarī,
O Pārvatī, Kulinī, Hariṇī, Māyā, Mahāmāyā, and Ambikā.
Raktakālī, Mahākālī, Ghaṇṭākālī, Vimātṛḍā,
Ūrdhvakeśī, Chinnamastā, and Mahālakṣmī reside within the triangle.
Mātaṅgī, Śivadūtī, Siddhāmbā, Padmamandirā,
Padmayoni, Nirāvādhā, Saliṅgā, and Bhagamālinī.
Known as Caṇḍā, she is the sustainer of the three worlds, situated within the Mother of the Three Powers (Triśaktimātṛkā);
she is Kapālinī, Mālinī, Kāminī, and Kamalānanā.
Maṃtreśvarī, Ugrakālī, Lakṣmīmālā, Mālikā, Kulālī, she known as Raktacaṇḍā, Kāmalakṣmī, and Manoharā.
Jinamātā, Jiteṃdrā, Sāradā, Ahaṃsavāhinī,
Mahāśrīvācasuramā, Bhadrā, and Manoharī.
She who dwells upon the peaks of horses, cows, and mountain crags;
whose limbs are adorned with dry kandalī stalks, and who carries dry kandalī stalks.
Daṃṣṭrinī, she known as Vikaṭā, Śivadūtī,
and Dyatastanī; her limbs are adorned with garlands of serpents, and she wears serpent earrings.
The Mistress of the Gaṇas has a garland of freshly severed heads hanging down as far as her feet;
she possesses many faces, many arms, and many feet.
Dwelling in the triangle and the bindu, she resides in the five stages;
established on the gross path, she is subtle, fiercely subtle, and the awakener of the intellect.
Residing in the *mūlādhāra*, having her own support, and making her abode in the fire-pit (*vahnikuṇḍa*),
she is the life-force moving through inhalation and exhalation, the one who causes exhaustion, and she rests upon the fire.
Arising from the threads of the creeper, she is the sixfold one who craves the taste of the six flavors;
she is the destroyer of the delusion of wandering within the rotation of the wheel of time.
Vārtālī and Meghamālinī are the ones who bring about excellent rain and cause it to increase;
she is the form of the letters A, Va, U, and E.
She is the embodiment of the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, clothed in the sky of the syllable *klīṃ*;
she is the color of vermilion-red and is fond of the vermilion tilaka mark.
She is dark-complexioned, possessing the seed-syllable of subjugation, and she manifests the subjugation of the world;
she has the face of an elephant, the face of a serpent, the face of a buffalo, and the face of a parrot.
She who moves among the Vibhākās, the supreme mantra that rends asunder;
she who possesses a thousand mouths, a thousand eyes, and bears a thousand arms.
She who traverses a thousand paths, who awakens the way of the hungry ghosts (pretas),
who possesses ten million faces, ten million feet, and always holds ten million arms.
O Great Plague, sleepless one, destroyer of lethargy and death;
you who resemble a fierce mandala and dwell within a fierce mandala.
Endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, free from desire, able to assume any form at will,
the Goddess is the bestower of the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) and the slayer of wicked *dānavas*.
Beginningless, endless, and inexhaustible, she bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
she resembles the *girikarṇī* plant and has eyes like autumnal white lotuses.
She is the knower of the past, present, and future; she brings about the contemplation of reality;
she is auspicious and of virtuous conduct; and she is the awakener on the path of the departed spirits.
Then there are Kubjikā, Kujā, Kubjā, Sumātā, Mālinī,
Jvālāmukhī, Vegavatī, Umā, and Śuṣkamaheśvarī.
She who desires auspiciousness, whose nature is that of a seer, who resounds with the roar of Rāva,
who stands in the center of the Krama-maṇḍala, the Mistress of Krama, and she who consists of nine aspects.
Brahmāṇī, Raudrī, Grahavatī, Vaiṣṇavī, Ghorarūpiṇī,
Narasiṃhī, Śakravatī, Cāmuṇḍā, Carvaṇā, and Bhayā.
She is auspicious, beautiful, fortunate, and possessed of great fortune and great power;
she is a Yoginī, passionate, delightful, and holds a jeweled water-pot.
Her limbs were covered with an elephant hide, a tiger skin was draped around her waist,
a lion skin was upon her hips, and a black antelope skin served as her upper garment.
She is the Fortune of the Universe, the Mother of the Universe, whose essential nature is the form of light;
she is the Vidyā consisting of all mantras, the supreme one composed of the syllables of all mantras.
Abiding in the midst of the circle of Mothers, she dwells within the circle of Mothers;
she is the pure mother of Kumāra, fair-faced, and the destroyer of sins.
Mānalakṣmī, Subhagā, Śītalā, Śīlasaṃyutā,
Divyastaṃbhā, Dākālī, and Pātālasphoṭakālikā.
She who is the banner of death, the banner of the wind, and the warder-off of the banner of Yama;
she who is unconquered, the unconquerable, the delightful one, and the nose of Rāma.
She whose abode is both dry and moist, the Terrifying One, the Most Terrifying;
the Mother of Rāma, the one worshipped by Rāma, honored by kings and honored by the kingdom.
Śivā, Mahātārīkā, Viśākhā, Bhahariprabhā,
Manonugā, Kaulīnī, Viśveśī, and Pāśatāriṇī.
Raktāraktā, Priyā, Aghorā, Karālā, Kekarā, Ghanā,
Karṇamoṭī, Yogeśī, Vinatsnānā, and Nivāsinī.
She who is garlanded with the moon, the beloved, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, the benefactress of the world;
she who laughs with loud, boisterous laughter, the laughter itself, she who wears a garland of diamond-flowers.
She who crushes with her machine, the mother of mantras, the illuminator of mantras;
she is the goddess Ruru, the lolling-tongued one, the one seized by the flame, the Śavarī, and the cow.
Marīcikā, Kālaghnī, adorned with black skins;
Śmaśānakālikā, Dhūmrakālī, the crusher of the universe!
Saṃgrāmakālikā, Kālavañcanī, Rāvaṇādini,
Jvālānanī, Karālī, Dhūmrakālī, and Raṇapriyā.
Amarāntarakālī is Caṇḍī, the protectress of the world;
Kulikāntarakālī is Māheśī, who is dark-brown.
She who dwells in the netherworld, the remover of sins, the shatterer of Pātāla, the auspicious one;
she who resounds with a roar, the fierce one, and the goddess who paralyzes the womb.
Akṣavaktrā, Caṇḍayogeśvarī, and Pratyaṅgirā are remembered;
as are Mṛḍānī, Svadhā, Svāhā, Dhūmrā, and Gaṅgāmahoddhṛtā.
Ādeśakālikā is at the time of the unshakeable; Melāpakālikā is at the time of the gathering;
Ākarṣakālikā is the attractor; Śāntinī is at the time of the clouds.
The bestower of boons, Mahākālī, Netrakālī, she who is resorted to by the gods;
she who is the object of devotion, she who is served by her devotees, and she who dwells in the abode of the lotus.
The mistress of the five vital breaths, the protector of life, Raktacaṇḍikā,
Śākaṃbharī, Viḍālākṣī, Nandā, Bhadrā, Ajitā, and Anaghā.
Mamommanī, she of the great fangs, who dwells in the *karavīra* tree;
she who resides in the *karavīra* cremation ground, Lakṣmī, who moves within the forest caves.
She is the slayer of the demon Caṇḍāsura and the bearer of the crescent moon;
she is embraced by the skeleton of Brahmā and adorned with the skeleton of Viṣṇu.
Mahāmantrakālikā and Mahābhīṣaṇakālikā;
Śyāmā, who loves the kundapuṣpa flower, and [Kālī], who loves the golaka flower.
Svayaṃbhū, Kusumā, Nandā, Dūtī, Ṣaṭkasamāgraṇī,
Veśyā, Sauṇḍinī, Brāhmī, Kheṭakī, Chippilī, and Kulī.
A washerwoman, a weaver’s wife, a woman of the lowest caste,
a fisherwoman, a Bhaṭṭa woman, a Kaula woman, a woman of the Vāli clan, and a low-born Kṣatriya woman.
The Cakriṇī, the Pauṣkaśī, the Śūdrī, the Dhīvarī, the Carmakāriṇī, the Mātaṅgī, the Narakī, the Veśyā, the Vāyakī, the Sānakī, and the Sarau.
Cāṇḍālī, Dhvajinī, Veśyā, Mahābhyantarajā,
Āśukī, Mahākramaṇā, Kālī, Kālakālī, and Kālīkā.
Mahāgaganakālī, Ekābhāsā, Kālikā,
Mānasikālī, Rūpakālī, Kanakakālī, and Kālikā.
Śabdakālī, Mahākālī, Kalikā, Brahmakālikā,
Svarṇakoṭīśvarī, Kālī, and Rājarājeśvarī are remembered [as her names].
Mahāḍāmarakālī, Bhāsākālī, and Yoginī;
Guhyakālī, Mahākālī, and Mahāśūlāgrakālikā.
The Yoginī is the goddess Kālikā, the ninefold Durgā, and the beloved of the nine;
she is Mātaṅgī, whose mind is intoxicated with wine, and who always delights in human flesh.
Śavarī, Śāvarī, Śīlā, she who is intent on those who have come for refuge; Vatsarā, the goddess Vāruṇī, Maheśī, and she of intoxicated gait.
Ūrdhvakeśī, Vikānāsthā, Cakrakeśī,
Mardinī, Oghakālī, Phetkālī, and Kāliśrīsiṃhakālikā.
Dharmakālī, Jñānakālī, Ravinī, Parā Kālikā,
Līlāvatī Kālikā, and thereafter Hrīṃkārī Kālikā.
Churikākālikā, Prāṇāhuṃkārarāvakālikā,
Mahāpheravakālikā, and Mahākarālakālikā.
Nandinī, Kālikāmodā, Svāninī, Nāmakālikā,
Haṃsinī, Kālikā, Kālī, and Kālibhuvanakālikā.
Kālī is the state at the time of creation, Kalā is she who exists at the time of maintenance,
Haṃsakālī is Yama, and Kālikā is she who devours Time.
Kālī who brings an end to obstacles, Kālikā whose banner is the bull,
Kālī whose banner is the cock, and Kālikā whose banner is the Garuda.
She who rides upon a peacock, Kālī, she who dwells on the swan-bannered one;
she is remembered as Kālarātri, Mahākālī, Caṇḍā, and Caṇḍeśvarī.
Kulālikā, Kuleśī, Mahānandanacāriṇī,
Vindhyavāsinī, Aparṇeśī, and Vīrālī, who is worshipped by all heroes.
Vīreśvarī, Kālikā, Mahākṛtāntakālikā,
Raktarakteśvarī, Kālī, Kālāgnikālikā, and the supreme [Kālikā].
Phetkāriṇī, Kroṣṭukī, Rāmā, the beloved of Īśvara,
Aparṇā, Tripurātārā, Ugratārā, and Kalaṅkinī.
Vārtālikā, Vārāhī, Ghanā with the face of a boar,
Krośinī, Ruṇdhinī, Kālī, Staṃbhinī, Mohinī, and Kalā.
Jaṃbhinī, Jayadā, Jaitrī, she who is worshipped by the world, the progenitor of the universe;
Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Kālī, Lākini, Sākini—the hosts of goddesses.
Kākinī, Hākinī, Śīlā, Yākinī, Dhātvāsinī;
Aṇimā, Laghimā, Prāpti, Mahimā—the beloved of the great ones.
46a) Who is described as Ipsitā in the Kali age? She who eats desires and goes to the essence; she who possesses a skeleton-garland, the Mistress of the Great Forest of the Ancestors.
Dwelling in the cremation ground, she is fierce, possessing a most terrible form;
she is the performer of creation, maintenance, and destruction, and the sustainer of the universe.
Moving through the course of the three paths, she dwells in the *brahmarandhra*;
she pierces the six chakras, remains hidden, and resides in the minds of those whose hearts are devoted to her.
She who gives birth, the mother of the three births, the sovereign of the assembly of victory-mothers;
she who is the knowledge of Brahman, she who is to be known by Brahman, pervading millions of cosmic eggs.
Vāmācārā, Ratavāmā, Nagnā, Dakṣiṇakālikā,
Jhaṃkāriṇī, Rāmavaśī, Ṭaṅkārī, and Vibudheśvarī.
With disheveled hair and distorted eyes, she bestows joy upon the world;
she is Jhaṅkeśvarī, who follows the path of the wheel of resonance.
She is the destroyer of the masses of light from a thousand billion suns,
and the bestower of the hearing of nectar from a thousand billion moons.
The Yoginī known as Guhyā, who bestows both the mortal and the immortal, should always be worshipped;
she stands upon twenty-seven skulls, has three faces, and nine eyes.
Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Sarvamaṅgalā; O Goddess who utters speech, who removes affliction, whose actions are binding, and who deludes with passion.
The mistress of phonemes, composed of phonemes, resplendent with the garland of letters;
the mother and protector of the three worlds, Tārā who moves through the sky.
She is eternally dear to the five elements, worshipped with the five offerings;
she is the embodiment of sound in space, and the form of form within the light.
In waters, you are the form of taste; in the five elements, you are their essential nature;
in flowers, you are the form of fragrance; and in Durgā, you are the form of the five [senses].
Kālī, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman, is the bestower of boons upon Jayadratha;
she is Durvāsas, the giver of perfection, as well as the Rākṣasī who agitates all beings.
Jayā, Vāgīśvarī, Drākṣī, Śrīvidyā, and Tripurāśritā;
Tripurā, Bhairavī, Jñānā, Kālikā, and Ālayabhairavī.
The goddess is of the nature of consciousness, Caṇḍabhairavī, and Siṃhikā;
she is Bhairavī who bestows prosperity, Mārgabhairavī, and Mārgiṇī.
Victory to Jayaśrī, Bhairavī, Kālī, and Mammonmodanabhairavī; to Harasiddhi, who removes the suffering of those who seek refuge, and the destroyer of the Dānavas.
Pūrṇeśvarī, whose mind is full, who is worshipped by the full god,
she who eternally delights in the full vessel, and who conducts herself according to the full conduct.

She who grants all desired objects, the foremost among those whose wishes are fulfilled; Kālikā, the destroyer of the sins of those who perform penance; the mistress of yoga, the greatly fierce, the exceedingly generous, and the great leader.
Emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the inexpressible—these are the states of the Bhāsakālika.
In the Guptakāla, she is Viśvamātā, Nirmāṇeśī, and Pareśvarī.

Thus, O Sovereign of the Universe, O You of Universal Form, having recollected this hymn of a thousand names of the illustrious Supreme Goddess— the assembly of mantras that destroys great sins and the secret essence of the Great Mantra— [one attains liberation].
By that [practice], one will swiftly circumambulate the excellent defilements and virtues, which resemble the circle of Mount Meru, just as fire consumes its fuel.
By bathing at ten million sacred fords, by reciting ten million mantras and the like,
by the gift of ten million cows, and by feeding ten million Brahmins—
Through ten million times ten million fire-oblations and through ascetic penance over ten million births,
he completely conquered the seven continents along with their oceans by means of his buffalo-demon form.
Whatever certain fruit one obtains by giving away all things moving and unmoving,
that same certain fruit one obtains as a portion from the recitation of these hymns.
On the eighth or the ninth lunar day, O best of those who know the Vedas,
it should be recited on a Tuesday, a Saturday, or even on a Sunday.
O Goddess, one should contemplate with one-pointed mind in a place perfumed by incense,
strewn with heaps of flowers, and prepared with the offering of bali.
Having worshipped the Lord with devotion for the sake of the secret mouth of man,
[one destroys] whatever sin has been accumulated through thousands of millions of yantras.
By merely reciting this, one will certainly obtain one's desired object;
one attains long life and health, and shall surely live for a hundred years.
By reciting it three times, one undoubtedly attains one's desired object,
whether during an eclipse of the moon or sun, on the ninth day (navamī), or during the autumnal festival (śāradotsava).
The meritorious soul shall obtain all accomplishments and merit within seven generations;
[he attains this] at the pīṭhas, upapīṭhas, sandohas, tīrthas, kṣetras, and so forth.
All deities without exception, the accomplishments (siddhis), caves, mountains, and forests;
the Tantras, Āgamas, and other scriptures, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the practitioners—[all these abide there].
Everything remains right there where this hymn of praise stands;
one should recite the Thousand Names, which destroy all defects.
47a) Harmful pretas, kuṣmāṇḍas, piśācas, bhūtas,
pūtanas, cruel grahas, śākinīs, and others who are evil-minded;
The ḍākinīs, the terrible rākṣasas, and whatever others are considered afflictions, as well as those who cause harm, will certainly perish; such is the command of Sāṃśākarī.
Those things do not arise there where this [mantra] resides in the home;
in battle it grants immediate victory, and their enemy is destroyed.
Having become long-lived and wealthy,
one is born fortunate and happy if one is submerged in the water of a river on a Saturday when the moon is in the constellation Bhūta.
By reciting it seven times, the Queen of the Gods will certainly be pleased.
Having worshipped a young girl with ritual offerings, one should have her recite it or recite it oneself before her.
That goddess becomes pleased, and one shall obtain all that is auspicious;
her name is a great deliverer from calamity and is formidable in the Kali Yuga.
She, who consists of all the gods, is indeed to be heard and to be saluted;
she alone delivers the universe, and she alone gives birth to the universe.
At the proper time, she herself withdraws that which is difficult to obtain on the surface of the earth—
sovereignty and happiness free from affliction— and one shall certainly attain liberation as a preta.
We bow to Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, who is intent on swallowing time, for whom the entire universe serves as a plaything like a ball.
We bow to that Kālī, the drawer away of Time, who devours the entire universe yet remains unsatiated, and who can assume any form at will.
She whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, who is inseparable from the Ultimate Reality,
who is the eternal Gaṅgā river, we praise her as Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī.
We bow to her whose head is ablaze, who is the manifold Kālī, most brilliantly radiant,
who delights in devouring Time, and who draws forth Time itself.
Licking [the world] excessively, most terrifying, and formidable,
we bow to Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, who is mounted upon the Great Man-Lion.
We praise her who is intent on devouring time, the attractor of time, by whom the universe is made to revolve for the sake of sport like a whirling firebrand.
I bow to that Kālakālī, who is intent upon devouring Time itself, and by whom millions of cosmic eggs are reduced to ashes.
I bow to Kālī, whose form is vast, who devours the conduct of primordial matter (pradhāna),
and who, for the sake of sport, creates the cosmic egg garlanded with clouds.
I bow down to Maṅgalā, who resembles a mountain of collyrium, whose splendor is equal to ten million suns,
and who is devoted to the protection of the three worlds.
Guhyakālī, Maṅgalā, Siddhikālī, Jayeśvarī, Carcikā, Tripureśī, Kālī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
One should worship the supreme ten-faced goddess, the glorious Maṅgalā Mahākālī, who bestows the state of Nirvāṇa, grants sovereignty, and constantly bestows wealth.

Thus ends the chapter on the Thousand Names of the Goddess Śrī Guhyakālī, within the Śiva-Pārvatī Sāmarasya section of the Mahātharvaṇa Saṃhitā, the thirty-six thousand verse collection of the glorious Hāhārāva Mahāmantra.
Now follows the meditation on the Fourth State (turya).
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees!
Out of my desire for the welfare of your devotees, I do not know the fourth state.
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Pārvatī, you are blessed, you have performed meritorious deeds, and you are the fourth among devotees;
O Goddess, having heard this, I shall relate it before you.
The fourteen worlds, including the earth, all that is stationary and moving, and even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna— none of these moving or unmoving beings perform worship unto Him.
Varuṇa [perceived] fire, wind, the moon, the sun, and the consumer of oblations;
the earth, the intermediate space, and the ether that sustains all things at the time of dissolution.
O Great Goddess, you are the form of Tuṃrī; yourself consisting of splendor and light, you are the singular embodiment of the universe, having attained the supreme second state.
Having seen Lomaśa, O Great Goddess, Mārkaṇḍeya then went there;
and Mārkaṇḍeya spoke to Lomaśa.
Salutations to you whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, who take the form of a multitude of beings;
salutations to you who are the Fourth State (Turiya), and salutations to you who are devoid of the individual soul (Puruṣa).
The Supreme Fourth spoke:
Listen to my boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever dwells in your heart;
if you desire the fortune of yoga, I shall grant it to you, of this there is no doubt.
The seer said:
"Salutations to you; I shall describe your great form, please accept it.
Thus spoke Turiya.
O highly fortunate assembly of sages, listen attentively;
I shall describe my own manifestation and the origin of Prakṛti.
From his forehead arose Brahmā; from his ears, the five deities;
from the tip of his nose, water; and from his mouth, fire was born.
From her tongue emerged the goddess Sarasvatī, from her two eyes the immortals,
from her throat the great goddess Nīlā, and from her arm Durgā, the crusher of enemies.
One should meditate on Kandarpa between the breasts, the seven oceans in the belly,
another deity in the center of the hands, and both sin and merit upon the chest.
In the heart is the moon and the gods; at the navel is he whose banner is Garuḍa (Viṣṇu);
on the left side is the Pitṛs, and on the right is Śakra and the host of kings.
One should worship Lord Gaṇapati in the secret place (guhya), Kālamṛtyuka in the thighs (uru),
the deity of the constellations (nakṣatradeva) on the back, and Sadāśiva in the generative organ (liṅga).
Rurumeśa is Manasādevī, and likewise Śirapā is Asthi;
Parvata is Rudhira, and the deity Dharma is the two shanks.
One should worship the Lord of the anus as a single deity, the sages on the two thighs,
and as many deities as there are tongues among Daityas, Rākṣasas, and humans.
Within the body is the god Kubera; O Sage, this is your wealth. Thus, this yoga of manifestation should be guarded with great effort.
The sage Pārvatī said:
Listen, O Lord of the World, Savior from the ocean of saṃsāra;
I shall describe before you where your abode is for them.
The Fourth spoke:
Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess! I am pleased with you, my beloved.
I shall tell you a secret that must be guarded with great effort.
I am the totality of all living beings, the fourth state (turiya), the immobile and the mobile,
the navel, the western path, and the remainder of the netherworlds (pātāla).
O Maheśvarī, from the navel to the throat is the ocean of the mortal world;
from the top of the throat to the head is the world of heaven.
Pārvatī said:
The peak station, the peak wheel, and the range of sound and the point—where is the abode of the Unmanī state? It is not non-objective; where is it all-pervasive?
Where is Brahmā? Where is Viṣṇu? Where is the Lord Sadāśiva? And where, O Śāmbhavī, is the thirteenth lotus and the state of Nirvāṇa?
Nirañjana, Sadāśiva, Mahāviṣṇu, and Maheśvarī;
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā; the six cakras—where do they reside?
Kuṇḍalinī, Haṃsa, Ajapā, and the lotus of the Formless;
thus spoke the Fourth.
Listen, O Goddess, and listen attentively, O Brāhmaṇa; I shall explain:
in the first [mandala] is the wheel of spokes (arucakra), joined with twelve lotuses.
May they remain in the heart of the Praṇava; Śakti remains there eternally. The second is the navel-cakra, which likewise possesses sixteen nirvāṇas.
In the midst of that is the god Viṣṇu, beautifully adorned with the power (śakti) Lakṣmī;
there reside the Kuṇḍalīs, whose bodies are like serpents and who bestow curses.
In the third [wheel] is the heart-cakra, endowed with fifty corners;
situated in its center is Brahmā, adorned by the power (śakti) Sāvitrī.
In the fourth [center], the throat-cakra, adorned by the goddesses and the classes of consonants (varga),
is the god Bhāskara situated within it upon his own lunar mansion.
In the fifth [center] is the tongue-cakra, endowed with a six-petaled lotus;
in its center resides the goddess Śāmbhavī and the stainless Mahāviṣṇu.
Haṃsa, Nirvāṇa, Śiva, and Unmanī-sthāna—
these, together with the six-petalled lotus, are united with Devaśāmbhava.
Above that is the palate-wheel (tālucakra), adorned with eight petals;
[therein reside] earth, water, fire, air, and space itself.
48b) One should not know the object [of meditation] as being in the middle; it is adorned with a golden lotus.
In its center, one should visualize the Goddess, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The exhaustionless "I" of that sound is called *haṃsa*;
in its former part, it is the *haṃsa* moving through three currents, abiding in the seed-syllable *praṇava*.
Iḍā is on the left side, and her form is red;
she is the goddess Iḍā, Gaṅgā, and likewise Yamunā is Piṅgalā.
One should meditate upon Yamunā in the form of Kṛṣṇa, filled with fish and tortoises,
and upon Sarasvatī as Suṣumnā of subtle color.
One should contemplate the bathing with the water of merit by means of the Lord of Eternal Yoga;
in its center is an eight-petaled lotus, and in the middle of that is a six-petaled one, wherein resides the Fourth State (turīyā).
In the center of that, within the lotus-petals, resides the sixfold tradition (ṣaḍāmnāya):
Pūrṇadevī on the eastern petal and Dakṣiṇakālikā on the northern one.
In the west is the goddess Kubjikā, and in the south is Sarasvatī;
Vaḍavādevī is on the path, and Tripurasundarī is above.
One's own vehicle and one's own power are filled by the sixfold tradition (ṣaḍāmnāya);
beyond that, there is a thousand and a most beautiful lotus.
The seed-syllable of the formless [consciousness] is in the aperture of the tenth door;
and there is a thousand-petaled lotus at its tip, encircled by a serpent.
It has eight petals and a thousand eyes, and is served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
in its center is a lotus of light containing a Person the size of a thumb.
In the midst of that, O Goddess, one meditates upon the Yoni, which is devoid of the Linga,
having the form of light, most fierce, and free from the three qualities (guṇas).
This meditation on the fourth Brahman is revealed through gross meditation;
it consists of six petals and the six traditions (āmnāyas), which is the form of that God.
Pārvatī said:
Listen to the great statement of Śiva, which I shall tell you, O God;
describe its characteristics to me, you who bestow grace upon me.
Śiva said:
On a mountain, during an eclipse, in a cave, in a secluded place, or in the presence of a deity—
the practitioner of steady mind makes his dwelling there.
There, being self-controlled and pure, one should worship Bhairava at the three junctions of the day;
O Dear One, with firm intellect and senses conquered, one should perform the fivefold *makāra*.
Eating at a single mealtime, much talkative speech, learning, making a loud noise,
little sleep, and eating during the day.
I shall accomplish the lotus posture and meditate upon the chosen deity;
one should constantly contemplate at the tip of the nose, extending the visualization as far as the crest-lock.
Success arises within six months; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The sage said:
What is the accomplishment, what is the yantra and mantra, and what recitation does he constantly perform?
49a) The fourth spoke:
The mantra of Kumārī has been proclaimed by me, joined with the method of visualization;
I shall now describe the specific characteristics of accomplishment as taught in the Brahmayāmala.
The fourth [state] bestows perfection; through it, the practitioner attains the state of Śiva.
At the end, they go to that which consists of Brahman, and at the end of that, to the deity Viṣṇu.
Having reached the great dissolution, one who practices the meditation on the Fourth State does not behold the door of rebirth merely by hearing the mantra.
Through the merit of the pilgrimage sacrifice and the vow, and by the mere sight of the practitioner,
the inner meditation and the fourth state lead the Brahmin to his own abode.
Thus, O Goddess, this secret, the most excellent essence, has been told to you;
it is more secret than the secret, O Goddess, and has been proclaimed out of affection for you.
It must be concealed, concealed, concealed with great effort;
one should reveal it only to a disciple or a practitioner endowed with devotion.
If one should give a book to a wicked person, to a fallen disciple, or to one who is averse to the state of the Goddess, death alone shall follow; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the eighth section of the Guhyakālī-prastāra within the Atharvaṇa-saṃhitā of the Śrī Hāhārāva-tantra.
49b) Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the well-honored worship of Kālikā;
I shall describe the Great Rite (mahākarma) of adoration, which is difficult to obtain within the three worlds.
Kālī, Dakṣiṇā, and Guhyakālī Pārvatī—
these three goddesses are remembered from this very day by their names.
O Dear One, one should worship Kulabhairavī as inseparable from Kālī, Kubjā, Siddhilakṣmī,
and Pratyaṅgirā.
He who worships without making distinctions [attains] that which destroys great sins,
even more than by the gift of ten million gold pieces or hundreds of millions of cows.
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, there are gifts of land up to the limit of the earth;
the worship of Mahākarma is performed upon a square,
yellow mandala, where the thread is drawn in sections with excellent water, having the form of the splendor of the wheel.
The red quality and so forth are divine.

In the mouth of Vāta is the six-cornered *ka* wheel, smoke-colored and equal to the clear [ether]; it is the presiding deity of space (*viyat*), the universe, and the five unmanifested elements, according to the scripture.
Thus one should meditate upon Maheśa, whose form is white and peaceful, four-armed, holding a white lotus, and seated;
in his right hands he holds a trident and a gift, respectively, and likewise in the others.
One should place the letter *kār* in the heart and the syllable *bhayaṃ* in the left hand; the body and faces consist of the fivefold mantra.
One should assign the eyes as zero (*śūnya*), the golden face, and the matted locks (*jaṭā*) in sequence by means of the mantras beginning with *dharā*.
When the *lakṣas* have increased by one hundred and three lakṣas, the wise one performs the oblation of one-tenth;
this Śrī-Pranaveśvara is the bestower of grace, the remover of the suffering of his devotees, and the giver of the qualities of the world.

O Sage, listen as I relate that which was heard long ago by the Daityas and Siddhas who had attained their station at the end of a purifying sacrifice, concerning the Goddess who is to be kept secret.
When the auspicious ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and asuras,
the goddess Mṛtā, a divine maiden of enchanting beauty, was born there.
Possessing great splendor and capable of assuming any form at will, she was like the sun at the end of an eon in her brilliance;
she was divine, resembling lac-dye in color and possessing a radiance equal to that of a ruby.
Her limbs were variegated with all kinds of jewels; she was Ambikā, whose form was composed of elemental spirits, possessing eighteen divine arms, and was intent upon various weapons.
The Goddess, who possesses various flavors, has no equal in the three worlds;
she holds a sword, a noose, and a goad in her right hands, and a skull-cup, a thunderbolt, and a banner.
Likewise, the chariot, the bell as the ninth, the bestower of boons;
in the *pheṭaka* [position], the bow, the noose, the *khaṭvāṅga*, the conch, and the water-pot.
The trident, the mallet, and the *vaitā* they hold in their upper hands;
having encircled the mandala, the river has been caused to flow forth by the Bhūtas.
They sprinkle all the fallen with the nectar-born Amṛtā, which removes all impurity.
Thus is the meditation on the goddess Amṛtā.
The goddess Mahāstrāghorasandevī is the celestial drum (dundubhi) composed of the three elements;
she is the goddess who rains down the nectar of accomplishment, [appearing] from the sky with her pair of eyebrows arched like a furrow.
Pages 48 and 49 are repeated, but the content does not correspond to the previous pages 48 and 49.
48a) One should meditate on the limbs as before, and upon the supreme among the supreme within the womb (yoni), which is red in color.
Listen to this true nature of existence and form, which bestows a multitude of virtues.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, endowed with fourteen arms,
with a mass of tawny matted hair standing erect, and adorned with a severed head, the moon, and serpents.
The god is joined with serpents, bones, and jewels; he has twenty-four eyes and is terrifying;
he is covered by an elephant hide and further enveloped by a tiger skin.
In the Dharāvitaraṇa rite, he is established as having a distorted face, seated upon a lotus made of a preta,
and dancing in the Vaiśākha posture.
One should meditate upon the Lord who dwells in the midst of the terrifying cremation ground, the crusher of all asuras,
the long-bellied Guru, until everything [is realized].
A trident, a spear, a discus, a noose, a skull-cup, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
a severed head, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a thunderbolt, a bell, a vessel, and the [mudrās] beginning with fear.
Thus ends the meditation for the placement (nyāsa) of the Aghora-weapon mantra:
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Huṃ Hraiḥ Prasphura etc.
[I meditate upon her] who has five faces, who is exceedingly fierce, and who is radiant with terrifying fangs.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of skulls,
in some places joined with red garments, it was terrifying, being haunted by hungry ghosts (preta).

She is seated upon a lotus marked by fire, possesses a variegated complexion, and has an upward-turned smile; her entire body is adorned with various ornaments, and she dwells in the midst of a great cremation ground.
[One should meditate on] Sitā, who is gentle and bestows boons, situated in the place of Mātṛkrīḍāvinoda;
likewise, [one should worship] the leaders of the Navātmanas during the recitation of the mantra.

That Dharma-dhātu, seated upon a lotus, the Lord of the battle against the enemy of Māra, is thus like the fire of universal destruction (saṃvarta) and likewise [like] Īśāna in the intermediate direction.
And likewise, he holds in his right arms a trident, a ḍiṇḍima drum, a mace, a spear, and a sword, as well as the moon, the sun, a shield, and a chisel.
He likewise holds a mallet, a serpent-noose, a bow, and a spear;
while in his left hands he holds a threatening gesture, a fruit, a jewel, a flute, and a shield.
The Veda is for the purpose of cosmic dissolution, and Kubjikā is indeed that Sovereign Goddess;
she is the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, and the granter of the fulfillment of all desires and aims.
Thus is the Saṃvarta meditation.
The great island Puṣkara is there; the god Mṛtodbhava resides there.
It is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, surrounded by a hundred thousand [yojanas], and ten thousand [yojanas] thick.
[He saw] Śrutidhara, the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), surrounded by a hundred yoginīs,
for the sake of slaying Vasantatvāka, until the teaching of Bhairava [was fulfilled].

O Dear One, Kālikā has protruding fangs, speaks with a terrifying voice, her lips are agitated by the portions of the sacrifice, her tongue-tip is marked with the letter *ra*, and she has four limbs and four eyes.
Khādakī, Rūpanāśā, Saṃhārī, Rakṣayantikā, Kṛṣṇā, Khaṭvāṅgadhāriṇī, Ataryonyaladharā, and Śubhā.
Thus ends the meditation on Śrutidhara Kṣetrapāla.
48b) Possessing the splendor of a blazing fire, mounted upon a cloud-sound Garuda,
with matted hair and hair reaching his cheeks, he holds a staff and wears tattered garments.
May Vaṭukanātha, who brings an end to the one who seizes the sons of Acaladuhitṛ,
be the bestower of accomplishments upon practitioners.
In the right hand. Thus is the meditation on Vaṭuka.
To the Great-Souled One with the face of an elephant, who has a serpent as his sacred thread, and who,
with a very loud elephantine roar, repeatedly tosses up his own form.
O Lord Gaṇeśa, who holds a rosary in your hand and whose vehicle is the mouse, may you destroy the multitude of my sins.
The Elephant Seal (gajamudrā). Thus is the meditation on Gaṇapati:
Seated upon a red lotus throne, red in color, possessing great splendor, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, of gentle form and great majesty.
"I bow down to my own Guru, adorned with all ornaments"—
thus is the meditation on one's own Guru, the venerable Tūṣṇīsānanda.
[He is] seated upon a white lotus throne, white in color, and of great splendor.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, he possessed a gentle form and great majesty.
I bow to the supreme guru, the illustrious Caryānanda, adorned with all ornaments.
Thus ends the meditation on the supreme guru, the venerable Caryānanda.
Seated upon a black lotus throne, sky-colored, possessed of great splendor,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and of gentle form and mighty power.
I pay homage to the most glorious Guru, adorned with every ornament and filled with the bliss of Maitrī.
Thus ends the meditation on the joy of Maitrī.
Seated in the lotus posture, established in his own state, ten-faced and three-eyed,
seven-colored and of great brilliance, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
The eastern face has six colors; the southern is adorned with black;
the northern should be black in color; and the one above that is dyed red.
The southern [face] is red, the northern is smoky-grey and white;
above that is yellow-colored, and the southern [face] should be yellow and black.
They say that red is superior, but white above that is most excellent;
it is endowed with eighteen arms and adorned with a severed head as an ornament.
The god holds a sword and a shield, as well as a trident and a goad;
he also holds an excellent spear, a water-pot, a hand-drum, and a skull-topped staff.
Holding an arrow and a well-joined bow, beautifully adorned with a hand-drum and a bell,
and likewise holding a discus and a mace in his hands, with his hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The vessel for the *bindu*, as well as its ornamentation, should be adorned with various decorations;
all should be yellow in color, established for the sake of happiness within the Teaching.
The person who, with a disciplined mind, meditates upon this ninefold mandala of form— the mandala of the Guru— attains accomplishment swiftly.
Her face is terrifying with fangs, she is adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she wears a tiger skin as a garment, and she is decorated with every kind of ornament.
Thus ends the meditation on the ninefold self.
Dark-complexioned, possessing great splendor, adorned with all ornaments,
with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, gentle in form and most beautiful.
Yellow in color, possessed of great majesty, adorned with all ornaments,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, she is perfectly formed and most beautiful.
I bow to the goddess Śrīśaktikā, who dwells in the realm of mortals;
she is smoke-colored, possesses great splendor, and is adorned with all ornaments.

With hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, possessing a gentle form and being most beautiful, she is joined with the fierce rays [of the sun] and stands to the south of the Guru-maṇḍala.
I bow to the Supreme Goddess of Speech, the Parameṣṭhin and others—
she who is red in color, possessed of great splendor, and adorned with every ornament.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, she is of gentle form and most beautiful;
joined with the syllable *mlūṃ*, she dwells peacefully within the circle of gurus.
I bow to the illustrious Goddess Jñānadevī, who is endowed with heavenly bliss,
white in color, possessed of great splendor, and adorned with all ornaments.
Her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she is of gentle form and most beautiful.
This is the meditation on the five jewels.
She is conjoined with the syllable *A*, at the western side of the Guru-maṇḍala.
I bow to the illustrious Ājñādevī, who dwells in the realm of the sky.
Thus concludes the meditation on Khasarpaṇa.
The goddess Aparā of the Śiva-tattva is white in color and has four arms;
she holds a trident and a skull-cup in her hands, while her other two hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The Śiva-tattva. The goddess Parā of the Vidyā-tattva is dark-complexioned, four-armed,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace, and is adorned with yellow garments.
The principle of knowledge (vidyātattva):
the supreme goddess Ātmatattvā is red in color, four-armed, and possesses a water-pot, a staff, a rosary, and a lotus in her hands; she is embodied in form.
The reality of the self:
the goddess Ājñāśrīkusumā is blue in color, four-armed,
with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and she is seated upon a blue lotus and a kuśa-grass mat.
Ājñākusumā; Pretāsanī is red in color, holding a sword and a shield,
as well as a rosary, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a *nāgapuṣpa* flower with its stalk.
I bow to the goddess Jayā, who stands in the prime of youth, possesses three eyes, is adorned with every ornament, and bestows the accomplishment of all desires and goals.
Jayā has the luster of the saffron-red color, possesses three eyes, and has a beautiful smile.
Her limbs are adorned with all ornaments; she dwells among the spirits and is both victorious and auspicious.
O auspicious Maheśvarī, who holds a sword, a shield, a skull-bowl, a staff, a severed head, and a discus, come here for the destruction of my enemies!
Vijayā:
The goddess resembles snow and jasmine, holding a sword and a shield,
as well as a garland, a khaṭvāṅga, nāgapuṣpa flowers, and a vessel.
One should meditate upon her standing upon a corpse, youthful, and three-eyed;
O Ajitādevī, O Durgādevī of the great tradition, salutations to you!
Resembling an Atasī flower, she holds a sword and a phetkāra-staff.
Ajitā [is adorned with] a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a shaven trident, and a beautifully decorated mendicant’s bowl;
she stands in the prime of youth, possesses three eyes, and is embellished with all ornaments.
I bow to the goddess Aparājitā, who dwells among the pretas; I worship her, the unconquered one,
who has transcended all suffering and resembles the flower of the pomegranate tree.

The goddess Śāntī is white in color, with her hair adorned by a crescent moon; she holds a jewel, a lotus, a bell, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and she is situated above the stage of "Beyond Peace" (śāntyatīta).
