I bow to the four-armed, large-eyed one who brings about auspiciousness; may there be peace. [I bow to] the great goddess of smoky hue, who holds a noose and a goad, and is composed.
And I bow to the Goddess who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is Vidyā, yellow in color, four-armed, and bearing a banner, a goad, and a bow.
I bow to Varadā and Pratiṣṭhā, the performers of auspiciousness; I bow to the goddess Nirvṛtti, who is dark-complexioned and beautiful in form. Pratiṣṭhā.
I bow to the goddess Nirvṛtti, who is dark-complexioned and beautiful in form.

Nirvṛti has four arms, holding a trident, a bell, a skull-cup, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. [The other deity] holds a sword, a *pheṭa*-staff, a trident, and a goad, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The Mistress of the Kula (Kuleśvarī) is white in color, large-eyed, and holds a vessel marked with a drop; she is Kulabhairavī.
The Great Hero (Mahāvīra) is black in color, holding a trident and a water-pot in his hands.
I bow to Kulanātha, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness;
O Kulanātha, you who are yellow in color, possessed of great splendor, and bearing the hand-drum (ḍamaru) and the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
I salute the illustrious Kulatuṃvuru, who has hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; I salute Kulatuṃvuru,
the dark-complexioned great hero, marked with the bow and arrow.
I bow to Kulakapāṭa, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness;
Kulakapāṭa, who resembles the moon, the sun, and fire, and who holds a bell, a jewel, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I salute the auspicious Bhairava, the knower of the Kula, who bears the *pātrabindu*.
He is the knower of the Kula.
[I salute] the Goddess, who resembles the fire of cosmic destruction and who wields a sword and a *pheṭaka* (shield).

The Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, who holds a discus in her hand, a mace in her hand, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she who bears the vessel of the *bindu* and is the Command of the Kula.
The Command of the Kula:
[She who is] holding a sword and a flaying-knife in her hands, and granting the boon and fearlessness with a vessel of nectar;
the primordial Kulabhairavī, lion-faced and possessing eight arms.
Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
her face terrifying with protruding fangs, and her hair matted and standing upright.
The Command Goddess of the Kula;
the Goddess wearing a garland of severed heads, holding a sword and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
adorned with a bell, possessing a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
I shall describe Kṣetrapāla, who has three eyes, a fierce form, who is the seed of all mantras, and who dwells in all places.
O Guardian of the Field!
With a protruding belly, a massive body, and a pot-bellied, short form;
marked with a rosary and an axe, and holding a root and a sweetmeat.
I bow to Gaṇeśa, the Supreme, who resembles a dark blue cloud; O Lord of Gaṇas,
I ever salute you who are seated upon a peacock and possess the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning.
I bow to the one clad in red garments, the bearer of the staff and the trident;
I bow to Vaṭukanātha, the youth who is the embodiment of auspicious prosperity.
O Vaṭuka!
[I salute] the goddess Kaumārī, the bestower of boons, who rides upon a peacock chariot;
she is the goddess clad in red garments, eternally manifest in a secret form.
Kaumārī:
I pay homage to the Guru-maṇḍala, to Bhairava, the glorious Navātman,
the god who removes all sins and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Whoever reads or even hears this meritorious hymn to the maṇḍala of the gurus will always be a recipient of excellent accomplishments and be highly honored by all the world.
Thus ends the hymn to the mandala of the gurus.

Salutations to the Mistress of the Application of Knots (Granthinyāseśvarī), who resembles a bandhūka flower, who is seated upon the back of a lizard, and whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The meditation for the placement of the knots (granthinyāsa):
Beyond this is the twelve-limbed [meditation] which removes the impurities of the elements and time;
salutations to Granthinyāseśvarī, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness.
The visualization for the placement of the knots:
KṢAIṂ ŚRĪṂ. Śambhu has declared this divine [mantra] as the girdle of manly power.
One should worship the four lords: Kūrma, Pūtanā, Kālī, and Ambikā.
The Indugam deity is situated at the zenith of the sky; she is dark-complexioned, imperishable, and born from him.
She has the form of a black elephant-faced one, and holds a sword, a book, and a bow in her hands.
Wearing a garland of skulls, of terrible form, and the fulfiller of all desires—
having first performed that very limb [of the body], one should then perform the divine placement (nyāsa).
Thus ends the twelve-limbed nyāsa.
Now the six-limbed nyāsa is described: [one should worship] the supreme four-faced Paraśambhu, who arises from the laughter of the Dhanaraudra mantra, and the supreme four-faced one.
Having first fashioned the peak-limb from black *meru* and white *udbhava*,
one should place the supreme deity upon a corpse, wearing a garland of severed heads.
Extremely fierce and most terrifying, it is endowed with wrathful substances;
it is black in color, possessed of great splendor, and filled with garlands of flames.
50b) Having first assumed such a form— with a skull in his right hand and a trident in his left hand— one should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Thus ends the meditation on the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Then follows the *Mālinī*:
"The dark [form] is in the left limb of the Goddess, and the red-colored [form] is in her right limb."
One should know that in the center is the white [syllable]; she has a charming form of three colors, six faces, and is the goddess Mālinī, beautiful and in the full bloom of youth.
Adorned with a garland of jewels shaped like suns and beautified by various forms,
she stands upon the threads of fire, setting in motion blazing rays of light.
The very gentle goddess laughs, adorned with eighteen eyes,
and holds in her right hands a trident, a rosary, arrows, incense, a goad, and a noose.
The form [of the deity] consists of a lotus, a serpent, a bow, a bell, a chowrie, and a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in the remaining [hands].
Then, one should contemplate the stream of verses and place the three syllables there.
Abiding in fear, the destroyer, and Mālinī—these are considered the threefold [nature].
Mālinī is meditation; she is the mass of sounds.
Perform the four-armed transition, as well as the fire-oblation of the vital breath;
pierce my Sāvitrī, which is difficult to overcome and filled with the jar of destruction.
One should meditate on the form arising from that, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, which has extracted the sound "kūṭa-pū" and is situated within the aperture of the head.
She is beyond peace (Śāntyatītā), three-eyed, wearing matted locks,
her body adorned with a forest garland, and seated upon a bull and a lotus.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, a hand-drum, a banner, a water-pot, a staff, a dwarf, five skulls, and the gesture of fearlessness.
In her left hands, she holds a blue lotus, a jewel, a book, and an axe,
as well as a conch, a discus, and a mace, and displays the gesture of granting boons.
Having meditated thus upon one’s own body, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed:
first performing that which ends with the *kūṭa*, and afterwards the primary and secondary divisions.
The aggregate of sounds, abiding in existence, consists of three abodes according to Sāṃkṛti;
it constitutes the vocative case and the dative case, and that is the sequence of the visarga.
At the beginning, there should be the Nyāsa upon that which is protected and freed from its banner;
one should meditate on the Goddess Śabdarāśi.
One should understand the two [mantras], such as Mālinī and the rest, according to the sequence of Śabdarāśi.
The meditation on the six messengers: Aiṃ 5. She is blue in color, extremely fierce, and renowned for her posture with legs drawn up (andha-paryaṅka).
Her hair is matted and stands upright as armor; she has three eyes, a crescent moon, and the fire.
In her left hands she holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a human head;
in her right hands she holds a tail; two-armed, she is the destroyer of tigers.
The Heart Messenger (Hṛdayadūtī):
51a) When the sun has risen, she is Trivaktrikā, whose belly is like that of Lambodara and who resembles the sun.
Her body was composed of jewels, snakes, and bones, and she was radiant with terrifying fangs.
She wears a garland of six-faced severed heads and is clothed in a tiger-skin garment;
her faces are black and white, and she has two breasts, one of which is deficient in the middle.
In her left hands she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga; with two [other] hands she displays the mudrā born of yoga.
Śivadūtī is dark-complexioned, possesses three eyes, and holds a sword and the tarjanī gesture upon a lotus.
In her left [hands] she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga, and with two [others] she displays the mudrā born of yoga. ||3||
She is yellow in color, five-faced, fierce, dwarfish, and with a protruding belly;
she holds a sword, an arrow, a goad, a knife, and a shield in her hands.
With her left hands, she holds a flower, a bow, a noose, and displays the gesture of fearlessness; she is Kavaca-dūtī. 4.
Now I shall describe Netradūtī, who is red in color and possesses a graceful form;
she holds a bow, an arrow, a trident, and a bell in her left and right hands respectively.
The messenger of the eyes. ||5||
In her left hand, she holds a blood-red vajra-khaṭvāṅga.
Brandishing a vajra in her right hand, Mūrtikeśinī has her garments worn away,
stands upon the fire at her feet, and is completely enveloped by the supreme light.
Her limbs are adorned with weapons and ornaments, she is radiant with formidable fangs, and she possesses three eyes; O Guhya, she is always known as Pratyangirā.
The messenger of the weapon. ||6||

The visualization of the six messenger-deities (dūtī) is as follows: the wandering [of consciousness] upon the head fixed on the devourer (khādaka). This is the placement (nyāsa) and meditation. The five jewels.
Gaganānandanātha is white in color, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Śakti is the beautiful young tree, and Vāgīśvarī is its form as the tender sprout. || 1 ||

Svargānandanātha is red in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he is embodied as Śakti, possessing the beauty of perfect youth, and his form is the embodiment of the vow of Sālankāyana. Indeed. 2.
Pavanānandanātha is smoke-colored, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
he possesses the form of Śakti, is in the prime of youth, and is adorned with a *sāla* flower. Mohinī has a form like that of a *sāla* tree. 3.
Martyānandanātha is yellow in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he is youthful, possesses ornaments, and is of the nature of Śakti. Jñānādevī is of that same form.
Gāyatrī, whose form is Śakti, possesses the nature of Sārakālāvrata; she is in the full bloom of youth, her hands bestowing boons and fearlessness, and she is Vāgānandanātha. 4.
The white-colored one is the Lord Ananta, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; the dark-colored one...
She is the embodiment of power, possessing that same form, adorned with ornaments, and in the full bloom of youth; she is like a sapphire. 5.
51b) On the crown of the head.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed at the center of the eyebrows, the mouth, the heart, the navel, and the secret place.
One should [visualize] the Lord, who is like a dark blue cloud, with matted hair standing upright on his head.
With a face made terrible by fangs, endowed with twenty-four arms,
eight faces, graceful limbs, and twenty-four eyes.
Bhairaveśvara, who laughs while being overcome by birth, death, and old age,
and who bears a banner with a trident, sword, mace, spear, and dagger;
She who produces the fruits of the moon and sun, flowing with the nectar of the Krama,
then holds a khaṭvāṅga, a mallet, a lotus, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated upon Mukharaka and the others, who possess bows, spears, and threatening gestures, one performs the ninefold self-meditation:
[the deity] with four faces and four arms, resembling black collyrium.
Resembling ten million suns, terrifying with twelve eyes,
the God who bestows the four aims of life and utterly destroys great death.
Holding a sword, a spear, a trident, and a mallet in his hand,
he possesses the brilliance of a thousand flashing lightning bolts and a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun.
The god who adorns his head with a skull, who fills the celestial vault with divine splendor,
whose limbs are decorated with serpent-earrings, and who is adorned with every ornament.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with a crown of matted locks,
he holds a *paṭṭiśa* spear in his right hand and an excellent sword.
In his left hand he holds a human skull and in his right hand a trident;
he is the constant crusher of enemy armies and the protector of his own side.
He is the refuge of all who are gentle, possessing a luster like crushed collyrium;
he is the cause of Brahmā and the others, and by renouncing him, one is eternally freed from the calamities of mantras.
Having dissolved the image into the *kusumāñjali*, one should place that [image] within this [receptacle];
having worshipped the image with the root mantra and by displaying the ritual gestures (*mudrā*).
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus, complete with filaments and a pericarp;
outside of that, a sixteen-spoked [wheel], and twice that size again on the exterior.
Having thus prepared the mandala, one should perform the most excellent worship;
then, having performed the rite for Vaināyaka, one should perform the six-limbed ritual at the end of the root mantra.

Having worshipped the Guru and Gaṇeśa, one should worship the object within the Ādhāra; then, having provided a seat for the deceased (pretāsana), the wise practitioner should invoke the deity's form.
Namely: *aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hraḥ prasphura*, and so forth.
This is the meditation on the Aghora-weapon (*aghorāstra*).
The meditation on the single syllable.
Having extracted [the syllable] ending with the seat (āsana), together with the Brahmin (v) and joined with the vital point (m),
one should meditate upon that which arises from it, yellow in color and situated in the center of the womb (yoni).
The goddess, whose form abides within the Śuklā river, holds a serpent, a trident, and an eye;
she consists of the three principles (tattvas) and is crowned with matted locks and a crescent moon.
One should place the cock-faced [deity] who utters a long *khaḍ-kara* sound;
she possesses the three knowledges (*trividyā*), consists of fifty syllables, is reversed, and is uttered twice upon the body.
The renunciation [of the self] arises from Brahma’s compassion.
This Māleya consists of the mass of sounds, the threefold knowledge, the ritual placement (nyāsa), and meditation;
it is the radiance of Śiva’s splendor, sounding with the syllable *raphet*, possessing a gentle luster like the brilliance of the sun.
One sees the center of the heart as red in color and brilliantly blazing;
having first performed this visualization of the limb, one should meditate upon the form arising therefrom.
The triple goddess, seated upon a white lotus atop a lion, is honored by the Bharanas;
she is red in color, exceedingly gentle, with one face and eight arms.
He holds the Veda, the staff, the rosary, and the water-pot in his right hands,
and he bears the mace, the discus, the conch, and the jewel in his left hands.
Thus, having meditated upon the form as the state of Śiva, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
This concludes the meditation on the Ghorikāṣṭaka-nyāsa and the meditation on Mahākāla.
Seated upon a great corpse-throne, dark in color and of great splendor,
with one face and three eyes, he is terrifying, with hair that is thick and stands erect.
With tawny eyes and tawny hair, possessing a massive body and a large belly,
he was clothed in a tiger skin with a lion skin as an upper garment.
Adorned with a red snake, bones, a skeleton, anklets, and other ornaments,
holding a sword and a *pheṭaka* in his hands, and carrying a skull-bowl, a drop, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.
Having thus meditated upon Mahākāla Bhairava, the Lord of the World, who possesses the great splendor of ten million lightning flashes and is adorned with a necklace of headless trunks;
Thus ends the meditation on Mahākāla.
The god who wears a garland of severed heads, who holds a sword and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
who is graced by the sound of the *pheṭkāra* roar,
whose brilliance is equal to ten million flashes of lightning, who has three eyes, and who possesses a fierce form.
I bow to Kṣetrapāla, who dwells in all places. [Kṣetrapāla]. Meditation on Gaṇeśa:
White in color, with two arms, and holding a rosary in the right hand.
In her left hand she holds an alms-bowl, and her lower garment is made of ketaki leaves.
Wearing a turban and a black antelope skin,
seated in the lotus posture, with armpits visible, and likewise holding a staff— the Lord.
One should worship everywhere that Lord Gaṇeśvara, who is white in color and possesses the same form as before. 2.
Red in color, adorned as before. 3.
White in color, with ornaments as before. 4.
His white-colored primary arms are adorned with ornaments. 5.
Black in color, with ornaments as before. 6.
Yellow in color, with ornaments as before. 7.
Black in color, with ornaments as before. 8.
52b) Black in color, with ornaments as before, 9.
White in color, with ornaments as before. 10.
White in color, with ornaments as before. 11.
The meditation on the lineage of twelve forms of the Guru, beginning with Bhujavastra (who is black in color), Ausana, Gaganānanda, Deva, and so forth. 12.
Thus ends the lineage of gurus.
Seated comfortably in the lotus posture (padmāsana), white in color, with three eyes and three faces—
the [central] face red, the [right] face white, and the [left] face yellow, adorned in the north.
The great hero has eight arms, holding a snake, a sword, a threatening gesture, a hand-drum,
a trident with its cord, and a blue lotus with its stalk.
One who causes drops to fall from the vessel is excellent; she with full and elevated breasts should be meditated upon as the Herb (Oṣadhī) for the sake of one who lives by deceitful means.
The meditation on the medicinal herbs.
Seated upon a corpse, red in color, holding a noose and a goad,
bearing a vessel of nectar in her hand, most excellent, three-eyed, and full of youthful vigor.
The agitator.
The goddess, resembling black collyrium, holds a sword and a shield;
she holds a rosary for recitation, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), various flowers, and a skull-cup (kādyaka).
Homage to you, Mohanī, who has three eyes and is mounted upon a corpse!
O Goddess Mohinī, who resembles the full moon and bears a sword and a shield!
I always bow to him who holds a rosary for recitation, a khaṭvāṅga staff, nāgapuṣpa flowers, and a skull-bowl; I pay homage again and again to the one whose abode is the cremation ground.
The Attractress.
The goddess resembles a blue lotus; she is the vanquisher who brings about auspiciousness, and likewise holds a sword, a shield, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a mace.
I bow to the Goddess who bestows boons and fearlessness, who destroys her own [enemies], who grants the boon of all desires, and who is the slayer of the Daityas.
Jambhanī,
possessing the luster of molten gold, holding a sword and a shield,
with a khaṭvāṅga and a severed head in her hands, bestowing boons and holding an alms-bowl.
I bow to Staṃbhinī, whose limbs are adorned with every ornament;
[I bow to] Staṃbhanī.
Seated upon a corpse-throne, she possesses a luster like that of blue collyrium.
The goddess holds a noose and a goad, carries a vessel of nectar in her hand, and is auspicious;
she is endowed with all ornaments and destroys darkness and the base.
The *kṣudrā* is the *chādinī*. Thus ends the procedure for medicinal herbs (*auṣadhividhi*). Śrīkaṇṭhanātha.
The god seated upon a bull-throne, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon;
he has one face and three eyes, possesses a divine form, and is most brilliantly radiant.
The great lord has four arms; he holds a trident and a rosary, and with one arm embracing the neck of the goddess, he holds a vessel full of nectar.
Having meditated on the chin of the Goddess, one should hold the sound within the hands;
the Goddess, dark-limbed and in the bloom of youth, has gone to stand upon the left thigh.
The goddess has hands granting boons and fearlessness, possesses three eyes, and has a divine form;
her body is adorned with divine red ornaments and she is beautified by divine garments.
Having thus meditated upon Mahādeva, Śrīkaṇṭha,
the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
"Brahmāṇī and the others are situated on the swan, the seat, and the water-pot," and so forth.
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady, the fierce and wrathful Great Goddess, the auspicious Bhagavatī,
who has the luster of molten gold and a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
She who possesses the splendor of a golden chest, has three eyes, and smiles beautifully;
she wears a crown and earrings, and is adorned with armlets, jeweled bracelets, and anklets.
Adorned with a variegated garland of jewels and draped with strings of necklaces,
she is endowed with eighteen arms and her limbs are decorated with divine garments.
She is resplendent, holding in her right hands a sword, an arrow, a discus, a goad, and a boon-granting gesture, as well as a hand-drum, a trident, and a vessel.
She holds a *pheṭaka* bow in her hand, beautifully adorned with a mace and a bell;
she carries a noose, a raised index finger, and a *khaṭvāṅga*.
In her left [hands], she holds the mass of hair of the Daitya and a hand marked with a dot (*bindu*).
Seated upon a lion-throne, with her foot placed upon the body of Mahiṣa.
She is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura and the destroyer of all the Daityas;
she is the Goddess who, with her entire being, bestows everything and grants the fruits of all desires.
Salutations to you, O glorious Ugracaṇḍī, who bestows the desired fruit!
O Ugracaṇḍī, [you who hold] the sword, the thunderbolt, the arrow, the discus, and likewise the goad.
He is resplendent with the boon-granting gesture, a trident, and a bowl in his right hands,
as well as a *pheṭaka*, a bell, a bow, a mace, and a noose.
On her left side, she displays the tarjanī, the hair of a demon, a bindu, and a mudrā;
she is resplendent with the form of a young woman mounted upon a lion and a buffalo.
And the Great Goddess meditates [upon her]; O Rudracaṇḍī, salutations to you!
[She holds] a sword, a spear, an arrow, a discus, a thunderbolt, and likewise the boon-granting [mudrā].
They likewise hold a trident and a bowl in their right hands;
furthermore, they carry a *pheṭaka* in the right, as well as a bow, a mace, and a bell.
She displays the tarjanī, the hair of a demon, and the bindu mudrā in her left hand;
she is mounted upon a lion and a buffalo, and her form resembles the color of the dawn.
To you, the Great Goddess of such a form, and to Pracaṇḍī, homage be paid! ||2||
A sword, a staff, an arrow, a discus, a vajra, and a trident granting boons.
And meditating on a vessel in [their] hand, they hold it in their right hands;
[they also hold] a *pheṭaka*, a bow, a noose, a mace, a bell, and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
She holds the head of a Daitya and the bindu-mudrā in her left hand.
Mounted upon a lion and a buffalo, with dark-hued limbs and ornaments, such is the form of the Great Goddess; O Candrogrā, salutations to you!
They hold in their right hands a sword, a jewel, a flame, an arrow, a discus, a thunderbolt, a goad, a trident, and an alms-bowl.
In their left hands, they hold a phetaka, a tarjanī, a bow, a mace, a bell, a noose, and the mudrā of the hair-tuft of the Daitya.
The Goddess seated upon a lion-throne, while Mahiṣa proceeds as her mount;
O Great Goddess of smoky hue, salutations to you, O Caṇḍanāyikā! || 4 ||
White in complexion, three-eyed, youthful, and beautiful in form, she holds a sword,
a noose, an arrow, a discus, an excellent thunderbolt, and a trident.
In her right hands, she holds a bowl, a jewel-adorned ornament,
a pheṭaka, a kusha-grass bow, a mace, a bell, and a threatening gesture (tarjanī).
She bears the head of a Daitya and the Bindu-mudrā in her left hands;
to that Goddess who is of such a form, obeisance be to you! (5)
O Great Goddess of dark complexion, you who move with the gait of a lion or a buffalo,
holding a sword, a banner, an arrow, a discus, a thunderbolt, and likewise the boon-granting gesture.
In her right hands, she holds a trident, a vessel,
a *pheṭaka*, a noose, a bow, a mace, a bell, and a raised index finger (*tarjanī*).
O Caṇḍavatī, salutations to you, who holds the head of a Daitya and the Bindu-mudrā in your left hands, and whose limbs are adorned with every kind of jewel.
Seated upon a buffalo throne, she possesses a complexion of yellowish-red radiance;
she holds a sword, a mace, an arrow, a thunderbolt, a goad, and likewise a boon-granting gesture.
In her right hands she holds a trident, a bowl, a pheṭaka, a discus, a bow, a bell, a noose, and the threatening gesture (tarjanī), adorned with various ornaments.
O Goddess with three eyes, who holds the head of a Daitya and the Bindu-mudrā in your left hands, you who are youthful— salutations to you, O you of fierce form!
White in color and possessing three eyes, she has sixteen arms;
in her hands she holds a sword, a trident, an arrow, a discus, a thunderbolt, and a goad.
She holds the boon-granting gesture and a bowl in her right hands, while in her left hands she carries a *pheṭaka*,
the hair of a demon, a bow, and a mace, along with a bell.
In their left hands they hold a noose, a threatening gesture, and the bindu-mudrā; having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess Aticaṇḍā, [one should say]: "Homage to you! (8).
Thus ends the meditation on the Blessed One, Navacaṇḍī.
An aged Mahattarikā, adorned with high and full breasts,
seated upon a lotus garland, three-eyed, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
O Vāgīśvarī, who possesses the hue of the bandhūka flower and wears beautiful garments—
may the meditation on the deity of the Krama system remove our impurity at will.
Blue in color, dancing with his feet in the upward-pointing paryaṅka posture,
appearing about sixteen years of age, and adorned with jewels, snakes, and bones.
Bhairava is situated upon the lotus at the navel of Fire; he is dark-hued, possesses a thumb, and holds a knife and a skull;
he is present in the forehead, the tiger-skin garment, the girdle, and the waist, and is endowed with a smile.
In his arms he holds a discus, a trident, a wheel, a banner, and an arrow;
in his hands are a garland made of *pārijāta* flowers, a rosary, and a book that bestows fearlessness.
With two other arms, his body covered by a tiger skin, he stands as the Lord of Gods in the Śmaśāna surrounded by deities. Thus he is ninefold.
In this context, I shall now describe the meanings of the groups of weapons in their proper order:
from the trident (śūla) comes gain everywhere, and for the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśa), there is the destruction of sin.
By giving [a gift] under the Dhvaja constellation, one becomes all-knowing;
under Pārijāta, there is the attainment of fortune, and the perfection of mantras arises.
As long as omniscience remains a mere book, there is fearlessness within fear;
the concealment of obstacles therein shall constitute the armor of Brahman.
For the sake of liberation, the goddess Lakṣmī is praised as being large and graceful;
just as the Lord of Gods is esteemed according to his own will for the remainder of the body.
In the rite of immobilization (staṃbha), it should be yellow; for subjugation (vāma), it is like saffron;
in the rite of eradication (uccāṭa), it has the appearance of smoke-colored ash; and in the rite known as inciting enmity (vidveṣa), it has the luster of a Dhava flower.
The *mohana* [stone] is to be known as being like a leaf; the *vaśīkaraṇa* [stone] is considered to be like a jewel. Resembling a sapphire (*indranīla*), it is the lord over all ritual actions.
In the state of peace and liberation, it is cool and resembles pure crystal;
when associated with the red and white [energies], it is said to be like the color of a lotus in the state of agitation.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord in the ninefold arrangement for the accomplishment of the [nine] groups;
in the rite of pacification, one should worship Him seated upon a bull, and in the rite of hatred, He mounted upon a lotus.
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), he is mounted upon a bull; for the rite of delusion (*mohana*), he is borne by a dolphin;
and for the rites of subduing (*yāmana*) and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), he has the form of a ram.
With the Senāstambha [mantra], one should perform the pacification of obstacles for the sake of the Śāraṅga [bow] which resembles a ray;
and with the Tīkṣṇātīkṣṇa [mantra], for the purpose of subduing the stubborn.
One should conquer the firm musical instrument, the lore, and the one seated upon the lion-throne.
O Goddess, Kubjikā has the appearance of blue collyrium and possesses a large belly.
Six-faced and twelve-armed, adorned with snakes, bones, and jewels, she wears a garland of severed heads; fierce and Raudrī, her face is terrifying with protruding fangs.
The goddess Aṣṭādaśāṃvikā has disheveled hair standing erect;
she is clothed in a tiger skin and wears a lion skin as an upper garment.
Her limbs were adorned with divine ornaments; she laughed with loud, boisterous laughter. She drank her water, and her face was of a most excellent, dark complexion.
The southern face is black, as was shown from the front;
the eastern face is red, and the Īśāna face is like crystal.
Resembling a thousand suns, with its face turned upward in the supreme expanse,
it abides well in the Hero’s Well, on the left, and in the right ear.
Vīracūlī is at the tip of the nose, while Vikramātmaka is on the base; I shall describe Śilācitra, Dārulepa, and Gatavaktra.
The water [element] and the Saumya [deity] are in the left side; Pūrvā is in the right ear-petal;
Paravaktra is in the region of the head; and Parāvidha is on the crown of the head.
Having cast forth all the terrible,
gaping maws and the weapons, I shall now declare the great [mantras] of Kubjikā.
And for one who understands, through the application [of visualization], there are a trident, a wheel, a vajra, a hook, an arrow, and a small knife on the right and the left.
On the right and left, he should hold a blue lotus together with a star;
the others are a severed head, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a bell, a book, and likewise a bow.
The skull-bowl is said to be on the left; the lion-throne is the corpse-seat.
The attainment of reality occurs in the Śūla-cakra, while that which consists of Māyā exists in the Cakra.
O Vajra, I am the destroyer of all diseases; where is the one considered to be the attractor?
And the arrow destroys the enemy; what is that which is devoid of the eighth?
From the lotus one obtains gain, and from the khaṭvāṅga, the bull for the sake of accomplishment;
from the bell arises the state of being filled with the meaning of the mantra.
O Great-minded One, [he attains] the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures, mastery over the body as pure as a book, the great siddhi of the skull, and the power of weapons.
Brahmā resides at her soles; Viṣṇu is said to be in her speech;
Rudra dwells in her heart; and Īśvara is in the circle of her throat.
Sadāśiva is on the forehead, situated above Śiva;
the moon and sun are his two eyes, and the circle of stars is his eye within the constellation.
One should visualize an eight-petaled lotus in the Svarga [cakra] and a corpse in the Preta [cakra];
one should contemplate the element of earth in the Svādhiṣṭhāna and water at the navel.
One should conceive of fire in the center of the heart, wind in the throat, and space in the forehead; everything is established within them.
She has ascended through thousands of millions of lineages in the teaching of the Kula;
even for the gods, the investigation of her essential nature (piṇḍavicāra) is difficult to attain.
Ananta and the others are proclaimed as her anklets;
Karkoṭaka is the girdle, and the Kaṭibandha is proclaimed as the waistband.
Takṣaka is his sacred thread, Vāsuki is his necklace around the neck,
Kulika is said to be on his ears, and he is adorned with earrings.
The lotus is situated between the eyebrows, and likewise the great lotus;
on all the staff-like arms, he is adorned with a thousand hoods.
Then, one should worship the four pedestals of the triangular peak,

[performing] invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (saṃnidhāna), and confinement (saṃnirodha), as well as offering sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), vermilion (sindūra), flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and sandals (pādukā).
Thus is the meditation on the Karma-devī. The meditation on Oḍḍiyāna.
Five-faced, of massive body, with three eyes and great splendor;
white in color, of vast form, a hero whose radiance is equal to that of the yoginīs.
He stands upon Ananta, possesses eight arms, wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
has a mass of matted hair adorned with a crescent moon, and is decorated with various ornaments.
In his hands [he holds] a trident, as well as an arrow, a shield, and a noose;
likewise, the gesture of fearlessness, a battle-bow, a razor, and a goad.
And likewise, O beloved, I have described that seat of Oḍḍiyāna as being such that it grants boons and delivers one from the belly of cyclic existence.
Thus [is] Oḍḍiyāna.
In the center is the five-faced, three-eyed one, resembling the bandhūka flower,
brilliant like ten million flashes of lightning, abiding in radiance, and possessing eight arms.
Adorned with various exceedingly fierce jewels of diverse colors,
it was deformed, licking [its lips], and terrifying to the six classes of beings.
In the eastern direction and the others, starting from the right side of the deity,
he holds a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), as well as a cat held in his hand.

The great pīṭha beginning with the syllable Ja has been described as that which is honored by heroes; it is Jālandhara. To the south is Pañcavaktra, who possesses great splendor, has three eyes, and eight arms.
His body is adorned by eight serpents and embellished with various jewels;
he stands upon a tortoise, possesses a full form, is yellow in color, and is most beautiful.
The arrow, the iron chain, and likewise the bow and the noose are declared to be in the right hands, while the goad is in the left; thus he is eight-armed.
The Great Goddess Pūrṇapīṭhā is described in the Kulatantra.
Pūrṇagiri, in the north.
Then [he saw] the god named Kāmākhya, three-eyed and possessing beautiful arms;
the excellent god Bhūtākaraṇa, adorned with great serpents.

The goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the triple body are proclaimed by me as being on the left; while the trident, the arrow, and the water-pot are held in the right hand, along with the gesture of granting boons.
Then,
from that [flame], she produced a hundred bows for the elephants that blaze like fire;
and there appeared the Supreme Goddess named Kāmā, dark-complexioned and seated upon a lotus.

The goddess has that same form and color; her first [two hands] display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the second holds a skull-cup with a chopper, and the third holds a vessel of nectar.
The fourth [form] embraces the right [hand], while holding a bowl in her left hand; she is Kāmarūpiṇī in the east.
There, upon that seat, is the Supreme Goddess (Parādevī), who resembles the complete ritual procedure itself.
There, one should worship Mātaṅga together with his Śakti, Mātaṅgī;
because of his ferocity, he has a massive body resembling pure crystal.
The Lord has six faces and twelve arms; he is short and pot-bellied.
He holds various objects that grant protection, and he is adorned with five skulls and other ornaments.
The crow is in the center; the hero-leader is surrounded by the two enemies;
[he holds] the trident of the Lord of All-Indolence, as well as the noose, the mace, and the club.
They bear the Hero in their left arms, with a khaṭvāṅga and a goad in the left hands; he holds a bow, a threatening gesture, and flowers, and possesses the splendor of many banners.
O Supreme Goddess, your form is thus the leader of the Śrī family, seated amidst the great assembly of pretas, holding the vessel of the bindu, and most excellent.
The seat of the Moon is in the west. 5.
Thus ends the Five Seats (Pañcapīṭha). Now, the Higher-Lower Seat (Parāparapīṭha). Then follows the meditation on the twenty-eight [deities] of the hexagon:
Oḍḍīśanātha is yellow in color, graceful, and holds a staff in his hand; his Śakti is also of that same form.
Jālandharanātha is dark blue in color and holds a noose in his hand; his Śakti is also of that same form. 2.
Pūrṇeśvaranātha is of a reddish-brown color, having the form of fire; Śakti also has that same form. 3.

Vāmeśvaranātha 4. Thus ends the group of four seats (pīṭha). In the center, in the southwest, and in the northwest, at the Avatārapīṭha and so forth: [the deity] is white in color, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; his Śakti is also youthful, adorned with ornaments, and identical in form to him. 1. [Another form] is red in color. 2. [Another] is smoke-colored. 3. [Another] is green in color.
4. Black in color; 5. White in color, like crystal; 6. Yellow in color; 7. White in color.
Red in color (9); green in color (10); black in color (11); white in color (12).
One should envelop the previously mentioned meditation, beginning with Mālinī, within a twelve-petaled lotus and a hexagon.
The Śākinī is black in color, naked, and holds a knife and a skull-cup in her hands; she has disheveled hair standing erect and is as inauspicious as a jackal, possessing that very form. (1)
Kākinī is white in color, naked, and holds a sacrificial knife and a skull-cup;
her hair is matted and stands upright, and Śivā has that very same form.
Rākinī is red in color, naked, and holds a curved knife and a skull-cup;
she has disheveled hair standing erect on her head. Śivā is likewise of that same form. (3)
Lākinī is dark-complexioned, naked, and holds a curved knife and a skull-cup;
she has disheveled hair tied upward, and Śivā is likewise of that same form.
The Ḍākinī is yellow in color, naked, and holds a flaying knife and a skull-cup;
she has matted hair standing erect on her head, and Śivā is likewise of that same form.
Hākinī is of the color of fire, naked, and holds a curved knife and a skull-cup;
she has disheveled hair standing erect on her head, and Śivā is likewise of that same form.
Yākinī is smoke-colored, naked, a Śakti holding a skull-cup, with matted hair standing erect on her head; she is Śivā, and they are of such forms.
Thus are the six ḍākinīs.
Having meditated upon the goddess Triya at the western corner of the hexagon, yellow in color, with hands granting boons and fearlessness—3;

upon the goddess Triya at the northwestern corner, white in color, with hands granting boons and fearlessness—3; in the northeast, [the goddess] red in color, with hands granting boons and fearlessness—3; and in the east, green in color, with hands granting boons and fearlessness—3.

In the southeast (Agnikoṇa), she is black in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness (varadābhayapāṇinī) [3]. In the southwest (Nairṛtya), she is white in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness [3]. One should surround the Trikadevī at the tips of the corners of the hexagon, each having the color of her respective direction. Thus are the eighteen goddesses, beginning with Manonugā. 18.
Viśuddha is in the eastern corner, while Anāhata is in the southwest;
Maṇipūraka is in the northwest, and Svādhiṣṭhāna is in the northeast.
The support is indeed the fire, and the command is said to be in the west;
she is yellow in color, graceful, youthful, possessing two hands, and is the power (śakti) in the form of a beautiful young woman.
Adorned with ornaments and possessing that form, she is proclaimed as Mitrā and the others: (1) dark-complexioned, with graceful hands;

(2) tawny-complexioned, bearing the form of fire; (3) smoke-colored, holding a banner and a goad in her hands; (4) white-complexioned, granting boons and fearlessness with her hands, possessing the form of Śakti, in the full bloom of youth, and adorned with ornaments—this is the group of four beginning with Mitrā.
1. Of that form; 2. red-colored; 3. smoke-colored; 4. yellow-colored; 5. dark-colored. This is the pentad.
White in color, with hands in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*); Śakti whose form is not distinct [from the preceding].
(1) 56b) Red in color (2); yellow in color (3); dark green in color (4). This is the group of four.

[Perform] invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpanā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and the offering of sandalwood paste, garments, ornaments, and sandals. [This is for] the illustrious Prayāga-kṣetra of the eastern region, belonging to the *a*-group of consonants, who is fair-complexioned, mounted upon a great preta (*mahāpreta*),
and who bears the sword, shield, trident, skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), vajra, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), and the water-drop (*bindu*) mudrā.

One should meditate [on the deity] adorned with a great garland of skulls, possessing the radiance of ten million suns and lightning, and so forth, extending to the east, west, north, and south. Following that is the meditation on the deities of the gates.
Now I shall describe the meditation on the gate-deities, which is concealed within the tantras.
Those who themselves cause the expulsion of the gate-gods from the divine gateway—
[namely] Pāśa, Aṅkuśa, Phala, Abhoja, Pāṇi, and Pātālatuṇḍila— [are destroyed].
I salute the heroic Vighneśvara, who has the face of an elephant and three eyes. Thus ends the meditation on Vighneśvara.
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, who has four hands shining with two lotuses, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, whose body is as fair as refined gold, and who possesses three eyes.
The meditation on Mahālakṣmī:
Sarasvatī has three eyes, holds a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting gesture in her hands; she is white, seated upon a white lotus, and clad in white garments.
The meditation on Sarasvatī.
Resembling molten gold, adorned with divine jewels,
Dvāraśrī stands upon an upward-facing lotus, her lotus-hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
White in complexion, with an elephant’s face, holding an axe, a staff, a noose,
and a trident in his four arms, he is seated upon a mouse.
I meditate upon the compassionate one of dark form, who bears a skull and a trident,
who possesses three eyes, is fierce, and who destroys enemies both within and without the realm.
He does not embrace the ten-armed Vasudharā, who has a beautiful protruding belly;
rather, he embraces Vasumatī, whose forehead is marked with the sign of a lotus.
I worship Māyā, who is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, and the root of saṃsāra; she holds a boon-bestowing goad and a noose in her hands.

I bow to Gaurī, who possesses the three eyes and the power of consciousness, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who has a reddish luster, is clad in red garments, and blazes with light.
One should worship Gaṅgā, the Great Goddess, the supreme deity who flows in waves, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who is gentle, and whose radiance is equal to ten million moons.
I bow to Kālī, whose form transcends time and space, who bestows boons and fearlessness,
who is mounted upon a black tortoise and a lotus, and whose neck possesses the luster of a blue water-lily.
I bow to the creator of the worlds, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
who is mounted upon Garuḍa, the sustainer, whose form is Kṛṣṇa.
I salute the Creator, who is red in color, seated upon a red lotus, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with a water-pot, mounted on a swan, and endowed with three eyes.
I bow to Dehalī, who is mounted upon a lion, dark-complexioned, bearing a sword and a shield, standing below, facing west, and most skillful.
Thus ends the meditation on the deities of the doors.
Within the center of the yantra is the invocation of the sixty-four Yoginīs:
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Bhīmā, as well as Kalā and the Aṣṭakās; Divyayoginī, Mahāyoginī, Siddhayoginī, and Gaṇeśvarī.
Śākinī, Kālarātrī, Ūrdhvakeśī, Niśācarī,
Gaṃbhīrāghoṣaṇī, Sthūlā, Yaṃvanāṅgī, and Ulisikā.
Bhīṣaṇā, Mahānandā, and likewise Jvālāmukhī;
Piśācī, Hastinī, Yakṣiṇī, and likewise Dhūrjaṭī.
Viṣabhakṣā, Sarvasiddhi, Stuti, and likewise Icchā;
Huṃkārī, Bhāsvarī, Dīrghā, Dhūmrākṣī, and Kalahapriyā.
Mātaṅgī, Kākadṛṣṭi, and likewise Tripurāntakī;
Rākṣasī, Ghoranādā, Raktākṣī, and Viśvarūpiṇī.
Terrifying, fierce, and loathsome, with withered limbs and devouring men;
Vīrabhadrā, Mahākālī, Kaṅkālī, and Vikṛtānanā.
Krodhanā, Bhīmabhadrā, Vāyuvegā, Abhayānanā, Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Carcikā, and likewise Īśvarī.
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and Śivadūtī— may this quartet of goddesses,
the great yoginīs, always accept this offering.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the form of the sixty-four [deities],
which is endowed with great fortune and distinguished by wealth and righteousness.
One should worship the goddess Vijayā, who bears a trident and lotus-seeds,
who is free from the stream of worldly obstacles, seated upon a lion, and the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
Maṅgalā should worship the Goddess, the bestower of all perfections,
who is seated upon a lion-throne and a lotus-seat, who is serene, and who wears a crown of matted locks.
One should worship the goddess Bhadrā, seated upon an auspicious throne, holding in her right hands a trident, a rosary, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness.
One should worship the goddess Dhṛti, who is seated upon a fierce throne and holds a blue lotus, rays of light, a rosary, and the gesture of granting boons.
Holding a lotus and a mirror, adorned with all ornaments,
Śānti should be visualized as bestowing peace, seated upon a lotus throne.
The goddess should be depicted holding a rosary, with her hands granting boons and fearlessness;
she is seated upon a bull, possesses three eyes, and has a hand displaying the gesture of granting boons.
She holds a hand-drum and a trident, and bestows fearlessness;
she wears a crown of matted hair with a crescent moon, and has a serpent fashioned into her bracelet.
Seated upon a lotus throne on the earth, with a sun-disk held in her hand,
she wears a girdle joined with a trident, and has a yogic cloth as her upper garment.
The goddess Caṇḍī, who bestows the boon of success upon those seeking accomplishment, should be visualized;
she is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and is adorned with a secondary sun.
And one should worship the goddess Tuṣṭi, seated upon a water-pot,
holding a noose and a goad, gentle in appearance, and bearing a lotus and a svastika.
Umā is to be visualized seated upon a lotus, surrounded by deer and lions;
she is auspicious, with her hands holding a yoga-staff, a water-pot, and wearing an upper garment.
Known as the Trident, she is the destroyer of enemies, surrounded by Jayā and the other goddesses;
she shines with a garland of planets and wears lotus-shaped earrings.
Listen now to how the goddess Puṣṭi, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, should be fashioned:
she has a sword in her hand, possesses a magnificent form, and carries a shield and a mallet.
Aśvārūḍhā, Sarūpā, and others should likewise be depicted as Puṣṭi;
and Śrī should be fashioned seated on a lotus, holding a lotus and a śrīphala fruit.
Being bathed by women with elephants holding water-pots, she is most beautiful;
one should worship Ṛddhi, who stands upon a lotus and has hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The goddess Rati, beautiful-eyed and seated upon a lotus, should be depicted with her hands raised in the gesture of giving and uttering auspicious words, even in the absence of musical instruments.
She should be depicted with blazing, fierce eyes, wearing radiant rays of light, seated upon a lion throne, possessing a pool of the Gaṅgā, and holding a lotus in her hand; she is most beautiful.
The goddess, whose splendor rests upon blue lotuses and who holds blue lotuses,
is adorned with a garland of swords and embellished with all ornaments.
Seated in the posture of royal ease (paryaṅka) within her womb, she should be fashioned as beautifully as possible;
holding a conch and a book, she is radiant with ornaments of garlands of flowers.
Lakṣmī is seated upon a lotus throne; Vīryā holds a lotus and the fruit of fortune;
and Īśvarī stands upon a bull, wearing a crown of matted hair.
The Goddess, who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament and is adorned with a trident and serpents,
stands upon a pitcher and holds a thunderbolt and a citron fruit.
She should be depicted as auspicious, wearing a yogapaṭṭa upper garment and holding a jewel-topped staff;
she is seated upon an elephant throne, holds a vajra in her hand, and is most beautiful.
Jayāvatī is seated upon a lion, auspicious, bearing arrows and a bow;
she should be depicted with a sword and shield in her hands, and granting the boons of *vara* and *abhaya*.
But Aparājitā should be depicted as mounted upon a lion, possessed of great power,
holding a Pināka bow and arrows in her hands, and bearing a sword and a shield.
The goddess Ajitā has three eyes, wears a mass of matted hair, and holds a snake; she holds a lotus and a goad in her hands and is seated upon a crocodile throne.
One should visualize her standing upon a chariot, holding a bell and a mallet;
the goddess holds a vajra and a goad, adorned with all ornaments.
Seated upon a white lotus, holding a staff and a rosary,
Diti should be depicted with four breasts and adorned with all ornaments.
The excellent Māyā, adorned with blue lotuses, holds a child upon her lap;
she wields the noose, the goad, and the excellent Māyā, and carries a fly-whisk.
Mahāmāyā, mounted upon a boar, deludes all that is moving and unmoving;
she is the enchantress, riding upon a deer, bearing a banner, a trident, and dice.
Those planets have bamboo-staves in their hands, drink liquor, and are adorned with armlets;
they are intensely longing, mounted upon elephants, and bear garlands and mirrors.
Mounted upon the corpse of Tārā, Vimalā is radiant with splendor in her heart;
she holds a rosary of pearls and a water-pot in her beautiful hands.
Gaurī is seated upon the lotus posture, her hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; the auspicious goddess holds a rosary and carries a water-pot.
Seated upon a lion, the refuge of all, she is the bestower of boons with a hand held in the gesture of protection;
Kauśikī, mounted upon a hawk, she bears a trident and a severed head.
Holding a skull and a knife in her hands, of terrible form and great strength,
she should be visualized as residing in the mind, adorned with all ornaments.
Skilled in playing the lute and beautiful while dancing,
she is the subduer of the enemies of Durga and others, the destroyer of the foes of Vrishabha.
Bearing the Pinaka bow, arrows, shield, and sword, she is the slayer of Mahisha.
Surrounded by her own warriors, she arose from that head with a massive body.
Threatened by those of great strength with eyes blood-red and deeply inflamed,
some were encircled by serpent-nooses and, their life-breath severed, went to the state of the dead.
The goddesses should be depicted as mounted on tridents, white in color, and facing forward;
each one is seated upon a lotus-throne and a lion.
In such a form Durgā is to be fashioned, and not otherwise;
she should be seated upon a cloth, beautifully adorned for her ritual performance.
They shine with flower garlands and are adorned with circles of light;
they wear girdles of serpents and are endowed with every beauty.
One established in the vow should fashion an auspicious image of Arundhatī holding flowers and water;
one should worship the goddess Ghaṇṭā, who holds a bell in her hand and carries a trident.
She should be fashioned with the form of Karna;
she should be made very beautiful, holding a lotus and a rosary, auspicious, and observing the great vow.
She should always be visualized as Kapālinī, bearing a skull and a trident;
she is of the form of Rudra, yet fierce (raudrī), seated upon a bull, and most beautiful.
One should worship Kālī, who stands upon a chariot, wearing a crown of matted hair with the half-moon, with Vāsuki as her armlet, and bearing a skull and a trident.
The auspicious Mayūrī should be depicted seated upon a peacock, holding a noose and a spear;
she should be fashioned with three eyes and adorned with all ornaments.
Seated upon a staff-posture (daṇḍāsana), bearing the lotus and the svastika,
one should worship the goddess in her own form, adorned with necklaces and armlets.
One should worship the goddess who holds a trident and a sword, who possesses many forms, who sits upon a man, who has three eyes, and who bears a spear and a shield.
Adorned with the moon upon the heads of matted serpents, she is the embodiment of Śiva;
for the destruction of enemies, she is the slayer of foes, bearing a thunderbolt, a discus, and a bow.
Likewise, one should worship Ambikā, mounted upon a horse, adorned with all ornaments,
and bearing a trident, a thread, and a rosary.
Now hear, O Lord of the Gods, concerning Carcikā, who is seated in the lotus posture,
the great goddess Pretārudrā, adorned with ornaments of serpents.
She should be depicted with hair standing erect, as formidable, holding a skull-bowl and a chopper,
honored by the gods, mounted upon an elephant, and possessed of great power.
Listen now to [the description of] the goddess who holds a vajra-hook, as well as Vaivasvatī:
she holds a skull-bowl and a staff in her hands, stands upon a boar, and has Yama as her seat.
The goddess Kaumārī is worshipped seated upon a peacock, bearing a spear;
she holds a triple staff and an arrow, wears red garlands, and is accompanied by a cock.
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, possesses three eyes, and bears a trident;
she is devoted to playing the lute and is adorned with necklaces and armlets.

Listen likewise to [the description of] Mahālakṣmī, the goddess who is worthy of worship with the conch, discus, and mace, who is Vaiṣṇavī, whose seat is Garuḍa, and who wears a garland of forest flowers.
Gaganobhāsī holds a trident and dances as Kapālinī;
she has a gentle countenance, is perfectly full, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with severed heads.
Facing her, one should fashion Kārtikī, who stands upon a corpse;
and Śivadūtī should also be made, radiant with youth and ornaments.
Śivā holds a vajra and a goad;
she is fleshless, with sunken eyes, lips that are closely set, disheveled hair, and bound by serpents.
Her ears adorned with mudrās, her left thigh resting upon her hand; she should be seated upon a pedestal, and likewise have a distorted face.
The goddess Cāmuṇḍā is worshipped; she has upright hair and is terrifying. Seated upon a corpse, she is fleshless and bears a garland and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Holding a skull and a trident in her hands, radiant with ornaments such as earrings,
her left finger rests upon her lower lip which is in the form of a seal (mudrā).
Clad in an elephant hide, fierce with liquor, and adorned with serpent ornaments—
thus has the form of the Goddess among the sixty-four deities been described to you.
And now, O Lord of the Gods, I shall describe the great splendor [of this practice],
wherein there is no end to the worship of the Goddess, just as there is none for Śiva.
Likewise, I do not see the end of the fruit obtained from the gift of gold and land, nor that of the gift of cows, even after sixty-four such acts of worship.
O Goddess, the fruit of that is greater than what is recorded here for the sixty-four [arts];
it pertains to the temple, the pavilion, the house, painting, clothing, and the four aims of life.
O highly fortunate one, the auspicious Catuḥṣaṣṭhī, when worshipped, bestows sovereignty;
having installed [an image of] Catuḥṣaṣṭhī, whether with thirty-two or sixteen [deities].
Then the goddess, whose number is that of the Vasus, completely crosses over all evil deeds.
Thus is the meditation on the sixty-fourth Yoginī.
I shall describe the characteristics of the Mothers as they were spoken in former times:
Brahmāṇī resembles Brahmā, having four faces and four arms.
She should be depicted mounted upon a swan, holding a rosary and a water-pot;
likewise, Māheśvarī is considered to have the form of Maheśvara himself.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, seated upon a bull, and having the moon as her crest-jewel,
she has four arms, holding a skull-bowl, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and bestowing boons.
Kaumārī has the form of a youth and rides upon a peacock;
she is likewise considered to wear red garments and to hold a trident and a spear.
Adorned with necklaces and armlets, she is Kṛkarā and likewise Kūṭarā;
she is Vaiṣṇavī, resembling Viṣṇu, and seated upon the throne of Garuḍa.
She has four arms, bestows boons, and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace;
she may also be seated upon a lion-throne together with Bālaka.
And I shall describe Vārāhī, seated upon a buffalo;
the goddess resembles a boar and holds a bell, a sword, and a discus.
She who holds a mace and a discus, who brought about the destruction of the hundred Indras under her control,
Indrāṇī, who resembles the moon and bears a thunderbolt, a trident, and a mace.
They praised that Goddess, mounted upon an elephant, surrounded by many eyes,
possessing a luster like the color of molten gold, and adorned with garments and ornaments.
Likewise, one should visualize this Yogīśvarī holding a sharp khaṭvāṅga,
possessing a long tongue, with hair standing erect, and adorned with fragments of bone.
One should likewise depict the goddess with a face made terrifying by fangs, with a slender waist,
wearing a garland of skulls and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
In his left hand he holds a skull-bowl filled with flesh and blood, and upon it a head with its hair; likewise, in his right [hand], he holds a trident.
The Gṛddhasthā, Vāsavasthā, Anirmāṃsā, Vigatodarī,
Karālavadanā, and likewise Āśā and Trilocanā should be depicted in this manner.
Cāmuṇḍā, Vaddhaghaṇṭā, Dvipī, Carmadharā,
Aśivā, Digvāsā, Kālikā, and likewise Rāsabhasthā and Kapālinī.
One should fashion Vināyaka adorned with deep red flowers and ornaments, together with a *vardhanī* vessel and a banner; likewise, one should perform the rite for the Mothers.
And the Lord Vīreśvara, wearing matted hair and mounted upon a bull,
holding a trident and a skull-topped staff, shall appear before the Mothers.
Thus ends the meditation on the Mātṛkā.
Alternatively, there is the meditation on the external Mātṛkā.
Her broad chest is divided by fifty-six folds, granting happiness;
she wears a radiant crown upon which the full moon is fixed, and her breasts are full and pendulous.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes, whose pure radiance is enhanced by her vows, and who holds in her hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and a book.
Thus ends the meditation. The meditation on Bhuvaneśvarī.

I worship the goddess who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, who wears Indra’s crown, whose breasts are lofty, who is endowed with three eyes, who is the face of Smara, and who holds the gestures of granting boons, the goad, the noose, and the protection.
And the meditation on Bhuvaneśī.

I bow to the eternal consort of Hara, who has a dark-limbed form and a moon upon her crest; she holds in her own hands a gesture of generosity, a red lotus, and a supreme goblet rich with blood that removes all fear; she is adorned with a pearl necklace and stands upon a radiant red moon.
I worship that primordial Bhuvaneśvarī, who is seated upon a lotus throne, who bears in her hands the gestures of meditation, the excellent goad, the noose, and the gesture of fearlessness,
who resembles ten million rising suns, and who possesses three eyes.

I worship the Blessed Lady, who is red in hue, clad in variegated garments, with a fresh crescent moon as her crest-jewel; she is intent on bestowing [boons] here, bent by the weight of her breasts, and thrilled upon beholding the Lord of Men, who has become a fragment of the moon.
The destroyer of the suffering of existence.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
In the delightful Pārijāta grove, within a pavilion with jeweled floors,
upon a beautiful throne of gems adorned with a six-cornered lotus design.
Below, one should remember the six deities of the Lord of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree:
[holding] a bow, a noose, a lotus, a water-lily, and a goad.
60a) Bearing a flower-arrow in her lotus-like hands, wearing a jeweled crown, and possessing three eyes;
shining with the luster of a golden lotus, bent by the weight of her breasts, adorned with jeweled anklets, and her body resplendent with necklaces and other ornaments.
I meditate upon the primordial power.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.
I bow to her who is dark-complexioned, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, wearing a garment of lotus fibers,
whose pair of breasts shine with a necklace of gunja berries,
who bears a girdle of bells upon her hips, who moves with the grace of a swan, and who is renowned for her playful artifice.
One should worship the three-eyed Goddess, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons, fearlessness, and the noose.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.

One should meditate upon the consort of Śiva, whose head is adorned with the crescent moon, who is worshipped by the immortals, who holds in her hands a noose, a trident, and a full skull-cup; she is red in complexion, dressed in garments smeared with red unguents, adorned with ornaments, possesses three eyes, and her limbs are overwhelmed with intoxication.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Seated within the interior of a red lotus on a red lotus-seat,
she is red-limbed, adorned with a crown upon which the crescent moon blazes, and possesses three faces and three eyes.
We take refuge in her who holds in her hands a citron, a noose, a goad, a lotus, a skull-cup, and a trident; whose limbs are bent in humility, and whose body is bowed by the weight of her breasts.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Seated upon a lion, adorned with a crescent moon on her crest, and possessing four arms resembling emeralds, she holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow;
graced by three eyes, with necklaces, bracelets,
tinkling bangles, a girdle, and jingling anklets fastened upon her limbs, may Durgā, who removes all misfortune, be my protection.
Her earrings shine with various jewels.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
I bow to her who resembles the luster of emerald, adorned with jeweled earrings, whose brow is marked by an eye,
and who stands upon the head of a buffalo;
she holds a conch, a discus, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a trident, and the threatening gesture.
With his own arms, [he grasped] the one whose crest is the moon.
Thus is meditation.
She who bestows fear upon the families of the letters *kā*, *la*, *bhrā*, *bhā*, *ka*, *ga*, and *kṣa*; who bears on her head a line of cow-horns;
who holds in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident; and who possesses three eyes.

One should meditate upon Durgā, who, seated upon the shoulders of a lion, fills the entire three worlds with her splendor; she is surrounded by the thirty gods and served by those desiring spiritual perfection, for the sake of the goal of victory.
Thus is the meditation: One should visualize the Lord of Beasts (Mṛgendra) as the object of focus, and [the Goddess] who, dark as a water-laden cloud, holds in her lotus-like hands a trident,
arrows, a flaying knife, a noose, a discus, a bow, and a sword.
She has the moon as her crest-ornament (or moon-like radiance), three eyes, a flame of fire upon her head, and a shield, together with the [ten] sovereign powers.
I meditate upon the wielder of the trident, who is served by maidens and strikes terror into her adversaries.
Thus is meditation.

May the Goddess of Speech protect you (us)—she who possesses the splendor of Śambhu with her full moon-like youth; whose limbs are bent by the weight of her breasts; who sits upon a blue lotus; and who holds in her lotus-hands a pen and a book, like the illustrious goddess of all learning.
Thus is the meditation:
[one should visualize her] radiant, clad in garments and garlands of translucent crystal, blissfully brilliant,
holding a book, a rosary, a jar of nectar, and the Vidyā struck by vajras.
I bow to the goddess of speech, who sits upon a lotus, whose breasts are slightly bent, who smiles gently,
who bestows the power of eloquence, who possesses three eyes, and who grants the wealth of good fortune.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
I meditate with devotion upon Vāṇī, whose face is as radiant as the full moon, who possesses the luster of camphor and the god of love,
and whose head is marked by the crescent moon; she who respectfully holds in her own hands a lute,
a rosary, a jar of nectar, and the goddess of learning, her body adorned with divine ornaments from the four oceans.
One should worship her as mounted upon a swan.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
May the Goddess of Speech (Vāgīśvarī) grant the welfare of all beings—she who holds a rosary of lotus seeds, a water-lily, two lotuses, and a book;
whose crown is bound with the crescent moon; who possesses the luster of the released moon and jasmine;
whose eyes meet upon her forehead; and whose breasts are slightly bent.
Constantly attended by hosts of deities and sages.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
May she who bears upon her head a pearl necklace and the crescent moon, who holds with her two arms a rosary, a garland of letters, a jeweled pitcher, and a book;
she whose waist shines between her high breasts like a window— may that Sovereign of Speech grant me long-lasting praise.
Seated upon a white lotus, she is bowed down by the three worlds.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.

With a face smiling like the moon, her speech as pure as a necklace of swan-pearls, her excellent countenance graced by a gentle smile, with a crescent moon bound upon her head, her hands radiant with the noose, the goad, the jar of ignorance, and the rosary, she sat upon a white lotus for the attainment of one's desired goals.
It should be the speech of Bharata.
Thus is meditation.
In splendor resembling gold,
[he was borne] by four elephants like the Himālaya mountains, which tossed golden nectar with their trunks.
I worship her who is seated upon a lotus, who bears the glory of being showered by jars, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her two hands,
who is radiant with a crown, whose silken garment is beautiful like the orb of the sun, and who rests upon a lotus.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.

I bow to the Lotus-Seated Goddess, whose splendor is like that of rubies, who is beautiful with four lofty elephants white as snow, their frontal globes raised high by the tips of their trunks and adorned with jewels, and who possesses the longed-for creeper of the Pārijāta tree.
Thus ends the section on meditation.
Seated upon a lotus, her face radiant with a smile, she bestows gifts, the gesture of protection, and a pair of lotuses with her lotus-like hands;
resembling lightning in her form,
she shines with large, lofty breasts adorned with strings of pearls.
May she who gladdens Hari with the splendor of the side-glances from her lotus-like face protect you.
Thus is meditation.
She possesses the luster of the rising sun, is radiant with a necklace of millions of shimmering crescent moons, and is adorned with jewel-ornaments;
she bears the beauty of blossoming jasmine clusters upon her sloping breasts, and like a lotus, she eternally holds the Kaustubha gem while smiling.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, who is endowed with three eyes and is exceedingly white.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
She possesses a luster red as vermilion, laughs like a lotus, and is an ocean of beauty;
adorned with millions of necklaces, earrings, waist-bands, and other ornaments that destroy the affliction of disease,
she holds in her lotus-hands a vessel of wealth, a pair of lotuses, and a mirror, while being intensely served by her supreme female attendants.
Should one meditate upon the beloved wife of Śārṅgiṇa?
Thus is the meditation.
Thus is the meditation on the retinue of Guhyakālī.
Again, he describes the meditation on Bhairavī, who is part of the retinue of Guhyakālī.

She possesses the radiance of a thousand rising suns, wears a crown of red silk and a garland of flowers, her breasts are smeared with red pigment, and she holds a rosary, the Vidyā, along with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting.
I bow to the Goddess who stands there, holding with her lotus-like hands the splendor of her three-eyed, radiant lotus-face, and whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.

She possesses the luster of a thousand copper-colored suns, with matted locks adorned by a crescent moon; her crown is embellished with various glittering pearls, and she is enriched with faces dripping with blood, resplendent with garlands of severed heads.
She is graced with the beauty of three eyes and endowed with a face like the full moon.
She wears a crest of pearl necklaces and is thick-breasted;
she is clothed in red garments and possesses a form intoxicated with youth.

One should constantly meditate upon her who holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary and the boon-granting gesture in her right hands; she is the human form who bestows great prosperity.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.

She possesses the radiance of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with various ornaments, and is as beautiful as a digit of the moon amidst a cluster of white water-lilies; she is auspicious and wears excellent pearls.

She is the eternal one, holding a noose and a goad, bearing a skull-cup in her left hand; she is enriched by the splendor of the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and possesses full, elevated breasts.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
I shall now describe the meditation upon this goddess, who destroys all beings,
who possesses the radiance of the rising sun, and resembles the hibiscus flower.
Wearing a beautiful garland of severed heads, with a face like the rising sun,
possessing breasts that are full and elevated like golden jars.
A noose, a goad, a book, and likewise a rosary.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Resembling a hibiscus flower, like the flower of the pomegranate,
she has a crescent moon in her mass of matted hair, possesses three eyes, and wears red garments.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
She possesses the radiance of a thousand rising suns, has the moon as her crest-jewel, and is three-eyed;
she is beautiful with various ornaments and is the destroyer of all enemies.
She who causes Yama, Rudhira, Muṇḍa, and Ari to act, she who is clothed in blood,
holding a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, and likewise a shield.
[One should meditate on her] seated upon the throne of Śiva, holding the Pināka bow, the noose, and the pair of goads in succession, as well as a book and a rosary, O Goddess of the gods.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Resembling the Javā flower and comparable to the Dāḍimī blossom,
she has a mass of matted hair adorned with a crescent moon, possesses three eyes, and is clothed in red.
Adorned with various beautiful ornaments, possessing full and elevated firm breasts,
she holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, taking refuge in Śiva.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
She has the luster of the color of molten gold, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
her crown is radiant with the splendor of all lights, and she is ruddy like saffron.
Clad in variegated garments, with squinting eyes and three eyes,
she possesses full, high, and firm breasts shaped like golden jars.
Śambhu, white as the luster of cow’s milk, five-faced, three-eyed,
with a gracious countenance, and resplendent with his blue throat.
Beholding the dancing Kapardin, adorned with serpents that shone like jasmine buds, she became supreme bliss itself.
62a) She has joyous, tremulous eyes, is richly adorned with a girdle, possesses shapely hips,
is constantly devoted to the giving of food, has a beautiful neck, and is auspicious.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.
One should worship Śivā, who possesses the luster of the orb of the rising sun, has four arms and three eyes,
and holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow.
Thus is meditation.
Then [he beheld] the Goddess, who resembles a lotus, radiant as the rays of the rising sun,
like the hibiscus flower, and comparable to the pomegranate blossom.
Resembling a ruby and appearing as red as saffron,
she is adorned with a shimmering crown-jewel and a network of tiny bells.
Her face, resembling the orb of the moon, possesses sprout-like curls that are dark as a swarm of bees and are curved like young shoots; it has the luster of fresh, glowing dawn.
I bow to the Supreme Goddess, whose forehead is slightly curved like a crescent moon, who wears a soft fillet, and whose eyebrows are shaped like the Pināka bow.
Her eyes were rippling with the waves of bliss, joy, and exhilaration;
she resembled the shimmering orb of the full moon with its throbbing rays of light.
Her breasts were nourished by the thread of Viśvakarman’s craftsmanship;
her lips, pierced by copper, were as red as the bimba fruit and like nectar.
Her hair was like the moonbeams, her nails were the light that spread across the expanse of the sky,
she was adorned with strings of pearl necklaces, and her breasts were high and full.
Adorned with three folds [of skin], beautifully graced in the middle region,
her waist was bound by a girdle set with priceless gems, and she possessed shapely hips.
The Mistress, whose limbs are as soft as the hair of a bound elephant, who has a slender waist,
and whose thighs are like the pure, smooth stalks of a plantain tree or a lotus.
Her knees were beautiful, shaped like blossoms of loveliness.
Adorned with a pair of shanks resembling plantain trees in their loveliness,
her two feet with concealed ankles surpassed even the beauty of tortoises.
Her feet were graced by lines that shone like slender,
long fingers, and her lotus-feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Resembling a hundred moons, she smiles with a continuous stream of light;
surpassing vermilion in its redness, she possesses the hue of a pomegranate flower.
Clad in red garments, with noose and goad raised in her hands,
she is seated upon a red lotus and adorned with jewel ornaments.
She has four arms and three eyes, holds five arrows and a bow,
and her mouth is filled with betel leaf mixed with camphor and areca nut.
Her body is intensely red with saffron, as magnificent as great musk;
she is enriched with every elegant attire and adorned with all ornaments.
She who generates joy for the world, who brings delight to the world,
who performs the attraction of the world, and whose form takes the shape of the world.
The visualization is as follows: [She who is] eternal and composed of all prosperity, auspicious and composed of all powers.
Resembling a hibiscus flower and similar to a red bandhūka, it is adorned with lines of passion,
existence, and darkness, and is beautified by the circle of the womb.
In the center, however, one should visualize that Great Goddess Chinnamastā, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
holding in her left hand the headless trunk of a woman.
With her mouth wide open, terrifying, and licking with a fierce tongue,
she drank a stream of blood flowing forth from her own throat.
With her mass of hair disheveled and adorned with various flowers,
she holds a razor in her right hand and is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
The goddess is naked, most terrible, standing in the pratyālidha posture,
wearing a garland of bones, and having a serpent as her sacred thread.
Seated for the sake of pleasure, her sprout-like feet are ever to be meditated upon;
she is eternally sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts.
And one should meditate upon her, who stands in the posture of inverted coition, possessing the nature of the mind-born [Kāmadeva],
as a maiden joined with a Ḍākinī through the union of the left and right [channels].
She is drinking the stream of blood gushing from the throat of the Goddess;
she is young, red in color, gentle, with loose hair and naked.
O Śiva, she holds a skull and a chopper in her left and right hands respectively,
is known for having a serpent as her sacred thread, and is ablaze with radiant splendor.
She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, supremely divine, with disheveled hair and naked;
she is eternally twelve years of age and adorned with a garland of bones.
On the left side, however, one should visualize the Ḍākinī, who resembles the fire of the Kalpa-sun,
with matted hair like lightning, three eyes, and rows of teeth like a flight of cranes.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, possessing full and elevated breasts,
the Great Goddess is most formidable, with disheveled hair and naked.
Licking her great tongue, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she holds a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, according to the arrangement of the left and right.
She is terrifying, her face made fearsome by a skull-cup held in her hand, as she drinks the stream of blood gushing from the neck of the Goddess.
The wise one should meditate upon that Goddess while these two are being practiced;
thus is the meditation (dhyāna).
One should meditate upon the divine Kālikā of the South— terrible with a gaping mouth, with disheveled hair, four-armed,
and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Her left lotus-hands are raised upward and downward, holding a sword with a freshly severed head,
while her right hands, likewise raised upward and downward, grant fearlessness and bestow boons.
