She has the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked;
she wears a garland of severed heads hanging from her neck, which is smeared with blood.
She had earrings made of human ears, was terrifying with her pair of severed heads,
possessed fierce fangs, a formidable mouth, and full, elevated breasts.
Her girdle was fashioned from the hands of corpses, her swan-ornaments were made from skulls,
and her face was illuminated by streams of blood flowing from her two breasts.
She is all-pervading, with her right side adorned with teeth, her mass of hair hanging down like pearls,
and she is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
She is surrounded on all four sides by jackals making terrible howls;
her face is serene and pleasant, with a smiling radiance like that of a reddish dawn.
In this way, one should contemplate the Goddess who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground;
then follows the worship of Kālikā at the tip of the secret *cakra*.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the Vidyā that bestows all fruits,
which directly grants the four aims of life and destroys even the greatest of sins.
The eternal Guhyakālī, the great vidyā who bestows all accomplishments, grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is exceedingly difficult to obtain within the three worlds.
Having first written the syllable "Indra" (I) along with the group-initial vowel (A), conjoined with the *rati* (S) and the *bindu* (M),
and having then tripled it, one should extract the syllable "Huṃ."
Joined with the sixth vowel and consisting of the bindu, nāda, and kalā,
one should then double it and extract the two lords (īśa).
The left eye (va) joined with fire (ra), adorned with sound (nada) and the bindu, is declared to be Guhyakālī; or else, one may speak of Dakṣiṇā.
Then, one should first join the seven seeds in their proper sequence;
thereafter, the Vahni-jāyā (svāhā) is declared—this is the Vidyā that fascinates the three worlds.
Then, from the Vedas, [the mantra] of Guhyakālī or Dakṣiṇakālikā is proclaimed:
the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), likewise the "kūrca" (HŪM), and at its end, Bhuvaneśvarī (HRĪM).
Likewise, in the Guhyakālika, there shall be two seed-syllables;
this vidyā, ending in svāhā, is said to be hidden in all tantras throughout the ages.
This is declared to be the sixteenth [mantra], which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life:
*klīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ guhyakālike klīṃ huṃ svāhā | klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ ūṃ ūṃ ūṃ īṃ īṃ srīṃ svāhā*.
First the two of one's own seed-syllables, then the two of Kūrca, then the two of Māyā,
then the two of invocation, then the two of seed-syllables, followed by Māyā, Vahni, and Vallabhā.
Excluding the two seed-syllables of desire, there arises the fourteenth vidyā. This mantra is without distinction.
The seven-seeded mantra was proclaimed of old, and furthermore, the secret Kālikā;
this vidyā, ending with svāhā, is hidden in all tantras.
This [mantra] also consists of fourteen syllables.

And likewise: if, having omitted the word beginning with her name, it is [placed] on the right, then it becomes fifteen syllables. And likewise: having uttered the word on the right, it becomes fifteen syllables. Likewise, by omitting the *kāmabīja*, it becomes sixteen syllables.

By this, there is the sixteen-syllable vidyā; in the absence of the kāmabīja, it becomes fifteen syllables. Having extracted the kāmabīja, one should place the two words ending in the vocative, then the kāmabīja again at the end, and finally the Sundarī of Fire (the svāhā).
This nine-syllable vidyā, when combined with Guhyakālī and the word *dakṣiṇe* at the end,
becomes the ten-syllable vidyā.
The shaking of these [limbs] is likewise [to be understood].
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before and worship the group of letters (*varga*) as before;
one should worship the Vidyā as before, for indeed everything is exactly as before.
The practitioner should likewise imagine the offering as before;
the mantra for the bali-offering is as follows:
Come, come, O Mother of the World, O Mother! Accept, accept my offering! Grant me success! Destroy my enemies!
Huṃ 2 hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, obeisance to Kālikā, phaṭ svāhā! Or alternatively, this is the mantra of Guhyakālī:
Come, come, O Guhyakālī! Accept, accept [my offering]! Destroy my enemy! Devour him! Hurry, hurry! Turu 2!
*Spuru spuru 2 siddhi dehi 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Likewise, this is the mantra for the seat (*āsana-mantra*): *Oṃ huṃ sadāśiva mahāpretāya guṇakālyai namaḥ guhyakālyai huṃ namaḥ*.
The mantras of Bhadrakālī and the others are now being told; listen, O beautiful one!
One should worship all the seed-syllables, beginning with the seed of desire (kāma), in both the preceding and succeeding positions.
One should likewise join "Bhadrakālī" and "Ṅeṃ Tāṃ" in the middle of the seed-syllable;
this Vidyā, ending with "Svāhā," consisting of twenty syllables, is declared by the supreme ones.
O Bhadrakālī of auspicious countenance, you are the knowledge that bestows the four aims of life;
having extracted the seven seed-syllables, you are likewise Śmaśānakālikā.
Furthermore, the seed-syllable followed by *svāhā* at the end bestows all accomplishments;
this mantra of twenty-one syllables is considered the *Śmaśānakālikā-vidyā*.
One should first utter the seed-syllables, then the word "Mahākālī," and at the end of that, the seven seed-syllables ending with "svāhā"; this bestows all accomplishments.
The twenty-leafed [plant] is proclaimed as the Mahāvidyā of Mahākālī;
for their recitation and worship, however, it should be accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Furthermore, in the Guhyakālī maṇḍala, there is the meditation on the retinue:
the goddess Mahāmeghaprabhā, who wears black garments.
With a lolling tongue, terrible fangs, and cavernous eyes, she has a laughing face;
she is adorned with a garland of snakes and bears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
One woman was binding her matted locks, while another was licking her own face; one had a serpent as a sacred thread upon her body, and another sat reclining on a serpent-bed.
She has a large belly and wears a garland of fifty human heads,
while upon her head is Ananta, endowed with a thousand hoods.
Guhyakālī is encircled by the hoods of nāgas in the four directions and adorned with Takṣaka, the king of serpents, as a bracelet on her left wrist.
She whose right-hand bracelet was offered as a gift by the Naga king Ananta,
whose girdle was fashioned by a Naga, and who wears jeweled anklets.
One should meditate upon the goddess as having two arms, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
and adorned with earrings fashioned from human bodies.
She has a serene countenance, is gentle, and is adorned with the nine gems;
she is the consort of Śiva, served by hosts of sages such as Nārada and others.
They draw her with a single matted lock of hair—laughing fiercely, most terrifying, and bestowing the desired objects upon the practitioner; "they draw" implies that they "wear" [it].
"Surrounded by Anantaśīrṣā and Guhyakālī"—this is an elliptical expression.
This is the visualization (*dhyāna*).
Having visualized the cremation ground there, one should then recollect the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) therein.
At its base is a jeweled pedestal, adorned with various garlands.
The Sage, adorned with various ornaments and jewels, was further embellished by the gods;
then he took delight in the auspicious flesh and bones of those who were devoted to him.

One should meditate upon Gaurī in the midst of that [place], which has four corners, is filled with heaps of severed heads, and is adorned with bones from funeral pyres, according to the yoga of meditation as described.
Thus is the meditation:
[one should visualize her] standing in the pratyālīḍha posture with the right leg extended, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
short-statured, with a protruding belly, terrifying, and wearing a tiger-skin around her hips.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with the five mudrās,
four-armed, with a lolling tongue, most terrifying, and the bestower of boons.
She is endowed with a sword and a knife in her two right and left arms respectively,
and is possessed of a pair of hands holding a skull-cup and a blue lotus.
One should meditate on her with a single tawny and fierce matted lock, adorned with Akṣobhya upon her crown,
and embellished with the five mudrās.
Thus is meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Resembling pure crystal, with four arms and a crown,
he holds a trident and a skull-cup in his right hands, while in his left hands he holds a noose and a goad.
"The wielder of the trident, who bestows the desired boons upon the practitioner possessed by the nectar [of power]"; such is the visualization.
Then, the supreme practitioner, with a steady mind, should meditate upon the Goddess.
Dark-limbed, with the moon as her crest-jewel, she sits upon a jeweled lion-throne.
The visualization is as follows: she holds a Veda, a staff-like arm, a sword, a shield, a skull-cup, a noose, and a goad;
she is seated upon a corpse, and her garments and ornaments are red.
Adorned with jewel ornaments and decorated with a necklace of gunja berries.
And she who is sixteen years of age, possessing full and elevated breasts,
holding a skull and a chisel in her hands, whose nature is the supreme light.
The best of mantra-knowers should meditate by means of the union of the left and the right.
Thus is the meditation.
[She who is] discolored, fickle, wicked, tall, and clad in dirty garments—
Her earrings were loosened, her teeth were rough, and she was like a widow with disheveled hair.
Mounted upon a chariot with a crow as its banner, her breasts were pendulous;
she was pale, exceedingly rough, holding a hand [in a threatening gesture], yet endowed with excellent qualities.
But Sudṛśī had a prominent nose and crooked, curved eyes;
she was constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and she gave rise to fear with her hideous laughter.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
Satiated, she declares this entire world to be but a single village;
holding with her two hands a fierce noose resembling a blazing flame of fire,
may that Bhadrakālī protect us from fear as she avoids it with her teeth, which resemble the fruit of the jambu tree.
Thus is the meditation:
[She is] possessing the luster of the interior of a saffron flower, slightly in the bloom of youth,
with arms as tender as fresh lotus stalks, adorned with armlets and bracelets.
Her two lotus feet were adorned with the shimmering tips of golden anklets,
and she was embellished with necklaces of rubies, a crown, earrings, and other ornaments.
She has eyes like blue lotuses, is graced by slightly budding breasts,
whirls a lotus with her two hands, and is clothed in red garments.
One should meditate upon that Goddess, the bestower of wealth, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the midst of a golden enclosure at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
The goddess, resembling collyrium and other substances, dwelling in the cremation ground,
with red eyes and disheveled hair, terrifying with her emaciated flesh.
She holds with her left hand a small bowl filled with wine,
and with her right hand, she holds a freshly severed head; may that auspicious goddess protect us.
With a smiling face, she is always on my left, chewing flesh and providing satisfaction.

Her limbs adorned with various ornaments, she is always intoxicated by excellent wines— thus is the visualization. She is seated upon a lion-throne at the center of a jeweled altar within a gem-studded pavilion in the midst of an ocean of nectar.
I bow to the Goddess, whose complexion is deep yellow, whose limbs are adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and jewels, who holds a mallet, and who seizes the tongues of her enemies.
I bow to the two-armed Goddess Pitāmbarā, who holds the tip of her tongue with her right hand, crushes the enemy with her left, and strikes with a mace held in her right.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Red in color, with black eyes and three eyes, she is short and has a protruding belly;
her tongue is as crimson as the bandhūka flower, she wears a garment, holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and has her face turned upward.

Salutations to her who has smoke-colored rays, whose matted hair is disheveled, whose two hands shine with a skull-cup, who is restless, the all-knowing one, who dwells having taken up residence in the heart of Smara, and who is worshipped by the Piśācas.

Thus is the meditation: one should contemplate the Youthful Lord (Kumāra), who is as auspicious as the moon, holding a book and a lotus in his hands, most beautiful and exceedingly peaceful, adorned with five topknots (pañcacūḍa), possessing vast and excellent liberation, with eyes as broad as lotus petals, and free from evil intellect.
I bow to the one who is skilled in burning and possesses a beautiful luster.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.

With the left hand holding a lotus, one should perform the worship consisting of recitation and so forth; indeed, with the right hand, during the ritual of practicing the erotic sentiment, one should meditate upon Him who is as white as the rays of the full moon, seated upon the head of a bull at the edge of a crossroads.
Thus ends the section on meditation.
O Great Goddess, I shall now describe the meditation that bestows all accomplishments:
[the deity] as white as the moon, holding a sword and a book in his hands, most beautiful and exceedingly peaceful.
I bow to Mañjuśrī, the youth with five topknots, who grants the most excellent and vast liberation, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, and who is skilled at incinerating the dull-witted.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
She was dark-complexioned, pot-bellied, and formidable, adorned with serpent earrings;
her hair was disheveled, her tongue lolled out, and she wore red garments around her waist.
The fierce Mistress of the Gods, whose breasts are full and elevated, is encircled by a great elephant;
she stands upon a corpse, and above that, upon a skull-bearer.
She is intent on meditation upon the tip of the nose, most formidable, the bestower of boons,
four-armed, with long hair, and riding upon a vehicle in the upper right.

The goddess holds a single lotus in her upper left hand and a drinking vessel in her upper right; she displays the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness in her lower right and left hands respectively.
To Sadāśiva, [I offer] the goddess who flows with streams of blood, whose drinking vessel is ever-present,
who bestows all siddhis, and who dwells eternally on the mountain.
She is endowed with three eyes, wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
has a long nose, long shanks, long limbs, and a long tongue.
Endowed with three eyes through the distinction of the moon, sun, and fire,
she is the Goddess who destroys enemies, possesses great luster, and bestows the highest boons.
With a tiger skin bound around her head, she illuminates the three worlds;
she brings happiness to practitioners and strikes fear into all the worlds.
Thus is meditation.
One should again meditate upon a jeweled lion-throne consisting of the moonlight of Durgā;
and upon that, one should likewise meditate upon the goddess Vāgīśvarī.
The Goddess, whose luster resembles the brilliance of pearls, who radiates a web of moonlight,
who bestows happiness upon practitioners, and who strikes fear into all the worlds.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
One should meditate on a jeweled lion-throne, and upon that, Durgā consisting of moonlight;
furthermore, one should meditate on the goddess Vāgīśvarī seated there.
The goddess, possessing the luster of pearls, radiating moonlight through her lattice-like ornaments,
adorned with a bright pearl necklace and graced by a beautiful crest of peacock feathers.
She holds in her two right hands a rosary of beads for the purpose of exposition and a divine jar filled with nectar, as well as a book.
Holding [something] with both her beautiful hands, endowed with the weight of her full yellow breasts,
slender-waisted, likewise translucent, and adorned with various ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon [the deities] according to their individual distinctions, one should then worship them in sequence.
This is the meditation.
Adorned by the lotus of her left foot upon the head of the deer,
and filled with the blood of the buffalo pierced by the tip of her right foot.
With a most serene countenance and a beautiful face, she is endowed with three lovely eyes;
she is adorned with anklets, armlets, matted locks, and a crown.
Clad in variegated silken garments and adorned with a crescent moon,
she holds a sword, a shield, a vajra, a trident, and likewise a three-pointed spear.
Holding a bow, a noose, a conch, a bell,
and a lotus in her graceful arms, the Goddess possesses a splendor equal to ten million moons.
She was always being praised by the gods dwelling in the sky, who were equal to the celestial beings,
and by the world-protectors and others, who were filled with joy.
Thus is meditation.
Having offered blue lotuses or water lilies, one indeed attains the state of Śravaṇā.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
[He saw] Mahākālī, who, like another fire of cosmic destruction, was chewing the asuras with her flickering tongue— she whose eyes were red and round.
Agitating the entire world, including the gods, asuras, and mountains— such is the visualization.
Mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, adorned with various ornaments,
the great goddess has four arms and wears a serpent as her sacred thread.
Clad in red garments, her body resembling the rising sun, she was served by hosts of sages such as Nārada; she is Bhavasuṃdarī.
[He saw] a lotus-stalk with a navel-base, encircled by three coils,
upon an island consisting of jewel-lamps and provided with a lion-throne.
One should meditate upon her, the mistress of worldly existence, seated upon a full-blown lotus;
such is the meditation.
[One should meditate upon] the two-armed Ambikā Caṇḍī, who holds a sword and a skull-bowl.
Adorned with various beautiful ornaments, wearing red garments, and auspicious.
Always sixteen years of age, with a serene countenance and three eyes,
beautiful with a garland of severed heads, and possessing full, swelling breasts.
Upon the corpse is the Great Goddess, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
the goddess who brings about the destruction of enemies and bestows the attainment of the practitioner's desired goals.
One should meditate upon her who generates all good fortune and bestows great prosperity. Thus is the visualization.
One should always worship Gaurī, who possesses a golden luster, who holds a noose and a goad in her arms for the accomplishment of her purpose, and who is adorned with all ornaments.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
May the goddess Vāruṇī— who bears on her head the moon-king with all its digits, whose hands are beautiful with the noose and goad,

who is surely the banner of the host of immortals, who is worthy of worship, and whose face is adorned with the flowers of asceticism— grant you prosperity, she who is peerless in the destruction of afflictions, like Pārvatī herself.
Thus is the meditation:

[one should visualize her] as five-faced, extremely fierce, deep red in color, and three-eyed, holding a spear, a trident, a bow, an arrow, a sword, a shield, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The visualization is as follows: [one should meditate on] the Goddess, holding [the goddess Dakṣāṃ] with her right arms, adorned with many ornaments.
With twenty crores of fangs, she stands upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa, holding the crescent moon in her hand.
With their right hands raised holding skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅga), they hold a noose and a head with their left hands.

Cāmuṇḍā— dark green in color, with tawny hair standing erect, holding a hand in the gesture of fearlessness, clad in a tiger skin, and mounted upon a corpse— is always to be meditated upon by practitioners during the rite of recitation.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
The Great Goddess is smoke-colored, three-eyed, and has the moon as her crest;
she is endowed with a mass of matted hair and is clothed in a tiger skin.

Her limbs were like those of a celestial being, her bones and flesh were firm, and she held a small knife in her lotus-like hand; she had deep-set eyes, beautiful fangs, and a belly as vast as the netherworld.
Thus is meditation.

O Gaurī, she whose face is like the full moon, who is multiform and holds the boon-granting gesture; she whose breasts are full and high, who dwells in the dance, who is all-knowing, and the bestower of fearlessness.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
She with the eyes of a deer, a face like the autumn moon, lips red as the bimba fruit, and anointed with the scent of sandalwood;
she who is without a bodice, possessed of full breasts, enchanting, youthful, ever-granting the fulfillment of desires, and wondrous.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
She has a serene countenance, is fair-complexioned, and possesses the beauty of lips like ripe bimba fruit;
she wears red garments, is youthful, and bestows the fruits of all desires.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.
Kāmeśvarī, who is as fair as the moon, whose eyes are like those of a playful khañjana bird,
whose gait is ever-fickle, whose splendor is radiant, and whose face is like that of the destroyer of the flower-arrowed god.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Golden-hued, fair-limbed, and adorned with every ornament,
she was beautiful for a moment upon the lotus with her anklets and necklaces.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
One should meditate upon her seated in the lotus posture, dark-complexioned, with full and elevated breasts,
possessing delicate limbs and a smiling face, her eyes like red lotus petals.
Thus is the meditation:
[one should meditate upon] the goddess Trailokyamohanī, who wears variegated garments,
is adorned with diverse ornaments, is delightful, and assumes the attire of a dancer.
Thus is the meditation:
[visualize her] resembling pure crystal, adorned with various ornaments,
embellished with anklets, necklaces, armlets, and jeweled earrings.
Thus is the meditation. I bow down to that Goddess Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed in the river Mṛt, whose eyes are like blue lotuses, and who is united with Vāgīśvara.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
One should meditate upon Bhadrakālī, who has eighteen arms, the moon as her crest-jewel, and the syllable Vāṃ;
she may also be endowed with sixteen or even ten arms.
He showed the Dānava the form of Ugracandrā’s body,
with a face formidable with flames and endowed with eighteen arms.
Equipped with divine weapons and missiles, terrifying with a garland of severed heads,
with split corners of the mouth and most fearsome due to his dreadful fangs.
Beholding that form, whose girdle was like a shimmering lightning flash and which was not harsh,
the Daitya closed his eyes.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
67a) She has a throat as dark as a rain cloud, extremely formidable teeth, and a flickering tongue; she is matted-haired and bears a sectarian mark on her left [shoulder],
while in the palm of her right lotus-hand she holds a crescent moon.

I bow to Kālī, the formidable one, who wears a garland of skulls as her girdle, whose face bears the non-duality of the two weapons of the Śṛṅkhalā and Pāśa, whose eyes are intoxicated with honey-wine, and who rests upon the heart of a corpse.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.

I worship that Great Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī, who holds a lotus, a goad, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands; who is seated upon a lotus throne; who resembles ten million rising suns; and who possesses three eyes.
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Upon the foundation [of the body], one should contemplate the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, as radiant as the rising sun and possessing the luster of gold;
and the seed-syllable Manmatha, resembling a moonstone, situated within the lotus of the heart.
In the aperture of the Brahma-abode, there is that which is most peaceful, stainless, moon-like in luster, and radiant;
O Śivā, I bow to that supreme Śaiva reality, whose two feet extend from the beginning to the end.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
Clad in yellow garments, with full and elevated breasts,
richly adorned with a crown of matted locks and full, uplifted breasts.
She holds the tongue and the mallet of the enemy as her supreme attribute. This is the visualization.
The Goddess is sixteen years of age, mounted upon a Śarabha, composed of the essence of Dāru, whirling, with a dark-blue body and reddish limbs.

One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī within the lotus of the mind— excellent, with broad breasts, adorned with a garland of guñjā berries, holding a stainless skull-cup and a sharp dagger in her two hands.
Thus is meditation.
The goddess has eighteen arms and eyes reaching as far as her ears;
she is three-eyed, possesses long and beautiful limbs, and resembles the fire of cosmic destruction.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.
Thus, by worshipping the Goddess, one is born as a bull among men,
such as Rāma among the Kṣatriyas and Purandara among the gods.
As Tārkṣya is among the serpents, as Śani is in cruel deeds, and as the powerful Senomantra-knower is among those skilled in the Śaṅku rites; so [is he].
This supreme secret has been told to you by me in brief;
this Vidyā which I have declared to you must be kept strictly hidden from those who do not practice it.
"Out of affection for you and out of devotion, I have become a *vaḍvā* (a mare), O Supreme Goddess.

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of the Mantras and Meditations of Various Deities" in the *Śrī Hāhārāvatantra*, within the *Arthavarṇasaṃhitā*, in the manual for the worship of Mahākarma.
67b) Now he states the specific application:
Śrī Bhairava said:
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and adorned with many kinds of flowers;
It was crowded with throngs of Apsarases, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
and graced by gods who were devotees of Śiva, as well as by celestial serpents.
It was filled with those who were uniquely skilled in the meditation of yoga and possessed of the realization of reality,
and with weapons endowed with consciousness that uttered cries of victory.
With one eye, with two eyes, and with yet other eyes;
with one foot, with two feet, and with three feet by the thousands.
It was resplendent with those who were exceedingly cruel, most terrifying, and formidable;
it shone with blankets, men, and serpents, and was graced by songs and instrumental music.
It was attended on all sides by the world-protectors beginning with Indra, by the asuras beginning with Bāṇa, and by sages beginning with Durvāsas.
When Kailāsa had thus become so, the Lord of Gods himself,
the Master, Sadāśiva— the embodiment of light, whose mantra is eternally recited by the deceased, and who is ever meditated upon by yogins— [resided there].
This unmanifest peak is where Śiva himself resides;
being praised by Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord was greatly delighted.
Once, in a secluded place above, the supreme Śiva—
the agent of creation and dissolution— was present with a joyful, nourished, and serene soul.
Having beheld the Lord of the gods in a secluded place, the Goddess, the Mother of the World, with a pure smile,
approached him and slowly spoke these words.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion!
O Lord, the castes, the stages of life, the duties, and my doubts have [been explained] by me.
O auspicious lady, I have heard all those ancient and other wonders from the Lord himself, for he is omniscient.
The determination of mantras, as well as the determination of yantras,
right conduct in this treacherous world, and the practice of yoga— these are very difficult to attain.
Indeed, through the practice of various meditations, someone is seen to have realized the Veda;
likewise, it is undoubtedly declared in the different Āgamas.
Thus, even the virtuous twice-born are seen to be partakers of suffering,
overcome by heretics, atheists, and revilers of the Vedas.
O Great Lord, without mantras, recitations, or fire-offerings, and without any hardship,
perfection arises at that very moment— perfectly accomplished and bestowing all desired results.
68a) In killing, expulsion, attraction, inciting enmity, as well as in paralyzing, bewildering, malevolent rites, and in all matters concerning one's objectives at all times.
In diversion, in debate, and likewise in the conquest of enemies,
all this indeed succeeds for the practitioner, O Lord.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, having reflected upon it, speak the supreme secret.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Vaiṣṇava, I have proclaimed the conduct of the Vedas for the high-souled sages,
as well as the dharma of the Siddhas and the path of liberation for the Vaiṣṇavas.
The Saura-sāṃkhya, which bestows success upon many, has been proclaimed by me;
and the scripture has been proclaimed in many ways, O beloved, as has Bhairava in many ways.
O auspicious lady, the knowledge of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa has indeed been revealed;
this is the supreme secret everywhere, without a doubt.
O lady of excellent hips, a mantra devoid of its secret essence, and especially its meditative visualization,
shall not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, show favor; O Master, tell me an easy means [to liberation], one that is secret, easily understood, and produces immediate conviction."
"O Lord, since one achieves perfection in the Kali age without fire-offerings, recitation, or preparatory rites, please tell me the means for that."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O lady of great wisdom, who acts for the benefit of the worlds! O lotus-eyed one, I have never been asked about this matter by anyone."
Listen with one-pointed mind to this secret that grants success in an instant—
the great [teaching] named Kalpacintāmaṇi, more secret than the secret.
It is the essence of all scriptures, the supreme essence of mantras,
and the highest of the essences of the Veda, which is the forest of meaning.
In this kalpa, O Goddess, there will be auspicious yantras made of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) that perform many kinds of desired actions.
He in whose house this ritual manual is always kept written down,
and who worships it every day, shall experience its power.
There is no fear of untimely death, nor is there any fear of thieves;
the power of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas does not arise at all.
In this doubt, it will certainly never succeed;
O fair-faced one, the practitioner must not harbor lack of faith.
The rite of sorcery (abhicāra) will undoubtedly succeed according to the ritual manual (kalpa) for those who lack trust;
however, a yantra performed with doubt results in the opposite effect.
Having bathed and become pure, one should worship the family deity;
one should diligently draw the supreme yantra in a secluded place.
This procedure has been proclaimed for whichever practice one undertakes; one should perform it for three days according to the rules for the yoga of worship.
For three nights he should sleep on the ground, remaining pure and devoted to celibacy;
O lady of radiant smiles, for three days the practitioner experiences no sleep.

The presiding deities of the mantra reveal in a dream the attainment of success (siddhi), the object to be accomplished (sādhya), the enemy, or indeed the certain state of "well-accomplished" (susiddha). They manifest these very things as a dream within the dream.
When no dream arises, then one should declare the goal accomplished;
otherwise, according to the auspiciousness of the dream, one should declare it in accordance with its true meaning.
Having heard from the mouth of the god that the accomplishment of the fruit [of the dream] would come through the prescribed rite,
when the dream was thus averted, then another supreme yantra [was revealed].
Whoever should draw [the diagram] in this manner and perform [the rite], success is indeed proclaimed for them;
for this very reason, many yantras are called "māyās."
By whatever means or by whichever machine one attains perfection, those very things must not be grasped; one should abandon that which is forbidden and leave the world.
In the Kali age on this earth, the Vidhirekha is indeed well-known among yantras;
therein, within the grid of mantras, practitioners perceive the categories of the accomplished (siddha), the achievable (sādhya), and so forth.
Success never arises for them due to various defects;
nor is there ever a single practitioner, for every person is of a singular nature.
O Dear One, there is not just one lunar mansion, nor just one family deity;
likewise, the yantra, the seed-syllable, and the mantra each exist in four forms.

The *siddha* is one who has already attained accomplishment; the *susiddha* is another such as that. The *siddha* attains success in time, while the *sādhya*, O Danavas, attains success through effort.

Is it "ariḥṣṇanta"? One who is well-perfected by the trident grants the desired goal at that very moment; therefore, likewise, [one considers] the zodiacal sign, the ascendant of time, and the rising of the planets.
Having correctly understood the mental disposition of the practitioner, one should act accordingly;
this is the supreme secret, which bestows joy and grants supernatural powers.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, O most beautiful one, listen to the great yantra for bringing kings under control;
it is prepared with pure ashes and other substances in a vessel made of bell-metal.
One should scratch with *jātikāṣṭha* wood, using *rocanā* and sandalwood;
one should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center and then encircle it with a circle.
69a) One should indicate eight petals upon that [mandala], at the tip of the wheel; then,
O Dear One, one should likewise encircle it with a circle.
Upon that, one should fashion a sixteen-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
the vowels beginning with 'a' should be written on the petals, and it should be worshipped in their proper sequence.
Then, one should properly encircle it with three lines and worship it with jasmine, *jāti*, and white lotus flowers.
Having worshipped the king of yantras known as Mahāmohana with other fragrant white flowers and white petals, [one should proceed].
Having performed this for seven days, one should then encase it with the three metals;
whoever wears it on the head, on the arm, or likewise on the neck, [attains the desired result].
Whether it be a perfected being (siddha) or even an ordinary man who has made a firm resolve,
all the servants (kiṅkaras) indeed always run toward him, having come under his control.
Hereafter, I shall explain the yantra known as "Bīja," which is excellent for bringing kings under control and likewise for subjugating the common people.
Having written four *hrīṃ* syllables in a single row,
one should then write the name of the person to be accomplished below, enclosed by *hrīṃ* syllables.
Furthermore, the wise one should write the four seed-syllables beginning with *hrīṃ* below, as well as two lines forming a quadrangle, upon a birch-bark leaf.
With yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, and likewise with sandalwood paste,
one should draw a very beautiful yantra using the ring finger mixed with red [pigment].
One should employ this yantra when the king is enraged,
when [the enemy] is suffering, bound in fetters, and even when all his possessions have been destroyed.
Then, having personally worshipped the King of Yantras according to the prescribed rite with various flowers, food offerings, and diverse auspicious meats;
Having fed the young girls and the Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity,
as well as the Yoginīs and the married women, one should offer salutations with firm resolve.
Taking that machine with his fist, he should indeed go to the royal palace;
it pacifies his anger and exerts power over subjugation by means of the noose.
Devotion arises at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim a heart-stealing charm for subduing one's master,
by which a man may bring his master under his control for as long as he lives.
One should draw two horizontal lines extending long from south to north;
at their ends, one should then form a pericarp (karṇikā) on both the southern and northern sides.

The practitioner should likewise write the Praṇava and the syllable Śrīṃ, as well as the name of the person to be accomplished; at the end of that, he should write the syllable Śrīṃ and the Praṇava, and place them in the center.
One should write the syllable *śrīṃ* on the upper petal, and likewise three [syllables] on the lower part;
then one should write them in sequence upon the petals in the south, north, and east.
The letters from *kṣa* ending with the *visarga*, together with the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, should be written in the corners;
having thus inscribed this yantra upon birch bark with yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
Having placed it in a pair of earthen saucers, one should then bake it with fire;
then, having removed it when it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, a person should drink the medicinal ash from the apparatus.
He shall remain under his control for as long as he lives; of this there is no doubt.
This third [method] is proclaimed as the supreme means for bringing a master under one's sway.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
When anyone has been expelled from the body by anyone else,
then, through great exertion, one should cause the divine wrath to descend.
Likewise, a wise person should prepare a divine [diagram] using Tamodanā;
with Gorocanā and saffron, one should draw a hexagon on birch bark or a lotus leaf.
A person should write the syllable *hrīṃ* in each corner and in the central region;
furthermore, one should write the syllables *hrīṃ* at the end of each corner, as well as on the outside of the enclosure.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center, enclosed by the syllable *hrīṃ*;
one should then write four letters, including the [initial] letter itself, above, below, and in the middle.
Having placed the pair of bowls together, one who acts with a spirit of devotion should perform worship;
then, having drawn the second [syllable] *hrīṃ*, one should well-worship the king of yantras.
At the time of the divine [mantra], having diligently bound the yantra upon the crest-lock (śikhā),
a person should, with great speed, write down the burden while observing silence.
At that time, nothing is burned; this is the grace of the King of Yantras.
He truly becomes a divine pillar and shall attain the state of a saint in the world.
One should not draw the yantra on a fine birch bark using yellow pigment (rocanā) or saffron;
rather, the yantra consists of *hrīṃ*, *saḥ*, *vaḥ*, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and likewise *hrīṃ* and *saḥ*.
Afterwards, one should properly unwind it and draw a four-cornered [square];
then, a person should write the syllable *kaṃ* within a triangle upon the upper, lower, and middle petals.
The syllable *hrīṃ* and the syllable *sa*, and again the syllable *sa* and the syllable *hrīṃ*:
thus, one should inscribe these four seed-syllables upon each of the petals.
Having placed it in a pair of earthen bowls and worshipped it according to the ritual procedure,
the mouths of the wicked are paralyzed, and he becomes submissive in an instant.
This supreme method for deluding the wicked, known as "the removal of royal wrath," should be practiced for seven days until the task is dried up.
When the Lord becomes angry and desires to act against you both,
then, for the sake of protecting one's own life, one should write the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra.
Having brought birch-bark leaves, one should write those respective [mantras] on both;
having written the name in the middle, one should enclose it with a four-cornered line.
In this manner, one should draw a sevenfold four-cornered figure with an iron stylus;
upon that, one should then draw three petals and fourteen [others].
One should write *lā*, *lī*, *lī*, and *lū* starting from Īśāna; *la* and *lau* in the south;
likewise *le*, *va*, and *laṃ* in the eastern corner of Aṅgāra; and *laḥ* in the north.
Having thus assigned one seed-syllable to each of the twelve petals,
a person should draw a trident with a bindu in the four corners.
Having brought a large stone, one should certainly throw it upon him;
thereafter, one should go toward him, for his anger will be directed toward the north.
This great yantra of Mṛtyuñjaya is the supreme protector of life;
for even when the invincible Kāla is enraged against one, it remains effective.
Even then, this king of yantras will protect [the practitioner], of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Bhairava said:
For the sake of victory in debate, one should construct a captivating yantra.
Then, having written the name in the center, one should surround it with a circle.
Then a person should fashion a four-petalled lotus provided with seed-syllables; having applied the syllable *hrīṃ* on each petal with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
Having written [the mantra] on birch bark, one should then cast it into the midst of the wicked;
thereafter, one may go for the sake of a dispute, and victory will be attained—of this there is no doubt.
This machine called Vijaya, which is honored among the gods in disputes,
belongs to whomever it may be who desires his own success.
But when wealth is lost through the power of destiny,
the creditor demands that wealth from the debtor by means of various kinds of pressure.
When his power of reflection is in no way possible due to the absence of a physical substance,
then, for the sake of bestowing that [power] upon him, there is a great, common yantra.
70b) Neither with yellow pigment nor saffron, but on a spread sheet of birch bark,
the name of the person to be accomplished is established in the center of a six-cornered [figure].
One should draw eight *kliṃ* syllables in the corners;
one should write a single *kliṃ* syllable well-positioned above the corners.
Then one should properly encircle that excellent,
circular yantra with twenty-five *hriṃ* syllables, surrounding it like a wheel.
Then, one should again properly wrap it into a circle as before;
thereafter, one should worship this yantra according to the rules for seven days.
A wise person should worship the Goddess Mahāmāyā every day,
[reciting] the supreme Devīmāhātmya as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
One should recite [the mantra] for as long as seven days; thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
At the conclusion, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and feed two ritual assistants (kalpakas).
Thereafter, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with each verse;
by performing that oblation, even a creditor shall come under one's control.
He does not beg for wealth, yet he gives it away for the sake of trade when the attendants in the royal court become wicked.
If they constantly engage in slander and malicious conduct day and night,
then one should employ the great yantra known as "Deluder of the Wicked."
Having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a circle;
having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus there, one should then write the seed-syllables.
The letters ending in *sa* along with the *visarga* should be written everywhere on its corners;
the *praṇava* (Om) should be written in the direction of the mouth and in the four directions in sequence.
Then, one should wrap that entire square with two lines,
having inscribed it beautifully upon a birch bark leaf with one's own blood.
Having worshipped this yantra, one should cast it into the midst of milk;
all wicked ones will perish, and thereafter the kingdom shall become prosperous.
For as long as twenty-one days, one should remain right there with the yantra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which increases victory in dispute.
One should install this yantra, which removes fear in legal disputes;
having inscribed "hrīṃ" and likewise "hrīṃ" in the first row.
Below that, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and encircle it with a square;
having formed a petal in each corner as well as in the center.
In the south are the seed-syllables of Rodana and Nauhṛt, as well as Pekṣa;
in the west are the seed-syllables of Staṃbha, and likewise Īkṣa in the northwest.
In the north, one should likewise place the seeds of agitation (kṣobha-bījāni) and the eye of Īśāna;
having thus placed these twelve seeds upon the eight petals.
Having placed the King of Yantras within a pair of shallow bowls (sarāva-sampuṭa) according to the prescribed method,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with eight lamps.
Having fully honored the world-protectors and fed the young maidens,
one should then worship them with offerings and lamps in the eight directions in due order.
One should worship with diligence as long as the task is not yet accomplished;
[this applies to] legal proceedings known as victory, as well as triumph in dispute.
In disputes among kings and their lineages, one shall be victorious; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through the grace of the King of Yantras, his honor shall be exalted.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O fair-faced one, if one wishes to bring [the deity] under control for as long as one lives,
then one should fashion a *yantra* dedicated to Gaṇapati that bestows success.
Having obtained birch bark that is even, free from holes,
and smeared with the blood of the ring finger as well as the ichor of an elephant;
Having combined the juice of barley, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā),
and these four ingredients, one should indeed draw [the design] with sandalwood wood.
O fair-faced one, seven *hrīṃ* syllables are to be inscribed in the upper row;
in the lower row, however, one should likewise inscribe *kroṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *klīṃ*.
Then, in the third row, [one should place] the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (sādhyanāma), followed by the scent (gandha),
and likewise the seed-syllables *klīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, the word "knife" (*kartī*), and again *hrīṃ* and *hrīṃ*.
In a single row, one should likewise write four *hrīṃ* syllables as the fourth; thus, twenty-two identical seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be inscribed.
One should properly encircle the western end [of the grid] in the east, west, and north;
then, facing east, one should carefully inscribe thirty-three letters beginning with the letter *ga*.
Having brought black-colored earth from a fertile field,
one should fashion Gaṇapati and place the yantra within his belly.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should joyfully recite this mantra:
"O Lord, please perform this mantra for me throughout my life."
Having recited this mantra and drawn [the design] measuring one cubit,
one should cast the dust of the path of the Gaṇas there and fill it with earth.
One shall remain under control for as long as life lasts through the grace of the Gaṇarāja;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for bringing people under one's influence.
Having written the name in the center, one should write the vowel *ī* below it;
"Oṃ namo namaḥ" should be written on the western and eastern petals.
Oṃ, one should write "Ajite Ajite" on the right and the left;
this is the captivating King of Yantras named "The Subjugator of Kings."
A man devoted to celibacy should worship daily for three days,
using gold, silver, or especially a silk thread.
One should wear the yantra on the back, at the base of the arm, or on the neck;
this is declared to be the rule for all yantras whatsoever.
O Goddess, by wearing this yantra, one becomes fortunate, handsome, and beloved by one's own kin; of this there is no doubt.
It should be written with camphor, saffron, gorocana, agallochum, and keśara.
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, listen to this most auspicious great yantra for subjugating the world:
camphor, musk, sandalwood, and likewise gorocana.
Having engraved [the syllables] with a *jāti* wood pen within the five seed-syllables of the *yantra*,
one should subsequently engrave the letter *ṭha* in the third row.
The syllable *u* is the name of the world, and the syllable *ṭha* follows immediately after;
then the syllable *hrīṃ*—in this way, indeed, is the pentad of seed-syllables within the Peaceful One (*Śānta*).
One should certainly inscribe the syllable *ṭha* in the fourth [square] of that as well;
having thus inscribed the seed-syllables, one should establish the four corners.
Having encased the supreme, great-bodied [amulet] that brings the world under control within two lines and wrapped it with three metals, one should wear it on the middle of the arm.
The world shall be under his control as long as the yantra remains,
provided that he first worships it constantly at the beginning of all rituals such as the worship of the deity within the yantra.
When one's own servant is enraged, he may reveal everything;
indeed, it is impossible to deny [the truth] by means of considerations of place, time, or power.
And likewise, for the purpose of deluding others while establishing one's own objective,
that which is called the Paiśācaka yantra should be constructed by the wise.
Having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a circle;
with effort, one should fashion a beautiful four-petalled lotus adorned with seed-syllables.
A person should write four *hrīṃ* syllables in the middle of the petals and in the four directions on birch bark with a pen and yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
Then, one should place that excellent and auspicious yantra into the midst of curd;
by the grace of this king of yantras, he [the target] will surely become submissive.
This supreme [mantra] called Yaṃtrapiśācikā, which brings servants under one's control,
must not be given to just anyone; this was spoken by Rudra himself.
When a master of cruel nature is served by people, he remains ever difficult to approach; even while being served, he indeed continues to be angry.
A king who is always surrounded by harsh men and is himself of wicked conduct— whether he be of high birth or low, or even a barbarian— will fall into a state of incompetence.
One should construct the Kālānala Yantra for the purpose of bringing [the target] under control;
the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be written within the interior of the syllable *hrīṃ*.

Furthermore, having written the *ikāra* mantra with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) upon a birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*), one should likewise write the syllable *hrīṃ* in the very same manner as that which is called the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*).
Having fashioned a long, triangular figure with three repetitions of four corners and provided with flour,
one should make an image of Rājikā from its dust.
One should cast the great Kālānala yantra of that [deity] into the center of the heart;
having worshipped the image there, one should bury it at the side of the hearth.
Then, for the pleasure of the guardians of the directions, an offering of food mixed with goat's blood, as well as incense, should be presented as a bali-oblation.
Oṃ, svāhā to Mahākāla!
With this mantra, one should likewise offer oblations one hundred and eight times;
at that very time, however, the offering should consist of cooked rice mixed with clarified butter and red flowers.
This [mantra] named Yaṃtrakālānala is worshipped even by the thirty gods;
it is for those engaged in trade, for the sake of commerce, or for the sake of gaining profit.
When any person among them becomes wicked,
whether he be a local official or even a sovereign, then one should employ this yantra.
One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the center of the interior of the syllable *hrīṃ*;
thereafter, one should place them above and then in the four directions in due order.
Afterwards, one should enclose the yantra with four sides using two lines;
one should then arrange two tridents in each of the four corners.
Having thus fashioned this excellent yantra and having worshipped it with diligence,
[one should write] with one's own blood mixed with yellow pigment (rocanā) upon a birch-bark leaf.
Having drawn [the figure] like a yantra and placed it in a secret location,
even a most cruel man becomes submissive at that very moment.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
When a powerful enemy desires to cut one down, then, for the sake of favoring oneself, one should employ a mechanical device as a protective suit.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center and encircle it with four petals;
the letter *i* and the letter *ka*, ending with the *visarga*, [should be placed] in the four directions.
Having written a single *kādyam*, one should then encircle it with a circle;
this should be drawn upon two *arka* leaves using cremation-ground ashes.
Having joined the two halves together, one should then pierce it with thorns;
one should draw and worship the yantra, which has been worshipped at night in a cremation ground.
A self-controlled man should offer a gift upon the ground;
at that very moment, an enemy becomes well-disposed, without a doubt.
The great yantra known as Kaṭukā is the supreme deluder of the wicked;
may Kālarātri, along with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity, be pleased.
Whether it be a friend, a kinsman, or even an enemy who becomes angry,
a wise person should then employ a yantra for the purpose of pacifying that anger.
Having written the name in the center, one should then pierce it with thorns,
specifically above, below, to the north, and to the south.
Then, having encircled the bindu-practice in the four directions, one should write it;
one should carefully write the syllable *huṃ* within the womb, in the middle of the bindu.
Having prepared both the right and the left [sides], one should encircle the name;
at the end, it should be joined with the syllable *huṃ*, while the center is to be written according to the prescribed method.
This [mantra] should be inscribed upon that very extensive yantra;
one should engrave it upon thorns and iron nails on a Monday.
Having placed the Goraka machine within the clay of a potter,
and having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, by that means one's anger is pacified.
The great yantra, when burnt at the proper time, is the supreme remover of immediate anger;
Jamadagni, firm in his vows, was free from anger and a speaker of truth.
"O Janaka of Rāma, you who are the manifest embodiment of pure being (sattva), obeisance to you!
Having thus recited this mantra at the conclusion of the worship, one should do so indeed daily.
In this manner, the offering of worship and ritual requisites should be performed for seven days;
on the seventh day, Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas should be fed.
And an offering (naivedya) should be presented for a month with great golden splendor;
then Krodha, through the heart-mantra and so forth, becomes pleased in an instant.
O auspicious one, one should draw three *hrīṃ* syllables in a single row;
beneath them, one should write the name of the enemy of the mind.
Then, in the third row, there should again be three *hrīṃ* syllables;
thereafter, one should properly enclose that with a line forming a square.
Then one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus and arrange the seed-syllables for each month;
one should place three instances of the syllable *hrīṃ* in the middle of each petal and arrange them in the four directions.
73a) Having placed a petal in each corner, the wise one should also place the syllable *hrīṃ*; likewise,
[he should apply] yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), musk (*mṛganābhi*), and sandalwood (*candana*).
Having unified [the elements], one should draw the yantra on a broad birch bark leaf during the bright fortnight of the moon,
while the practitioner faces north.
O fair-faced one, one should worship that yantra daily, night after night,
with various kinds of enjoyments, flowers, garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Having performed this for seven days, at its conclusion one should feed four women endowed with good fortune, numbering seven in total.
"May the Goddess, beloved of Śaṅkara, be pleased with Lalitā;
grant her beauty, grant her fame, grant her good fortune, and grant her every desire."
Having recited this mantra, one should then dismiss it;
having wrapped that yantra with a thread, one should then wear it around one's own neck.
Endowed with an auspicious form, she shall become even more beloved by her husband;
this great yantra called Lalitā brings about good fortune for women.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen attentively, O Goddess, to the yantra which is the third means of accomplishment;
having written it auspiciously, with the names of the beloved interwoven within it.
O auspicious one, two forms with distinct shapes should be drawn, one above and one below;
then, one should properly encircle them with a single circular line.
Upon its upper surface, one should write eight petals together with the syllable *hrīṃ*;
this should be inscribed on birch bark using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
One should worship daily for three days, night after night, as previously described;
then, having bathed on the fourth day, one should worship the one of auspicious limbs.
"O beloved of Anaṅga, O Goddess, may you be dear to me;
thus, O Smara-vallabhā, act to bring about my great subjugation of the beloved."
Having recited this mantra and worshipped those women,
one should fashion that yantra from metal and wear it around the neck.
By the grace of Yantrarāja, her husband shall become a servant;
incomparable good fortune arises for her—of this there is no doubt.
She does not go to her husband's kin, being adorned with all auspiciousness;
she, as an *ekā-suvāsinī*, is to be worshipped on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
This yantra, which increases good fortune and should be worshipped constantly for the sake of pleasure and affection in every fortnight,
must never be given to those women [who are unfaithful].
The illustrious Bhairava said:
I shall now proclaim the method for bringing women under one's control; listen, O Goddess, to this most auspicious [teaching].
[It is prepared] with *rocanā*, saffron, sandalwood, and musk.
The yantra should be inscribed upon birch bark with a stylus made of *jāti* wood;
first [the seed-syllables] *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, then the name, and likewise again *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*.
Having thus performed the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭita*), one should encircle the four corners; having carefully inscribed two seed-syllables (*bīja*) above and below as well.
Aiṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, and likewise Akṣiṃ, and Aiṃ again at the end;
likewise, the seed-syllables Aiṃ, Hrīṃ, and Klīṃ are also placed in the corners and the directions.
An image of Madana should be fashioned from wood;
having placed the yantra within it, one should worship it in all respects.
Every night, at the end of each day, one should perform [the worship] daily with auspicious enjoyments, various perfumes, incenses, lamps, and fruits.
When this is performed, that woman will certainly become a slave;
[this is] the supreme yantra known as Śrī Kāmarāja, which brings about subjugation.
In this [rite], people should worship with sandalwood and not with mustard seeds;
Kāma, Anaṅga, Pañcaśara, Kandarpa, and Mīnaketana [are the names of the deity].
"O Lord, son of Śrī Viṣṇu, be gracious to me, O Master"—
this mantra should be recited until she comes under one's control.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this yantra, which crushes the pride of the arrogant; it is exceedingly rare in the world and destroys the fame of those who are conceited.

With the blood of a horse, one should write the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), as well as *hrīṃ*, and the individual letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*).
All the letters of the name should be enclosed by the syllable *hrīṃ*;
likewise, the *praṇava* (oṃ) should be written at the beginning and at the end in a single line.
Then, one should properly enclose that with a line forming a square,
and having drawn [lines] above and below, one should place the seed-syllable in its "encased" form as before.
In the horizontal portion, in two rows, one should form the *tantrasampuṭa* as before;
having made a petal-shape in the corner, one should place the *madanotkṛti* in the center.
Having thus carefully drawn the yantra and a beautiful image of Madana,
one should fashion it from wood, show it to the mind, and place it within the heart.
One should make the heart vulnerable so that the yantra remains well-established;
having wrapped it, one should certainly cast the yantra clearly upon his chest.
Then, having worshipped me with red sandalwood and garlands for twenty-one days, she came into the presence of his mouth.
Hereafter, I shall explain that which brings a king’s wife under control,
so that by the casting of a mere glance she becomes as if struck by the arrows of Love.
74a) Seeing it, women intoxicated by passion fall down suddenly;
furthermore, a person should not write with yellow pigment (rocanā) or saffron on birch bark.
The yantra, together with camphor, should be fashioned according to the prescribed rite upon a *jātī* wood block;
the name of the person [to be protected] is established in the center of that hexagon.
The syllable *krīṃ* should be written everywhere above the corners on all sides;
however, in the intermediate space of the eastern corner, one should write two instances of the syllable *hrīṃ*.
One should likewise write the syllable *hrīṃ* in the middle of the corner, situated toward the east;
one should encircle all of that with a beautiful, circular line.
One should draw three petals in the south and likewise one petal in the northeast; one should inscribe the syllable *hrīṃ* in the middle of each petal in due order.
Having thus drawn the yantra, one should worship it with a spirit of devotion,
wearing white garments oneself, using perfumes, flowers, incense, and food offerings.
One should meditate upon that woman standing before the yantra at night;
one should do this for seven days, and at its conclusion, [feed] three Brahmins.
Having fed her with various kinds of foods, thinking "may Kāmākṣā be pleased," the practitioner should give a sacrificial fee according to his ability and feed his own wife.
Having encased it with three metals, he should wear it at the base of his arm;
upon seeing it, the king’s beloved was tormented by the blazing fire of passion.
One should always personally seek [this], for what else could be said regarding other women? Hereafter, I shall proclaim my own singular practice of great fruit.
Whoever constantly wears it shall become most beloved by women;
and whatever woman wears it with devotion shall become possessed of good fortune.
This seed-syllable generates good fortune, especially for men;
this syllable of the seed must be kept secret and should not be given to just anyone.
The letter *sa*, the letter *ha*, the letter *ka*, and likewise the letter *ra*,
the letter *da*, and that which is established in the vowel *i*.
In this manner, one should gradually join the group of six syllables,
conjoined with the vowel *i* and adorned with the *bindu*.
A person should write [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment mixed with water;
having performed worship for three days, one should then encase it in gold.
A man should wear the king of seed-syllables at the base of his arms, and a woman on her neck; for it clearly destroys misfortune.
"Which produces great good fortune and was previously proclaimed by Śrī Śiva," [thus] Śrī Bhairava said.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the yantra that bestows good fortune;
this yantra, known as Karaṇa, is specifically prescribed for women alone.
By retaining this very [mantra], even a barren goddess shall become pregnant;
and a woman whose children have died shall likewise [attain success] through this supreme yantra.
One should wear it; then the goddess Jīvaputrā will be born, of this there is no doubt. One should then write [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma).
One should first write the Praṇava, and immediately after that, the syllable Hrīṃ;
then follows the Lord Ramanātha, established with the syllable Hrīṃ at its end.
One should assign the letter *ha* in the middle of the petals in the four directions;
one should also write the syllable *krauṃ* once each above and below.
One should place the letter *ha* in the middle of the petals in the four directions;
likewise, one should write the syllable *oṃ*, as well as *hrīṃ* and the letter *ya*.
Furthermore, these four seed-syllables should be written within the interior;
they should be written in each corner and on each petal, O practitioner, as well as in the central region.
Having thus drawn the yantra, one should worship it for three days and feed a single couple, saying, "May the Lord of the World be pleased."
Afterwards, having especially wound it with threads and encircled it with gold, one should fashion it into a circle and wear it in the middle of a necklace.
O Goddess, from its retention arises incomparable and great good fortune;
she shall surely have living children, and barrenness is pacified.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, the great yantra called Kāmalā was created by Brahmā; it must not be given to just anyone by a practitioner.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the visualization of the yantra alone,
using red sandalwood mixed with one's own blood upon a birch-bark leaf.
Then, having written the name in the center, one should surround it with a circle;
thereafter, one should fashion a four-petaled lotus, beautiful and joined with the seed-syllable.
One should then inscribe the syllable *huṃ* sequentially upon each petal; having thus properly prepared the yantra, one should worship it with pleasing offerings of oblations and flowers.
One should cast it into the midst of clarified butter; attraction shall occur after three days.
This yantra is to be kept strictly secret and must be guarded with great effort.
It must not be given to just anyone if one desires success for oneself;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the great Traipuraka yantra.
A person should write [the mantra] on birch bark using a mixture of yellow pigment (rocanā) and liquid;
having written the name in the center, it should be auspiciously enclosed by the syllable *huṃ*.
One should draw a hexagon, beautiful with the name placed within its center; from the letter *sau*, one should write [the letters] in the corners, adorned with a *bindu* in the middle.
Having thus thoroughly worshipped the yantra, one should place it in the midst of ghee;
one should recite the mantra daily at all times and again offer prayers to Tripurā.
O Great-Velocity One, draw forth Devadatta, who is dear to me;
O Goddess of the gods, may she grant him to you in Tripura.
One should pray with this mantra and accomplish the Tripura yantra;
when this is done, O auspicious one, attraction occurs on the seventh day.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious method for subduing an arrogant woman,
which is a secret of all yantras and bestows accomplishment at that very moment.
This king of yantras, which is extremely difficult to accomplish, must not be told to just anyone.
One should draw it on the palm of the left hand with blood from the ring finger.
A person should likewise write the Praṇava (Oṃ) and "klīṃ klīṃ" in this row;
below that, he should write the triad "tryaṃ tryaṃ" in sequence for each element.
O lady of virtuous vows, one should also write the name of his beloved below that;
thereafter, O dear one, one should encircle the triangles above the seed-syllables.
Having performed this and worshipped right there with auspicious flowers, that woman will arrive within a single watch (yāma); of this there is no doubt.
The yantra known as Śrī Kāmarāja is difficult to obtain even for the gods;
therefore, I shall now fully describe the yantra called Devamātṛkā.
O Goddess, hear about the great fruit of attracting men and women:
[one should apply] lac juice, turmeric, and madder upon birch bark.
One should diligently write this supreme yantra in a secluded place;
having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a triangle.
Thereafter, O beloved, one should carefully wrap that [thread] into a circle;
upon it, the sixteen vowels beginning with 'A' should be inscribed.
Then, one should encircle it entirely with lines numbering as many as the eyes [nine], and then,
using the dust from its own feet, one should fashion a Śālabhañjikā figure.
Having condensed the King of Yantras and well-consecrated it within her womb,
when this is done, she will undoubtedly be drawn forth and arrive.
What is the use of speaking much here? One should bring forth this king of yantras, which is equal to the Lord himself, highly secret, O God, and known by the name Mātṛkā.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this great yantra which paralyzes all enemies;
in disputes and legal proceedings, one will certainly become a stammerer at the mouth.
When discord arises due to the influence of an untimely woman,
then one should employ the supreme great yantra known as the Tongue-Piercer.
One should well-draw and carefully polish a six-compartment grid upon a birch leaf using yellow pigment (rocanā), using two sets of lines.
One should write the seed-syllable in the middle of the enclosure; the lover goes together with [the beloved] as a single unit.
Then follow the letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, and immediately after that, the letter *la*.
The letter *va* and the letter *ra*, established with the letter *ya* at the end,
joined with the vowel *u* and adorned with the letter *ra* on its head.
The six letters joined in union, conjoined with a single bindu and half [a bindu],
united with two vowels and adorned with a bindu.
In this way, the seed known as "mouth-paralysis" (mukhastaṃbhana) is produced;
indeed, one should inscribe each of these excellent seeds individually within every single chamber.
In this way, having inscribed the seed-syllables on the second line,
one should place them above the seeds, with the divisions of the corners in the four directions.
Above the outer line, tridents should be drawn over the head;
at the end, one should draw tridents all around in sequence.
In this manner, twenty-two [deities] are established upon the tips of the tridents;
one should likewise draw them in sequence everywhere within the intervals of the tridents and above.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the beautiful pillar for the procession;
it should be beautifully inscribed with yellow pigment within a casket of veins.
Rocanā, yellow orpiment, turmeric, realgar,
and saffron— these are declared to be the yellow substances.
A person should write the seed-syllables of the Kumbhamohana mantra in a single line;
beneath that, he should write the name, established at the end of the word "mohana."
Then one should properly enclose that with a line, making it four-cornered;
and in each corner, as well as in the center, one should likewise draw a trident.
Having thus fashioned eight tridents situated upon the yantra,
one should worship the most beautiful King of Yantras with yellow flowers.
Having thus worshipped the yantra with incense, lamps, and food offerings accompanied by various acts of devotion, one should then cast it into the middle of the earth.
Having filled [the area] with earth in a level place, one should diligently cause the movement of the machine above it to be arrested; thus, by means of reflection, the "avam" should be performed.
Just as even vessels that have been sown do not always come to fruition for me,
so now, O beautiful one, I shall fully explain the paralyzing of speech.
This yantra, renowned on earth as the "Paralyzer of the Opponent's Mouth," should be drawn with yellow pigments in the center of a stone casket.
Having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a triangle;
thereafter, one should properly enclose that again with a circle drawn with a line.
76a) Thereafter, one should fashion eight petals upon that;
in the middle of each petal, one should place the seed-syllable *la*, adorned with a *bindu*.
In this manner, one should draw [the deity] upon an eight-petaled lotus and worship it with auspicious flowers of yellow hue, as well as with incense, lamps, and auspicious food offerings.
One should feed a single Brāhmaṇa with milk-rice (pāyasa) and jaggery;
then, having sat down upon the ground, the installation [of the vessel] follows as before.
The mouth of the opponent becomes paralyzed; there is no doubt about this.
O Mahādevī, this yantra, which must be kept strictly secret, has been told to you.
Karṇikāra, kulattha, campaka, svarṇaketakī,
dhattūra, pītavahidrā, and likewise nāgakeśara.
Then, O beloved, one should quickly construct an easily accessible yantra that bestows the attainment of results, having drawn it with chalk upon one's own body.
O Dear One, having written the name of the enemy in the center according to the prescribed rule,
eight lines are drawn in sequence situated above it.
One should draw a trident in each of the eight directions;
having worshipped it well right there with white flowers and auspicious fruits.
And with other white perfumes and beautiful white garments,
one should feed a single Brahmin, thinking, "May Śiva be pleased."
May this [mantra] cause the mouth to become paralyzed even in debate and in the assembly;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the captivating immobilization of fire (vahnistambha).
O fair-faced one, at an auspicious time, one should fashion a most beautiful king of yantras,
having drawn it with yellow pigment upon a birch leaf.
Without writing the name in the center, one should write the *saṃpuṭa* beginning with *kroṃ plāṃ*;
one should also write the beautiful syllable *kroṃ* above and below.
Then the Goddess should encircle it with a line to form a square;
above that, four lines should be carefully drawn.
Having written the letter *la*, adorned with a dot (*bindu*), within the intermediate corners,
one should likewise write four such seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the letter *la*.
O beloved, one should draw eight tridents at the corners in every way;
thus, one should draw the eight tridents and then worship them.
Having honored and fed a Brāhmaṇa, one should place the yantra on the ground;
having positioned the yantra in the center according to the rising and setting of the [planetary] movements.
As long as the water flows over it with a fierce roar, for that long the great pillar remains burnt; of this there is no doubt.
This yantra, named Divyasaṃstambhana, is highly honored by the gods;
it should not be given to just anyone if one desires success for oneself.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the yantra that wards off fire;
in whichever house this yantra is situated, there shall never be any fear of fire.
For one who always and constantly holds this captivating king of yantras in his hand,
the fear of fire never arises, even in a dream.
O beloved, the taking up of the fire must be performed by force,
even when a yantra or a medicine of superior power is present.
Just as a snake, when touched by the foot, bites without any other thought,
so too, O Goddess of gods, does pride arise in people through either speech or action.
O Goddess, just as the medicinal elixir removes untimely death,
so too, O Sovereign of the Gods, does the yantra remove the fear of an intermediate state.

One should smear the yantra upon birch bark (*bhūrja*) according to the prescribed rite with sandalwood paste (*śrīkhaṇḍa*), yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and snow (*hima*). Having written one's own name in the center, one should encircle it well with a circular line.
Above that, one should certainly draw a petal adorned with a dot (*bindu*).
Having encircled all of this— namely the east, the south, the west, and again the north— one should draw a four-cornered [mandala] with a line.
Having encased it with the three metals, one should place it at the base of the arm,
or else in the middle of the arm, or finally, immerse it in milk.
Having thus constantly worshipped him, who bestows victory like a god,
whatever fear may arise in him from the presence of fire—
One should feed a single Brāhmaṇa for the satisfaction of Yaṃtrarāja.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe that which causes the subjugation of one's beloved.
O fair-faced one, when anyone approaches by force even though he has been restrained, then one should perform that paralyzing rite whenever he becomes slightly smiling.
Whatever fruit arises from a mixture with yellow liquid that results in suffering,
one should draw the yantra on a piece of chalk or in a vessel made of wood.
The letter *ya* is established in the center of the womb with the name of the person to be accomplished;
then, one should properly encircle it with a line forming a quadrangle.
Above that, the wise one should draw a second square;
he should make the corners have the shape of petals, with [lines] here and there in the central region.
O Dear One, one should write the letter *la* joined with the *bindu* in the center;
having thus written and worshipped this supreme yantra according to the rules.
One should fasten a water-pot upside down in the middle of the house;
there, O Goddess, a paralysis shall occur— of this there is no need for deliberation.
Nevertheless, even after having gone there and brought that minister under his control,
I shall now proceed to explain the supreme method for paralyzing an enemy.
Having drawn [the diagram] with chalk, one should place it within a stone casket;
therein, in the center of the interior, is the syllable *hrīṃ*, established with the name of the person to be accomplished.
Then one should properly encircle it with a line to form a quadrangle;
having thus drawn this supreme quadrangular yantra, the supreme diagram.
In the corners at the end, one should draw four tridents in each of the four directions;
one should worship this yantra according to the rules with auspicious flowers.
Having written [the mantra] within a casket and placed the yantra in an auspicious spot, the mouth of the enemy will be paralyzed at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the Picchūna yantra,
the most excellent, which, O fair-faced one, paralyzes the speech, movement, and intellect of an enemy.
One should write a very beautiful yantra with yellow pigment (rocanā) on birch bark;
the syllable derived from the name should be enclosed by the syllable *kro*.
Then, the second syllable is enclosed by the syllable *hrīṃ*,
