and as many syllables as there are in the name, they too are similarly encapsulated.
Then, one should encircle it entirely with a line in the form of a square;
in each corner, one should fashion a petal, encapsulated by the long seed-syllable.
The letter *ya*, the letter *ma*, and likewise the letter *ra*;
the letter *i*, the letter *va*, and immediately after that, the letter *ya*.
In this manner, one should sequentially join the group of six syllables,
conjoined with the vowel *u* and adorned upon its head.
One should draw [the seed-syllable] joined with the *bindu* and *nāda* in the middle of the petal;
having thus drawn the seed-syllable upon the petal, O goddess worshipped by the gods.
One should draw the syllable *kroṃ* in the intervals between the petals and likewise in the four directions;
having thus drawn the yantra, one should worship it with red sandalwood.
O Brahmasambhava, a beautiful woman should offer red flowers, garments, and her own blood as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to her capacity.
One should feed the Brahmins afterwards and must not practice stinginess regarding wealth;
thereafter, one should have the yantra drawn and deposit it within the ground.
O fair-faced goddess, by [this means], a slanderer instantly becomes paralyzed in body, paralyzed in movement, and paralyzed in speech; of this there is no doubt.
77b) The Goddess said:
I bow to that Tvaritā, who was worshipped by Rāmacandra upon seeing Rāvaṇa slain in battle by her glance.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen with diligence, O Goddess, to this diagram that increases misfortune,
by which constant strife between men and women arises.
O fair-faced Mahādevī, one should not write the yantra on a birch bark leaf using yellow pigment or saffron, for it destroys various forms of good fortune.
O lady of beautiful smiles, one should draw horizontal lines situated from east to west; indeed, one should make eight long lines within the grid-square.
And in the middle and upper portions of that, one should write each [syllable] in sequence;
in the center, the letter of the nose (nāsākṣara), the goddess, twice again and again.
In the center of that, one should neither place nor draw a wheel;
instead, one should write "Ajite" at the top, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*.
Having thus inscribed the yantra, one should go to the bank of a river;
auspicious earth should be taken from both banks by one who observes silence.
Having made Gaṇapati [the presiding deity], she should place the yantra within his belly;
O beautiful one, she should perform the consecration of the King of the Gaṇas with cow’s milk.
Then, one should worship with various flowers and many modakas;
having honored the children with edible offerings, one should say, "May Gaṇeśa be pleased."
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the King of the Gaṇas, O lady of pure smiles,
one should place him within a hollowed pair of shallow bowls and set it down upon that vessel.
One should place the mantras "Aghora" and "Amogha" upon the casket;
having placed the casket on the ground, one should bury it and then worship it.
O lady of virtuous vows, having encountered incomparable misfortune, even a woman of beautiful form sinks in despair day and night along with her husband.
A woman cannot endure a yantra applied to a man's body;
O Goddess, this is always the supreme secret that causes estrangement between husband and wife.
O my beloved, this yantra must not be employed for any other purpose;
it should not be given to just anyone, for otherwise it will produce contrary results.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite for inciting enmity among enemies;
through it, a great mutual hatred arises among foes.
O fair-faced one, on the fourteenth day, one who is intent on causing enmity should write [the name] upon a cloth from a cemetery using a pen made from a crow's feather.
Then, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* and the syllable *a* joined with a *bindu*,
and thereafter, the third *hrīṃ* syllable, all written in a single line.
Then, below that row, one should encircle the name within a four-petaled lotus;
thereafter, one should fashion another four-petaled lotus adorned with two [syllables] denoting hatred.
Likewise, it should be drawn within the circle, and similarly in the central region;
the blood-offering (naivedya) should consist of blood mixed with goat's blood.
Then, O fair-faced one, having worshipped the yantra with offerings of leaves and flowers at night,
one should diligently worship the Guru and feed a single Yoginī.
There is no doubt that the yantra should be installed in a temple of Śiva or in a cremation ground; however, it should never be installed in a house.
Hatred toward enemies arises in due course, without a doubt;
indeed, there is no king of yantras that yields such great fruit as this, which causes all enemies to be filled with hatred.
Having observed this at the end of the ritual procedure in a secluded place,
I shall now fully explain the supreme method for inciting enmity among kinsmen.
On a cloth from a cremation ground, one should write with a pen made of a crow’s feather,
using charcoal produced from a cremation ground ground with the blood of a ram.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should then encircle it with a triangle;
having written the letter *ra* above and below, this should be drawn on the nights of the spirits (*bhūta-rātri*).
Then one should properly encircle it with a line forming a square,
and at each corner, four tridents should be drawn.
It should be drawn equally in the four directions, situated above the four lines;
thus one should draw the yantra, and having worshipped it again as before.
Then, having drawn [the lines] seven finger-breadths wide, one should fill the center of the ground;
subsequently, during their journeys and on the road, one should cast [the contents] right there.
Great mutual hatred arises among kinsmen;
even she who falls at one's feet becomes a vessel for misfortune.
There is no doubt that this occurs through the power of the King of Yantras. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the incantation for causing enmity among one's own kin and servants.
On the fourteenth day, at the dead of night, one should write [the mantra] on a cloth in a cemetery using a stylus made of some kind of wood, with ink mixed with poison.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished within the center and then encircle it with a circle;
furthermore, one should place three *rakāra*s above and below that.
The letter *ya* should be written first, with two seed-syllables in the transverse position;
the letter *ya* and the letter *ra*, ending with the *visarga*, are established there.
Having thus drawn the yantra, one should then encircle it with a circle;
having thus drawn the yantra, one should bury it on their path.
Great hatred between master and servant is always born [from this];
as long as the yantra remains on the ground, the mutual enmity continues.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the supreme yantra known as Bhayānaka, which causes aversion toward the world and increases misfortune.
Furthermore, for the purpose of writing down misfortune, one should use a pen made from the blood of a crow or an owl, or the blood of a Rishabha, along with a quill made from a crow's feather.
O Dear One, one should scratch the name of the person to be accomplished upon a birch leaf at night;
on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should draw the captivating yantra.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the center, surrounded by the syllable *ṭha*;
one should always surround it with an odd number of *ṭha* syllables.
Then, having surrounded it with a circle, one should surround it with *durbhaga* grass;
having properly established this yantra on the ground or in the midst of grass.
As long as that [enemy] remains in his house or at his workshop, he too will always be present in that house;
until then, he becomes an enemy to the entire world—of this there is no doubt.
As for the sequence of worship, the previously mentioned yantra always [brings success] to men;
Śrī Bhairava said:
Hereafter I shall describe the yantra that utterly destroys enemies.
Having carefully drawn this yantra upon a human skull, [one should proceed].
Having ground charcoal from a cremation ground with the juice of *dhattūra* in a skull-cup,
the practitioner, with a steady mind, should draw [the diagram] in the cremation ground itself.
Afterwards, one should encircle the triangle, adorned with two rows of dots;
moreover, O fair-faced one, an upward line should be drawn everywhere.
Having placed [the offering] in a pair of shallow bowls (sarāva-sampuṭa), one should thoroughly worship that yantra with offerings of meat,
blood, and water, especially with one's own blood.
One should bury this yantra in that very place where one intends to perform worship;
by that very process, one shall suffer from a great disease and subsequently meet death.
By offering a bali-oblation consisting of a single living being, he indeed lives once [the victim] has been extracted;
otherwise, he goes to the city of Naciketas—of this there is no need for deliberation.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
79a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the yantra that destroys enemies;
it brings about the death even of a powerful foe, and not otherwise.
A person should write [the mantra] on birch bark with poison and yellow orpiment,
having first written the name of the target (sādhya) using a pen made from a crow’s feather.
The procedure for writing is exactly the same as that previously stated for the rite of killing;
what is the use of repeating it again and again? It would only serve to cause prolixity in the book.
The syllable *hrīṃ* is established in the center of the womb, with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) situated therein;
then one should properly encircle it with a triangle as before by means of the three [syllables].
Having drawn a trident in every corner, one should then perform worship;
the procedure for worship that has been declared applies everywhere, even in rites of killing.
One should cast the well-consecrated yantra into the hollow of a human foot;
having cast it, one should place the tube together with the yantra upon the ground of a cremation ground.
His death occurs suddenly; there is no doubt about this.
The previously mentioned favor applies everywhere, even in the case of killing.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Henceforth, I shall explain the rite of killing for those born in distant lands:
one should grind charcoal from a cremation ground together with the blood of a goat.
Having ground poison itself, one should cast it into a human skull;
and having written [the mantra] upon a cover, using a pen made from a crow's feather.
One should draw the sādhana-āmali in the center, auspiciously encased by the syllable *hūṃ*;
then one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus and install it in the house as prescribed.
Having inscribed "huṃ phaṭ" in the four directions in the middle of the petals,
one should then properly encircle that with two circular lines.
O Dear One, one should subsequently encircle it on all sides with *huṃ* syllables joined together;
then, O Auspicious One, one should fill that casket within the *mela* with ashes.
Having placed it before the form and filled it as prescribed,
fever arises even for an enemy who has gone to another country.
Every day, however, Sundarī would kindle it little by little;
on the twenty-first day, she ignited it completely throughout the night.
At that very moment, O beloved, the death of the enemy occurs.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the method of killing all embodied beings:
one should plant [the seed] with human blood and charcoal from a cremation ground.
Likewise, one should write [the mantra] with poison on a cloth from a cremation ground;
having written the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), one should likewise include *huṃ phaṭ* three times.
O fair-faced one, having thus drawn it three times in three rows,
one should then properly encircle it with three circular lines.
One should fashion an image out of mustard seeds and the dust from the feet of an enemy;
having inserted a yantra into its heart-center, one should slowly heat it in a crucible.
For the enemy, burning and grief arise gradually, step by step,
just as a headache manifests on the third great day.
If there is pain in the hands and feet, death will occur on the seventh day;
this shall happen without doubt, and there is no uncertainty that he will not be released.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the method of killing all embodied beings,
as well as the yantra for both women and men;
one should draw it upon a leaf of the *vibhītaka* tree using ashes from a cremation ground.
Having mixed the menstrual blood together, one should write the name of the person to be subdued in the center with a pen made from a crow's feather,
joined with the *sābhani* mantra upon a pillar.
Then, having encircled a triangle and likewise a pentagon above it,
one should cast the man into the hell and worship the man with a thread.
Then, by the power of that thread, one should worship the Goddess who arises from it;
thereafter, one should bury it in the center of the earth or in a cremation ground at night.
Thereafter, after the restraint, the enemy dies within seven nights from the sight of a friend; the method of release is indeed as previously stated.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite for the eradication of enemies; O fair-faced one, it should be written with the blood of a nameless finger on a birch-bark leaf.
O Gaṇapati, one should know that the syllable *praṇava* and so forth are dispatched;
having written them in a single row, as well as the *huṃ* and the name itself.
Having written the second [syllable] in the row, one should then write the third;
having written "huṃ gandhaḥ svāhā," the person should proceed in due order.
Then one should properly enclose that with two lines forming a square;
the goddess wears red garments and has red unguents as her ointment.
On the fourteenth day, during the great night, the practitioner should draw [the mandala] in due order and perform worship with red flowers, red perfumes, and auspicious fruits.
A maiden [should offer] food at night, and a sacrificial fee according to one's ability;
the beautiful woman [should perform] meditation upon the God of gods, Gaṇanātha.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for immediate eradication:
one should draw a crow using poison on a palm leaf and indeed on a *pannaka* leaf.

On a writing tablet made from a skull-bone found in a cremation ground, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished using a pen made from a monkey’s tail; subsequently, one should write the word *vāyasodara* in the center.
The previously mentioned procedure is prescribed for both worship and transcription;
however, that skull should be turned face down, with its tip measuring only a *lava* toward the south.
One who is self-restrained should tie [the mantra] to the right side of a Vibhītaka tree at night;
when this is done, on the third day, there shall be expulsion from one's place by means of the syllable *hrīṃ*.
O Lord, as long as this machine remains situated there, the man who is anxious will find no happiness anywhere, even in his own home.
There will be travel abroad for him, and his life will be lived in uncertainty.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Hereafter, I shall explain the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) for all embodied beings.
A person should write [the mantra] on birch bark with the blood of a crow and an owl.
Then, having written the name in the center, one should surround it with a circle;
thereafter, one should fashion a four-petalled lotus adorned with three lines.
Established within the belly of the letter *ya* and ending with the visarga,
the sequence of worship is as previously described, yet it is devoid of even meditation.
Having broken that yantra into pieces and mixed them with leftover rice,
it should be given day after day for the crows to eat.
Having abandoned the country, he surely departs; what then need be said of a village? Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme yantra for eradication.
It should be written with the juice of nimba leaves using a pen made from a crow’s feather;
it is enclosed within a birch-bark leaf, for the ritual procedure is indeed as previously described.
Then, having written the name in the center, one should encircle it with a circle;
thereafter, one should fashion a beautiful four-petaled lotus adorned with seed-syllables.
Having worshipped the seed-syllables "ra-vau-ha" individually in the center of each petal as before, one should then bury them and subsequently worship [the deity].
Then, having turned that machine face-down according to the previously mentioned procedure, if this is done, it will cause expulsion on the seventh day; not otherwise.
Wandering through one's own country and foreign lands alike, one is treated with contempt like a blade of grass.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the yantra for the expulsion of women;
it should be drawn with the blood of a donkey using a pen made from a crow's feather.
Having drawn [the design] upon a wooden board, one should then encircle it with a circle;
thereafter, an eight-petaled lotus, beautiful and adorned with seed-syllables, should be fashioned.
Having carefully drawn the yantra with the letter *kha* ending in the visarga, followed immediately by the syllable *hrīṃ*, one should worship it according to the prescribed ritual.
Having buried it in the ground and filled it up as before, yet with the face turned downwards,
one causes [the target] to be expelled from their place or to move like a leaf in the wind.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme rite for the eradication of the three worlds:
a man should write [the mantra] upon birch bark with the blood of a black cock.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should then encircle it with a triangle;
O fair-faced one, having again drawn a second triangle, one should surround it.
Above that, in the division, there should be four instances of the syllable *hrīṃ*;
having drawn this division with twelve seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Then, having drawn a circle, one should worship it again as before;
having performed this, the son should bind that yantra around his neck.
Just as it is devoid of number, so indeed in this world,
O celestial nymph, one shall undoubtedly cause [the enemy] to be expelled in that very instant.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme yantra for eradication;
it should be written on birch bark with the juices of night-stalkers, without a doubt.
Having written the name of the person for whom the rite is intended, one should then encircle it with a circle;
having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus around that, it should be beautiful and endowed with seed-syllables.
Then, one should write "phaṭ" in each of the middle of the petals;
thereafter, one should properly encircle it by drawing a single circle.
After worshipping it according to the prescribed rules, one should then crush the yantra;
if it is administered in food or drink, expulsion occurs with certainty.
I bow down to Rāma, who formerly went to the forest at the command of Janaka’s daughter, and having crossed it, reached the end of the cold [Himālayas].
I shall now declare the ritual procedure which destroys all calamities;
it brings peace, nourishment, and happiness within the seventh chapter.
This [tantra] known by the name Śāntirakṣākara is renowned as difficult to find everywhere;
it should not be given to just anyone if one desires success for oneself.
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret yantra which provides ultimate protection;
it is known to grant great protection to children, women, and men alike.
Furthermore, on an auspicious day and a favorable lunar date, one should write [the mantra] upon a bell-metal plate using yellow pigment (rocanā),
saffron, and especially camphor.
A person should draw eight vertical lines with sticks of *jāti* wood smeared with musk; these lines are situated there upon the chest.
If there are nine compartments in this manner, designated as a row,
then the vowels beginning with 'a' should be written, having been inscribed in that very same way.
The consonants should be written in sequence, yet not in that same sequential order;
having thus written the seed-syllables, one should then write the tridents.
One should certainly draw a boundary line on the other side, sequentially in the four directions;
six *kroṃ* syllables are to be written in the east and likewise in the west.
Having thus drawn that yantra, one should worship it with a spirit of devotion using white lotuses,
blue lotuses, and charming hundred-petaled lotuses.
And with *mālatī*, *yūthikā*, *ketaka*, and *mallika* flowers, as well as *vakula* and whatever *phalakeya* and *phalodbhava* flowers were available.
One should carefully avoid a flower that is red in color but lacks fragrance;
[one should worship] with camphor, betel leaves, incense, perfumes, and white utpala lotuses.
Having thus worshipped for three days with various food offerings, O Dear One,
one should daily recite the Saptaśatī while feeding Brāhmaṇas for those three days.
Having fed him with milk-rice mixed with as much ghee as desired,
he should sleep on the ground for three days following the meal, the application of fragrant unguents, and the feeding.
Having extracted [the essence] and formed it into a pill, one should then encase it with the three metals; O fair-faced one, one should likewise drink the remaining liquid and apply it to the hands.
The agitation of a fool arises when he is indeed employed by means of the vidyā.
O Goddess, one should wear the pill at the base of the arm or on the neck.
By wearing that yantra, misfortune is dispelled,
as are ill fortune, quarrels, and especially bad luck.
Whatever has been performed by another, all of that perishes;
even the rites known as *śāntika* and *pauṣṭika* are difficult to obtain even for the gods.
First is that which is called the King of Yantras, which produces all forms of conviction.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the yantra that wards off thieves;
when this yantra is held in the palm of one's hand, there is no fear of snakes or tigers.
81b) The procedure for writing is as previously stated, and the materials are indeed those previously mentioned.
In all cases of pacification (*śāntika*), O Goddess, no other procedure exists.
The worship is exactly as previously described, and for this [deity] as well, one's own [mantra] is likewise [to be used].
Having inscribed the second excellent yantra upon birch bark, [one should proceed].
The syllable Hrīṃ is situated in the center of the womb, with the name of the person to be accomplished established therein;
O Goddess, the syllable A should then be joined immediately after that.
The letter *la*, the letter *ya*, and the letter *ya* are firmly established;
the letter *ū* joined with a vowel is the seed-syllable of peace, captivating the mind.
Then, one should properly wrap it in a square shape with two lines,
enclose it with the three metals, and place it at the base of the arm or on the neck.
It destroys the fear of snakes and tigers, as well as the fear of thieves; it wards off various calamities—there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the yantra that destroys misfortune,
especially for women and always for men as well.
The procedure for writing is as previously stated, and the materials are likewise as previously described;
having first specified the pen, a person should write upon birch bark.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should draw a triangle with two lines;
above that, a quadrangle adorned with three lines.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should place a trident in each corner;
having encased it with the three metals, it should be worn either at the base of the arm or on the neck.
Whether it be a woman or a man, one should wear this according to the prescribed rite;
it destroys various calamities and protects the fetus.
Nourished by incomparable good fortune, he always rejoices like a god.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme destroyer of fever;
this [mantra], proclaimed in the Veda, destroys fever born of malevolent spirits.
Then, on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, he should bury [the image] as before;
however, during the day, the man should remain without food in a cremation ground.
One should draw a square, and from its corners, an eight-petaled lotus as it appears;
having written the name in the center, one should then form the enclosure of the hell-dweller.
In the middle, within the interval, the letter *ra* is firmly established;
thus there shall be twenty *rephas* according to the sequence of all the tantras.
O Earth, by worshipping with beautiful offerings of flowers and oblations,
that terrible spirit in the form of fever departs at that very moment.
82a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the yantra that brings peace to children,
which is the most excellent protector and the destroyer of all calamities.
The manuscript should be written according to the previously mentioned procedure using the materials specified before, in due order;
the worship of the goddess upon the birch-bark leaf is performed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a circle;
thereafter, an eight-petaled lotus, beautiful and endowed with seed-syllables, should be fashioned.
One should place those ending in *sa* and those ending in *visarga* on each petal;
having worshipped them according to the rules, one should subsequently place [the mantras] at the base of the arms and at the throat.
One should wear this yantra, encased in lac and wrapped in three layers of metal;
by this, the Śākinīs, the Ḍākinīs, the Bālagrahas, and others [will be subdued].
They depart, leaving behind the child, through the power of this royal [mantra].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the third [mantra], which destroys fever.
According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should write on a beautiful birch-bark leaf;
having written the name of the person to be accomplished, it should be enclosed within the letter *ya*.
Having encircled the triangle, one should place the seed-syllables upon it;
having thus drawn and worshipped [the diagram], one should bind it on the right arm.
In matters concerning fever, for the purpose of a ritual offering, one should consume curd with rice;
whether a child or an elder, one shall be freed from fever at that very moment.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the destroyer of children's fever,
which, when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, wards off all fevers.
Having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a circle;
above, it enters the womb, and on the back, it is within the enclosure of the letter Va.
Then, an eight-petaled [lotus] should be made, with the seed-syllable joined on all sides; moreover, in the middle of each petal, the letter *na* should be adorned with a bindu.
In the *Dalākara*, however, one should place the syllable *hrīṃ* [in the appropriate location].
Having thus drawn [the diagram] and performed worship, one should cast it into cool water.
One is undoubtedly freed from fever within three days;
when combined with warm water, even a persistent fever is destroyed.
Likewise, when bound at the base of the hand, this "Surasundarī" spirit-machine destroys fever arising at the [specific] time; of this there is no doubt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the characteristics of children at all times,
as well as the yantra known as Jvaraṇarakṣā, which is supreme for increasing longevity.

82b) One should write it according to the previously stated procedure using the auspicious materials mentioned before; having inscribed it upon birch bark, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) should be written in the center.
Then one should properly encircle it with a line to form a square;
above that, one should draw a square and tridents at each corner.
In the corner of the square, one should write the seed-syllable *va*, adorned with a bindu;
above it, in the moving space, the wise one should inscribe the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Having thus inscribed that yantra and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should encase it with the three metals and bind it around the middle of the neck.
By that [practice], whatever afflictions there may be— whether physical or mental,
such as envy, anger, lines [of fate], or even the appearance of teeth— shall no longer arise.
It never causes any harm from defects in the mother’s milk to the infant. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the remedy for the destruction of epilepsy caused by spirits.
If one is seized by a Śākinī, a Bhūta, a Vetāla, or even by those belonging to Varuṇa,
then for the sake of liberation from that, one should construct a captivating yantra.
One who is healthy should, however, perform [the rite], for he is not seized by the faults of enemies;
then, the document should be written with the materials previously mentioned, according to the previously stated procedure.
O fair-faced one, having written the name in the center on a birch-bark leaf, one should encircle it with a circle; upon that, one should inscribe the eight petals.
One should then write the syllable *hrīṃ* within the center of each [section] again;
having thus written it out and performed worship, it should be encased in the three metals.
Gold, silver, and copper are known as the "triloha" (three metals);
the Tripurabhairava yantra should be worn on the hair or on the arm.
O fair-faced one, a child is liberated from diseases such as epilepsy;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme protection against snakes.
Just as a child or even an adult is not bitten by snakes and the like, O Goddess, so may you not be harmed through negligence;
having written [the mantra] according to the previously mentioned rule and having worshipped it according to the injunctions.
Having written the name in the center, one should draw a circle with two lines.
Having wrapped the eight petals individually with the *haṃsa* seed-syllable,
and having encased them in the three metals, one should wear it at the root of the arm.
Upon his mere sight, venomous serpents from the four directions perish;
though they have fallen at his feet through negligence, they remain as if paralyzed.
Now, for the purpose of paralyzing snakes so that the poison does not ascend at all due to the bite of negligence,
there is this *yantra* spoken by Garuḍa.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme protection against ḍākinīs;
[protection] from bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others, as well as from ḍākinīs and brahmarākṣasas.
When any enemy— whether a man, a woman, or even a hero— is present,
one should then employ a mechanical device (yantra) for the purpose of destroying spirits and rākṣasas.
Having written with chalk upon a cloth in an auspicious place,
one should draw four horizontal lines across and a vertical line below them.
In this way, O fair-faced one, there are twelve squares for the syllable *bhavāṃ kāṃ*; having written the syllable *hrīṃ* in each square, one should worship it.
Then, having offered oblations of rice, flowers, and incense, one should fill [the vessel] with dust;
having placed beautiful forms before it, one should kindle a fire of khadira wood.
Seeing a great being weeping as a metaphor for flight,
he abandons the child at that very moment and departs by leaving the country.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme destroyer of fever:
one should write [the mantra] upon a betel leaf using the thorns of the *cañcu* plant.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, auspiciously enclosed by the syllable *kroṃ*,
one should place the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) in the center of a hexagon and in its corners.
One should then inscribe the syllable *hrīḥ* in sequence upon each corner;
having honored it, betel is offered for the purpose of consumption.
By consuming the yantra, O Goddess, fever departs without a doubt; even a fever occurring every other day vanishes in an instant—no deliberation is required here.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for protecting the fetus;
it should be inscribed with elephant-ichor upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf.
Due to the absence of rut in the elephant, one should smear the throat and lips on all sides;
having written the name in the center, one should form a square with two lines.
The pericarp-surrounding petals should be made circular in the four directions;
the syllable *ya* and the syllable *ra*, each ending in a visarga, should be placed individually.
One should draw [the design] in the center of the pericarp as before and worship it in due order;
having encased it with a single piece of metal, one should place it around the neck of a pregnant woman.
Birth becomes easy, and the vulnerable openings are destroyed.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the protection for a pregnant woman.
Just as a machine enters the womb, so does the movement that destroys all beings.

The wise one should write [the mantra] on birch bark (bhūrjapatra) according to the previously mentioned procedure, using the materials specified before, in due order, following the ritual rules of the Middle Country.
One should write the name beginning and ending with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the syllable *hrīṃ*,
encircling it within a circle, a square, or a long rectangle using a line.
Above and below the three-petaled [lotus], one should establish [the syllables] in each corner;
likewise, one should write "hrīṃ kṣaṃ" and "hrīṃ" located in the corners and on the petals.
When this yantra is thus drawn, there is no doubt regarding any undertaking:
womb-pain, headache, and afflictions caused by malevolent spirits are destroyed.
Birth becomes easy, free from pain; this is certain. This great being, the king of yantras, has been declared as a secret.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the third [rite] for the destruction of fever;
it should be written on birch bark with the aforementioned substances, O fair-faced one.
Having written the name in the center, one should again encircle it with a triangle;
above that, the wise should draw a four-cornered figure in the shape of a peak.
Then, one should encircle it with the letter *ya* and the visarga at its end, placed at the odd positions;
having worshipped it at that time, one should bind it upon the right hand.
There is no doubt that fever born of spirits (bhūtajvara) or tertian fever (tṛtīyaka) will depart;
however, the disease does not simply vanish, for it may return once again to the forest [of the body].
Thus, O Goddess, the supreme practice of the yantra has been told to you in brief; O Great Goddess, now hear the Indrajāla [spell].
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Accomplishment of Yantras" in the Atharva-saṃhitā of the Śrī Hāhārāva-tantra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for paralyzing an army,
as well as the characteristics of the various types of kettledrums, clay drums, and war-drums.
The stone known as *anvitam* was fashioned by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*) for the purpose of heating;
it is auspicious when conjoined with the asterisms Anurādhā, Puṣya, Ārdrā, and the three *natitraya-jayā*s.
On the day of the Sun, Venus, Moon, and others, during the bright fortnight,
the benefics situated in the second, trines, or angles, while the malefics are not in the third house, [bring prosperity].
And one should have the work performed while the *bherī*, *mṛdaṅga*, and *paṭaha* drums are being beaten;
at a very pure moment of time (*lagna*) made of iron, the skillful artisan should carry out the task.
One should perform that which is firm conduct, stainless, and increasing victory—
at dawn, at noon, at midnight, when the hair is loose, and from the moment of the ascendant.
Having gone toward the western direction outside the city,
the leather-worker should properly prepare the hide at sunrise according to the rising of the sun.
By the sound of that low humming, the supreme enemy flees;
or else, one becomes bald by using the root or the bulb of red dhattūra.
One should grind together the ashes from a funeral pyre combined with the root of the plantain (kadalī), along with vīta, markaṭī, and lotus; this is the "madalagnā" situated in the middle.
Upon hearing a long-drawn-out cry, the army flees;
however, the lizard, the house-godha, and the vātāli bring auspiciousness and relief from suffering.
One should grind [the substance] with mustard seeds and smear it upon one's own body;
seeing that, O Lord of the Earth, they will drive each other away as if into a forest.
Thus ends the paralyzing of enemy armies.
Now follows the immobilization of the sword.
One should apply *ketakī* to the head, the eyes, the base of the palate, and the mouth;
with a sword [applied] to the feet and the heart, the sword becomes a pillar.
One should drink these three roots ground into powder with clarified butter;
thereafter, for a day and night, and indeed for as long as one lives, one is not afflicted by weapons.
One should take the root of the śirīṣa tree and its flowers, boil them in water, and then grind them with water;
having fasted for half a day, one should subsequently drink half a measure of that liquid.
As long as it is beneficial, its falling does not cause distress through clothes;
and having tied its root to the neck, it does not cause distress through swords or rams.
One should place a thread extracted from a *puṃkhī* flower upon the belly of Varadā;
one should then insert a *ṭaṃvarāṭa* fruit, which has a hand [carved] in its center.
That fruit, situated within the mouth, is a supreme neutralizer of weapons;
when the sun has been swallowed [by Rāhu], one should extract it together with the *śarapuṅkhī* plant.
He who holds this in his mouth while observing silence is not pierced by a sword;
he should fill [the vessel] with the Viṣṇukrāntā plant, including its roots, leaves, and branches.
Then, having prepared [the substance] fried in oil, one should rub it upon the limbs;
this will provide protection in battle against all weapons, such as swords and the like.
Having heated pure iron and combined it with the ashes of *kāntaloha*,
one should then [heat it] seven times in a sword-shaped crucible using liquors produced from wine and the juices of heroes (*vīra*).
Grind the seeds of the Brahma-tree, black mustard, and *nirājikā*,
along with *vadhī* and *viṃvā*; having ground them, perform this auspicious rite.
That which was previously ground into a ball and cooked with light *mattapuṭa* [firing] should be held in the mouth; it is a supreme means for paralyzing weapons.
For all the aforementioned yogas, one should remember Kumbhakarṇa in the heart;
he wards off weapons and missiles approaching from the front and from above.
Oṃ! Aho! Kumbhakarṇa, great rākṣasa, born from the womb of Kaikasī, destroyer of enemy armies, destroyer of enemy armies, Rudra commands you, O Mahāsacā, svāhā!
By reciting this mantra one thousand and eight times, success is attained for all yogas. Here, one should uproot all medicinal herbs while facing the north.
Thus ends the immobilization of the sword.
Now, the suppression of fire.
The juice of the *kola* tree combined with the fat of a ram,
when merely smeared upon it, causes even a metal [object] to burn in the midst of fire.
The root of *nalukāpāṭalī* and *rauvālaka* flowers in equal parts,
ground with the fat of a frog and smeared on the body, prevents one from being burned.
Indeed, by anointing all one's limbs with the juice of white guñjā,
one does not burn even while wandering in the midst of a heap of glowing coals.
Now, the fire-stopping pill.
Having grasped the left foot and the left hand of the chameleon as before,
with the *siddhaka* [herb] wrapped around it, the immobilization of fire (*vahnistambha*) remains within the mouth.
Foot-ointment, fire-walking,
the removal of withered flowers and discarded offerings, the *paribhadraka* plant,
and *maṇḍaka* cooked with fat should be prepared over a mild fire after being thoroughly kneaded.
With that foot-ointment, one should wander on the Aṅgāra mountain;
one should cook it with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* buds and the fat of a frog.
Then, by means of a mild fire, one should fashion two foot-rests from the clay smear of the feet.
For the purpose of smearing with the juice of *gālū*, *vartita*, *masṛ*, *ājaśaikasāhī*,
they become as cool as the moon through touch.
Then, having first burnt the wood of *tulasī* to arrest the cooking of the food, one should sprinkle it over the rice-pot; or else,
one should place the burning charcoal from a donkey's hoof-print onto the blazing hearth.
Even with a hundred loads of wood, cooking food does not occur;
rather, there is the consumption of embers.
Having repeatedly crushed long pepper and drunk ginger, [the fire still does not burn].
85a) A man eats glowing charcoal, yet his mouth is never burned at any time.
Now follows the rite for paralyzing arsonists.
If one recites the Himavat mantra seven times and sprinkles water [upon it],
even a fierce fire will be extinguished when a house is burning.
Oṃ! On the northern side of the Himalayas, there is a rākṣasa named Mārica.
With his mantra and excrement, I paralyze the sacrificial fire, svāhā!
Now, here are seven methods for paralyzing [an opponent] through divine play:
having taken the root of the *śirīṣa* tree on a Sunday while the sun is in the eastern quarter,
one should rub it with water and apply it as a mark (*tilaka*) upon the forehead.
One will achieve victory in gambling with heated dice. Having ground the thread of a young girl and smeared it on one's hands and arms,
one will not be burned by glowing coals or heated metals when accompanied by the mantra.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should smear one's hands with the fat of a ninth-month frog;
one may then hold heated iron, for this is the supreme method for arresting fire.
The immobilization of boiling ghee:
[Take] *kāminī*, *kuṣuma*, *sīsī*, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, water, *ṭiḍḍibhadra*, and *duḥkhasamāsya*; these are ground together with *bhakta* (boiled rice).
When one touches the root of the hand [with this mixture], even if one touches boiling ghee or oil as much as desired, one is not burned.
Following that, the divine ordeal for poison is described:
O child, as soon as it has been prepared, the stool of a cow should be taken;
having consumed the poison from it, one should eat [the food]; thus, victory in the divine ordeal of poison shall be achieved.
If even a single niṣka of the marrow of the *jīvaphala* fruit is consumed, one obtains a son.
One should eat poison that was swallowed while asleep at dawn; thus, victory over the enemy will be achieved. Now follows the ritual for the ordeal by rice (taṇḍuladivya) and its suspension.
When black pepper and ginger have been chewed and swallowed,
even a fault committed regarding divine rice produced from grains becomes purified.
O Vārāhī, if the root of śikhin (Agasti) ground together with milk is applied,
it will cause even divine rice to sprout again.
Now follows the rite for the immobilization of lightning.
The stake of that woman who died on a Sunday is to be driven in;
having taken four stakes for the four directions, one should mark them oneself.
One should protect them with great effort, consecrated by the Rudra-mantra;
one should place them in the hands of the four who run with speed.
Thunderbolts, locusts, and hailstones fall of their own accord;
as long as they remain at a distance, no harm exists.
When the [victim] has reached the end of his life there, one should recite the mantra for the measure of a fathom;
one should drive stakes into that spot and return to one's own abode.

Having collected that ash, one should throw it into the house of the enemy;
his expulsion will be accomplished and he shall be driven away within three days, without a doubt.
Oṃ huṃ kūṭayaḥ vāma-vāhu ucche vichalacilliṇi karahakaccora-rajemokija iti ha ane moha devarasaṃ tatage deśāntara-sarge śaśyed bhurate uccāṭaye svāhā. With this mantra,
one should offer two hundred oblations of *villini* seeds into the fire while remaining composed.
The eradication of the enemy occurs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is known as the rite of inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa),
by the mere consumption of which one shall go to death at that very instant.
That fang causes distress due to the cutting of the wound by blood;
then, one should administer *bhallātaka* combined with honey and clarified butter.
At that very moment, one dies from the limb where it is applied; it is like poison at the tip of its crest.
Likewise, having seized a blue fly by the tail, or a jackal in the same manner, [one dies].
Having combined them, one should offer the gift; it certainly causes death by poison.
One should place *guñjā* seeds into the mouths of both a jackal and a vulture and hold them there.
Afterward, one should extract that *guñjā* seed and cause it to be consumed;
then, terrible pustules arise, resembling the most virulent poisons.
Oil extracted from the seeds of the *hanī* and *guñjā*, as well as that produced from the *siddhārtha*, should be administered in food and drink; this is the supreme method for slaying an enemy.
Having taken the root of the *palāśī* plant combined with pungent oil,
one should mix it with the seed-mantra of Devapriya and administer it.
There is no doubt that he dies here, even if it were Śakra himself,
if [the powder] from fresh karavīra roots is combined with oil of white mustard seeds.
The conjunction with the seed-syllable *mohavīja* is the cause of immediate death;
one should consume *sphaṭikī* with seed-oil, and *kanaka* becomes [the state of] existence.
If it is given for consumption, there is no doubt that one will die;
if it is given with milk, the tongue of even Hālāhala [poison] is neutralized.
Especially at the time of the *puṭaka* [offering], one goes to the abode of Yama;
having combined it with the milk of a *vajrī*, one should cook the flesh of a woman who has recently given birth.
The enemy dies at that very moment; what is the use of much talk?
One should cause [the substance] to be administered mixed with putrid urine and pungent oil.
By merely consuming it, one certainly does not die;
having taken the *māṇikya* meat, one should combine it with pungent oil.
By merely consuming ashes, one dies; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, one should saturate seeds of gold with the juice from the root of the *kṛṣṇā* plant.
One should provide food and drink that is excellent for slaying enemies:
namely, the root of red *citraka* and the powder of conch-shell lime.
Having combined these, one should administer them together with *vīkīra* powder;
by consuming this, a man impelled by Time dies instantly.
The wise man should cause the enemy to swallow them while they are still spotted;
at that very moment the enemy dies, and no remedy exists.
One should give a span's measure mixed with honey for the consumption of one who desires [the fruit];
the consumer attains immediate death—of this there is no doubt.
That man who consumes [the substance] placed within the belly of a peacock by means of a thread goes immediately and irresistibly to the abode of Yama.
Whoever should eat [this] mixed with honey and clarified butter at a single mealtime will die instantly; he is truly incurable even by the gods.
If one who has a short lifespan consumes oil mixed with ten million poisons and salt, he will die; of this there is no doubt.
Having brought the mouth of a snake and grinding it in a tiger-pit, it should be administered in food and drink; he will die, of this there is no doubt.
Taking the eight [parts] of a hunter, as well as the dung of a porcupine,
combined with *karavīra*, this is certainly an immediate means of killing.
These yogas have been fully described, arising from various mantras;
they all grant immediate accomplishment and must be guarded with great effort.

Thus ends the chapter on the application of various mantras and the art of sorcery (*indrajāla*) within the *Śrī-Hāhārāva-tantra*, specifically in the section on the compendium of syllables (*athavarṇasaṃhitā*).
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim this supreme remedy for great diseases,
which pacifies illness instantly and is renowned throughout the three worlds.
First, I shall properly describe in brief the remedy for leprosy (kuṣṭha):
the *saraṭa*, the *ṣaṭpada*, and likewise the *karpaṭavṛścika*.
Having reduced it to powder, one should cast it into oil and subsequently rub it onto the body.
Merely by anointing the limbs, leprosy is certainly destroyed;
having extracted the worms from the head, one should fill [the mouth] with betel leaf.
A disease of the mouth occurs for him, proclaimed as the "hāhārava" (the cry of "hā hā");
having seized the *saṃkocaka* thorn, one should place it in his midst.
In him there arises a pain that is most terrible and exceedingly cruel;
likewise, the forest-rat, the female mongoose, the female swan, and the peacock [portend] misfortune.
For Ajitā, one should write [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with Svāhā;
for Aparājitā, one should place it in the lower part, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā.
Having thus inscribed the yantra, one should go to the bank of a river;
auspicious clay should be taken from both banks by one observing silence.
Having offered oblations to Gaṇapati with that [mudrā], she should place the yantra upon it;
the beautiful woman should then perform the satiation of Gaṇanātha with cow’s milk.
One should worship him with many flowers and offer many sweetmeats (modakas) while praising him; having honored the children with snacks, one should pray: "May Gaṇeśa be pleased."
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods with a beautiful smile, O King of Gaṇas,
one should place [the deity] within a pair of shallow bowls (saṃpuṭa) and then set the vessel upon a pedestal.
One should place the mantra "Aghore" over the *saṃpuṭa*;
having formed the *saṃpuṭa* resting on the ground, one should then bury it and worship it.
Having fallen into a state of misfortune, a woman cannot endure it day and night; nor can a man endure her, even if she be beautiful and devoted to virtuous vows.
A yantra joined with the masculine gender endures various [obstacles],
but for the estrangement of a married couple, O Goddess, this is always the supreme secret.
This yantra, which is dear to me, must not be employed for any other purpose;
it should not be given to just anyone, for otherwise a contrary result arises.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed mantra for attaining success (*siddhi*):
*Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya yamarūpiṇe kālasaṃkṣepāya: ete saṃhara 2 śatruṃ 2 nāśaya 2 amukaṃ hana 2 paca 2 ghātaya 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. By means of this mantra...
What is being proclaimed? By consecrating any syllable whatsoever with this mantra, the destruction of one's enemies occurs. Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya.

And for the benefit of all beings, may the Blessed One, the Lord of All, quickly act! O Goddess, [act] quickly! *kuru* 2! *mocaya* 2! From all the Rudras! Homage be to you! *svāhā!* By means of this mantra, applied at the end of the previously mentioned yoga of re-entrance (*pratyānayana*), one will thereafter become healthy. *Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya*.

O you whose form is Śiva, bind the topknot! May there be auspiciousness for all women and for all men! O Nara, protect, protect! Cause fear to all beings! Muru, muru! [Protect] from all fears, svāhā! Now, when this Vidyā-yoga is employed, one should bind it upon one's own body; it becomes a protection. *Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya vyāghracarma* (Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lord Rudra, the tiger-skin wearer).

To him who has clothed himself, who has let out a loud laugh, *mana* 2, *satyaṃ kṛt*, establish your presence 2, *sasa* 2, *dhara* 2, *svāhā*. A person should employ this mantra in conjunction with the rites for eradication (*utsādana*).
By this very method, peace is attained; it is not otherwise. *Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya*.
To the one of terrifying form, the fierce one: expel the root of [name], bind, bind! slay, slay! burn, burn!
cook, cook! quickly expel, indeed! *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having consecrated [the object] with this mantra one hundred and eight times, it causes everything to be expelled.

By means of a *homa* sacrifice using the wings of a crow and an owl, one causes [the enemy] to be driven away at that very moment. *Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya gara 2 dara 2 bhañja 2 kuru 2 moṭaya 2 nagara-maṇḍala-pati-rājñā pacati svāhā.* Having consecrated with this mantra a substance that has been defiled by impure persons, one should cast it [into the fire].

The water becomes as clear as cow's milk; poison becomes non-poisonous. Beyond this, there are further [remedies]: having collected the eyes and the snouts of a jackal and a boar, as well as their mantras and blood.
One should extract it by grasping it evenly at its very point of initial emergence.
One whose eyes are anointed with this becomes invisible in an instant to the owl,
the vulture, as well as the cat and the boar.
Having taken the eyes of these [beings], together with *śrota* collyrium,
one should make a fine powder for all mantras and for the application to the eyes.
One sees the long path of the enemy as clearly at night as by day— whether that of a peacock, a vulture,
a buffalo, or two cats.
One who is skilled should collect the eyes of a crow and a boar,
and having combined them with *srotoñjana*, apply it as an ointment for the eyes.
One whose eyes are anointed with this shall see at night as if by day.
This is the mantra for these formulations.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, to Rudra, to Śiva, the face of light; may [he] grant the directions, svāhā! Having become established for one night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, being composed and having performed worship according to the rule, one should remain at a solitary liṅga.
While it is blazing, one should cause it to be entered by the foot of that very person;
then, one should burn it in a cremation ground and have it buried in a donkey-shaped mound.
Having taken that very house and a lacquered casket,
one should write the name of whichever person is to be seized, whether quickly or otherwise.
Oṃ! O crow, destroy the fever of [Name] upon this black antelope skin, svāhā!

Having climbed a jambū tree, one should recite this ten thousand times; then it becomes perfected. Oṃ! O Cāmuṇḍā, kha 2, khāhi 2, do not cause [Name] to enter the house, svāhā! By means of this mantra, [one should take] a human skull...
Having taken [the substance] and reduced it to powder, it is offered as incense to Cāmuṇḍā.
By taking [it] under someone's name, that person is seized; by means of guggulu incense, there is liberation.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme practice of moving about on foot.
The wise man, having gathered the root of the white *kākajaṅghā*,
should extract its juice and cook it with sesame oil.
Having fashioned a sandal known as *auṣṭracarma* (made of camel-skin), the wise man should consecrate it with that very mantra and then anoint his feet with oil.
Having become all-powerful, one should turn back at the place of the cows;
with the fat of an owl, one is successful, and sandals should be made from the skin of a camel.
Having gone five yojanas, it continues again without end;
there is no doubt about this, according to the word of Uḍḍīśa.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra; O you who speak in various ways, move, move! Svāhā!
Having fasted for four meals and being composed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the Lord Īśāna and offer an oblation according to the prescribed rite.
Facing the northwestern direction, one should consecrate the oils with mantras;
then success arises, just as the word of Uḍḍiśa declares.
Eight thousand [verses] of these have already been prescribed;
this is declared to be the means of accomplishment for all yogas whatsoever.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, who makes himself known, who moves along the path of the shore, whose valor is immeasurable, the knower;
svāhā!
[This is] the measure of the bitter oil from the cotton-tree on the Golden Mountain.
One should combine all these together with muscle fat and honey in a single place.
Having gathered its pungent parts, one should place them in a concealed spot;
then, having consecrated the oil, one should churn it eight hundred times.
Having anointed his feet and face, he may travel a hundred yojanas;
then, once he has quickly reached the sky, he returns with all his enemies slain.
Having ground the powder of a dead lizard,
one should burn it in a smokeless fire within a pair of earthen saucers, together with the white powder of white mustard seeds.
If one should cast that which has been taken from mixed ashes into someone's house,
then the women of that place shall always remain deluded.
That same powder, mixed with the dust from one's own feet and consecrated seven times with mantras, should be placed on the path;
that same powder, mixed with one's own semen, when given to someone, causes them to come under one's control.
Having placed that same powder inside a cow's horn, one should bury it; he for whom it is buried becomes impotent.
Having made a forehead mark (tilaka) with that same powder mixed with gorocanā, one becomes beloved by kings.
Oṃ, homage to Rudra! Udyādana! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Quickly bring [the person named] so-and-so under control, svāhā!
Having taken the root of the *kāsmarya* tree, along with *savaraka* flowers and *ketakī*, grind them together with *lakṣaṇa*.

Having rinsed the mouth with bhr̥ṅgarāja juice mixed with triphalā and oil, one should apply iron powder to the fine hair; this instantly makes it as dark as a swarm of bees, resembling the luster of black bees. As for the collyrium, one may use the root of the lotus or even that of the blue water-lily.
Take *ayorañja*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and the leaf of *savarasā*;

having obtained one *kuḍava* of oil along with these, one should cook it over a gentle fire combined with a decoction of the juices. For half a month, one should administer this as a nasal drop (*nasya*) while consuming a diet of *kṛśara*. Then, on the day that is a quarter [of the total duration], it should certainly be applied.
One with a black head-hair tuft, a youthful appearance, and a mouth possessing the fragrance of a blue lotus,
shall live for more than a hundred years, free from wrinkles and grey hair.
Having taken sesame seeds, flowers, clarified butter, and likewise the horse-syllable (hayakṣara).
One should apply a head-ointment mixed with honey;
by this ointment, hair grows even on the palms of the hands.
One should place blue lotus mixed with milk and meat upon the ground;
when heated with oil, this is the supreme collyrium for the hair.
Blue lotuses, sesame seeds, kuṣṭha, and yaṣṭīmadhuka,
when boiled with oil and applied to gray hair, are an excellent means for dyeing the hair.
Then one should prepare a powder of *nāga* (lead), along with pearls and *rasāñjana*;
by means of this powder, hair grows even on the soles of the feet.
One should cook blue lotus, musīla, sandalwood, nāgakeśara,
śāli rice, nakha, and kuṣṭha with goat’s milk.
Let oil be prepared from these as an excellent hair-dye:
the three myrobalans (triphalā), nimba seeds, vacā, utpala, and sārivā.
One should collect iron powder, sesame seeds, and fresh butter derived from goats, buffaloes, cows, and other such sources, combined with *bhṛṅga* and *madhuka*.
Having stirred it in an iron vessel, one should place it upon the ground;
by smelling this, the growth of hair on the head and teeth will be destroyed.
One should bring forth a woman with hair as fine as a lotus fiber and one who is deaf;
she should burn everything on all sides with blue-black hair, *saṃdhanya*, and rice husks.
With a thread wrapped around the head, one should burn black rice and mustard seeds;
indeed, the black rice and mustard seeds situated on the head shall be consumed by fire.
One should burn the head-hair along with the fallen filth; then, black hair will grow, accompanied by triphalā and honey. One should nourish the hair for a month with realgar and oil.
Bhallātaka, viḍaṅga, iron filings, and iron rust are the best for the six types of hair-removal applications and for the growth of hair.
One should cause black sesame seeds mixed with *sauvaccala* to be given;
then, having applied a paste to the head, one should place [the image] in a clean spot.
Furthermore, for the supreme dyeing of the hair on the head of a bride,
one should use the heart of a crow, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the juices of bhṛṅgarāja.
These [substances] should be taken in equal parts; likewise, they form a single ointment.
Having cooked oil with these, it will cause the hair to grow long.
Likewise, her hair is curled in form and resembles blue lotuses at the ears.
99b) Oṃ, O Kṣipanī, [lead] from the wrong path to the right path; release, release! Svāhā!
This [mantra] for one who has recited it over water causes her to give birth easily;
likewise, the roots of the world, combined with white guñjā seeds, [achieve the same].
Equal parts of these, applied as an ointment to the vulva with honey,
will cause her to give birth to a handsome son endowed with strength and vigor.
Having drunk a mixture of blue flowers, *saunika*, *citraka*,
along with *vacā* and *kuṣṭha*, a woman gives birth.
One should grind together the seeds of the bottle gourd, vetasa, the two types of rajani, apuṣpī, vacā, vāsā, and sandalwood.
Having smeared the womb with this, one should engage in sexual intercourse;
thus he procreates a son who is pleasing to the heart and dear to the mind.
If one takes one *prastha* each of cow’s urine and oil, and one *kuḍava* of [the medicinal paste],
even a woman who has bathed after her menses, or even one who is barren, shall give birth.
Equal parts of *akṣimahiṣagarbhinī*, sheep's urine, and *śatāvarī*,
combined with goat's ghee.
Even a barren woman, if she bathes after her menses, shall give birth;
provided it is during the bright fortnight, at the conjunction with the flowering of the *vaṭa* tree.
By drinking water boiled with *ṛtusnātā* (the plant used for ritual bathing after menstruation), a woman shall become pregnant;
likewise, milk boiled with *aśvagandhā* and cooled should be consumed.
By drinking this, even a barren woman gives birth through sexual union;
likewise, by consuming the seeds of the citron or the powder of *nāgakeśara*.
Having drunk this, one should resort to that which brings delight to the womb of the unborn;
it consists of sugar, blue lotus, liquorice, red sandalwood, and *śarivā*.
When the fetuses are leaking, rice should be prepared by one who acts with care;
[the remedy consists of] the roots of the red and blue lotus, madhuka, sugar, and sesame seeds.
When the fetuses are being miscarried, the rite for stabilizing the fetus is supreme.
Thus ends the section on stabilizing the fetus.
Madhuka, candana, and likewise ghee and raw sugar—
Even if a woman has a hidden pregnancy, she will give birth very quickly.
One should smear the roots of the *ajara* plant upon the navel and the vulva;
as soon as they are smeared, a woman will give birth very quickly.
One who is composed should apply the root of *pṛṣṇiparṇī* with its flower for the treatment of a feverish patient,
for causing the expulsion of a *visalpa* (cutaneous eruption), for exhilaration, and for the delivery of a concealed fetus.
One should smear the navel of the leaf of the *panasūra* with a paste; by smearing the navel for the sake of the desired purpose, there is the extraction of that which is situated within the womb.
In the case of a miscarriage, one should throw powder of long pepper and other such drugs into the womb;
or else, a measure of one akṣa of rice-root, with sour gruel, at dawn.
And with the root of the *kaluṣa* plant, or with *lāṅgulī* or *vṛṣa*, ground together,
she should smear the vulva and the navel with it along with a vulture’s [feathers].

One suffering from wind-disorders (vāta) and palate-heat (tāluya) should drink a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla) combined with heated iron to destroy the diseases of the postpartum state (sūtikā).
Having drunk blood mixed with sugar, a woman gives birth;
likewise, having fumigated the vulva with the incense of *nisvakāṣṭha*.
If a woman gives birth to a human child through sexual intercourse,
she should drink the juice of a *palāśa* sprout on the tenth day after her menses.
The fetus of women miscarries; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Equal parts of *lohitapitta*, *tagara*, black pepper, and long pepper [should be used].
One should smear the vulva with these [substances] in equal parts mixed with honey;
having applied this ointment during the day, one may engage in sexual intercourse at night.
A woman who desires fortune through the *bhaga* (private parts) will always give birth to a nourisher;
[she obtains] cow-horn, enjoyment, *sahadevī*, and *priyaṅgu*.
One should grind the fluid of peacock eggs together in one place;
having smeared the vagina with this, she who engages in sexual intercourse [shall obtain a son].
If those [women] conceive a fetus,
and if there is a miscarriage, one should apply a ball of red ochre the size of an axle-pin and bathe [the woman].
By drinking the water under the Tiṣya constellation, one enters the womb and is born;
one should apply a fine paste of red ochre and turmeric.
But when the third month has passed, the following is the best method for causing the destruction of the embryo:
the root of *lāṅgalī* should be ground into a paste and combined with the water of *kulattha*.
When drunk with a strong [substance], it is the supreme destroyer of the fetus.
Thus ends the section on the destruction of the fetus.
One should boil the roots of *citraka* over a gentle fire.
One should wash the vulva with that; thereby it attains firmness.
One should boil powdered *khadira* with *saurāṣṭrī* over a gentle fire;
when the vulva is washed with this, firmness is produced.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, vacā, māṃsī, and likewise somarājī,
when combined with buffalo butter and its paste, constitute an excellent means for thickening [the mixture].
One should prepare equal parts of *tuṃva*, *patra*, and *lodhra*;
by applying this as an ointment to the vulva, one will become preeminent in sexual enjoyment.
She who always applies this powder to the vulva will,
upon discharging her seed during sexual intercourse, become desirable once again.
The wise and discerning one, having ground *padma* and *tamāla* into a powder,
should grind it with goat’s milk and form it into pills.
But she who has given birth for ten nights, having been cast into the womb like a maiden,
eternally attains the state of virginity through this yoga.
Having smeared the vulva with the fruit of the *palāśa* and *udumbara* trees combined with sesame oil and honey, it is the best means for making [the union] firm.
Thus is the method for making it firm.
One should cook the juice of *mātuluṅga*, honey, collyrium, and *kaṇṭhakālikā*; this king of ointments causes the infatuation of a woman’s mind.
The dung of a pigeon, along with *koṣṭhikāraka* worms, *kuṣṭha*,
and the seeds of *madhuśirīṣa*— this ointment brings an end to leprosy when applied while reciting the mantra.
These two kings of ointments have been brought down for Pradyumna:
*garbhitā*, *strīṇāmājaṃsinmikaṃ*, and *vyugni*. [Also] *aṃjana*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *devadāru*, and sugar.
One should grind two parts each of long pepper, vacā, and kuṣṭha with elephant urine.
This drink should be administered to a woman who is pregnant:
[a paste of] *śatapuṣpā*, honey, *ketakī*, and the fruit of *vṛhatī*.
This ointment should be applied; it is the supreme means of subjugation.
[It consists of] sayyāda, priyaṅgu, tagara, and the filaments of the lotus.
One should grind cow's urine with honey and apply it as a paste; this paste brings comfort to those women who are tightly bound by their husbands.
Long pepper, rock salt, kuṣṭha, and likewise sea salt,
combined with realgar— this ointment brings about death.
Pippalī, taṇḍula, madhu, and madhuka,
combined with the juice of kapikacchu— this ointment brings about death.
This ointment, consisting of the resin of *kanakavīja*, honey, long pepper, and rice,
combined with the juice of *vārtāka*, brings about death.
Oṃ naṭe kucaṭe svakinī svāhā. Brahmadaṇḍī, curd-juice, long pepper, and black pepper— this ointment should be applied to the hearts of women to bring them under one's control.
Oṃ caṃcabhā devīra, homage to you, svāhā! What is said regarding one's own self is as follows: the impurities of one's own ears, as well as one's own semen, are equal to foam.
Food, drink, fruits, flowers, as well as perfumes and garments, should be offered to her who is pregnant; then the servant shall remain under her control.
With her hair disheveled, her earrings like those of a wandering bee, and wearing the garland of a corpse,
this woman, her limbs smeared with ashes, stands weeping at every step along the road.
The seeds of the Puṣkara, Pippalī, Taṇḍula, Añjana, Dhāva, and Puṣpa flowers, or the Manu-mantra, constitute an excellent drink.
Goat's urine that has lost its pungency, along with long pepper, rice, and honey,
should be given as an excellent drink for women who have conceived.
Having combined these— all of them together— namely, gorocanā, kulattha, a paste of bilva, and manaḥśilā, one should place them in a copper vessel.
One should cause sesame oil to remain there for seven nights;
having smeared that oil upon the vulva, one follows after women with devotion.
Once she has attained the state of sexual maturity, she will make her husband a slave;
[the remedy is] saffron, *śatapuṣpa*, *priyaṅgu*, and two *locanā* plants.
Combined with horse urine, it brings others under one's control;
one should take the fruit of the citron and dry it especially well.
One should place sea salt and powder therein,
and having processed it for seven nights, one should saturate it with one's own urine.
Having placed it in a hollowed-out pair of earthenware bowls, one should burn it with smokeless fire;
this is the supreme method of pulverization at a crossroads or in a cremation ground.
He to whom this is given comes under one's control; there is no doubt about this.
101b) Oṃ namo bhagavati prītirī svāhā.
Dog’s tongue, *vacā*, costus, and even discarded flower offerings—
when combined with this mantra, they bring those who are unwilling under one's control.
Oṃ vacakutrāya svāhā. Having made a fine powder of añjana, haritāla, vacā, and likewise kuṣṭha, this is the supreme means of subjugation.
Oṃ kuṭu 2 svāhā. Having consecrated this powder with recitation for seven days, it should be given to women; it causes madness.
[Also, one may use] urine and feces, indragopa insects, ṣkarasāñjana, guggulu, bark, lac, kuṣṭha, and seeds.
For gold, however, this incense should be prepared; one should combine it with jaggery.
This incense brings about profit from the sale of all types of merchandise.
Oṃ cili 2 mili 2 puttalīke vaśamānaya svāhā.
Indrayava, vacā, kuṣṭha, tagara, and likewise mustard seeds,

Fumigated by this, even a woman who does not give birth— a woman among those unfortunate ones— quickly undergoes a transformation [to become fertile] through her husband.

A woman should smear her slender body with the paste made from lotus petals;

Oṃ, to Mahāsena, who possesses great strength and prowess, the great leader, the renter of the earth, the wielder of the spear: rending all mechanical devices, crush! crush! threaten! threaten! pulverize! pulverize! cause to fall! cause to fall! Svāhā!
Having prepared mustard seeds, *ājuramaṇḍika*, and *atiyaṃvajrasūci* with this mantra, [one should perform the ritual].

Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should strike a mountain. Now, for the rite of splitting the earth, one should strike the ground according to this mantra-vidhi; it splits the earth. This is the procedure for making a site suitable for a temple.

He to whom a well is to be given must be told: "Even if it is only four finger-breadths deep, whoever drinks its water shall go to the abode of Yama. Likewise, one should crush a chameleon, a crow, a cock, and a monkey.

Excluding the act of bringing it back,

One should burn it with wood from the *vibhītaka* tree, ensuring there is no smoke;
then, having collected salt, the wise practitioner should give it to the enemy.
If the ritual treatment is not performed, one quickly becomes insane;
by the consumption of *dhībhitaka*, it arises in the eye.
Thus concludes the ritual for bringing [the deity] back.
The wise one, having ground together the powder of *mātulī*, *mātuluṅga*, *vṛścika*, and *hālāhala* poison, [should proceed].
This should be offered as food in the vehicle [of the deity] for the destruction of all enemies:
a musk-rat, sesame seeds, pungent oil, and radish.
If a person does not give that [offering] for a fortnight within the month, his enemy shall prevail;
by failing to give it for a month, a tumor and piercing pain arise from poison on the ninth day.
Peacock, crab, meat, and likewise the deer;
long pepper, ginger, asafoetida, and likewise sauvarcala salt.
And the wise one should boil the *dīpa* together with the root;
by merely consuming this, one should apply it once the colic has arisen.
Bījapūraka, musk, and lotus stalk,
combined with sauvarcala salt, constitute the most excellent means of restoration.
One should quickly give [the medicine] that destroys dropsy to the enemy;
if no treatment is applied, he will die within four months.
A wise man should offer a rohita fish for the sake of the gods;
by that, the seed sown in the waters of Puṣkara yields happiness.
And food should be provided— either meat from the wilderness or human flesh—
at the root of the *kṣīrī*, *akṣīrī*, *agastya*, and the *sarṣapa* tree.
A young woman, when her menses have ceased, should drink a dose of red ochre (*gairika*) mixed with *tikṣṇa* salt; this is the supreme means for creating the opening of the womb.
If a woman has never given birth to a male child,
one should fumigate her with the incense of *nimba* wood; then, having performed sexual intercourse with her,
she shall never again fail to give birth to a son.
Bhallātaka-rasa, guñjā, and likewise maṇḍalakārikā.
The man who offers incense mixed with house-lizard [dung] will develop leprosy within seven days, and intense pains will arise.
Having boiled sugar and neem together with milk in a vessel made of *dhātṛ* wood, one should give it as food to the enemy.
On the eighth day, he should cause that enemy to be slain; he is not honored by the foe in Vaikuṇṭha.
One should perform the re-consecration according to what was previously stated.
One should cook chicken meat, cow-tusk [meat], and likewise fish meat,
as well as snake and *mocaka*, with sesame oil.
One should cause him to drink a preparation consisting of *ahinirmocaka* mixed with sesame oil and *śasyoma*.
A piercing pain arises in his heart; this is what has been described. I shall now declare its pacification, by which well-being is attained.
One should have the meat of a peacock and a cock ground together;
when combined with ghee, it destroys even long-standing diseases.
For Jala, having seized the mouth and dried it with effort,
should cast the great poison Nābha into that person's mouth.
103b) To whomever this is given, even if poison has been administered,
that enemy dies at that very moment; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Having taken earth from a palace, one should place it into the mouth of a snake;
one should then bind it with a black thread, whereby the path is obstructed.
Desiring to bring [the patient] back, one should move him very slowly;
[using] well-prepared clay, *mārkaṣaka*, *pṛṣṇu*, and the plowshare of *kuruka*.

The physician should administer all these powders in equal proportions. If this treatment is not performed, a person who has not eaten will suffer from a loss of appetite and face the destruction of his vital strength. One should drink milk with sugar, along with the leaves of *carī*, *nimba*, sixteen leaves of *bilva*, and sixteen *bhallātaka* fruits.
Likewise eight, and twenty likewise;
this should be given as powder, specifically for consumption rather than for drinking.
Also, peacock meat, dahilāvyā, and bhṛtīrekākṣinī.
This should be administered for consumption or in drink;

One should cook the heart of an owl together with the tongue of a boar using *ehibhili*; with that [ointment], one should smear one's own limbs and massage whomever [one intends].
What is its remedy? It is easily cured; it perishes within three days by means of goat’s milk, cow’s ghee, and *jyeṣṭhī* combined with honey.
This should be given for drinking as the supreme means of restoration:

Then, having made equal portions, one should grind them with elephant urine;
the wise person should fashion pills of the size of a *varamātra*.
Among them, one should not first rub a pill;
one should give this [medicine] to drink, and when five nights have passed, [the patient] is afflicted by jaundice.
If no ritual action is performed, one will die within a single month;

By merely adorning it with that, happiness is attained there;
for [the remedy consists of] the slough of a snake, asafoetida, bile from a mongoose, and indeed [the bile] of a mongoose.
104a) For one who certainly suffers from throat disease, a drink should be administered;

One should cause [the victim] to swallow black aconite, cow dung, the root of *lāṅgalikā*, and the poison of the *vatsanābha* variety, along with the excrement of a white dog.

Having prepared this powder, the wise man should touch all living beings—elephants, horses, buffaloes, and cows; by the mere act of touching them, there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Now I shall fully explain the destroyer of all poisons,
whether it be located [there], prepared, or whose powder one administers.
Having collected the fat derived from the flesh of a house lizard, a snake, a porcupine, and a boar,

it should be placed within a girl who is pure and dressed in white garments.
While drinking that paste, one should recite this mantra:

Oṃ, obeisance to the Perfected Being (Puruṣasiddha), obeisance to the Purifier; to the Lord of All, the Sovereign of Remedies, perform, perform! O Āsurī, destroy, destroy the unrighteousness! Establish, establish [the righteous]!
Svāhā!
Merely by being smeared with this, all kings shall become well-disposed;

When seven days have passed, one should diligently bring it back;
