Drink and food should be given; by that, happiness is attained.
For the meal, cooked rice with ghee and milk should be provided.
One should administer liquorice, ghee, and honey in equal measures;
within seven nights, one will be liberated from the previously mentioned Bhairava.
Having made a fine powder of spider, monkey, guñjā, the white tail of a lizard,

Or it may become eightfold by means of its fruit.
Guñjā, markaṭī, kṣāra, and likewise the poison markaṭaka.

Wherever a man is bitten by a snake that has died while facing downwards, [this remedy should be applied].

Food and drink mixed with it should be given; the man will become healthy.
This is the boar's vomit; it is the blood of a man.

Having ground together the bone of a monkey, a vulture, and likewise white excrement, one should apply this powder as an ointment;
otherwise, one should cause the dung of a jackal to be given to him for drinking.
If one were to smear the back of Kuśa even with a mere measure of honey and ashes, [it would become pure].
For that very person, leprosy arises after five nights;

The seed of the śirīṣa tree, māṃsī, and likewise mustard seeds.

Kukūṭī, gojihvā, the flesh of a black serpent,

this destroys heart disease.
One should cause boiled rice with goat's milk to be offered for seven nights,
as well as the flesh of a hare and the flesh of a black snake.
Then, having made equal portions, one should saturate them with milk and ghee;

Then, by the mere touch of his body, leprosy (kuṣṭha) arises;

Oṃ trailokyamohani sarvabhūtavaśaṃkarīṇi hrīṃ svāhā.
If one recites this one hundred and eight times, it brings gods and asuras under control.
By taking the eye of a man and [anointing it] with the ichor of an elephant...

O beloved, having consecrated water for drinking, ointments, and incense with the mantra one hundred and eight times, he quickly becomes submissive; he shall become a giver of wealth and a giver of life.
Having prepared incense made of guggulu mixed with priyaṅgu buds and offered it as smoke one hundred and eight times, one becomes truly fortunate.
Even a man who is deficient in form attains beauty and a state of auspiciousness through the offering of incense, which is mixed with the fragrance of flowers and lasts for a long duration.

A fire sacrifice (homa) performed with the Aghora mantra using salt mixed with sesame seeds destroys hatred within seven days; even those who are arrogant toward travelers will come to him with affection.
One should offer mustard seeds, honey, milk,
and ghee mixed with cow dung, using the previously mentioned mantra.
When the mustard seed has been prepared, it is the firm conclusion of the scripture that one should collect the dust from the feet of eight men belonging to the woman to be accomplished.
One should perform the fire offering during a lunar eclipse;
having offered one thousand and eight oblations while reciting the name of a person, one swiftly draws that person under one's influence.
Having taken the charcoal from a cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight,
one should draw the form of either a woman or a man with focused intent.
O highly fortunate one, having ascended into his heart, one should first recite the mantra a thousand times, interwoven with the name of the person to be accomplished.
Avoiding that during an eclipse of the sun,
one should diligently strike [the image] with a red karavīra flower.

With heads adorned with disheveled hair and the like strewn about, and women who are naked and utterly distraught, one should mutter the *dhātu-mantra* while being emaciated and deprived of physical beauty.
But for those who have brought [the enemy] under control, their own lord has taken away their sins; O you whose doubts are destroyed, join with the Goddess, who is likewise red.
On the day of the moon's conjunction (the *somaparvan*), one should take [the substance] joined with *sahadevā*;
it should be recited over with this mantra while combined with *rocanā*.
A wise man should apply a *tilaka* [made from] *somarājī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and charcoal from a cremation ground; by doing so, he shall bring both women and men under his control.
Having ground these with effort, a person should fashion them into pills;
by bringing flowers, fruits, and roots under control, he becomes worthy of royal honor.
One should recite the previously mentioned mantra one hundred and eight times.
Now, I shall explain the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) in brief, but not in detail.
When a solar eclipse occurs, one should take the excellent root of the lāṅgalī plant,
combined with charcoal from a cremation ground and accompanied by a banner of the gods.
The wise one should quickly enter his house with this mantra:
*Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Bewilder so-and-so! Terrify him! Expel him! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!*

Having consecrated mustard seeds twenty-one times with this mantra, if one buries them in someone's house, that person is expelled. [Likewise, one may expel] a corpse's hair, bone, or even the remains of offerings made to Śiva.
If one places a Vibhītaka seed within someone's house,
I shall declare the supreme mantra for that person which effects their eradication.
Oṃ hāṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
This mantra, which was previously well-guarded and now made manifest, shines forth for you.
Through one hundred thousand recitations, it becomes fully perfected and shall accomplish all rites.
If one performs a rite even when unaccomplished, how much more so if one were to accomplish it?
Having become one whose face is turned toward the sun and other [deities], one should recite the mantra a thousand times.
By practicing this for seven nights, one may cause an enemy to be expelled by means of clarified butter,
having first performed this rite while inserting the name of the foe [into the mantra].
This mantra, which brings about expulsion and victory when recited seven times, is undoubtedly effective;
it is declared by the tradition to be a mantra that accomplishes even what has not yet been achieved.
Having uttered the name of the enemy, one should enclose the mantra for the purpose of worship;
this is done by the sacrificer with a mind possessed by wrath.
Facing the south, one should perform a fire offering with red karavīra flowers and blood, causing the enemy to be eradicated in an instant.
It banishes thousands of enemies and even causes them to depart.
Now I shall describe another yoga that is very difficult to find on earth.
Whether one should cause [an enemy] to be eradicated, or increase the pride of a fool,
or [perform rites] for one's own people and retinue along with their mounts, it should be done immediately.
The King, the king of mantras previously proclaimed, is interlaced with the name [of the target].
One should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*), consisting of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpya*) in a cremation ground or a place of deafness.
When the state of the ten-fold portion of the *homa* has been reached, one should offer guggulu resin and *rājīkā*. Then, at the time of dawn, for all of them...
Having placed the collection of bones in the four cardinal directions, one should cast them into the ten directions.
A king of noble vows can swiftly cause expulsion even without material resources;
having purified the previously mentioned mantra, he should then commence the rite.
Perform the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) by means of the flow through the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the great and specific method of eradication.
One who possesses wisdom should begin with the previous mantra;
having constructed a sacrificial pit at a crossroads using the feathers of a crow and an owl.
By means of a complete fire-oblation, expulsion shall occur at that very moment;
or else, it may be accomplished by another method—listen to that means according to reality.
One should fashion a great doll and write its name;
by condensing the syllables of that name, one brings about the destruction of enemies.
By means of those mantras, quickly perform the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) on that day; it will certainly succeed.
Or else, [perform it] against an enemy who is arrogant due to his increased strength.
O son of Pṛthivī, listen as I shall proclaim the mantra for the ritual placement (nyāsa);
having taken a cotton wick soaked in clarified butter, it should be infused with the name of the enemy.
Having turned it face-downward, one should then fill it with ashes;
having established it on a riverbank, one should make it radiant according to the prescribed ritual.
Having established the vessel on the path of knowledge, one should then perform the fire offering (homa),
using black mustard, salt, poison, and indeed *nāgara*.
By practicing for seven nights, one will certainly die again;
therefore, one should perform fire oblations for seven nights with the previously mentioned king of mantras.
One should begin with one hundred and eight peacock-feather [amulets] for bile,
and one thousand and eight should be given for one made of iron.
Furthermore, by practicing for seven nights, one will certainly die;
therefore, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the previously mentioned king of mantras and the seven-navel [substance].
One should begin with one hundred and eight recitations for the father,
and one thousand and eight for an image made of iron.
Facing south, with hair loosened and wearing black garments, one should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa) through the flow of one's own right channel.
One should remain intent upon that purpose near the peacock-shaped sacrificial pit;
by this very mantra, one may slay even the most formidable enemies.

Oṃ huṃ huṃ kṣāṃ rāṃ [name] māraya rāṃ kṣāṃ huṃ huṃ svāhā. This seventeenth vidyā-mantra is proclaimed in its syllables for the purpose of slaying all beings within the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
O King, that wicked-souled one who reviles Brahmins is a transgressor of the sacred law;
he is a slayer of mother and father alike, and he is eternally devoted to that [evil path].
O King, Śaśakamāra lived among the people without being hated;
otherwise, one should never act otherwise, even for hundreds of crores.
In the first [case], it is deluded; in the second, it is a peacock;
when raised in the third, it is situated above; and in the fourth, there is stability.
In the fifth [month], the spinal cord is broken; in the sixth, the semen reaches the head;
in the seventh, he dies upon the earth—he dies, there is no doubt about this.
Now I shall proclaim the ritual application which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
I shall describe in brief the method for the immobilization of all beings.
Viṣṇukrāntā, Sarvākṣī, Nāgaparṇī, and Valā—these should be gathered under the Puṣya asterism; [otherwise] the practitioner does not succeed through the mantra.

On the days of the new moon and likewise on the first day of the dark fortnight, one should deposit all the medicinal herbs, empowered with mantras, into the house of the enemy; by this means, I shall describe the destruction of everything. [The herb] Viṣṇukrāntā...
Oṃ ṣajya huṃ huṃ huṃ [name] staṃbhaya 2 huṃ hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ phaṭ.
By this mantra one paralyzes; there is no one who can give it away, nor anyone who can awaken from it.
This great mantra for self-concealment shall paralyze even the source of the bilva tree.
When recited, it brings about the purification of accomplishments and produces immediate conviction;
[one should offer] buffalo butter, vermilion, and golden fruit.

Sudarśana, nīlapuṣpī, and nāgī come together with great power; when they are applied, the earth becomes motionless. Pratyāyanavimardaka, malakākṣīraka, sarpākṣī, jñānajihvā, and the fruits of madana [are used].
The lizard, the monkey, the kalaśa-bone, the chameleon, and blood.
Having taken all of this along with the fat, one should make it into a dry powder;
mixed with great oil (mahātaila), it is to be applied as an ointment for whomever it is given.
When combined with the previously mentioned mantra, it brings about the immobilization of a man;
furthermore, those mantras for bringing [the object] back are not always understood.
If my queen should cause the construction of a pleasure garden,
then I shall have it built by the wise for the sake of sport.
Gojihvā, sālaparṇī, as well as saṃkocapatrikā,
vajrī, ruska-kṣīra, and likewise śatruparṇī.
Having collected these in equal parts, one should reduce them to a dry powder and then carefully mix it with the oil of the *śiśumāra*.
If it is sprinkled with oil consecrated by the recitation of the mantra one hundred and eight times,
it effects the immobilization (*staṃbhanam*) of all quadrupeds, such as buffaloes and the like, equally.
Having washed them with warm water, they return unharmed; in this way, the species of cattle, buffaloes, and other animals become healthy once more.
Likewise, the trident-shaped [seeds], white mustard seeds, bibhītaka fruits, thorns, vermilion, and bitter bottle gourds.
O practitioner, with this mantra, one should prepare hot water for the subject:
*oṃ huṃ kraṃ hastastambhana svāhā*.
By anointing both hands with this mantra, one paralyzes even a divine being.
Sarṣapa, white guñjā, and jalakuṃbhī are the third [type].
With palms joined in reverence, one should have a fine powder prepared;
having taken the skin from a frog and a water-snake, one should saturate it [with the powder].
One should awaken the mantra of the body of the lake-element:
Oṃ, you are water, the sustainer of all worlds; O mantra, pillar of pillars, svāhā!
Just as one moves at will upon the water amidst the shifting whirlpools;
likewise, one should prepare a dried powder of māṃsī, kanakapuṣpā, saptaparṇī, and vacā,
combined with the bile of a crocodile.
The wise man, having applied the simple ointment, should lie down upon the sacrificial fire.
Oṃ namayopanidīyani staṃbhani rīṃ rīṃ rūṃ rūṃ huṃ svāhā. One should recite this twenty thousand times in the presence of the two deities; thereafter, success is indeed attained.
[The ingredients are] cotton-seed, turmeric, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and suvatsalī.
One should also cast a snake, joined with the root-mantra of Nāgārī, into its mouth.
A snake along with its pillar approaches and remains as if fast asleep.
*Oṃ huṃ* Koṭarākṣi Vagalāmukhi, O you who grant long life, paralyze the movement of the malevolent sorceress, *svāhā*.
The root of the Kumārī plant, the Varjanī, and the Śarapuṅkhī, combined together [are used].
By means of this application of incense, there is the binding of the pits of serpents.
Thus ends the subduing of serpents.
O God of gods, salutations to you, Bhairava with the terrifying countenance;
I shall now describe the subduing of armies as it was taught by Bhairava.
Whether at a self-manifested image, a Jantu-linga, a temple, or before Keśava,
the all-pervading one, remaining there with a concentrated mind, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
I shall proclaim the nine-syllable great mantra; listen attentively:
*oṃ saṃ raṃ kṣaṃ saṃ laṃ vaṃ dhaṃ krīṃ svāhā*.
This is your king of mantras, which wards off wicked enemies.
And the destroyer, having thus broken through, protects his own army.
One should always recite with diligence this mantra that increases victory;
by remembering this king of mantras, one becomes free from fear and disease.
When great danger has arisen, we shall take auspicious clay from a place of pilgrimage;
then, having gathered it repeatedly, we shall smear the surface of the earth.
One should likewise draw an eight-petaled lotus with this [mantra];
then, a wise man should place a water-pot in each of the four directions.
Endowed with the five jewels, possessed of the two-fold increase, it is victorious; likewise, there is the seed-mantra, as well as *vacā* and *parājitā*.
One should place Sahadevī, Lakṣmaṇā, and Śaṅkhapuṣpī as the seventh,
along with Aṣṭā and Somarājī, inside the water-pot.
One should clothe it in white garments and anoint it with divine perfumes;
then, having joined it with sprouts of *bhūta* grass, one should place the mantra upon it.
One should worship the deity in the maṇḍala and perform worship with their respective mantras;
recitation (jāpya) should be performed before him, as well as the fire-oblation (homa), continuously.
Then, with red flowers, one should worship the Lord Bhairava, the all-pervading master; having paid homage to the God and the Goddess who are covered with the dust of the menstrual flow.
One should sprinkle all the sacrificial posts with water mixed with gravel from a field that lacks water;
likewise, one should also sprinkle the elephants and the people with water.
Having consecrated the bow, the thunderbolt, the sword, the mace, and the supreme Kṛṣṇa— the Great-Souled One— there shall be the destruction of the enemy host.
If a person should fashion a human figure according to this rite, it will,
when brought under control by the command of the deity, bring about the destruction of enemies.
If even Indra, the enemy of Sambara, is paralyzed by this,
then follows the accomplishment of the Vetāla:
having taken the *rocanā* (gallstone) and the ashes from a corpse.
A wise person, having burnt the wings of the crow and the owl, brings about their destruction.
And the wise one should perform [the rite] consecrated with this mantra:
Oṃ kṣāṃ kroṃ svāhā.
And one should prepare the collyrium; then one will certainly see the Vetāla, who, having arrived in an extremely terrifying form, is most radiant.
Tell me what must be done by me for those great-souled ones,
so that the practitioner may obtain whatever is desired by his own will or wished for in his mind.
Everything will be accomplished for you; all this shall come to pass, so there is no need for hesitation here.
By taking refuge in a single liṅga and reciting the three-syllabled king of mantras, [all goals are attained].
Having performed the recitation, one who has conquered anger and subdued the senses should wait until midnight has passed; then he indeed arrives.
One should draw a lotus with eight petals, including the filaments, the receptacle, and the pericarp; one should write the mantra in the center and know that it should be applied to the petals.
With yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, and musk, mixed with the juice of *kāca* and *pārā*,
one should write the name and the syllable *hrīṃ* surrounded by a black circle on a birch bark leaf.
And having increased it on the hand and the neck, that man shall become auspicious;
he shall wander over the entire earth like another Kāmadeva.
I shall now fully proclaim the Mohanī, which is renowned throughout the three worlds;
by knowing it, all sentient beings attain a state of auspiciousness.
Oṃ krīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ. When this supreme protective vidyā is recited, it becomes effective.
Oṃ klāṃ, the heart; oṃ hīṃ, the head; oṃ su, the crest-lock; oṃ haḥ, the armor; oṃ hrīṃ, the feet; oṃ krīṃ, the knees; oṃ līṃ, the thighs; oṃ rīṃ, the hips; oṃ sa, the genitals; oṃ oṃ.

At the Maṇipūraka: Oṃ vāṃ, on the belly; Oṃ vāṃ, on the heart; Oṃ hrīṃ, on the arms; Oṃ hrīṃ, on the throat; Oṃ huṃ, on the eyes; Oṃ krāṃ, on the head. By this ritual placement (nyāsa), one becomes Vāgīśvara himself. Indeed, there is but one fault regarding this vidyā: while it is being recited, all people—both men and women—become as if possessed by it.
The wise one attains the fruit:
whatever has been spoken or not yet spoken, by a single recitation the practitioner becomes equal to the Lord, even compared to hundreds of millions of other mantras.
Now I shall further explain the supreme characteristic of the root,
by the mere knowledge of which self-conviction arises.
109b) He becomes fortunate, the sole leader among all men and women in the world;
even an enemy turns into a friend— what could he do that would not be accomplished?
Wicked thieves, kings, serpents, tigers, jackals, and the like—
all these come under one's control and constantly carry out one's commands.
Oṃ bhave bharokṣa bhūkṣo bhayamohaya sarvasattvaṃ vaśamānaya kuru me hīṃ mohinīye svāhā.
This is the root mantra (mūlamantra). Its subsidiary mantras (jāti) are as follows: Oṃ bhūte is the heart mantra (hṛdaya). Oṃ bhūge bhaga... [is the head mantra].

Thus for the head. *Oṃ khaṃ bhakṣau bhayaśikhā* (Oṃ Khaṃ, O you who devour fear, [be] the crest-lock). *Oṃ sarvatva ca mama kuru kavacaṃ* (Oṃ, and make everything mine; [be] the armor). *Hrīṃ mohinīye netrābhyāṃ svāhā* (Hrīṃ, to the Enchanting One, to the two eyes, svāhā). *Astrāya phaṭ* (To the weapon, phaṭ)—this is the meaning. Having thus performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should recite [the mantra].
Having become a needle and being concentrated in mind, one should perform a hundred thousand recitations at a solitary liṅga,
using deep-red tamāla flowers consecrated with the three sweets.
Through many hundreds of homas, the desired perfection is attained;
it endures [the practitioner] in eating and drinking, fulfills desires, and brings success in ritual actions.
In this, the practitioner succeeds without delay; of this there is no doubt.
Having consecrated white mustard seeds with the mantra, one should offer them to the esteemed women.
If one performs the rite on the head when the moon is in Puṣya, and again on the root when it is in Punarvasu,
that woman becomes submissive both in person and through her wealth.
Alternatively, one may perform [the rite] upon a man, because there is no difference between the mantra and the name;
by employing it twenty-one times, one brings the man into a state of servitude.

In the presence of kings, however, the practitioner who removes the thorns [of their adversaries] shall recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; then they will become submissive, and not otherwise.
Then, at the beginning of the recitation for one who is being consecrated, one should apply a tilaka with the word "Svāmin"; this destroys all calamities.
Then, through its application, all accomplishments come to pass;
even for wicked women who are arrogant with the pride of intoxication.
O wise one, listen to this [instruction] for the purpose of subjugation:
one should take up the dust arising from the left foot with the left hand.
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, a man should apply it as a *tilaka*;
he becomes a master of the woman from whose feet its origin arose.
This yoga must be kept strictly secret and should not be given to just anyone;
it is the truth, the truth, and again the truth, as is the mantra of Bhairava.
It should not be given to wicked beings; one should always keep it secret until [the time] has come.
It should be bestowed upon one who is devoted to the treatise; otherwise, one should certainly not do so.

For the subjugation of a man, having taken dust from his right foot and eight grains of rice, one should offer them into a great fire; at the conclusion of one hundred and eight oblations of excellent liquor with the mantra "svāhā," one shall attain success.

Oṃ kroṃ huṃ hrīṃ hīṃ hrīṃ hoṃ! This queen of mantras is certain for the eradication of enemies of knowledge. Having recited it ten thousand times, one becomes accomplished; one will surely achieve this, there is no doubt.
One may cause an enemy to be expelled even from afar, let alone when he is nearby.
First, one must prepare the site, and afterwards, one should commence the recitation.
One should visualize the syllable Oṃ, yellow in color, at the crown of the head;
one should contemplate the syllable Kroṃ at the heart, resembling red mercury.
One should contemplate a white syllable *huṃ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
thereafter, one should contemplate the syllable *hrīṃ*, which has the luster of the color of blazing fire, with the mantra *oṃ varvasanabhyātyagni*.
One should contemplate the syllable HOṂ as being black in color and pervading all the limbs.
Having thus first performed meditation upon Śambhu, one should undertake everything;
furthermore, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), listen to the description of the second location.
Having visualized the enemy as black in color and oneself with disheveled hair,
bound indeed by the noose of Time, one should strike him with those of great power.
Seen by all the men, he fell from that place outside;
having sent away the men, he closed the gate and was confined within the mountain.
In this way, meditation should be practiced; for the enemy of the senses is like a foe.
Once the six aggregates have been destroyed from their station, what need is there even to mention bathing or other such acts?
Oṃ! One should worship Mahākāla, who is formidable, most terrifying, and exceedingly fierce in his transformations, whose form is like that of a mountain.

Oṃ lava-lā! O you who are like fire, burn this heart; burn his limbs, burn his joints, burn his bones, burn his marrow! Lava-kāla-vana! You cut [them] asunder; lava-nā-vi-bhati-lavana! You cut them asunder thirty-five times! Where is the blood? Where is sleep? Where is pleasure?
Even if she dwells a hundred yojanas away, beyond rivers that are impossible to cross,
bound within a wall of nagas, or enclosed by a fence of black serpents— she will indeed come there quickly.
The slaughter of Lavaṇa was performed by him in a previous life.

Oṃ ciṭi 2 vikrāmi 2, accomplish [the task of] so-and-so together with his retinue, or bring him under control, svāhā! Oṃ karṇapiśāci parṇasavarī, you who destroy all calamities, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Śiva! Ṣaṃjarīṭa, Sīto, and Śiva—[this offering] combined with the *nirmālya* should be given at the root of a tree; that tree...
They abandon their flight. One should make a pill from *ṣaṃjarīṭa* with blood; whoever touches it becomes submissive.

Having sprinkled the heart of *ṣaṃjarīṭa* with water or the body with oil in secret, one becomes defeated in battle. And by [applying] the hair from the head of *ṣaṃjarīṭa* to the secret parts and the impurities, he becomes submissive.

Having made a powder of *manaḥśilā* (realgar) from the root-buds of the *ṣaṃjarīṭa* plant, he to whom it is given becomes submissive. Likewise, by giving *karañja* seed, *vālaka*, and *kaurmapī* with affection, even a barren woman gives birth.
This powder, including the flower of the *mṛtaka* plant, should be administered; the woman becomes invisible and submissive. Oṃ.

"O Cāmuṇḍā, bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā! Having recited this mantra seven times, whoever it is to whom [the offering] is given becomes submissive. Having made a pair of deer bones into a stake the length of a finger, if one buries it in the name of someone, that person becomes like a corpse. Oṃ.
*Vaṭadahi svāhā*. Furthermore: *Oṃ kāmeśvarīye svāhā*.

By reciting this mantra twenty-one times over betel leaf or a flower and giving it to someone, that person becomes submissive. Having prepared collyrium from *chuchundarī* oil, if one applies that ointment to the eyes so that someone looks upon them, that person becomes submissive.

It comes to pass. One should apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with this ointment; one will become beloved by kings. Having ground turmeric and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) into an equal powder, one should cause it to be applied to the heads of women; the man will be brought under their control.
Yellow orpiment and *gorocanā* should be given; having caused a forehead mark to be made with blood from the nose, whatever one desires, that one shall obtain.

To the limbs, the limbs, svāhā! Tagara, rock salt, uśīra, yaṣṭīmadhu, and likewise honey—if a man possessing these [ingredients] approaches women, he becomes beloved by royal ladies. [The root of] vātāri is superior.

Having produced [the substance] under the constellation Hasta, one should grind it into a fine powder on that same day and prepare a pill (*vāṭikā*). It should be placed upon the heads of women; they will become submissive. *Oṃ namo bhagavate amuka-vaśo bhava | oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* Having recited this mantra over betel leaves and other items one hundred and eight times while chanting, [one should apply it].

If this [mantra] is recited seven times over [an object] and given to someone, then that person will become submissive. *Oṃ raladāya oṃ ali 2 kalivala dhūlī cauraghra yogaṇḍa sarpāvināvaddhnāmiva svāhā*. Having consecrated a piece of wood four finger-breadths long with this mantra seven times, it should be placed in the right ear.
By reciting this while departing, there will be no fear of thieves, tigers, and the like. *Oṃ rāma-nija-mme?

sthaubhaniṃ staṃbhane mohanī mohe andhanī andhe amukasya hṛdaye cakṣuḥ śiraḥ sarvāṅgaṃ mohaya he phaṭ astrāya svāhā.* One should proceed on the journey after reciting this mantra seven times. This is the Vidyā.

This is the *kevalikā*. One should apply a *tilaka* (forehead mark) with eight thousand recitations of *rocanā* (yellow pigment); whoever sees it becomes submissive. This mantra, when one goes into the royal court, makes one very dear: *Oṃ maṃtranāthāya trailokyavijayaṃ strīpuruṣasya hṛdayam asādhitasya karma bhavati*.

Having risen in the morning, one should take collyrium, consecrate water seven times with the mantra, and wash one's face. Whomever one has seen, by likewise consecrating oil and a tooth-stick seven times with the mantra and consuming them, that person becomes submissive. *Oṃ hāṃ vadha svāhā*. *Oṃ hili 2 mānuṣī phaṭ svāhā*.

O Bull, at the end of the day, [recite] at will: *oṃ klaṃ rakṣame huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, which bestows accomplishment, [say]: *hrīrakṣāya namaḥ*. On this Sunday, standing facing the sun, fixing it in one's mind, perform the recitation, O Sage; it is certain: *oṃ cūrṇaparṇenaktaṃ haḥ*.

Reciting "ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ" twenty-one times while uttering the name [of the person], an ointment made of ghee, honey, and *madana* fruit increases the moisture of women; likewise, one should know that it is effective when prepared with long pepper (*pippalī*) and rice.
111b) Pigeon droppings mixed with honey— this ointment is a binding by means of oil.

Having ground together one’s own blood, the powder of *satapuṣpā*, water, *karavīra*, the fruit of *bṛhatī*, mustard seeds, *priyaṅgu*, *tagara*, lotus filaments, and cow urine— prepared to subjugate women— one should administer a dose of one *tulā* of this mixture with honey along with *yākīnī*; this is the supreme means of subjugation.

An ointment composed of vulture excrement, meat, human flesh, bone, and one’s own enemy brings about subjugation that ends in death. Having recited "Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Sa" while holding the thumb and ring finger of the Vīrabhava [mudrā], one should apply a *tilaka* on the forehead.
He who brings the three worlds under his control is therefore called a practitioner (*prayogadhāra*).
He whose banner is the ocean does not know [this], for he wanders upon the surface of the earth;
however, that man who knows this science shall become a bull among men.

Oṃ hrīṃ! Homage to the sandals of the Guru-nātha, the power of consciousness (vijñāna-śakti). Oṃ hrīṃ! Hara! O Ārāhasana-bhiva! Hrīṃ phaṭ 2! Strike 2! Seize 2! O you who dwell [therein]! Ye rārīmāra-stambhaniye! Paralyze! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! For paralyzing thieves of cows and the like.
It destroys the fear of tigers and misfortune.

One should recite it with the firm conviction: "O Siṣirāvatī, grant me great accomplishment! Furthermore, by taking this mantra—*siṣiyīsisvāṃ*—and binding it upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*) at the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the Sun, or likewise during a solar eclipse, using *rocanā* (yellow pigment), [one attains success].

By performing the *tilaka* [mark] with this [mantra], one paralyzes [the opponent] in all undertakings. Now, the paralysis of the sword (*khaḍga-stambhana*) is described: Oṃ pātulaṃthe kalikamalaku apretalalitaṃ ya | bhūratasaruvadhamotasilaṃ sarvanāśaye ṣaḍete taṃ kavarigrahanumaṃte yaha hanayā udyāvatānepi ca | [Recite] one hundred and eight times.

The practitioner, having consecrated water with mantras and recited them over it, should drink it again, saying: "May the waters be most excellent for me. Having seen a fragrance as if it were gold, one should gaze at it with a pure mind; this is called the "divine paralysis" (divyastaṃbhanati). Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, to the Blessed One, O divine yoginī, paralyze the divine [powers]! Agne, Manu, O axe of the mind, do not let them pass!
Māra ṭha jalamaḥ aṣṭadivyāni maṭha oṃ Siddhiśvarī Bhagavatī mama divya-stambhaniye svāhā. 112a)
The *Sitalīpatra* is known as the "Lion's Vehicle.
When recited with great mantras, it bestows success and grants all accomplishments (*siddhis*).
By this very mantra alone, one should likewise perform the *japa* and the *mudrās*.

Grind wood from a *vahutagraha* tree together with *maṇḍūka*, animal fat, lac, and *asita-nīpa* leaves using water decocted from leaves. By means of that [mixture], having made a circle and a pillar, one should cause water to flow. Then, having taken up two feet with that [mixture], one should carry them around the fire. Oṃ, salutation to Narasiṃha, the destroyer of the race of Asuras, huṃ.

*Phaṭ kālī kachulīnāya eti vīmaśānaṃ ca ivīmaśca eyiśikara śubhitaiḥ |* Having consecrated water in a jar with the mantra *sneho hanna uttārade vahni kaṭi ājñā na* repeated one hundred and eight times, one should wash the feet. [The result is] the immobilization of heated iron and the like. Taking red and yellow [pigments], as well as a widow's [garment], in that same manner...

Having cast [the substance] mixed with *vacaka* into the mouths of tigresses, one should wrap it around with a footprint. Having cast it into flowers, the wise man should effect this "stambhana" (paralysis) of water. Regarding kings and the like, in matters of equality and so forth, he should utter a single word; this is the supreme essence. Those [mantras] for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*) are now being told. [The city...]

When the dust has been applied to the root and the grain is obtained, if one then raises the arms and, having done so, does not follow along but whirls [the arms], and casts the dust into someone's house, they shall be made to hate one another. Wherever the syllables *ka-kha-ho* are constantly deposited in the house, [the effect occurs]. *Oṃ ṣaradhīranī 2 vidveṣanī dhūlanīye svāhā*.

"O you who effect expulsion, create enmity between [Name] and [Name], svāhā! Having drawn them in with the Jvālinī mantra, it is said that when both have been rendered mutually hostile, one should take their dust and cast it into a fire of *niṃba* wood or embers; thus they shall be made to hate one another. Enemies are to be dealt with here in this manner.

Investigation: Oṃ! Kālī, Karālinī, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura! [To] Amukā, the hater of Amuka, svāhā! On the delightful summit of Kailāsa, frequented by gods and gandharvas, strewn with various trees and creepers, and adorned with various flowers, [he was] seated comfortably.
Bhairavī asked Hara, the Lord of the World, who is Bhairava and the beloved of Bhairavī, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, omniscient Supreme Lord!
There is no other brother for me in this world, nor in the three realms with all their mobile and immobile beings.
O Lord of the Gods, you are the brother of all beings and the bringer of welfare to the worlds; therefore, for their benefit, speak in brief.
Now, in this world of various views, people are afflicted by hatred;
tormented by many mouths, they are constantly agitated in mind.
When there are many afflictions and one's own intellect and prowess are so slight,
how is it that all these beings continue to suffer while the Lord exists?
Singing your name and its virtues again and again, those who share in the burden of afflictions tremble;
terrified, they abandon falsehood and become worshippers of the gods and guests.
By what means is it that there is never a lack of accomplishment for them?
O Lord, the commitment made by you is never lost through its practice.
How then, O Mahādeva, does even the performance [of rites] perish?
O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, tell me this, for there is doubt.
To the gods who were shaken, afflicted, and distressed, the Lord of the Gods,
Śrī Bhairava, said:
O illustrious lady, acting for the benefit of the worlds, I shall speak;
I will not elaborate, but shall tell it briefly and in summary.
O beloved, that which has not been told to anyone— the most essential of the essential—
is indeed known by the name Ḍāmara, for its name is difficult to obtain.
I shall briefly declare its most essential core:
this most excellent treatise is for the benefit of the three worlds.
For those who are distressed, for daughters, and for those born into royal lineages,
I shall declare the expedient means for those who are broken and whose splendor has been destroyed.
O lady of excellent hips, I shall briefly explain [it] in due order;
I declare that it must be performed with diligence and kept secret.
This is true; O Bhairavī, listen as I shall describe the ritual applications.
Having become pure and composed on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should proceed.
In a secluded place, one should diligently perform [the rite] with a non-conceptual mind;
having then smeared the four corners with cow dung, [one prepares] the mandalas.
Having offered perfumes, flowers, and incenses,
one should present a silk thread that has been smeared with vermilion after bringing it forward.
Just as a sword-blade is held by its own [scabbard] when it is without support, so too [the disciple] should be supported;
I shall now declare the mantra by which one should consecrate that [disciple].

Oṃ, salutations to Caṇḍikā, girīṃ turī ṭha ṭha. With this mantra, one should consecrate [the object] up to one hundred and eight times. Having worshipped a young girl with that [consecrated substance], one should show the cloth according to the prescribed rite. For whomsoever [this is done], whatever was intended—whether lost, stolen, life, or even death—[shall be realized].

[This is] the *vastraprasannā*. Now, therefore, follows the *khaḍgaprasannā*. Having performed its worship according to the previously mentioned procedure on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*), one should observe a fast and then recollect the mantra before Caṇḍikā:
*oṃ caṇḍikāyai kliṃ 2 ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. This mantra [is to be recited] on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.

One should repeat [the mantra] one thousand times. Then, at the time of dawn, having worshipped the Goddess according to the ritual with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), and having brought a hundred flowers while all are seated upon their seats, the Goddess should be struck with each flower consecrated by mantras. There, one should worship the sword, having smeared it with *alika* [pigment] in front.
One should show it. They ask about the auspicious and the inauspicious, and whether the sword is being held.
Now I shall explain another [method] which produces immediate conviction;
it must be performed without conceptual doubt, for success occurs in no other way.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, as well as on the eighth, one should satisfy the *citila*;
then, indeed, he should build a house for it, which shall dwell there again,
having been worshipped with oil, perfumes, and flowers, and adorned with beautiful blossoms.
Having placed it by the mother's side, one should tie it with a red thread;
having worshipped it especially, he shall dwell upon the surface of the earth.
One should worship with this mantra and not deliberate upon that door;
thereafter, he should enter the supreme house with a mind free from conceptual construction.
Then, one should show him everything that is desired by the mind;
there, one should diligently remember this mantra which is worthy of worship.
Oṃ, homage to Maheśvara, the lord of Umā, for the accomplishment of all aims!
Homage to the Uṣṇīṣa, the Great Karabhrāja, Vikara-hīṭha-strīya! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
113b) The obtaining of a maiden and so forth, as well as coming and going;
joy and gain, and likewise what has been and what is yet to be.
Life, death, illness, health, and what is dear—
as well as what is joined with and desired— these are the subjects of all discourse.
Thus it is, O Goddess Umā, you who move with the power of Varāha;
you are the mother of all beings, showing them what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Thus ends the section on ritual applications (*prayogakhaṇḍa*) in the *Śrīhāhārāvatantra*, which is a compendium of the Atharvaṇa.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O delighter of supreme bliss!"
Be gracious, O speaker of secrets; speak, O you who are so pleasant in speech.
That which is hidden from the five-faced one in all tantras and mantras— that known as the secret— reveal it, just as you have revealed it to me, O beloved.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
How shall I speak to you, O fickle-souled one, regarding that which is secret?
For by your very nature as a woman, you know the Great Principle (Mahattattva) which bestows happiness.
I shall become perfectly steadfast; never should anything be spoken [that would disturb me].
Then your meditations will be focused upon the accomplishment of the mantra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The deity, the guru, and that which is called mantra are said to be a single realization.
The mantra is the guru and the deity; the guru is indeed the deity.
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāguhyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Bhedavicchinnamastā, and likewise Vidyādhūmāvatī.
Vagalāsiddhividya, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā—
these ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the Great Goddesses.
Kālikā, Karālī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Chinnamastā, as well as Bhairavī; Harasiddhā, Siddhilakṣmī, Bhrāmarī, and Vātavī likewise.
Mahāmārī, Tāmasī, Mātaṅgī, Śavareśvarī, Carcikā, Śivaruṇī, and Mahāmahīṣamardinī.
Ugracaṇḍā, Kulikā, Phetkāri, and Guhyakālā—
these are your fierce forms, as well as those that are gentle, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Extremely rare in the world, these are honored by the six traditions;
they are supreme vidyās, difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Bestowing happiness and liberation, eternal, and not to be achieved through mere hardship—
by whatever means possible, such [attainments] shall be realized upon this earth.
114a) I shall tell you everything solely out of affection for you;
herein there is no consideration of the lunar mansions such as Aśvinī and the like, nor any calculation of the Siddha and other yogas.
There is no need for the purification of time and so forth, nor the elimination of enemies and the like;
this great vidyā of accomplishment is easily accessible even with little effort.
O Great Goddess, there is never anything that causes suffering;
she who is the supreme knowledge at the time of death is proclaimed as Tārā herself.
The supreme Tārā, who was previously described as being fourfold through ignorance—
it is indeed by virtue of the distinction between these two that the mantras come into being.
That which was spoken by me in the Kālikā-kalpa and the Tārā-kalpa—
the Great Vidyā of sixteen syllables that was previously described as fourfold— [is this].
Through the distinctions of the Lakṣmī-bīja and others, that [mantra] becomes fivefold here;
previously, the great one-syllable vidyā was devoid of seed-syllables.
The three-syllabled Bhuvaneśvarī is proclaimed as the Great Goddess.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, this desired Vidyā has been mentioned, but it has not been revealed."
And he gives, O Nandasundara, out of a disposition of compassion through his teaching.
The illustrious Bhairava said: In ancient times, this great lore, the Mistress of the World, known by the name Vajrā-mohinī, was indeed propitiated by the King of the Gods.
The single-syllable [mantra] is devoid of seed-syllables; by means of the Vāgbhava [syllable], it overcomes fevers.
This [mantra] is perfected through the Puṣpadhāvinī, known as the Kāmarāja-vidyā.
Formerly worshipped by Śakra, she was proclaimed the Sovereign of the World; and this Vidyā, who is Kumārī, has descended from you as Satyavatī.
Vidyā is established in Māyā; she is solely of the nature of Śiva and solely of the nature of Śakti, the savior whose form is like the moon.
Bhairavī is indeed the Great Vidyā, the bestower of great prosperity;
Chinnamastā is she whose true nature is fondness for wine, meat, and blood.
The great vidyā Dhūmāvatī is intent upon killing and eradication;
Vagalāmukhī is endowed with various qualities such as subjugation and paralyzing.
Mātaṅgī is indeed the Great Vidyā who brings the three worlds under her control;
Kamalā is said to be of three kinds, and likewise exists as the Single Syllable (Ekākṣarā).
But Guhyakālī alone is the great source of prosperity, the bestower of happiness and liberation; she is the Great Vidyā, exceedingly difficult to attain within the three worlds.
The Goddess said:
"The rosary has been described with effort, yet it was not fully revealed."
What is the name of this "rosary of the eyes," and what is its fruit? Tell me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The rosary (akṣamālā) is indeed the Goddess of the gods, and it is manifold according to the different types of seeds;
listen as its various classifications are described by me in detail.
By means of the swift speech of the letters in both direct and reverse order,
the Supreme Goddess [is realized] through the sequence from the first letter to the last, and from the last back to the first.
One should never place the letter *kṣa*, which has the form of Mount Meru, at the bottom;
for a rosary that is devoid of Meru, or one that consists of only a single string, is deficient.
Devoid of faith and lacking luster, the garland of fat becomes fruitless;
the Viśinī, which lacks the manifestation of the twenty-six principles, has entered the interior of the Brahma-nāḍī.
Strung together by her, it bestows all desired fruits when recited one hundred and eight times; having performed this, one should employ the *klība* mantra.
The three classes [of consonants] beginning with *kṣa* are called *taṃtu*,
while the neuter is said to be the eighth of the groups (*varga*), according to the sequence of the divisions of desire.
From the eight groups beginning with *a*,
*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*, there is the attainment of liberation through crystal [rosaries], while the lotus-seed (*padmākṣa*) yields many sons.
O beloved, a rosary made of *putrajīva* fruits bestows wealth, one made of stones bestows all enjoyments,
and a pure crystal rosary bestows great prosperity.
In the rite of Dhūmāvatī,
a garland is made from wood from the cremation ground or from the bones of human fingers, strung according to the divisions of the joints.
Bestower of all accomplishments, giver of liberation, she of excellent complexion;
she who is to be worshipped when the task involves the weaving of various seats, and who is fond of the red lotus at the navel.
O beloved, it should always be guarded with effort, like a mother's secret or a lover's;
this rosary, which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments, has been described as being of five kinds.
A garland strung with pearls bestows the fruit of all sovereignty;
so too do those made of precious gems, coral, gold, and silver.
O beloved, the garland composed of the foremost ancient texts, which bestows the fruit of all liberation,
is strung together with the channels (nāḍīs) and grants great spiritual accomplishment.
The thirty [deities] bestow the fruit of sovereignty; the twenty-five, however, bestow liberation.
Consisting of fourteen, she is the giver of liberation and the increaser of enjoyment.
The Goddess, consisting of fifteen aspects, is established for killing and expulsion;
she is also present for paralyzing, bewildering, subjugating, obstructing, and summoning.
In connection with the accomplishment of the sandals (*pādukāsiddhi*), the number of recitations is proclaimed as follows:
one should perform one hundred and eight recitations, or otherwise, that which grants all desires.

One should always perform the recitation (japa) with the hand according to the rule for those seeking specific desires; however, O Priyaṃvadā, one may also perform even the recitation for desired results with the hand if one possesses a rosary (mālā).
In this matter, one should perform the recitation (japa) with the fingers; one should recite using all the fingers including the thumb.
Any ritual action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless.
Starting first with the two ring fingers (anāmikā) and proceeding in order from the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) to the base of the index finger (tarjanī),
this is proclaimed as the hand-garland (karamālā).
Circumambulating Mount Meru by way of the root-joint of the ring finger, one avoids the fault of overstepping Meru; otherwise, the result is produced differently.
Starting from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction,
one should not cross over [the lines], keeping Mount Meru in the center from the middle to the base.
If a person joins the tips of the index finger and the middle finger there,
his four things— life-span, knowledge, fame, and strength— will perish.
One should not worship with a single finger; rather, one should contract the strength slightly.
Now, therefore, I shall describe the stringing of garlands and the consecration therein.
Having first performed worship with devotion while remaining pure and having fasted beforehand,
the practitioner himself, observing silence in a secluded place, should string the garland.
Having performed his daily rites and being pure, the knower of mantras, in a pure field,
should [offer] at the proper time and according to what is available, with diligent effort.
They should be uniform in shape, neither too thick nor too thin,
free from defects such as insects, and not marked with lines.
Having washed each of those separately with the five perfumes,
O best of brahmins, [he should take] that which is fashioned by a virtuous woman and is free from knots.
Having tripled a threefold [cord], or likewise a silk thread that is white, red, and black, one should place them in the prison for the sake of pacification and ashes.
One should place there a white gem, washed with fragrant scents, upon nine horse-leaf-shaped lotuses arranged in a circular pattern.
Or with water from a cremation ground, or with water used for washing the ritual seat;
or with pure water, blood, musk, and saffron.
Having placed the Tāra-śakti, the Mātṛkā, the thread, and likewise the jewel,
one should worship them and diligently offer oblations with clarified butter.
If one is capable of performing the fire sacrifice (homa), one may perform the recitation (japa) even if it lacks certain qualities;
the wise practitioner should take each individual bead and thread it onto the string.
One should join mouth to mouth when feeding, and tail to tail;
or else, one should act according to the term "cow's tail," or it may take every form.
One should place a single eye at the junction of those two, and at the front, one should arrange a single jewel for each on Mount Meru, while fashioning Brahma-knots in the middle.
Having prepared the rosary, one should then perform its consecration;
one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using water [recited over] with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta!
In every birth, in non-birth, and in the state beyond birth, may Bhava protect me; salutations to Bhavodbhava.
Having first uttered "Oṃ" and then "Namaḥ" before this [name], one should circumambulate the lotus of the feet with Vāmadeva,
using sandalwood, agallochum, incense, and other such substances.
Oṃ, homage to Vāmadeva; homage to the subduer of strength, the tamer of all beings, the one who causes the destruction of pride;

homage to the one who creates power, homage to the one who creates heroic might, homage to strength! Homage to the subduer of strength, homage to the tamer of all beings, homage to the one who transcends the mind and the transmental!
One should fumigate with the Aghora mantra and likewise with the Tatpuruṣa mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the terrible, to all, to every one of all forms!"
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us from there. This mantra is indeed for the fifth [face]; one should recite it one hundred times for each [face].
Īśāna, the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the sovereign of Brahman, the overlord of Brahman...
May Sadāśiva be Brahmā; may he be forever all-pervasive.
One should consecrate Meru with the great mantra beginning with the Praṇava, "Sadāśiva," in due order, using that very mantra for the fifth [element]. Then, one should perform the consecration.
Having thus consecrated the garland, the wise one should establish its vital breath therein;
O Goddess of Gods, he should worship it with devotion using the Bhūta-mantra.
Having worshipped the guru, one should receive the rosary from his hand;
one who is impure should not touch it, nor should one show it even to the guru.
For enjoyment, liberation, or likewise for malevolent purposes, the wise one should mutter the middle [finger-mantra];
however, for subsequent rites, he should mutter with the thumb and ring finger.
One should recite for the rites of killing and expulsion with the joining of the index finger and the thumb;
one should recite for the rite of killing with the joining of the little finger and the thumb.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should worship that rosary and keep it well-concealed;
for during the time of recitation, the auspicious recitation rosary must be kept well-guarded.
The wise man should reveal the Guru, but never the mantra;
nor should he ever reveal the rosary or the mudrā.
Since spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas,
and nāgas carry him away while he trembles, one should therefore practice in secret.
If the thread has worn out, one should tie on a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times;
if it falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
"O Goddess, having first washed that rosary which was touched by those whose touch is forbidden, it was then offered to me; this rosary has been described as one difficult to find on earth."
"It must always be guarded with great effort, since you are difficult for me to obtain.
Śrī Devī said:
O God of gods, while he was speaking of the beautiful bliss regarding the postures and seats,
[he said that] when there is no delay by the preceptor, all mantras bestow excellent accomplishment.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
On a riverbank, at the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, in an empty house,
in a great forest, on a mountain, or wherever the mind may find its dissolution.
O Goddess, the place has been described to you; now the seat is being told:
for the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi), it is a tiger skin; for the attainment of knowledge (jñānasiddhi), it is a deer skin.
A seat made of cloth removes disease; one made of cane increases affection; that of silk is said to bestow nourishment; and a seat made of [other materials] alone grants all perfections.
Whether it be white or black, or especially a red woolen blanket,
that soft woolen blanket which was spread out has indeed fallen in battle.
That which has been killed by a living being, or is dead, is not a fit seat;
nor is the skin born from the womb of women, even if it be the skin of one who has miscarried.
O Goddess, you bestow all accomplishments and grant the abundance of all enjoyments;
and you shall make the place of Raurava free from coughing and affliction.
A householder who has not been initiated should never sit upon a seat made of wood from a cremation ground, nor upon any wood that is harsh, even if it is variegated with black and white stripes.
Furthermore, one should not sit upon that seat where a celibate practitioner (brahmacārin) has previously sat; nor,
O man, should one sit upon grass or deerskin that is not trimmed at the corners and is not even on all sides.
On a pure seat, one should prepare a platform measuring one or two cubits and raised four finger-breadths high; thereafter, one should perform the consecration and worship.
The tortoise posture (kaurma-āsana) bestows enjoyment and grants yoga;
they call it the lotus posture (padmāsana), which yields the fruit of all sovereignty.
O Goddess, the heroic posture (vīrāsana) is a seat that bestows success upon men;
one should stand with feet raised before the Goddess, specially adorned.
Or rather, O Goddess, even the *sarvāsana* is most excellent and very difficult to perform;
yet by means of the *padmāsana*, O Queen of the Gods, you remain established within the subterranean abode (*pātāla*).
Whoever worships the Goddess at night shall become wealthy and possessed of sons;
O Goddess, among all sacred seats (pīṭhas), the Caturdhā seat is the most excellent.
Jālandhara is the great pīṭha, and likewise Pūrṇagiri shall be the bala;
O Great Goddess, Oḍḍiyāna and the great Kāmarūpa are likewise [pīṭhas].
In the Kṛta age, Jālandhara is to be known; in Tretā, Pūrṇagiri;
in Dvāpara, Uḍḍiyāna; and in the Kali age, Kāmarūpa.
In this world, it bestows great fruit and grants supreme accomplishment through its consumption;
indeed, among the fifty sacred seats (pīṭhas), Kāmarūpa yields the greatest fruit.
There, the fruit of recitation and worship becomes a hundred-thousandfold for the Goddess;
though the Goddess is described in many ways, what need is there to further extol her virtues?
Wherein she herself abides in the form of the Yoni, consisting of ten million qualities.
The Goddess said:
"May Caṇḍikā be satisfied by the mere offering of the *bali*."
O Śaṅkara, protector of the Kurus, you have previously told this to us; now reveal it [again].
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent hips, I shall now describe the extremely secret ritual procedure for the worship with offerings; remain steadfast for now.
Curd, milk, jaggery, cooked rice, and milk-rice (pāyasa) combined with all [these];
honey from milk-rice, meat, coconut, and sweetmeats (modaka).
The *rāsaka*, the *bhikṣu*, the *khaṇḍa*, the *sārdraka*,
the *sakṣākara*, the *raṃbhāphala*, and the *laḍuka*— these, when conquered, provide nourishment.
The black goat, the "great meat" (mahāmāṃsa), the monitor lizard, the doe,
as well as the water-born fish meat, and the meat of the gaḍakī.
Pāvīna, moreover, should offer the flesh of the śāna fish, as well as the kulamvika,
the madgu, and the buffalo.
O lady of excellent hips, there was the flesh of birds, the emergence of various kinds of young animals, various seeds, human excrement, and condiments mixed with honey.
117a) One should offer an oblation of desired items smeared with ghee, either at night or during the day,
especially on an auspicious day during the dark fortnight.

If the Moon is in Dhanu, there will be the acquisition of elephants; if in Mīna, the acquisition of teeth is certain; in Māheṣa (Makara), there will be success in wealth; and in Mṛga (Capricorn), the fruit shall be enjoyment.
In Pakṣidanta, even one of great supernatural power may achieve wicked siddhi through the Anuttara [tantra].
[The mantras] are located on the forehead, the hands, the heart, the head, and in the middle of the body.
When one’s own body-blood is offered as a gift, the dissolution of Rudra’s body is supreme;
by the offering of a lotus-stalk oblation, great siddhi is produced.
By the gift of *surā*, O Goddess of Gods, one becomes a great lord of yoga (*mahāyogeśvara*).
The goddess *surā* is indeed threefold: *sphāṭikī* and likewise *ḍākinī*.
A gift of black crystal brings unsurpassed increase of wealth;
by the mere gift of a *ḍākinī* stone, one will certainly become the subduer of all.
The passionate goddess Kāmākī should worship the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī) with wine,
by means of pills, collyrium, paralysis, killing, expulsion, and so forth.
Having become a lord of great siddhis, one shall dwell for ten thousand kalpas;
O Maheśānī, when the arghya is offered, unsurpassed great siddhi is attained.
O Great Goddess, by offering red sandalwood, bilva, and so forth, as well as the javā flower and varvara grass, all desires, purposes, and accomplishments are attained.
Through the offering of wine and the presentation of arghya, one becomes dear to the Yoginīs;
O Goddess, by means of the waters used for washing the sacred seats (pīṭhas), one becomes a Mahāyogī.
With flowers of the *svayambhū* tree and with ivory, one may accomplish the six rites (*ṣatkarma*);
likewise, with very cool water mixed with musk and saffron, one may fill a pond.

By means of the *vāñjī* arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, one becomes the lord of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). That which arises on a Saturday at twilight is the *kuṇḍabhūta*, which bestows prosperity.
O Goddess of gods, a *gola* produced from a widow on a Saturday bestows success upon the earth; having drawn it in with the root mantra, one should remain pure and fearless.
The wheel is worshipped with the left foot;
the self-arisen flower, O Goddess, is born on earth in three ways.
The sixteenth, when married to an unmarried woman, bestows all accomplishments;
the middle one, when married by force, increases enjoyments.
And the Rājayoga is another, which is inferior yet bestows happiness;
one capable of worshipping the Virgin (Kumārī) should meditate upon the goddess Kroṇārī in sleep.
Having drawn out the semen produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* by means of the yoga of binding,
one who is fearless and pure-minded should diligently perform everything [with it].
In a copper vessel, or a skull, or one fashioned from the wood of a *vāṇaśāna* tree,
on a Saturday or a terrifying day, [one should place] the body of a deceased person.
Having worshipped the discus made of gold, silver, or iron according to the prescribed rite,
one should likewise offer flowers that are black or white as specified.
Likewise, O beloved, white and red flowers, as well as karavīra,
tagara, mallikā, atimuktaka, varvarī, and yūthikā;
Dhattūra, Aśoka, Bakula, white and black Aparājitā,
red flowers, Bilva leaves, Campaka, and Nāgakeśara.
O Priyaṃvadā, Mallikā, Kiṭīkācī, that which is proclaimed as Rakta, Arkapuṣpa, and Javāpuṣpa are the others.
On the eighth day, Pārvatī is especially pleased with him;
all the deities are pleased with a red lotus flower.
Whether she be Kṛṣṇā or the joined Kālikā, she may be a granter of boons;
yet she is not at all pleased by the cemetery weapon, for the supreme one smokes [with anger].
Kālī is satisfied by the flowers of the cremation ground,
while the supreme Pārvatī is satisfied by various wild forest flowers.
Pārvatī is pleased by the leaf of the āmalakī tree and by its flower;
one should worship her with various flowers on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
In a cremation ground, or at the end of the night on a Saturday or Tuesday, or at night;
the Illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord, tell me the procedure for the *puraścaryā*, which is the most secret of secrets."
Speak from the heat of the turban, for all desires shall indeed be fulfilled.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Having received initiation from a true guru at an auspicious time, whether by day or night, the Vāmamārga is the best; he who has been so initiated is indeed of middling status.
He who is indeed the self-born, supreme teacher, consecrated by liquor,
served Hariśambhu for fourteen thousand years.
Then that man becomes devoted to the worship of the Goddesses through body, mind, and speech, O best of gods, by means of matted hair and other such observances.
Having satisfied [the guru] with supreme devotion, one should undergo the initiation of the guru; then,
resorting to the previously mentioned place, one should take recourse in recitation and worship.
Beginning at dawn and continuing until midday, one should perform the recitation;
it should be recited on the first day, and it should be recited day after day.
One should not recite with deficiency or excess; one should always recite until it is completed. When the first month has passed, however, the limit is until the third watch of the night.
It should be consecrated at night, and one should not recite during the remainder of the night;
being a solitary hero and well-restrained, one should always consume sacrificial food (haviṣya).
A young woman, devoted to worship, should immediately prepare the offering;
she may worship her own wife or another woman on every sacred festival day.
One who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings should not associate with the base;
for whichever [mantra] is prescribed for recitation by whomsoever, its specific quality follows that [person] in due order.
At the conclusion of each recitation, one should perform a fire offering (homa) day by day with the respective substances;
it is taught that the number of offerings should be one-tenth of the total recitations.
The head-massage is prescribed with a tenth part of the libation;
with a tenth part of that, one should honor the best of Brahmins and young maidens of noble family.
One should unite [the deity] with various kinds of substances accompanied by joy;
if one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and other rites for the Lord, one should perform a recitation (japa) possessing that same number of repetitions.
If, due to a lack of materials, one is unable to perform worship and so forth, O beautiful one,
the rite of *puraścaraṇa* is prescribed by means of recitation alone.
Whether on a tripod, in the sky, or on the ground, the supreme practitioner,
being devoted to acting according to his own will, should always offer [the oblation] in a solitary place.
One who is capable may perform the preliminary rite with the sound of fish, meat, and so forth,
at night in a cremation ground, or near a corpse or a large tree.
I have taught the ritual procedure of the Bhairavī-kalpa, O lady of excellent complexion,
[to be performed] in a sacrificial pit one cubit in size, or in a secluded forest frequented by heroes.
O Goddess, this practice for the accomplishment of heroes, which destroys suffering on earth, has been declared;
indeed, by the worship of a young maiden alone, the rite of *puraścaryā* is considered fulfilled.
A maiden of various births endowed with youth,
or a girl who is exceedingly mature, like a cuckoo that speaks most melodiously.
One should worship with various substances, excellent fruits, and auspicious foods and edibles,
with supreme devotion, [offering] many beautiful and charming forms.
A sister, a daughter, a granddaughter, or even a daughter-in-law—
regardless of their various castes— are always to be honored, with the exception of one's mother.
Alternatively, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
beginning at sunrise until the sun sets.
Reciting it one thousand times is prescribed as the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight or the ninth day, [one should perform it] with great festivals.
One should especially perform worship on the eighth or the ninth day;
O Dear One, one should break the fast on the ninth day with fish, meat, and other such offerings.
Devoted to a state of pure devotion, one should recite [the mantra] six thousand times daily,
beginning from the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] until the next fourteenth day.
O Great Goddess, when that many recitations have been performed, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is considered complete;
the mantra is perfected by recitation alone, and not otherwise.
Without the performance of fire-offerings and other rites, and especially without the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas),
no seat is equal to the Yoni-pīṭha, nor is Kāmarūpa equal to it by others.
O Rudra, one of those two is like another body;
[it is especially so] at every sacred ford (tīrtha), particularly during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
The acceptance of the guru at the time of initiation is remembered as auspicious;
now I shall proclaim the secret [teaching] of the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds.
Formerly, all the kings were to be propitiated by you; formerly you were Brahmā, Rudra, the thousand-eyed Indra, Māyā, Śiva, Savitṛ, and Bhava.
O Maheśānī, Śakti is Māyā; she is the imperishable, supreme Vidyā.
Her seers are Brahmā and Virāṭ, her metre is Gāyatrī, and her deity is the Purifier of the Worlds.
She who is renowned as Mahāmāyā is proclaimed as the seed-syllable Lakṣmī;
the power of Maya and the Kilaka are declared to be the body of Śiva.
Then, one should perform the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) through Māyā for the sake of liberation from long [saṃsāra].
O Goddess, I shall now describe the meditation (dhyāna) which bestows the fruit of all sovereignty.
The goddess, resembling a mass of lightning, seated upon a red lotus throne,
three-eyed, clothed in a tiger skin, and endowed with twenty arms.
Yellow, red, white, black, smoky-grey, skull-white, pearl-white,
and blue-black— these indeed are said to be the colors of the purifiers.

Holding in her hands a sword, a trident, a mace, a discus, a conch, a bow, arrows, the *kartrī* mudrā, and likewise the *yoga* mudrā; the Goddess who bears the trident and spear, the bestower of the fruits of all supernatural attainments (*siddhi*).
119a) I shall now describe the yantra for worship: a hexagon joined with power (śakti),
followed by a lotus of six, eight, and sixteen petals, endowed with the vowels.
One should worship the Goddess in the triangle, excluding Māyā, Vāṇī, and Hari;
thus Prīti, Kṣamā, Tuṣṭi, and Mano-bhavā are to be worshipped in the [remaining] squares.
One should worship Yoganidrā, Mahānidrā, Mahāmāyā, Sundarī,
Mahāmudrā, and Mahāsvapnā upon the six petals.
She is knowledge and supreme ignorance, the great knowledge that bestows boons;
she is gentle, supremely gentle, the great gentleness, and the ultimate refuge.
Kālarātrī, Mahārātrī, Mahāgātrī,
Mahātmikā, Prakṛti, Vikṛti, Medhā, Viśvarūpā, and Kramādipā.
Mahāmattā, Pragalbhā, Unmattā,
Madagāminī, Mahāprahlāda, Vikalā, Harṣaṇā, and likewise Vihvalā.
Vikaṭā, Bahurūpā, Mahārūpā, Mahipradā,
Ghorarāvā, Mahānityā, and Bhañjabhuñjalabhāṣiṇī.
O beloved, Sundarī should always be worshipped according to the most excellent procedure;
thereafter, Indra and the other deities are to be worshipped in all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, at the four gates, one should worship Bhagaklinnā,
Bhagakṣā, Bhagamedhā, and Bhagākhyā, according to the rite, by way of counter-clockwise rotation.

Having thus worshipped the Goddess, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times; O Dear One, one should perform the fire oblation and other rites according to the prescribed rule, in the manner of a tenth part of that number.
By this method of non-duality, O Goddess, one becomes a lord of great siddhis;
wealthy, possessed of sons, wise, an enjoyer of pleasures, and of great strength.
Indeed, the son of a goddess always attains royal fortune;
for the Goddess Bhuvaneśī, the consort of the Lord, has been worshipped by me.
The seven-syllable mantra of Mahādevī bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
One should visualize the goddess, who resembles the color of gold and is adorned with every ornament.
She is clothed in linen, possesses three eyes, and is accompanied by a mountain peak;
or else she is Śailasimhā, Indrāṇī, the deity of the chariot.
Having meditated thus, one should first recite the entire [mantra] in brief;
at that time, that mantra to be recited bestows all prosperity.
O Dear One, Śiva is joined with the left [nostril], and the pair [of letters] with the ear;
Brahmā is joined with the mouth, having been repeated twice in the order of the mantra.
Endowed with the eye and accompanied by Śakra and her [the consort],
this compassionate Manu has arrived, bestowing the fruits of all vidyās.
The seed-syllable, the power, and the peg, through their application at the beginning, end, and middle;
one should fashion the six limbs with the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels.
Kālī, with a terrifying face, adorned with a garland of human heads,
possessing four hands and three eyes, holding fish and meat in her lotus-like hands.
She holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, speaks with a terrifying voice,
is clothed in a skirt of human skin, and is fierce with her flesh dried up.
Her mouth devours the three worlds, she is terrifying with her two tongues,
and she is adorned by three sunken, round, and blood-red eyes.
Having meditated thus, the Goddess [should then visualize] upon the beautiful family-seat (kulapīṭha) a triangle,
a square, a hexagon, and a nine-cornered figure.
The wise man should draw a circle, a figure with eight petals, and a square;
within the triangles, he should worship the goddess Caṇḍā, whose face is fierce and formidable.
Having recited the six mantras in sequence— Caṇḍakālī, Caṇḍālī, and Pracaṇḍākālanāyikā— one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite.
Japatuṇḍā, Mahogrā, Bhīmā, Bhīmakapālikā,
Aṭṭahāsinī, Vidyā, Nityā, Pragalbhā, and Ghorarūpiṇī.
One should worship the goddess Śuṣkabhīmā, who is the supreme self of ten million Vasus;
she is Atikālī, Mahākālī, and Mahānityā, who yields great fruit.
Having offered [oblations] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should worship the goddess Aghorā, who is multiform, of variegated appearance, and who utters terrifying roars.
Then Indra and the others should worship her and constantly recite the Lakṣmī-mantra;
he shall obtain all desires and divine enjoyments from the netherworld (rasātala).
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great fruit of the Mahāvidyā;
the seed-syllable of Māyā, joined with Nāda and Bindu, has been thus declared.
The seed-syllable joined with the mantra and accompanied by the *pāta* is dear;
endowed with *nāda* and *bindu*, it is the second, most excellent seed-syllable.
The supreme mantra is "sarve sūryapradaṃ vahnim"; Sadāśiva is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is called the meter (chanda).
O Goddess of the gods, you who crush the splendor of the [asura] Śumbha and are saluted by all the deities;
now, O Mistress of the Gods, perform the six-limbed ritual with the six long vowels.

Now, therefore, by means of the yoga of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should meditate upon the body of the Goddess as the power of the seed-syllable— three-eyed, with eyes like those of a serpent, and possessing excellent vision.
Her limbs are like the petals of a lotus, her face is as beautiful as the moon,
she possesses eighteen arms, and she is eternally seated upon the back of a lion.
Worthy of worship with millions upon millions of virtues, she holds in her hands the noose,
the goad, the bow, the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the bell, the mallet, and the sharp-edged spear.

[She who possesses] leather, sword, and the great sixth [day], who is harsh with skulls and [the sound of] horses; then she who delights in the completion of a hundred [sacrifices], holding a vessel in her hand.
Within the triangle is a hexagon, beautifully adorned with eight petals;
in the center of that lotus within the triangle is the creeper of the primordial digits (kalā) beginning with Śivā.
In the hexagon, one should worship the goddess Kālīcaṇḍā Pracaṇḍikā,
whose form is will, who is eternally formidable, and who is auspicious, by way of the path of Vāsava.
Then, in the center of the eight-petaled [lotus], the Mothers beginning with Brahmā are placed in sequence:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Skandī, Vaiṣṇavī, and likewise Sāṅkarī.
Likewise, Narasiṃhī, Caṇḍī, and Śivadūtī, according to their divisions,
are the hosts of Yoginīs who bear [their forms] in accordance with their respective colors and scriptures.
Then Indra and the others are to be worshipped; O one of great strength, one should worship Dvāra, Nandin, and Paramavijaya by offering handfuls of flowers.
One should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times, and perform the fire oblation (homa) and other rites with a tenth part of that amount.
There is no knowledge equal to this; it is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
O Maheśānī, Kulasundarī alone, having been described with great effort,
should indeed worship this entire Vidyā in due order.
For him, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain; O Goddess, all happiness in this world exists beyond that [state]. One must protect it with great effort and not bestow it upon just anyone.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for Guhyakālī in the Atharvaṇasaṃhitā of the Śrī Hāhārāvatatantra.
The illustrious Bhairava said: One should bow down to the guru, the brahmin, the mother, the father, and the king.
Having bowed to the Supreme Goddess, he who is devoid of the sixfold ritual placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) [should perform it].
Before long he meets death and falls into hell; one should never deposit a deposit with anyone other than a trusted person, nor ever with one who is untrustworthy.
She, whose body is composed of a thousand grains of rice, worships with offerings preceded by ritual salutations;
she is bound to his left side as his Śakti and gazes upon him with affectionate sidelong glances.
Betel leaf, musk, nutmeg, camphor, grapes, and so forth;
likewise, *kramaka*, *kalāgali*, *devapuṣpa*, *jātiphala*, *vātimatsya*, or *amiya*.

Having placed in his mouth that mantra which was spoken by his own guru— a mantra such as this does not exist anywhere else in the entire circle of the universe— by the mere recitation of which one certainly becomes a king of kings;
indeed, this very Vajrapañjara resides within the midst of the fourfold cage.
It was created by the Lord himself for the purpose of slaying Tripura.
By the power of that [divine armor], Rudra became a conqueror of the three worlds;
and by the mere wearing of the divine armor of the Goddess of Devas, Bhairava likewise attained such power.
In the Mahāyogabrahmataviya [Tantra], the Supreme Śiva himself became manifest;
I have no doubt regarding my Navātman, which is capable of both restraint and grace.
By means of the great sixfold nyāsa of the vajra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all other gods pay homage; how much more so, then, other lords of sages?
He who daily performs the worship of the six Kālīs and their consorts is saluted by all the gods; I bow to him, without a doubt.
Whatever merit is obtained by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) existing here on earth, in heaven, or in the sky, is gained simply by placing [the image] down.
What is the use of giving gifts at Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu?
What need is there to cast off the body at Kāśī or Prayāga? [If one dies here, that alone suffices.]
What is the use of offering funeral cakes at Gayā? One should perform the sixfold ritual placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*).
What is the use of renunciation, yoga, or even the knowledge of Brahman?
But what is the use of giving away men, or even wool,
when one should properly bring about prosperity through great gifts and many other means?
Whether it be a quarter, a half, or even a fourth of the *ṣoḍaśī* [offering],
one has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
Even millions of sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, are dissolved;
indeed, whatever sins have been described by the sages [are likewise destroyed].
All those [faults] perish for one who has attained the supreme sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
There is no placement equal to the sixfold, and no recitation equal to the sixfold.
