Worship with the sixfold [method] is not possible, nor is the recitation of mantras a thousand times;
having renounced all ritual actions, one should perform the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*).
In this very life he shall attain happiness and will certainly become a king of kings;
that prosperity which belongs to the Lord of Wealth shall indeed belong to the practitioner.
All enemies shall perish, as shall the fourfold collection of living beings;
the Brahmin shall become radiant like Brahmā, and the Kṣatriya shall become disciplined.
A Vaiśya, moreover, shall obtain the happiness of a Śūdra through [the possession of] many riches and jewels;
he should observe celibacy during the day and may act as he desires at night.
One should perform the great nyāsa through the union of the left and the right;
it revolves a thousand times and is thus called puraścaraṇa.
By that very number, O Goddess, one shall attain the perfection of the Command (ājñāsiddhi);
by ten thousand repetitions one becomes a sky-walker (khecara), and by a hundred thousand, one becomes Bhairava.
The state of union and nirvāṇa will certainly be attained through the two lakṣas;
there is nothing higher than this in the Kaulika teaching of the Kula.
Truth, truth, again truth; truth, truth, again and again! There exists no science equal to this in the three worlds.
This alone is the supreme reality; this alone is the supreme austerity;
this alone is the supreme knowledge; this is the means to liberation.
O Pārvatī, having abandoned all actions and all dharmas,
perform this supreme and most excellent nyāsa through my grace.
Even when one has reached any state whatsoever, that which is well-taught by the true Guru in the Kālikā lineage must not be abandoned, provided that the sixfold [practice] is obtained.
There is nothing on the surface of the earth more venerable than one's mother;
one should not grant [this knowledge] to one who is devoid of the traditional lineage, even if he possesses power.
For the knowledge of Brahman, which is her very nature, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
she must always be guarded with great effort, like one's own private parts.
O Dear One, without the grace of the Guru, if anyone sees and recites the sixfold rite of Kālī,
the host of Yoginīs shall devour him.
One would cause even one's ancestors to fall into a dwelling in hell;
therefore, one should not take back an empty-handed deposit that is honored by the world.
Even after hundreds of years, he does not achieve the supreme [attainment] if he acts with wealth;
a wise person should not make a guru rich with money, but should satisfy him [with devotion].
First, one should satisfy the Guru with elephants, horses, or wealth, as well as with extensive offerings of garments and ornaments, and with many beloved ones dear to oneself.
One should not speak falsely, nor should one ever deceive the Guru;
when the Guru is satisfied, Kālikā will grant satisfaction.
Without the grace of the Guru, one certainly does not attain accomplishment;
whatever desire one contemplates, that one obtains with ease.
Success is not attained through the consumption of *vīrasā*, nor by the practice of the four seats (*catuḥpīṭha*), nor by bowing at night;
rather, Bhairavī is realized through the proper ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Having become the Goddess herself, the practitioner may roam the earth;
he may consume the rites of others and so forth, including malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), planetary afflictions, and the like.
Bhairavī perishes all at once by means of the fierce placement;
even with a thousand recitations, one becomes directly the Supreme Lord.
There is no doubt regarding this mantra; it is capable of both subjugation and grace. Within the teaching of the Kālikāstra, there is nothing equal to it—there is truly nothing equal to it.
Having meditated, "I am Bhairava, I am Śiva," one should then perform the placement (nyāsa) with great incense, a lamp, or with liquor (ali).
By the union of the flower of human intellect and by pleasing the Guru,
[one attains success] through the *svayambhū* flower and indeed through that which arises from a *kuṇḍagolaka*.
Having dried a pill made from nābhi, kāśmīra, and red sandalwood, one should apply it as a *tilaka*.
Then, having performed the great nyāsa, he becomes united with Śiva and Śakti;
for him, the perfection of the Command (ājñāsiddhi) shall come to pass—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī.
His success will truly be realized in the Kaulika tradition of the lineage of Kālikā.
Hereafter, I shall explain the ritual application; listen to it.
Thus, in the glorious Hāhārāvatamtra, within the Atharvaṇa Saṃhitā, is the chapter on the praise of the Guhyakālī-Ṣoḍhā.
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Bhairavī, the Kula-Ṣoḍhā assignment (nyāsa) in the Kālikrama is difficult to obtain.
Whoever performs [this] at the dead of night, his command prevails throughout the three worlds.
Through the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Great Sixfold Kālikrama, one becomes Śiva directly;
for without that, there is no accomplishment, nor is one capable of performing restraint or grace.
O beloved of the Kālikula lineage, he who performs [this] through the process of transference shall become Viṣṇu, Keśava, and Śakra; thus shall he be one who carries out the command.

Regarding this *praṇava* [mantra] of the Śrī Kālī Kulakrama Ṣoḍhānyāsa: the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the supreme Krodha-Durvāsas; the meter (*chandas*) is Bṛhatī; the deity (*devatā*) is the supreme Śiva, who is the Guhyakālikā consisting of the five transmissions (*pañcakramātmaka*), [invoked with] *strī phreṃ phreṃ*; the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the *ājñā-siddhi* through recitation (*japa*).
122a) Meditation.
Now I shall describe the meditation on the Great Goddess according to the sequence of yoga,
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall become a partaker of accomplishment.
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, fashioned from sapphire,
she stands in the midst of a circle of light, her brilliance swelling with the radiance of the rays of primordial wisdom.
Mahākālī has nine faces, twenty-seven eyes,
and fifty-four mighty arms, with the face of a man.
Above the goddess is the lion throne, white in color and of auspicious appearance;
below that is the black Trailokyadaṃmara with the face of a crow.
The face of Kapīdra on the left is red in color and greatly radiant;
the face of Bhakṣa in the southwest (Rakṣe) should be smoke-colored and terrifying.
The face on the left is that of Tārkṣya, yellow in color and very desirous;
the face on the right is that of a crocodile, proclaimed to be greenish-yellow.
One should contemplate the elephant-faced [form] on the left as white in color and exceedingly fierce;
one should meditate on the horse-faced [form] on the right of Kālī as dark in color.
With all her fangs bared and a mouth formidable, she has three eyes and a terrifying roar;
with eyebrows knitted in a frown, she is fearsome, with a face like Time (Kāla), yet another is Śrīmukhā.
Her tawny matted locks are bound with the crescent moon as a crest-ornament;
she wears a white skull-garland upon her head, adorned with various jewels and the heads of Kinnaras and others.
The head-garland is proclaimed as consisting of twenty-seven heads, joined with blood and entrails, and adorned with a garland of vajra-flowers.
He holds the jewel of consciousness, the noose with a hook, the spear, the khaṭvāṅga,
the skull-bow, the thunderbolt, and the bell of beautiful sound.
The hair-ghost, the mountain, the skeleton, and likewise the clan,
the serpent, the procuress, the hexagon, and again the oḍikā.
She holds in her left arms a fire-vessel, a triple staff, a *śruva* ladle, a pearl necklace, a sword, a garment, a mallet, and a *ḍamaru* drum.
The index finger is a cutter of the row of consciousness-jewels;
the kusha-grass staff is a jewel-filled flask; and the trident is the destroyer of desires.
The five Pāśupatas, Vārṇa, Padmadvipa, Matāṅga, Kunta,
Pārijāta, Churikā, and likewise Tomara.
A garland of flowers, a drum, a vulture, a svastika, a vardhanī vessel, a water-pot, and a sacrificial ladle— these indeed bring about the fear of pale and emaciated beings.
With their right arms, they fashion a *naṃdyāvarta*, an earring, a well-adorned lump of flesh,
a *vījapūra* fruit, and a needle.
Clad in a tiger skin with a black antelope skin as an upper garment,
she is enriched by the splendor of a network of tinkling bells and resounds with the sound of heroic bells.
Terrifying with the fierce sound of *ghara-ghara*, she was adorned with bracelets,
armlets, and anklets, and beautified by great bones.
A garland of severed heads hangs from the Goddess’s neck, reaching down to her feet;
likewise, she wears a garland made of red lotuses and dried skulls.
The goddess shone with a waist adorned by a girdle of gold,
her neck radiant with a sacred thread, and wearing a meditation band as an upper garment.
Adorned with gentle head-ornaments and decorated by the kings of the Nāgas and others,
she is seated upon the fivefold throne of the beauty of her ears with red earrings.
Oṃ. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five Kaulas possess yellow, dark blue, red, fixed (yellow), and white complexions.
Those bearing weapons such as the staff, face, spear, trident,
and khaṭvāṅga, with the threatening finger raised, bring about liberation from Śiva’s lower realms.
She is tawny-eyed, three-eyed, and indeed terrifying with her howling;
she has adamantine fangs and the touch of her claws, she nourishes the lotus, and is the supreme Śiva.
One should contemplate the Goddess, ever-arisen, standing upon a lotus and dancing; her tongue-tip emits the syllable *hūṃ*, and she is licking it.
Thus, Mahākālī, who is terrifying and in the prime of youth, resides in the center of the sequence of parts; she is most fierce and has the form of Time.
Having meditated thus and worshipped the mind,
this sixfold placement (nyāsa) is proclaimed: the weapon of one's own Kālī-kula, the seat of the fierce Mothers, and the group of mantras arrived in their proper sequence.
Then follows the Kālīkrama Nyāsa:

Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ phreṃ phreṃ akhphreṃ, I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī; [place this] on the head. Oṃ 4 āṃ khphreṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī; [place this] in the mouth. 5.
Iṃkhphreṃ Mahācaṇḍā Yogeśvarī Śrī [at] the ten eyes; 5 Īmūla Śrī [at] the nostril-passage of the left side; 5 Ḷṃ 1 Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī Kīlakuli Śrī [at] the right cheek; 5 Ḷṃ 1 Mahācaṇḍayogikālī.
123a) On the left cheek: 5 Oṃ 1 Mahācaṇḍayoginī Siddhikālī Śrī. On the upper lip: 5 Aiṃ 1 Mahācaṇḍayoginī Siddhikālī Śrī. On the upper lip: 5 Aiṃ Mahāśaṅkhayoginī Kālī Śrī.

On the lower lip: 5 Oṃ 1 Mahādivyayoginī Siddhikālī Śrī. On the upper teeth: 5 Auṃ Mahāpadmayoginīkā. On the lower teeth: 5 Aṃ 1 Mahābhakṣaṇakālī Śrī. On the palate: 5 Aṃ 1 Asyamahāriṇī Kālī Śrī. On the mouth: 5 Kaṃ Mahāraktakālī Śrī. At the root of the right arm: 5.

Khaṃ 1 Mahākṛtāntanāśanī Kālī Śrī [at the elbow] 5; Gaṃ Mahāyāmabhakṣaṇakālī Śrī [at the wrist] 5; Ghaṃ Mahākālarātrī Kālī Śrī [at the base of the fingers] 1; Ḍaṃ 1 Mahāsaṃhāriṇī Kālī Śrī [on the nails] 5; Caṃ 1.

Candracandreśvarī Kālī Śrī, at the base of the left arm (5 chaṃ 1); Caṇḍeśvarī Kālī Śrī, at the elbow (5 jaṃ); Mahākālāgnikālī Śrī, at the wrist (5 rūṃ 1); Rudrasaṃhāriṇī Kālī Śrī, at the base of the fingers (5 ñaṃ 1);
Mahābhairavasaṃhāriṇī, at the tenth [digit] below (5 aṃ 1).
Mahābhakṣaṇakālī Śrī is at the knees (5) with AṂ 1; Mahāsaṃhāriṇī Kālī Śrī is at the mouth (5) with KAṂ 1;

Mahāraktakālī Śrī is at the base of the right arm (5) with KHAṂ 1; Mahākṛtāñjalipāḥ [is at the fingers] (1); Mahākālarātrī Kālī Śrī is at the bases of the fingers (5) with CHAṂ 1; Mahāsaṃhāraṇī Kālī Śrī is at the [heart].

Candrakālī, Jālandharī, Candrakālī, Udyānī, Raktakālī! Grant the attainment of all pledges (*samaya*)! Grant the pledge of perfect accomplishment! *Śara*! O Śrī, spread forth! *Hansa* twice! *Kha* twice! *Hrīṃ*! *Huṃ*! *Vāhī* twice! *Kāhī* twice! *Khe* twice!
*Huṃ*! *Lāṃ*! *Khāṃ*! *Khāṃ*! *Chāṃ*! *Huṃ*! *Phāṃ*! *Vāṃ*! *Hrīṃ*! *Śrīṃ*! *Huṃ*! *Sauṃ*! *Hraḥ*! *Huṃ*!
Huṃ haṃ hreṃ namaḥ svāhā | [To be placed] on the head. Thus is the placement (nyāsa) of the thousand-syllable mantra-group.
He who places this mantra at night acquires merit a hundred times greater than that of daytime.
Whether one has already eaten or has not yet eaten, one shall attain perfection within a month.
One attains the perfection of command and the warding off of all calamities;
that which does not exist [in this] cannot be perfected—such is Kālī in the Kaula Kulārṇava.
Thus ends the chapter on the Guhyakālī Ṣoḍhā-nyāsa in the Atharvaṇa-saṃhitā of the Śrī Hāhārāva-tantra.
Now, the worship of the Kaulika.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme worship of the Kaulikas;
for the wife of a Sādhaka, indeed, she becomes the manifest Īśvarī herself.
A Kaulika who desires sexual union with her becomes a denizen of hell,
as does one who eats from the same seat or from the same vessel as a woman who has defecated.
If one drinks from the same vessel, you both will certainly go to hell;
therefore, one should lift the vessel for common use and pour it into separate vessels.
One should not move the vessel; one should make the vessel itself the deity Śaṅkara.
O beautiful one, one should not touch the remains of food or the Kula substances within the circle.
Having washed them outside, one should not cause the vessels and ritual materials to be given [to others];
that which is performed by one devoid of the five purities is as if it were not performed at all.
Without the fivefold purity, worship serves only for the movement of the sacrificial fire.
These are: purity of self, purity of the place, and likewise the purification of the mantra.
Purity of the body and purity of the ritual substances—thus is purity declared.
Worship performed without mantra and libation offered without meat [is incomplete].
Whatever falls by the power of destruction, all that becomes partless (niṣkala).
By the word "or" (vā), one should drink the substance; likewise, one should not fill [the vessel] with it.
Having performed mutual salutations, one should drink the divine nectar once again.
Sacrifice is said to be threefold, following the sequence of the Divine (divya), the Heroic (vīra), and the Animal (paśu).
The divine drink before the Goddess is the "heroic" (vīra), which is to be consumed on the first day;
however, that drink which is unrefined is known as the "Pāśupata" drink.
The refined [speech] produces accomplishment, while the purification consists of penance and so forth.
Having lifted the vessel with the *sadya* [mantra] and formed the *mudrā* for the sake of the cattle (*paśu*),
one should effect the union of the piercing (*vyadhra*) through yoga, without [ordinary] conjunction;
just as water becomes pure when it flows toward a river.
Likewise, wealth from the house of a barbarian is pure when placed in the hand of a yogi.
A yogi should not be a seeker of enjoyment, nor should he be like a worldly enjoyer;
therefore, because he possesses both yoga and enjoyment as well as the Kaula, the yogi is indeed a Kaulika.
With one dry piece of wood I drink from a jar; suddenly with salt water from the ocean I drink from a well;

if I drink from a pond, O Rohita, it is a mere fragment of a shaven head; if I drink from the Gaṅgā, it is the Yamunā; and suddenly in the ocean, whether it be a mother, a sister, or even a maiden-jewel.
When intoxicated by honey, that which ought to be said is not even mentioned;

they drink liquor in the houses of the Ikṣvākus, and having fallen into deep sleep, they do not wake in the houses of courtesans. They partake of food in every house; thus, O practitioner, would one become a universal monarch (cakravartin) by whom the fish have been devoured with his nails—he is indeed a "forest-eater" (vanakhāda).

The prostitute was not embraced by him, yet he consumed meat despite having been warned by his own brother; the maiden was not served by him, yet he drank wine despite having been forbidden from such talk of pleasure;
thus everything was in vain, for he did not follow the discipline of the lineage of Gurus nor the tradition of Maheśvara.
Whatever fruit one may obtain by performing that rite correctly,
one obtains that same fruit through devotion by beholding the Śrīcakra.
He should first offer to Vījayā, the second vessel to Śrī, the third vessel to Guru and Pāvaka,
the fourth vessel to Gaṇeśa, and the fifth vessel to the deity of the path.
The lineage of Pañcālya Pānna was indeed established by Bhairava through the sixth transmission (*ṣaṣṭhakrama*) of the fathers and mothers;
in the seventh transmission, the twenty practitioners were established according to the sequence of the names of Śaśakti.

The mother, father, and brothers represent one's lineage and modesty; likewise, the teacher and the practitioner represent the guru, the wife, spiritual accomplishment, the dawning of knowledge, and its subsequent increase.
[The materials for the vessel are] gold, silver, stone, tortoise shell, skull, water-born [conch], earthenware, coconut,
conch shell, pearl, and that which arises from oyster shells.
A wise person should fashion an alms-bowl produced from a tree of merit;
one should avoid one that is too fine, too thick, cracked, or perforated.
Wood made from metals such as copper and bell-metal becomes fruitless;
however, vessels of gold and silver grant all accomplishments.

For pacification (*śāntika*), a stone bowl; for immobilization (*staṃbhana*), one made of clay; for subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like, a coconut bowl; and for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one made from tortoise shell.
The conch bestows knowledge; the pearl-oyster shell grants wisdom;
and the skull, the lotus, and the vessel bring about the perfection of yoga.
Born from the tree of merit, supreme and the remover of all sins—
one wise man should place one [such pillar] at each end of the white [altar] when it has been described.
O beloved, the merit gained from seeing a sacred ford (*sutīrtha*), hearing its story, or remembering it,
is ten million times greater than the merit gained from seeing ten million scriptures.
If, through seeing after seeing, one were to become a creator of thousands of millions of ultimate realities by means of the vision of the ultimate truth, [then that would be so].
For those for whom the Guru alone is the refuge, established as the source of the Gaṅgā and the Gītā,
one should serve the family Guru with body, mind, and speech, O Dear One.
Having seen [the deity] and completed the worship, one should not depart without filling the vessel with red [substances].
Having offered whatever is dear to oneself and prostrated with the five limbs, [one should depart].
If it should arise from egoism, desire, or greed,
then life, knowledge, fame, and strength will all perish.
The body is to be understood as the tantra, and the mantra becomes embodied;
through the union of tantra and mantra, one who follows the path of the Guru shall achieve accomplishment.
In whatever mantra and at whatever time the movement occurs, such is the true nature of reality;
one must not entertain delusion therein, for it causes the loss of accomplishment.
Having bathed daily at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
and having performed internal worship there, one should meditate upon the form with the mind.

One should perform the ritual of the offering (bali) endowed with both substantial and non-substantial elements, and may slaughter various animals according to the procedure taught by Dhanya; if this is performed according to the rules, the Lord of Beings himself [will be pleased].
If one takes the substance from the Guru’s vessel with one’s own hand and drinks it,
filling one’s own vessel, then having drunk it, rebirth no longer exists.
Having drunk again and again, having drunk repeatedly, he falls to the ground;
rising up and drinking once more, rebirth is no longer found.
Resembling a dark rain cloud, beautified by a blue elephant,
enriched with the adornment of blue flowers, and decorated with blue ornaments.
She whose body was the color of blue sapphire, wearing a garland of blue lapis lazuli,
with rays fixed by sapphires and adorned with highly precious jewels.
Mounted upon a blue horse, bearing a supreme blue sword as her weapon,
she [covers] the fourteen worlds with a blue veil of sleep.
O Hero, protect her who deludes with great illusion, who consumes the storehouse of material wealth, who delights in the drinking of blood, and who guards [us] on all sides.
She covers the divine Saṃketamaṇḍala with her own garment;
she is Paramānandabhairavī, whose body is supreme bliss.
I bow to Parāvikā, the generator of supreme bliss;
the wise practitioner, having placed the vessel in his hand, may accomplish all rites.
One attains prosperity in this world and becomes Bhairava at the end of the body;
all the deities residing within the body are the elephant-faced ones, the lords of the fields, and the Bhairavas.

May the Yoginīs, the Vaṭukas, the Pakṣapitṛs, the Paiśācas, the servants (Ceṭakas), and others who move on earth and in the sky— the Pratikhas, Vetālas, Bhūtas, and Grahas— be satisfied by the drinking of the wine, the lamp, and the sacrificial pap (Caru) of this son of noble family; and may they be purified by the enjoyment of wine, meat, women, and pleasures.
I am one whose nature is cultivated through the undertaking of the manifestation of the glory of the multitude of people;
I am liberated from the state of ordinary folk; I am Bhairavī, born of the Mother; I am one who bows at the feet of the Guru; I am Bhairava; I am Śiva.
I am one whose self is purified by the initiation mantras of all the gods;
I am one who is oriented toward the path sought through the various practices of the gods.
I am the one whose nature has forever transcended birth, death, and suffering through the constant internal growth of complete and incomplete worship;

I am endowed with supreme, stainless, eternal bliss and consciousness; I am devoted to the feet of the Guru; I am Bhairava, I am Śiva, I am the stainless one, I am the ancient one, I am intent upon Sundarī, and I am devoted to the feet of the Guru; I am Bhairava, I am Śiva.
I am the growth of the state of the co-emergent; I am the essence of both the worshiper and the object of worship; I am composed of abundant bliss; I am truly rejoiced.

I have taken refuge in Śiva; I am worshipped by the world of devotees; I delight in the feet of the Guru. I am Bhairava, I am Śiva, I am Śiva, I am the embodiment of Śakti, I am the God, I am the Danuja (demon), I am the Yakṣa, I am the human, I am all, and I am everything that exists.
I am the mantra, I am the ritual manual of mantras, and I alone am the recitation of mantras;
I am the creator of mantras, I am the knowledge of mantras, and I am also the very essence of bliss in the mantras.
I am the object of worship, I am the one worthy of worship, and I alone am the worshiper;
I am the act of worship, the one who causes worship to be performed, the essence of worship, and I am the sacred pledge (samaya) of worship.
The vessel for the folds [of the skin], the Yoginī-vessel, and the two vessels for the Śrīpātra and the Guru-pātra;
the Guru-pātra, the Kumbhaka-vessel, and the Vīra-pātra at the two tips.
O Maheśānī, the vessel of peace is said to be the supreme vessel;
when satisfied, they grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation to all the worlds.
One should cause the ritual of worship to be performed with all available means;
without the perfuming of substances, there can be no recollection of the mantra.
O Goddess, listen as I declare that for those great fools who remember [this], there is suffering at every step; yet here, by worshipping Indravī, one shall become worthy of honor.
Gaudī, paiṣṭī, as well as dhī, ṛtunārī, and nārikelajā; having offered those born from palm, wood, and grapes, these are the various types of liquor.
The armor is red; for the pearl and coral [beads], they are made of gold;
for the crystal and those called coconut, they are made of the skulls and jawbones of hell-beings.
Bring these vessels, which are prescribed for the ritual of worshipping the deity:
the dancer, the protector of the well, the courtesan, the washerwoman, and the woman with yellow limbs.
The daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, the daughter of a Śūdra, likewise the daughter of a cowherd,
and the daughter of a garland-maker— these are proclaimed as the nine types of maidens.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain what one should do in the absence of the ritual substances:
milk, curd, ghee, honey, oil, and collyrium (sauvīra).
Grapes joined with Ārdrā, coconut water, or water produced from cows,
humans, elephants, horses, buffaloes, boars, goats, or deer [is auspicious].
A rabbit joined with meat that causes delight to the deities,
fresh from being slaughtered, along with the head of a female monkey and the five types of meat.
Garlic is prescribed as a substitute for meat for the Mahādevī;
in the absence of fish, betel nut and betel leaf may be used, as well as whatever else is fit for a woman.
One should contemplate the mudrā, or rice, or food, and so forth, with devotion;
these nine vessels are proclaimed as the "Hāhārāva" [offering].
By the power of his merit, even if he were equal to Śakra,
[he would be protected] during a pilgrimage to a temple or at the royal gate in the midst of great danger.
The minister, having gone a long distance with great effort, beheld that multitude;
for I am manifest within the multitude, and the multitude is the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The multitude is Keśava, O Goddess, while the multitude is indeed Purandara; the multitude of people is Nārāyaṇa, and by nature, every living being is Sundarī.
"I shall dwell there with you according to my desire.
Having praised her thus, the practitioner should then worship her with the affliction of passion.
130a) According to whatever is obtained— by means of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth—
the great accomplishment is established within the assembly of young women.
Is there ever seen a diminution of the merit of that very worship?
Whoever worships the Goddess in this manner attains success; of this there is no doubt.
Having beheld Maheśvara, one should worship him according to the prescribed rites; and having offered the five elements in their respective forms as they exist in phenomenal existence.
Kālī shall always be well-pleased even with all your desires;
otherwise, no accomplishment will arise, for she becomes a fierce Yoginī.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving the entire earth to a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas,
that same fruit is obtained in the worship of the Kaulika.
The fruit that one obtains by witnessing thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices is attained through the worship of the Kaulika.
And likewise, the gift of gold equal in weight to Mount Meru to a Brāhmaṇa.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving [such gifts], that same fruit is obtained through the worship of the Kaula;
as also the fruit one might obtain by constructing wells, ponds, tanks, and the like.
From worshipping the Kaulikas, one obtains a hundred thousand times that fruit;
and whatever fruit a man obtains by giving a tawny cow (kapilā), [that too is obtained].
The fruit of that is multiplied ten millionfold by worshipping the Kaulikas;
for nothing whatsoever is done without a man having performed [the preliminary rite].
Likewise, without Śakti, the Goddess is indeed not capable of bestowing the fruit;
therefore, having united with the Power of the Puruṣa, one should accomplish the mantra.
O Kaulika, on this path, a male deity does not attain success;
rather, one should meditate upon oneself as Śiva and the deity in the form of Śakti.
His deity is well-pleased when he sports with the five *makāras*;
his attitude toward women on the path of the Dakṣas is like that toward his mother, and likewise on the Kaulika path.
For one whose conviction has become firmer, the deities are indeed pleased;
this secret has been declared, which must be guarded like the secret of a mother’s paramour.
O Pārvatī, the Śaivas, the Smārtas, and the ritualists do not construct a funeral pyre for those who are Kaulas,
knowers of the Āgamas, and practitioners of the Tantric way of life.
130b) Likewise, for those who provide substitutes and those who remain indifferent,
as well as for those whose minds are fickle and who perceive women merely as goddesses.
For those devotees of Śubhakālī who are always resolute in mind,
the worship of the Power (Śakti) is as essential as the worship of the sacred seat (Pīṭha), O Sovereign Goddess.

Kālī, who is none other than the Buddha herself, should be worshipped with a mind free from the agitation of desire; those who are liberated from the four states of existence are devoted to the worship of Kālī for the sake of liberation.
Whether they follow the Kaula path or the Akula path, those who abide by this truth— Śiva,
the enemy of the cities (Puradviṣ), has told me that for them, the worship of the Nityās is eternal.
O beloved, that power (śakti) should be known as twofold: one's own and the wife of another; that which is born of one's own caste and has been duly married is the "own" [power].
Having thus explained that which pertains to the scriptures, it is now praised;
I shall now describe in order the fivefold types of praise pertaining to others.
For one whose husband is living is indeed one thing, while another is one whose beloved is dead;
likewise, a courtesan, a maiden, and a married woman—each subsequent one is more highly esteemed than the preceding.
A young woman who has not yet given birth is praised this very day;
however, even one who has given birth is considered firm in her resolve throughout all time.
In the absence of each preceding [form], it is to be grasped by practitioners as the subsequent one;
and for the Kaula [practitioner], it is likewise for the female practitioner, and the male practitioner is also the same.

O Goddess of the Gods, without the means of accomplishment (sādhana), mantras are not effective for a noble person; they are not remembered as being efficacious for men even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Sexual union with another's wife, intoxication by liquor, or the killing of animals—even if for one's own sake—leads only to hell; any merit earned thereby is rendered futile.
O Queen, I do not understand how these [acts] produce joy;
likewise, they do not produce evil for that reason, even when performed by those who slaughter animals.
Likewise, there is no sin such as sexual union with another's wife;
nor are there those with missing limbs, nor those with extra limbs, nor those who are excessively stout or excessively thin.
Neither one whose fingers are severed or destroyed, nor one who is tall, nor one who is dwarfed;
neither one who is shaven-headed, nor one who is hunchbacked, nor one who is dull-witted, nor one who is deaf.
Neither those with squinting eyes nor the lame, nor women of mixed birth with sagging breasts,
nor those with very young children should be made into Śaktis, like the [inferior] powers [of the gods].
I declare her to be most worthy and preeminent, by whom Kālikā is pleased:
she is fair-limbed, youthful, with a face smiling like the plantain flower, and possessed of a beautiful form.
Her breasts were large, full, high, and intent on quivering;
her expansive hips were graced by the three folds of skin.
She had beautiful flanks and a slender waist; she possessed a lovely voice and curled locks of hair.
She was adorned with various garments and ornaments, and she wore diverse and wonderful raiment.
Adorned with various garlands, she bestows manifold delights;
her face is ever serene, and she is devoted to the service of the Goddess.
She knows the reality of the Kaulika conduct, is devoted to the practitioner,
free from fear, mindful of the face [of the deity], and always speaks kindly.
One who is perfected in the conduct of the samaya, knowledgeable in mantra, free from fear,
clever, unmarried, and endowed with fortitude and independence.
One should worship all women endowed with such qualities;
in every way, O Goddess, one should act thus, for it cannot be otherwise even in ten million aeons.
O Goddess of the Gods, those who perform the recitation of ten padmas do not indeed achieve success;
therefore, with every effort, one should follow the sequence of one's own vidyā.
One's own power and that of others are both merely the Great Goddess;
she is worshipped with all ritual offerings through the intellect as the presiding deity of the mantra.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites with devotion using various fruits, betel-leaves, and all kinds of golden ornaments, one should cause many gifts to be bestowed.
He who performs the worship of Śakti while maintaining the latent impression of sensual enjoyment will always encounter enemies and will certainly become a denizen of hell.
What is the use of many nets of excellent verses? Listen to the rule in brief:
the worship of Śakti is prescribed for the Kaulikas day after day.
The daily taking of wine and likewise its daily acceptance is declared to be a constant duty for those devoted to the Kula path, O Goddess, regarding both [the male and female] practitioners.

O Dear One, in the discernment between what is to be abandoned and what is not, those among the Śaktis who provide even a secondary alternative (anukalpa) are indeed rare; for [the primary practice] is indeed eternal.
Indeed, among those [deities] who are excluded from the *vihāya* [rite], only those who are capable and suitable are accepted;
for others, there is the worship of power (*śakti-pūjā*), which may be performed for specific desires or on occasional occasions.
O Pārvatī, for those whose minds are established in samādhi, there is the rejection of all other desires; now I shall describe the ritual procedure and the mantras as well.
She was bathed, wearing divine garments, adorned with various ornaments,
a young woman with full breasts, and likewise possessing a beautiful form and a pleasant countenance.
Having grasped her by the hand, one should place the supreme Śakti upon his left thigh; if he is unable to carry her, he should then place the two goddesses upon a seat.
On the left side, one should draw a triangle within a lotus-circle,
colored with white and red, and its stalk smeared with vermilion.
The practitioner, facing east, should worship the Goddess while facing west;
he should worship Uḍḍīyāna in the Tretā age and Pūrṇagiri in the Kṛta age.
Jālandhara in the Dvāpara ages and Kāmapīṭha in the Kali age—
these four, which are more secret than the secret, I shall now declare.
The entire body of Śakti is considered the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri;
its head, located in the region of Candra, has been described by me as Udyāna.
The two breasts are called Jāladhara, and the vulva is known as Kāmapīṭha.
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and other elements.
One should first perform the rite for the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth, and thereafter perform the purification;
the rite for the seers and so forth is now [to be explained] here by this one who praises the gods.
For this worship of Śrī Śakti, Gonarda is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi);
Vikṛti is said to be the meter; may she who is the form of Śakti grant [blessings].
Mahākālī is the deity, Kām (Klim) is declared as the seed-syllable (bīja),
Vadhū the Bhuvaneśī is the power (śakti), and [Klim] is declared as the peg (kīlaka).
Through application in the light of the equilibrium of Śiva and Śakti,
the six-limbed [mantra] is formed by the union with the five long [vowels] and the seed-syllables of the Vadhūs.
Having performed the assignment of the limbs of Śakti within oneself, or otherwise one may perform it;
if [the recipient] is a woman, the word "Bhairava" should take the place of the word "Śakti."
If there is a location for the *yoni-pada*, there should be the conceptualization of the *liṅga-pada*;
and that too, O Queen of the Gods, is either through the instruction of the Guru or by one's own meditation.
Modification (ūha) must be performed everywhere, both in the gender and in each respective word;
however, it is restricted to the Gāyatrī, for that remains uniform in both cases.
Listen attentively to this perpetual extraction of the nyāsa:
[the syllables] Trayā, Kāmoramārāma, and Yoginīroṣayoṣitau.
The Ḍākinī is Pralayohāra, Phetkārī, and Karṇikā;
the Preta is Nṛsiṃha and Kulika; and the power of consciousness (cicchakti) resides at the very end of all.
One should give each individual seed-syllable, honored by the gods, following the names;
it should not be otherwise at the beginning, [but] the *kaulīkī* mantra follows immediately after the *bhagamālinī*.
Likewise, Ratipriyā, Anaṅgā, Kulā, Samayapālinī,
Madanonmādinī, Kāmā, and immediately after her, Veśinī.
Then there is Smarā, who agitates the mind and likewise draws one toward slaughter; she is the form of the bodiless god of love, and immediately after her comes Hr̥tpramodā.
O you who are worshipped by the thirty gods, after that come Saṃtāpinī and Saṃkṣobhinī;
at the very end of all, she should be known as having the nature of equanimity (sāmarasya).
These sixteen [mantras] should indeed be employed, ending in the dative case and joined with the word *pūrvāṇa*;
when used for the female gender, they take masculine forms, and the mantra for the rite of worshipping Bhairava is "namaḥ."
Now, in all the remaining locations, one should assign the parts by means of a digit (kalā):
the head, the two cheeks, the neck and shoulders, the chest, and likewise the belly.
The sides, the belly, the navel, the folds of skin, and the groin; the thighs, the knees, the shanks, the feet, and the generative organ—these are the remaining parts of the body.
O Goddess, one should perform the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya) with her as if she were alive;
this alone is declared to be the purification of Śakti.
Having performed what is difficult to do and having placed victory in her heart, the Goddess is then at Kāmapīṭha; in the opinion of Nābhaumīliyakī, she is not on the earth.
Chanting the *mantra* that will be described— whether once, three times, or seven times—
one should perform this purification of the power (*śakti-śodhana*), which consists of the placement of the vital breaths (*jīva-nāsa*).
By this, the power (śakti) is purified, and not otherwise even by ten million mantras;
[the mantras] are Māyā, Kāma, Vadhū, Lakṣmī, Kūrca, and Prāsāda.
One should first visualize the Śākinīs and Ḍākinīs, as well as the eight seed-syllables;
then the enjoyments, the bliss, the Kula, the speech, and the individual soul (jīvātman) and the supreme soul (paramātman).
The reflections, which serve as a treasury through the nature of non-dual cognition, are declared in sequence as the ten peaks; then [follows] that which is the opposite of the Brahma-island.
The pair at the end of the ten should be uttered, measured one above the other;
then one should say "mamānu hṛdayam" followed by "tavānu hṛdayam."
O lotus-faced one, having first uttered the words "Dadhātu mama vācyutkā," one should then recite [the mantra] over the vital points (marmans) and the sense organs.
Do not overwhelm my senses; rather, take pleasure in my words.
Therefore, O Kucā, grant me the power that brings about success.
"Whoever you are, I am indeed that; whoever I am, you are that"—one should say this, and then both should proclaim their union with Śiva.
Having commenced from Śiva and Śakti, and immediately thereafter having attained that [state],
one should recite "we two shall accomplish that oneness," and thus proceed.
The *saṃdhi*, the *tāra*, the heart, the head, and then the weapon—
this is declared to be the mantra for the rite of purifying the *śakti*.
It consists of one hundred and eight syllables, neither fewer nor more;
its meditation is that which was previously described by you, O Bhagavatī, as being free from decay.
One should meditate on the Śakti as having such a form, perceiving her as a collection of limbs;
and one should contemplate oneself as being identical to the meditation on Bhairava.
Then, the practitioner, using the añjali mudrā, should invoke the Goddess upon the limb of Śakti, which resembles a pedestal, with the mantra that is about to be described.
Neither Māyākāmā, Vadhūrā, Kamalā, Yoginī, Ruṣā, nor even Ḍākinī or Phetkārī sing in the Vaitānya and other regions.
"Come, come, O Blessed One! Having joined [with the mantra], Mahākālī should utter:
'Obeisance to the Seat of Power (Śaktipīṭha)'; she should cause the presence [of the deity] to descend and then extract [the essence]."
Then, having inscribed [the mantra] with the syllable *asahaṃ*, one should carry it forward and recite it;
then, having addressed those whose forms are identical to all powers (*sarvaśakti*), one should speak as follows.
Listen to the mantra consisting of Tāra, Pratiṣṭhā, and Śīrṣa, followed by the root of Śakti:
one should then utter Māyā, Rāva, Smara, and Nārī for the sake of Śakti.
The mantra for the rite of worshiping Śakti is declared to consist of nine syllables;
it has no seer (ṛṣi) and so forth, nor does it have a meter, seed-syllable (bīja), or power (śakti).
However, the water for the feet and so forth, up to the food offering, are the causes for the offering of all the requisites;
nor indeed should the mantra be recited half-way, according to the word of Bhairava himself.
One should offer all the ritual services (upacāras) according to one's capacity;
however, whatever is desired—from the offering of water for the feet (pādya) up to the offering of food (naivedya)—should be presented.
In my view, there is no other mantra distinct from that of the Goddess of the Universe;
as for that "kūrca" which the followers of the Kaula tradition [employ], let it be understood that it is rootless.
Whatever remains of the worship of Śakti— the flowers, garlands, and unguents—
that which is offered to oneself constitutes the worship of my state of non-dual identity (sāmarasya).
Then the mantra should be performed according to this command of Īśāna;
thereafter, having placed the hand upon the seat of the Yoni, one should perform the recitation (japa).

The practitioner, renowned for his practice, should perform the recitation of the Śakti-gāyatrī one hundred times, or even half of that, or half of that again, upon the Yoni-pīṭha; indeed, no other recitation exists anywhere equal to this.
It is the supreme seat for mantras that generates the power of truth,
for those mantras whose strength has been maintained and whose application has exhausted the mind [of obstacles].
For those whose lifespan has not yet been extracted, there is dependence on [the remaining] years, whether they be fewer or more;
likewise, even for those who desire their teacher, there is the giving away of their vigor through lack of strength.
This is the procedure for ignorance regarding the names of the offerings and the recipients of the vessels—
those who have renounced, those who have forgotten, and likewise those who lack spiritual power.
Both were spoken by the Enemy of Tripura for the purpose of kindling [the fire];
thus, having encapsulated that recitation with the Nirvāṇa mantra.

In the Kaula seat, there is no other practice of recitation (japa) than the sacred site of the womb (yonipīṭha). The Kaula seat is the sacred site of the womb; therein lies the restraint of the mantra through women.
Or, having united with the Guru’s wife or a Śakti, one should perform the recitation for both;
this supreme kindling with other mantras brings about a further increase in the power of the Vajra.
Now, therefore, O Goddess, hear the Śakti-Gāyatrī of great fruit: one should first utter the Bhagavatī from the Kāma-bīja, ending with "Ṅe".
After that, one should say "vighnaha yonimālinyai dhīmahi," and then,
having uttered "tatra śaktiḥ," one should conclude with "pracodayāt" at the very end of all.
For this Śakti-Gāyatrī is well-guarded by all the Āgamas;
without these [mantras], the recitation performed with the *vitāna-śakti* and the *niśakty-ṛc* is [ineffective].
Having recited this according to one's capacity and having offered it to Śakti,
O Dear One, one should sit on the left side and perform the recitation of the root mantra (mūlajapa) in this manner.
One should worship the temple of Madana, anointed with red sandalwood;
for in her venerable vulva, there flow three streams upon the seat of the vehicle.
The lunar channel flows inwardly alone, while the solar flows outwardly;
the fiery channel is not to be known by others—the practitioner who seeks success should worship them.
The lunar [power] flows as blood, the solar [power] flows as the menstrual flow, and the fiery [power] flows as the seed;
one should worship them by their respective names.
With a well-pleased mind, one should worship using the syllables beginning with Vāgbhava joined with *namaḥ*;
O Maheśānī, one should perform meditation upon the crocodile-faced goddess in the cavern.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, the Vidyā who deludes the world, situated there, having the form of a copper-colored cock's crest and a splendor equal to that of the elephant-faced one.
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable (AIM) at the end of the word "bhaga," followed by "bhage" and "bhagini.
Then [one writes] "bhagodarī," and at the end of "bhaga," [the words] "bhagamāle" and "bhagāvahe."
In the secret place of the vulva, at the edge of the vulva, at the edge of the womb, at the end of the vulva,
at the edge of the womb, at the end of all, and then, O Sovereign Goddess, [reside] there.
O you whose form is the vulva, O you with long, lotus-like eyes,
O eternally moist one, O you whose nature is the edge of the vulva— one should draw everything in its true form.
One should write "bhagāni me hyā" at the end of the word *namaḥ*, followed by "varade tha".
Then, [one writes] "rate", "svarate", "bhagavan", "klinne", "klinne", and then "drave".
Then, O Mistress of the *bhaga*, moisten and dissolve all sentient beings!
O Amoghe Bhagavice, cause everyone to see and shake all things!
Bhageśvarī should address sentient beings with the Vāgbhava mantra beginning with *vrūja*:
*bhaṃ vlūṃ mauṃ vlūṃ*, and after that, *klinne*.
And one should cause all the vulvae to contract with the mantra "saṃvānaya," and at the end, one should take away the seed of the woman by means of the syllable consisting of the letter *va*.
Having drawn Bhuvaneśī, this is the Vidyā Bhagamālinī;
one should worship the Goddess at the end of the dative case and cast a flower upon the bhaga.
Having washed [the image] with family substances (kuladravya), one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should thereafter worship the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa).
In this case as well, there is no invocation; Maheśvarī is the installation of the living soul.
Thus, according to this procedure, these [deities] are not [worshipped] with the sixteen types of offerings.
Having worshipped one's chosen deity, one shall become a master of all accomplishments;
thereafter, one should worship one's own Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Now I shall explain another [method]: one should meditate upon the Self as Śiva;
one should install the five-faced Mahādeva, endowed with his aspects (kalās), in due order.
Śaśinī is the first digit (kalā) of Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences;
thereafter, Aṅgadā belongs to Īśvara, the Lord of all beings.

At the end of the word *brahmādhipati*, [one says] "the lord of Brahmā"; furthermore, [one says] "may Śiva, the bestower of the desires of Brahmā, be present. One should then install the *marīci* enclosure.
Having uttered Sadāśivām, then Aṃśumālinī, and Parā;
that which is proclaimed as "Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe kalātīte" [is the next].
Mahādeva, Adhimahī, Kalā, and likewise Vidyā;
after that, Rudra is the Pada, and Pratiṣṭhā is said to be the Kalā.
Having fully uttered "pracodayāt," there shall then be cessation;
this occurs during the first and last watches of the night, while in the northern [watch] one sleeps according to the sequence.
Then the goddess should place the digit (kalā) "aghorebhyaḥ" in the heart;
thereafter, she should place "mohāṃ" from "ghorebhyaḥ" in the neck.
After *ghorānta*, the *kriyā* [kalā] should be placed;
subsequently, one should place *namastestu* on the right shoulder, and then *kṣudhām* on the back, placing the *kalās* in their proper sequence.
At the end [of the mantra], "To those who have the form of Rudra," there are three *tāra*s and *namaḥ*.
"Salutation to Vāmadeva"—this mantra should be placed on the secret region;
having applied it to the right side of the face, one should perform the protection with "Salutation indeed to Jyeṣṭha."
"Obeisance to Rudra; [I offer] this digit of the face on the left, Rati, behind [him].
At the end of 'Obeisance to Kāla,' Pālinī is on the right thigh."
Having uttered the word "namaḥ," one should place [the hand] on the right knee for the sake of restraint, while the Goddess of the Gods, desiring time, is on the left for the sake of transformation.
The two *valakriyās* (hand-gestures) are prescribed for the left side and for the *vikaraṇa* (withdrawal);
having uttered "Vṛddhi" at the end of "Namaḥ," one should place [the hand] slightly on the right.
One should place the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to the one who expands the quarters" on the left [side] as the Night;
at the end of "Oṃ, salutation to the subduer of all beings" is the Brahmā-kalā.
Having placed the Mohinī-kalā at the end of the mantra upon the region of the hips,
one should place the radiant Unmāyā, preceded by "namas," on the right side.
The practitioner should correctly place the eight kalās arising from Sadyojāta in sequence upon the two feet, the two breasts, the nose, the head, and the pair of arms.
Now, therefore, O beloved, I shall fully explain the determination of the vessels:
one should worship Guhyakālī with eighteen great vessels.

"Having made [the disciple] drink his own power and the power of the Hero (vīraśakti), who is consecrated and embodied as the Guru, he himself should drink the serpent; such is the definitive conclusion of the scripture."
Therefore, having worshipped the auspicious Śakti with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, one should, perceiving her as the deity, present the vessel of enjoyments.
The nectar-essence from the crest of the glorious Bhairava, which has been completely drenched and overflowing,
is worshipped by the lords of the sacred fields (*kṣetra*), the *yoginīs*, and those who have attained perfect accomplishment (*susiddhi*).

I salute this first vessel of Śrī, which is the ocean of nectar consisting of nine parts, containing the triple-portioned nectar of the three worlds, joined with the lotus-hand that bestows purity. || 1 ||
Having seen the golden fish-essence offered by his beloved with lotus-like eyes slightly tremulous, he was fully propitiated by her and others.
I bow to the second vessel, which, by placing the hand that effects the purification of purity upon its own left side, now increases singular bliss. || 2 ||
It is endowed with a multitude of arts that serve as its support, revealing a sense of wonder,
and is attended by Candra, Upendra, Śaśāṅka, Śambhu, Varuṇa, Brahmā, and others.
Salutations to the third vessel, which is always meditated upon by the hosts of gods and the nine classes of beings seeking liberation, which ever increases the worlds and bestows happiness. || 3 ||
134b) Wine, which brings forth the essence of fish, is honored by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others;
it is devoted to the practice of the *mudrā* of sexual union and relies upon salty, sour, and bitter [flavors].
Salutations to the fourth vessel, purified by the flesh of Siddhibhairava through the eight teachers, and accompanied by the reality of the five *makāras*. 4.

This eighth [treatise] on the family of sacrifice, which removes delusion, is secret and endowed with esoteric knowledge; it is spoken by the Vedas as being superior even to one's own ancestral dharma traditions.

This vessel, the fifth nectar, is not for one who has not tasted the essence of the yogis—the drop of the lunar stream arising from bliss—and the terrifying Bhairava who has drunk the essence of Brahman. || 5 ||
The parasol, the chowrie, the auspicious throne, the supreme food, the beloved wife, the kingdom of Rāma, the essence of delightful happiness, and the bestower of the empire of union—
[all these] remove the darkness of various diseases arising from worldly existence and destroy rebirth in other lives.
And the sixth vessel is the ocean that delights the eyes of the illustrious Suṃdarī. || 6 ||

May that Kuṇḍalinī, who bestows the direct realization of consciousness in the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the Fourth (turya), who resides within the bow of lightning, sun, fire, and moon, who moves upward through the middle of the Iḍā and Piṅgalā along the triple-fold path, and who is praised by the filling of the seventh vessel— may She, possessing supreme bliss, protect me.

May that vessel protect us— the vessel proclaimed by the world as the means for attaining the sword, sandals, collyrium, the pill of Sarasvatī, and the state of noble station; the vessel that brings about success, stabilizes the mind, exerts control, and is the cause for remaining embodied even amidst the dense thicket of formidable deeds and the words of Death.
And the eighth [chapter] is always mature and serene, bringing about the eight supernatural powers.
This is the vessel that brings joy to all, bestows the singular liberation of the pair of feet of Sadāśiva, grants sovereign dominion and happiness, fulfills desires, destroys ignorance,
increases longevity, fame, and glory, cuts through the delusion of saṃsāra, and is a worthy recipient.
The ninefold power of the illustrious Navanātha has arisen with full and mature majesty.
I bow down to the tenth vessel, which is especially difficult to obtain and purifying for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the goddesses. 10.
I bow to the eleventh vessel, which destroys sin, bestows peace, is pure, and has the nature of giving joy; it is the ultimate goal for those devoted to the service of the Guru.

Neither by residing in a hermitage nor by remaining in the womb, nor even by bathing at sacred fords, is there liberation; rather, through remembrance and performance [of this], I bow to the supreme twelfth [name].
Setting aside dharma and adharma, and regarding myself as a constant human being, I,
a man, always delight in the practice of eating [the fruits of] my senses.
One should never hold the bowl in the hand while performing yoga, nor recite hymns with it in the mouth;
I bow to Svachanda Bhairava, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 14 ||
The alms-bowl is in the hand, the hymn of praise is in the mouth, and bliss is in the lotus of the heart;
on the head is the lotus-foot of the venerable Guru—by remembering these, one should proclaim the Supreme.
Having drunk again and again, and having drunk until one falls to the ground, and rising once more to drink, there is no further rebirth. || 16 ||

Upon the base, which is the circle of the earth encircled by the king of serpents, the vessel is the orb of the world; the wine is the water of the seven oceans, and the meat is the eight elephants of the quarters.
Thus, O Bhairava, every day I am honored by hosts of stars, by the gods and asuras led by Āditya, and by my command-following servants. || 17 ||
In her left hand she holds a skull-cup filled with blood, and in her right, a beautiful vessel;
before her are the *mudrā*, the *caṇaka* (peas), the *vaṭuka*, a pig, and dried meat.
In the *Skandha*, the Kaula Dharma—most profound and inaccessible even to yogis—is revealed through the activity of true gurus by one who is auspiciously adorned with the lute of melody. (18)
Having abandoned all dharmas, one should practice the dharma of one's family;
having abandoned the dharma of one's family, one goes to the Raurava hell.
The highest worship is that which is performed constantly; the middling is worship on festive occasions;
the lowest is said to be monthly worship; beyond a month, one becomes a mere beast.
Whether once a month, every three months, every six months, or even once a year, one should worship the venerable Guru with devotion; thus one obtains [the blessings of] wife, sons, and so forth.
There, devoted to the worship of the *cakra*, the auspicious one (*śiva*) should satisfy a person of noble lineage and his disciple who is a yogin with the substances of the *kula*.
Thus ends the chapter on the determination of the worship of Kālikā in eighteen vessels, within the Atharvaṇa-saṃhitā of the Śrī Hāhārāva-tantra.
